name: Ancient historiography and Greek/Latin documentary sources on Alexander (incl. fragments, epitomes, papyri, inscriptions, Byzantine chronicle versions)
overview: There is still no Russian translation of the fragmentary and late-antique Alexander historiography. The narrative core does exist in Russian: Arrian, Plutarch, Curtius, Diodorus XVII, Justin and Orosius, plus Photius' summaries of Arrian's Anabasis and Events after Alexander (cod. 91–92), now on azbyka.ru. I found no Russian collection of the FGrHist 117–153 historians. Those fragments can only be read in Russian inside the host authors (Strabo, Plutarch, Arrian, Athenaeus; Nearchus through the Indica, published in ВДИ 1940 no. 2). I also found no Russian version of the Metz Epitome, the Liber de morte, the Itinerarium Alexandri, the Heidelberg Epitome, the Alexander papyri (Prandi's corpus of 10) or the non-Photian fragments of Arrian's Diadochi history. Russian translations of Alexander inscriptions are scattered across articles (e.g. Ladynin 2014 on the Bahariya altar). The Byzantine chronicle accounts of Alexander in Georgios Monachos, Zonaras IV, Kedrenos, Glykas and Joel have no modern Russian translation, only Old Slavonic versions. Malalas is the exception: a full Russian translation appeared in 2014–16. English coverage is uneven. These have full English translations: Robinson 1953 and BNJ (fragments), Davies 1998 (Itinerarium), Heckel 1988 (Liber de morte), BNJ 155 (Heidelberg Epitome) and Jeffreys 1986 (Malalas). These do not: the full Metz Epitome (only a 2026 Otago thesis, embargoed until 2027), Georgios Monachos Book I (a French thesis only, 2024), Zonaras IV, Kedrenos and Glykas. Spanish translations of the Metz Epitome and the Liber de morte appeared in 2025–26 (Aprile, Circe), and an Italian Itinerarium (Tabacco 2000). The strongest openings are therefore the Latin epitomes, a Russian corpus of the fragmentary historians, and the Byzantine chronicle accounts of Alexander, which have no English translation either.
already_translated_ru: Verified in this sweep: Arrian, Anabasis (Сергеенко 1962) and Indica (ВДИ 1940, no. 2). Plutarch, De Alexandri fortuna aut virtute (AST edition). Diodorus XVII (separate Russian edition). Photius, Bibliotheca, cod. 91 (Г.П. Власов) and cod. 92, the summary of Arrian's Ta meta Alexandron (Д.В. Мещанский), both on azbyka.ru. Malalas: Book V (Л.А. Фрейберг 1968), selections by Аверинцев (1987), and a complete Russian translation 2014–16 per the dissertation on dissercat.com. Not re-verified this sweep: Curtius (МГУ 1963/1993, with appendices of Diodorus, Justin and Plutarch); Justin (Деконский–Кашинцев 1954); Orosius (В.М. Тюленев 2001–03); Plutarch's Alexander; Polyaenus (2002); Aelian, Varia historia (Сонкина 1963); Athenaeus. So the fragments of the Alexander historians can be read in Russian only inside these host texts.

candidates.title: Epitoma rerum gestarum Alexandri Magni (Metz Epitome) + Liber de morte testamentoque Alexandri / Metz Epitome & Book on the Death and Testament of Alexander / «Мецская эпитома» и «Книга о смерти и завещании Александра»
candidates.author: Anonymous
candidates.tradition: historiography (vulgate/Cleitarchan epitome) + political pamphlet shared with the Romance (α III.30–33); Late Antique Latin
candidates.size: Epitome §§1–86 (330–325 BC) + Liber de morte §§87–123 (Thomas numbering); c. 35–40 Teubner pp. (estimate)
candidates.edition: P.H. Thomas, Teubner 1960, 2nd ed. 1966 (in copyright; a user scan is at archive.org/details/EpitomaRerumAlexandri). Public-domain base: O. Wagner 1900 (Jahrb. f. class. Philol. Suppl. 26), scan not yet located.
candidates.ru_evidence: Searches for «Мецская эпитома» and for «завещание Александра» + Liber de morte returned no Russian translation; neither text is in the ancientrome.ru author index.
candidates.en_evidence: Metz Epitome: excerpts only in Heckel–Yardley 2004; a full translation is in M. Watts, Otago PhD 2026, embargoed until 29.4.2027. Liber de morte: English translation in Heckel 1988 (Historia Einzelschriften 56).
candidates.other_translations: Spanish, both by G. Aprile in Circe: Liber de morte in 29/2 (2025); Epitome in 30/1 (2026), billed as the first Spanish translations. Amateur English (K. Soundy, pothos.org forum).
candidates.value: An independent vulgate witness for 330–325 BC, with unique details (Sogdiana, Roxane, India). The Liber de morte is the poisoning/testament pamphlet that links historiography to the Romance (α III.30–33, Julius Valerius III), which fits a Romance-specialist commentary perfectly.
candidates.ai_feasibility: High. Plain late Latin; the corrupt passages are documented in Thomas' apparatus. Greek and Latin expertise is enough.
candidates.pilot_unit: Liber de morte (§§87–123, c. 3,000 words, estimate) with a synopsis against Ps.-Callisthenes α III.30–33 and Julius Valerius III.

verification.title: Epitoma rerum gestarum Alexandri Magni (Metz Epitome, §§1–86) + Liber de morte testamentoque Alexandri (§§87–123) / «Мецская эпитома» и «Книга о смерти и завещании Александра»
verification.ru_found: No Russian translation of either text, full or partial, so the "none" claim holds in substance. The only Russian renderings found are tiny: (a) one sentence of Liber §97, translated as Onesicritus F 37 (FGrHist 134) in a fragment collection taken from simposium.ru and reposted at https://facetia.ru/node/3243; (b) short passages quoted in the authors' own translations in articles: О.Л. Габелко in «Исторический вестник» 2018 (Epit. Mett. 121), Е.О. Стоянов 2016 and О.М. Ян 2013 (both cyberleninka.ru), and А.С. Балахванцев's dissertation (ivran.ru). N. Gorelov's «Жизнь чудовищ в Средние века» (Азбука-классика 2004) cites Thomas's 1966 edition only among works used in the notes; it does not translate the text (https://facetia.ru/taxonomy/term/239). Queries run: «Мецская эпитома»; «Мецской эпитомы» перевод; "Liber de morte" Александр перевод; «о смерти и завещании Александра»; "Epitoma rerum gestarum Alexandri" перевод; site:facetia.ru; site:ancientrome.ru/simposium.ru/vostlit.info (zero hits). Ru.wikipedia only names the work («Книга о смерти и завещании Александра Великого»). Not verified in this pass: the Russian translation of the Armenian Romance (Дарбинян-Меликян 1986) should contain the parallel Romance version of the testament (III.30–33), but that is not the Latin Liber.
verification.en_found: The two texts must be split. The LIBER DE MORTE is fully translated into English several times. (1) T. Howe, C. Dunn, D. Lunt, Successors to Alexander the Great: Historical Sources in Translation (Wiley-Blackwell, © 2026, released Dec. 2025; ISBN 9781119688280), pp. 142–149. The book itself says "a translation of the complete text of the Liber de Morte", §§87–123 (Google Books id Mt-UEQAAQBAJ, search-inside verified). (2) Heckel & Yardley, Alexander the Great: Historical Sources in Translation (Blackwell 2004), pp. 281–89, "the Pamphlet" (per D. Grant, The Last Will and Testament of Alexander the Great, 2021, notes). (3) Heckel 1988 (Historia Einzelschriften 56): Appendix 1 prints the Latin of the Liber and the parallel texts (Ps.-Call. A III.30–33, Julius Valerius, Leo); the testament from §115, supplemented from A, is translated by J.C. Yardley (p. 24, "The translation is by J.C. Yardley"). (4) An amateur complete translation of §§87–123 by Karl Soundy on the defunct Google Site "Alexander Sources", archived at web.archive.org/web/20200615190249/https://sites.google.com/site/alexandersources/romance-and-other-sources/liber-de-morte. The METZ EPITOME §§1–86 has no published full scholarly English translation. Printed excerpts are in Heckel–Yardley 2004 and in Howe–Dunn–Lunt 2025/26 (Metz Epit. 5–6 at pp. 116–117; 28–31 at p. 50). Soundy's amateur full translation is on the same archived site (Part II = §§32–86, archived 2020-06-15; Part I's capture is not retrievable). A full scholarly translation is M.H.O. Watts, "The Metz epitome: translation and historical commentary", PhD thesis, Otago, 9 Apr 2026. It is embargoed until 29 Apr 2027 (abstract only; https://ourarchive.otago.ac.nz/esploro/outputs/doctoral/The-Metz-epitome-translation-and-historical/9926852167501891, hdl 10523/50348). Expect it to be published in English soon.

Bencivenni, Storicamente 9 (2013) no. 39, DOI 10.12977/stor492. No Italian translation of the Epitome was found. SPANISH, confirmed and open access: G. verification.source_text: Best public-domain text is O. Wagner, «Incerti auctoris epitome rerum gestarum Alexandri Magni e codice Mettensi», Jahrbücher für classische Philologie, Supplementband 26 (Leipzig: Teubner 1901 [the issue part is often dated 1900]), pp. 91–167. It contains both the Epitome and the Liber de morte (testament §§115–123 confirmed in the OCR). Google-digitized scans on the Internet Archive: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_MAYaAQAAIAAJ (title page reads "Sechsundzwanzigster Supplementband… 1901", Wagner at pp. 91–167); a second copy is https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_q0XnAAAAMAAJ. The standard edition is P.H. Thomas, Teubner 1960 (2nd ed. 1966), which is in copyright. Its readings should be collated and cited, not reproduced. Note J. Hunt, "Textual Problems in the Metz Epitome", L'Antiquité classique 2005 (DOI 10.3406/antiq.2005.2575). The single manuscript, Metz 500, was destroyed in 1944, so Wagner is a primary witness to the codex, not just an outdated text. DigilibLT (digiliblt.uniupo.it) has an entry for the Epitome; its text basis and licence were not checked.
verification.recommendation: Still a good Neoscholia candidate for RUSSIAN, with the main unit being the Metz Epitome §§1–86, ideally published together with the Liber §§87–123 (about 40 Teubner pages in all). The Liber is weak as an English-first unit: there are at least three English translations, the most recent explicitly complete (2025/26). There are also French (Callu 2010), Italian (Ravazzolo 2012) and Spanish (Aprile 2025) versions. Base the work on Wagner 1901 (public domain) checked against Thomas's readings. Only Latin is needed, but the corrupt Late Latin text calls for a textual-critical reviewer; for the commentary use the parallels in Ps.-Call. α III.30–33, Julius Valerius, Diodorus and Curtius. Watts's English thesis comes out of embargo in April 2027, so the English slot for the Epitome will soon close.

candidates.title: Fragments of the Alexander historians (FGrHist/BNJ 117–153); pilot: Onesicritus of Astypalaea (FGrHist 134) / «Фрагменты историков Александра»: Онесикрит
candidates.author: Callisthenes, Onesicritus, Nearchus, Aristobulus, Cleitarchus, Chares, Ephippus, Medius, Polyclitus, Ephemerides, etc.
candidates.date: 330s–c. 280 BCE (transmitted by Strabo, Plutarch, Arrian, Athenaeus, Pliny)
candidates.size: Corpus of several hundred fragments. Onesicritus c. 40 fragments and testimonia (estimate); could become a series of one author per volume.
candidates.edition: Jacoby, FGrHist II B (1927–30; not public domain). Public domain: C. Müller, Scriptorum de rebus Alexandri M. fragmenta, Didot 1846 (archive.org/details/arrianianabasis00arrigoog). BNJ online (subscription).
candidates.ru_evidence: Russian searches found no collection. The ancientrome.ru index has no entries for these authors. Fragments exist in Russian only inside host authors; Nearchus via Arrian's Indica (ВДИ 1940, no. 2).
candidates.en_evidence: C.A. Robinson, The History of Alexander the Great I (1953), translates all fragments plus the Ephemerides; livius.org calls it the only thorough English translation of the Ephemerides. BNJ entries include English.
candidates.other_translations: German commentary by Jacoby; Italian commentaries on individual authors.
candidates.value: The primary layer of Alexander historiography, which Russian readers have never had as an annotated corpus. Onesicritus (gymnosophists, Musicanus utopia) leads straight into the Brahman tradition (Palladius, Collatio, Romance III).
candidates.ai_feasibility: High. Greek/Latin. The main work is giving each fragment its source context; flag Latin fragments from Pliny.
candidates.pilot_unit: Onesicritus, all fragments and testimonia from Müller 1846 checked against Jacoby (c. 40 items). Alternative: the Ephemerides (FGrHist 117).

verification.title: Fragments of the Alexander historians (FGrHist/BNJ 117–153); pilot: Onesicritus of Astypalaea (FGrHist 134)
verification.ru_found:
The "RU none" claim is wrong. A full Russian version of the pilot exists online, but it is amateur and unattributed.

(1) simposium.ru, project «Фрагменты греческих историков» (https://simposium.ru/ru/node/12345, an alphabetical index of about 610 FGrHist authors). Uploaded by user "agnostik", 2016–2019; no translator is named. Contents for the Alexander historians:
- Онесикрит Астипалейский (https://simposium.ru/ru/node/13803, 12.04.2017): every Jacoby item, T 1–13f and F 1–39. Mirrored at https://facetia.ru/node/3243 («Онесикрит Астипалейский. Отрывки», source line «simposium.ru»).
- Неарх (node/13842)
- Аристобул Кассандрейский (node/13784; plus node/14300)
- Харет Митиленский (node/13785)
- Птолемей Лаг (node/13599)
- Эфипп Олинфский (node/13457)
- Медий Ларисский (node/13521)
- Бетон (node/13523), Диогнет (node/13541), Никобула (node/13526), Антиген (node/13525), Кирсил (node/13533), Марсий Пеллейский (node/13542), Аминта (node/13535), Гегесий (node/13538), Андросфен Фасоский (node/13520)
- Каллисфен (node/13869): selected T only; the fragments are numbered 1–51 on Müller's system, not Jacoby's, and include contamination from Ps.-Plutarch's De fluviis.
- Клитарх (node/13856): mixed up with the gnomic Clitarchus (the Sententiae).
- Not found in the index: the Ephemerides (117), Polyclitus (128) and Strattis (118).

How the Russian was made: wherever a Russian translation of the host author already exists, the passage is that published translation, reused without credit (Strabo/Стратановский, Plutarch, Arrian/Сергеенко, Diogenes Laertius/Гаспаров, Lucian, Gellius). The remaining passages (Pliny, Aelian, Tzetzes, Metz Epitome 97, the Byzantine poem) are rough new renderings. The source labels are BNJ-style English headers (e.g. P.Oxy. 4808 for Clitarchus T 1b), so these renderings were probably made from the English. There is no Greek text, apparatus or commentary.

(2) Russian translations of host authors carry many of the fragments:
- Arrian, Indica (Nearchus F 1, Onesicritus T 4). ВДИ 1940 №2, с. 230–263. Bukharin names the translator as О. В. Кудрявцев; ru.wikipedia says С. П. Кондратьев, so the attribution is disputed.
- Arrian, Indica ch. 1–17, tr. О. В. Смыка with notes by А. А. Вигасин, in «История и культура древней Индии» (М., 1990).
- Arrian, Indica, new full translation by М. Д. Бухарин in «Индия и античный мир» (М.: Восточная литература, 2002); online at facetia.ru/node/2757.
- Strabo XV, Plutarch, Athenaeus (Голинкевич), Pliny VII (Маркин, 2010).

(3) No scholarly Russian collection with commentary was found. Checked: CyberLeninka API (7 queries: Онесикрит; Каллисфен фрагменты перевод; Аристобул; Клитарх; Харет Митиленский; Эфемериды Александра; историки Александра фрагменты), ru.wikisource API (7 queries), the ancientrome.ru author index (no Alexander historians) and the vostlit.info indexes (medieval sources only).

The WebSearch quota was already used up, so all checks went through site search pages and APIs.
verification.en_found:
Both English claims are confirmed.

- C. A. Robinson Jr., The History of Alexander the Great, vol. 1 (Providence: Brown University, 1953; Kraus reprint 1977). The archive.org record lists vol. 1 as "An index to the extant historians. The fragments." Identifiers historyofalexand0002robi and historyofalexand0000robi; borrow-only.

Latin and German:

Spanish: none found (OpenLibrary query only).
verification.source_text:
The standard edition is Jacoby, FGrHist IIB no. 134 (1929/30), numbering T 1–13, F 1–39. It is not public domain (Jacoby died in 1959). BNJ 134 is online but subscription only.

The public-domain base is C. Müller, Scriptores rerum Alexandri Magni, in Arriani Anabasis et Indica, ed. F. Dübner (Paris: Didot, 1846). Copies: archive.org/details/arrianianabasis00arrigoog; reprint archive.org/details/anabasisetindica00arri (1865). It has a facing Latin translation, but its numbering differs and it lacks later-identified items: Jacoby's F 37 (Metz Epitome 97, edited by Wagner in 1900) and F 39 (the Byzantine poem, ed. Wagner 1881) have to be taken from those editions.

A practical alternative: rebuild each fragment from public-domain editions of the host authors (Strabo, Plutarch, Arrian, Pliny, Aelian, Diogenes Laertius, Tzetzes), keyed to Jacoby/BNJ numbering. Greek and Latin are enough to check the result.
verification.recommendation: Weak candidate, because it fails the "untranslated" test. Onesicritus already exists in full in English (Robinson 1953; BNJ 134), in French (Auberger 2001) and in an unattributed Russian web compilation (simposium.ru, 2017), and most of its fragments are also in published Russian translations of Strabo, Plutarch and Arrian. If pursued at all, the only real gain would be a first scholarly Russian edition and translation from the Greek with commentary, keyed to BNJ numbering. The best unit would be the items missing or garbled in the Russian web set: the Ephemerides (117), Polyclitus (128), and Callisthenes (124) redone on Jacoby's numbering.

candidates.title: Itinerarium Alexandri ad Constantium Augustum / Alexander's Itinerary / «Итинерарий Александра»
candidates.author: Anonymous (sometimes attributed to Julius Valerius)
candidates.tradition: historiography (Arrian-based epitome) + panegyric/mirror for Constantius II's Persian war
candidates.size: Short treatise, c. 25–30 printed pp. (estimate)
candidates.edition: A. Mai 1817/1818 (editio princeps). D. Volkmann, Naumburg 1871, public domain at archive.org/details/itinerariumalexa00unse. R. Tabacco, Olschki 2000 (critical edition with Italian translation).
candidates.ru_evidence: A Russian search for «Итинерарий Александра» or Itinerarium Alexandri + перевод found no Russian translation; not on ancientrome.ru.
candidates.en_evidence: Iolo Davies, 'Alexander's Itinerary', Ancient History Bulletin 12 (1998) 29–54.
candidates.other_translations: Italian: R. Tabacco 2000 (first modern Italian translation).
candidates.value: A 4th-century imperial reading of Arrian: Alexander as the model for Constantius against Persia. It is transmitted alongside Julius Valerius, which makes it a natural companion to the Romance and evidence of late-antique imitatio Alexandri.
candidates.ai_feasibility: High. Latin. Lacunae can be checked against Arrian.
candidates.pilot_unit: Proem plus the Gaugamela chapters, with a synopsis against Arrian III.

verification.title: Itinerarium Alexandri ad Constantium Augustum (Anonymous, sometimes attributed to Julius Valerius, c. 340–345 CE, Latin)
verification.ru_found: The sweep's RU "none" is refuted: a Russian translation of excerpts exists. V. V. Latyshev, «Известия древних писателей греческих и латинских о Скифии и Кавказе», vol. II (Latin authors), St Petersburg 1904, pp. 311–313, section «ITINERARIVM ALEXANDRI. ДОРОЖНИК АЛЕКСАНДРА». It has the Latin text after Müller 1846 with a facing Russian translation of chs. XVI (Thracians, Euxine, Maeotis, "Gothi"), LXXIV–LXXV (Drangians, Arachosians, Caucasus/Paropamisus), LXXIX (Maracanda, Tanais), LXXXI (Abii Scythians, Alexandria Eschate) and XCV–XCVI (Abian embassy, Pharasmanes of Chorasmia), in Müller's numbering. That is roughly 1–1.5 pages of Latin. I checked it in the scan at https://archive.org/details/Latyshev2 (djvu text). A second scan is izviestiiadrevni02laty. The passage is quoted in Russian as "перевод В. В. Латышева" in Stratum plus 2000 («Восточные германцы в Приазовье», cyberleninka.ru/article/n/vostochnye-germantsy-v-priazovie-v-iii-iv-vv-n-e), following Budanova 1990. Latyshev's translations were later reprinted (ВДИ 1947–1952; book reprint 1990s), but I did not check that this passage is in the reprints. I found no complete or other partial Russian translation. Searches: cyberleninka (Итинерарий Александра; Дорожник Александра; Юлий Валерий Полемий; Itinerarium Alexandri; Путеводитель Александра Констанций), ru.wikipedia and ru.wikisource (no article on the work, no text), ancientrome.ru author index and anon-lat page (not present). Russian scholarship only cites the work (e.g. «Ornamenta regia», 2015, quotes ch. 64 in Latin).
verification.en_found: Complete: Iolo Davies (tr.), "Alexander's Itinerary", Ancient History Bulletin 12 (1998) 29–54. It is listed in the AHB vol. 11–15 back-issue store at $1 (ancienthistorybulletin.org/volume-11-15-purchases/), so not open. Bibliographies describe it as a complete translation; I did not see the text. Partial English translations: (a) J. W. McCrindle, Ancient India as Described in Classical Literature (Westminster 1901) 150–155, chs. 103–117 (the Indian campaign to the Malli town and the return to Babylon), public domain. Checked at archive.org/details/dli.ernet.107414; a reprint PDF was on SDSU Project South Asia (web.archive.org copy of sdstate.edu/projectsouthasia/upload/The-Itinerary-of-Alexander-the-Great.pdf). (b) M. H. Dodgeon and S. N. C. Lieu, The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars AD 226–363 (1991) p. 176 (§7.3.1), the preface, Itin. Alex. 1–11 ed. Volkmann pp. 1–2 (checked via Google Books in-book search). (c) W. Heckel and J. Yardley, Alexander the Great: Historical Sources in Translation (Blackwell 2004). Its acknowledgements say it reproduces "with minor changes, portions of his [Davies'] translation of the Itinerary of Alexander" (Open Library search-inside). Stoneman's Legends of Alexander does not contain the work, which is historiography rather than legend; this is inference, not checked against the table of contents.

verification.recommendation: A weak candidate under the "never translated" rule. Complete translations exist in English (Davies 1998), Italian (Tabacco 2000) and French (Brenez 2003, open access), and Russian has only Latyshev's 1904 Scythian excerpts. It is only worth doing as the first complete Russian translation with commentary. The whole work (about 120 short chapters, roughly 25–30 printed pages of Latin) fits as one unit; a pilot could be the dedicatory preface and portrait (chs. 1–7), the mirror-for-Constantius section. Only Latin is needed, but the Latin is terse, mannered and transmitted in a single corrupt manuscript, so an expert Latinist must review it against Tabacco's text, with Arrian as a parallel.

Slavonic additions and omissions are marked with brackets. So this is not a translation made from the Greek alone, but it is a published, annotated, complete modern Russian version of exactly this chapter. I verified it through Open Library full-text search of the 2012 edition (archive.org legendsofalexand0000unse, lending-restricted). It runs from p. 25, «ALEXANDER OF MACEDON. After Philip, Alexander his son was King of Macedonia», to p. 33/34. It covers the Jerusalem episode with the high priest's vestments (pp. 26–28), Kandake (p. 30, «King Alexander…»), and the Long-lived Ones/Brahmans (p. 31). It also covers the Odontotyrannus (p. 32) and the laws catalogue including the Gelae women and «The Amazons have no husbands» (pp. 32–33). It closes with «his kingdom was divided into many dominions...», directly before ch. 4 (Palladius). The notes cite Bardesanes' Book of the Laws of Countries. The ellipsis suggests the satrapy list of the Diadochi may be cut; otherwise the chapter is translated in full. Independent confirmation: Di Serio, «An Ethnographic Catalogue in George the Monk's Chronicle», Studia Ceranea 11 (2021) 145–164, doi:10.18778/2084-140X.11.07. Her notes 12, 55, 56, 68, 76, 86 and 96 cite «Georgius Monachus I,19 (p. 35–39 de Boor), translation in R. Stoneman, Legends², 2012, p. 30–33», and she quotes Stoneman's English. Her article is a study, not a new translation. I did not see the 1994 edition itself; the 2012 catalogue record says the book was «originally published 1994».

Caire. Confirmed on theses.fr (https://theses.fr/api/v1/theses/these/2024AIXM0146). Its Greek text reworks Dmitry Afinogenov's unpublished edition, which uses Coislin 305 (P) and the Letovnik, with an apparatus against de Boor; a French translation follows. The record says it is not accessible online («accessible: non»). MEDIEVAL VERSIONS: the 11th-c. Slavonic Vremennik (Istrin 1920–30, reprinted Munich 1972; Матвеенко–Щеголева 2006) and the 14th-c. Bulgarian Letovnik. Russian Wikipedia also mentions a Georgian translation; I did not verify it. SOURCE PARALLELS already translated elsewhere: the Jerusalem episode comes from Josephus AJ XI.317–345. The Brahman section is almost verbatim Palladius, De gentibus Indiae I (EN Stoneman 1994/2012; FR Maraval 2016; RU Taronyan 2007 per the earlier sweep). The laws catalogue derives from Bardesanes via Eusebius PE VI.10 and Ps.-Caesarius (IT Ramelli 2009, per Di Serio). The surrounding Greek text is therefore almost entirely available in modern languages.
verification.source_text: C. de Boor, Georgii Monachi Chronicon, vol. I (Leipzig: Teubner 1904), Book I ch. 19 at roughly pp. 25/26–40. Public domain. Correction to the sweep: archive.org «georgiimonachic00boorgoog» is VOLUME 2. Volume 1, which contains the Alexander chapter, is https://archive.org/details/georgiimonachic01boorgoog (marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT, PDF available). The archive.org OCR of the Greek is unusable (Latin-alphabet garbage), so a new Greek OCR or manual keying would be needed. Other Google scans exist (bub_gb_s55EAAAAMAAJ, bub_gb_dp1EAAAAMAAJ; I did not check which volumes they are). The Wirth corrected reprint (Stuttgart 1978) is still in copyright. The Coislin 305 (P) redaction is unpublished; the Afinogenov edition is available only inside Picciola's thesis.
verification.recommendation: Not a Neoscholia candidate. The whole Alexander chapter (I.19) already has a published, annotated modern Russian translation (Матвеенко–Щеголева 2000, made from the Slavonic collated with de Boor, free on vostlit) and a near-complete English translation (Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great, 1994/2012, pp. 25–33). A French translation also exists in Picciola's 2024 thesis. The only defensible niche is a fresh Russian translation directly from the Greek of de Boor I.19, or later of the Coislin 305 (P) redaction once Afinogenov's text is published. That would be a retranslation, not a first translation, so drop it or keep it at the bottom of the list.

(1) ru.wikisource, page «Изложение истории (Зонара)» (https://ru.wikisource.org/wiki/Изложение_истории_(Зонара)): «ПЕРЕВОДЧИК = нет». The other two vostlit items are articles, not translations: Удальцова 1971 (on Malalas) and Черноглазов, «Хроника Иоанна Зонары и её источники (IX–XI вв.)», ВВ 63 (1999), which deals only with Books XVI–XVIII. (3) The 19th-century Russian Zonaras volumes (Правила… с толкованиями, 1876–1881) are the canon-law commentaries, not the Epitome. (4) Russian Wikipedia mentions only the medieval Slavonic translations. The only East Slavic witnesses are medieval Church Slavonic: the Paralipomenon (Bodyansky 1847) and the full Slavonic translation, whose Byzantine part was reprinted by Fink in 1970 ('Die byzantinische Geschichte bei Joannes Zonaras in slavischer Übersetzung'). I did not check whether the Paralipomenon includes the Alexander chapters. My CyberLeninka API queries returned 0 hits, which may be a failure of the API rather than a true null.
verification.en_found: No published English translation of Book IV was found. Banchich & Lane, The History of Zonaras (Routledge 2009; archive.org banchich-lane-2009-zonaras-history) translate only the Prologue, XII.15–XIII.19 and the Postscript. Their introduction (p. 18 and n. 33–34) lists all prior translations they knew of, and none covers Book IV. It also gives a useful note (n. 16) on IV.8 and IV.15 following Josephus AJ XI.8.2–5. Other English material is partial and elsewhere in the work: the Loeb Cassius Dio (Cary 1914–27) and Foster's 'Dio's Rome' (1905), which contain Zonaras VII–IX and later Roman passages; DiMaio's dissertation on the neo-Flavians (1977); and Tada's MA thesis on XVIII.20–29 (1999). One caveat: Agnes Wenman (d. 1617) made an unpublished English translation from Jean de Maumont's French adaptation. It survives in Cambridge UL MSS Mm.3.32, Dd.1.18 and Dd.1.19, covering Maumont's Book 1, 'Histories' 1–20, per the Harvard/AMDigital catalogue notes and Banchich & Lane p. 18. I could not tell whether those 'Histories' reach the Alexander chapters. Short quoted passages in studies (e.g. Kampianaki, John Zonaras' Epitome of Histories, OUP 2022; Jouanno on Byzantine chronicles) are possible but were not verified.
verification.other_found: The sweep's 'none found' is wrong for other languages. (1) Modern Greek: I. That is likely but not confirmed: check vol. Α's contents. (2) Latin: H. Wolf, Basel 1557; reprinted facing the Greek in Du Cange's edition (Paris 1686) and the CSHB edition (Pinder, vol. 1, 1841, Alexander at about pp. 328–358; verified in the archive.org scan ioanniszonaraea01pindgoog), and in PG 134. Ferentilli 1570/1572 (bub_gb_SmAhD-2JmSAC, bub_gb_McLGe7WDMvsC). (4) French: Jean Millet de Saint-Amour, Chroniques ou Annales de Jean Zonare (Lyon, Macé Bonhomme 1560, three parts); Jean de Maumont, Les Histoires et chroniques du monde (Paris, Vascosan 1561; 1583 ed. in three books), a free adaptation with material from other sources. (5) Partial modern translations that do not touch Book IV: German, E. Trapp 1986 (969–1118); Aragonese, Libro de los emperadores (Heredia, ed. Álvarez Rodríguez 2006, XV.10–XVIII); Turkish, 'Tarihlerin Özeti' (Arkeoloji ve Sanat, about 2010), apparently the Byzantine part only (not verified). So in practice the only modern translation of Book IV is very probably Grigoriadis's modern Greek; no modern Western-language translation is known.
verification.source_text: The unit is IV.7 (end, from the Sanballat/Manasses episode, Josephus AJ XI.302–312) through IV.15, optionally with the start of IV.16 (the partition of the empire). It is about 5,500 Greek words. (1) Dindorf, Ioannis Zonarae Epitome historiarum, vol. 1 (Teubner 1868), public domain: IV.8 starts p. 284.17 and IV.15 ends p. 306.26. I checked this against the OCR at https://archive.org/details/cuaioanniszonara01zona (file cua_ioanniszonara01zona_djvu.txt); there is also a Google scan, iannoytoyznapae01canggoog. Dindorf's source notes give IV.8–14 as Plutarch, Alexander 2–77, with p. 304.20 ff. (the Nonacris poison and Roxane's stopping his attempt to drown himself in the Euphrates) 'fortasse ex Arriano 7, 27', and IV.15 as Josephus AJ XI.8.3–7. (2) Pinder, CSHB Ioannis Zonarae Annales vol. 1 (Bonn 1841), public domain, Greek with facing Latin, a useful crib; Banchich used Pinder as his base text for Books I–XII: https://archive.org/details/ioanniszonaraea01pindgoog. There is no modern critical edition of Books I–XII; Büttner-Wobst (CSHB vol. 3, 1897) covers only XIII–XVIII.
verification.recommendation: This is a good, low-risk candidate: no Russian or English translation of Book IV exists. Start with IV.7 (end) through IV.15 (about 5,500 words, Dindorf vol. 1 pp. 283–306), with commentary keyed to Plutarch's Alexander, Arrian 7.27 and Josephus AJ XI. Note the probable modern Greek version by Grigoriadis; Greek and Latin expertise is enough to check the work. Its value lies in reception history (a 12th-century chronicler epitomizing Plutarch and Josephus, set against the Romance-based chronicle tradition), not new facts.

verification.ru_found:
I found no modern Russian translation of the Alexander sections of any of the three chroniclers. The "untranslated" claim mostly holds for Russian, but with one 18th-century caveat.

(1) Kedrenos. There is an old Russian translation in Church-Slavonicized language, printed in Cyrillic at the Synodal press: «Деяния церковные и гражданские от Рождества Христова до половины пятнадцатого столетия, собранные Георгием Кедриным и другими», translated by I. I. Sidorovsky, Moscow 1794, 3 parts; it was reprinted in 1820. Sources: ru.wikipedia «Георгий Кедрин», which links an NEB scan at https://rusneb.ru/catalog/000199_000009_02000026808/ (geo-blocked, so I could not open it); the РБС entry at ru.wikisource «РБС/ВТ/Сидоровский, Иоанн Иоаннович»; and Evgeny Bolkhovitinov's «Словарь исторический», which describes it as «…собранные Георгием Кедрином, с продолжением других». By its title it begins at the Nativity of Christ, so it very probably leaves out the pre-Christian Alexander chapter (Bekker I 264–273) and the Jerusalem visit (I 340–342). This still needs checking against the scan. Fyodor Polikarpov's Slavonic translation of Kedrenos (1720s) was never finished and exists only in manuscript (РБС «Поликарпов-Орлов»).

(2) Glykas. The only Russian translation is of his prison poem, by М. Е. Грабарь-Пассек in «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (1969). Two Russian scholars publish on the Chronicle but have translated nothing on Alexander: Л. Т. Авилушкина (2007–2019, manuscript studies) and В. Ю. Жаркая (2012, 2020; her own translations of other passages). Byzantinorossica (Бибиков) covers only passages about Rus'.

(3) Joel: nothing found.

Searches run: CyberLeninka API (Михаил Глика, Георгий Кедрин, Иоиль хронист, «Александр Македонский византийская хроника», Глики хроника перевод), ru.wikipedia/ru.wikisource search, and Google Books (Russian queries on Кедрин/Глика/Иоиль plus Alexander/brahmans). Gap: the WebSearch quota was used up, and vostlit.info refused the connection, so it is unchecked.
verification.en_found:
I found no published English translation of the Alexander sections of Kedrenos, Glykas or Joel. Three caveats:

(a) Kedrenos is being translated into English. Roger Scott, Byzantine Chronicles and the Sixth Century (Routledge 2018; Google Books uvZKDwAAQBAJ), says: "An English translation is being prepared by J. Burke, R. Scott and P. Tuffin". The same team has published studies: Brill Companion to Byzantine Chronicles 2024, ch. 13 (doi 10.1163/9789004711266_016); Brill 2024 (doi 10.1163/9789004707603_020); Routledge 2021 (doi 10.4324/9781003021759-11). I found no published volume. Byzantina Australiensia runs to vol. 27 (2024) with no Kedrenos, and a Crossref book search found nothing. Its status in 2026 should be rechecked before committing.

(b) The Brahman sequence in Kedrenos and Glykas derives from George the Monk. Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great (1994/2012) has an English translation of that George the Monk excerpt (1.19; doi 10.5040/9780755625741.ch-003). This is a close parallel, not a translation of Kedrenos or Glykas.

(c) Studies that paraphrase or quote snippets: Jouanno, "Alexander Romance and Byzantine world chronicles" in Stoneman/Nawotka/Wojciechowska (eds.), The Alexander Romance: History and Literature (ANS 25, 2018), 225–244 (doi 10.2307/j.ctv13nb6rb.16); Jouanno, "The Alexander historians in Byzantium" (Harrassowitz 2018; she discusses Kedrenos citing Diodorus); Jouanno, "Byzantine Views on Alexander" (Brill 2018); Kaldellis, CUP 2022 (doi 10.1017/9781316711798.011).

Ruled out:
- McCrindle, Ancient India (1901), translates Kedrenos only on Metrodoros (Bekker I 516–17), not Alexander.
- Priaulx (1873/JRAS) only discusses Kedrenos's sources.
- English Wikipedia says no modern-language translation of Glykas's chronicle exists.
verification.other_found:
This refutes the sweep's "Other translations: none".

- Joel, Italian: F. Iadevaia, Ioel, Chronographia compendiaria: introduzione, testo critico, traduzione, note e lessico (Messina: EDAS 1979). It is a complete Italian translation. Confirmed by the Google Books record lI2IZwEACAAJ and by Quaderni medievali 1984: «edita e tradotta in italiano da Francesca Iadevaia».
- Kedrenos, Italian edition: L. Tartaglia, Georgii Cedreni Historiarum compendium (Bollettino dei classici Suppl. 30, Rome 2016, 2 vols). It is Greek only (introduction, text, indices). The H-Soz-Kult review (https://www.hsozkult.de/publicationreview/id/reb-25574) says a translation is still needed.
- Latin: Xylander 1566 for Kedrenos and Leunclavius 1572 for Glykas, both reprinted facing the Greek in Bekker's CSHB volumes.
- Not found: any French, German, Spanish or modern Greek translation of these chapters. Mavromati-Katsougiannopoulou 1984 is a source study of Glykas, not a translation.
- Romanian (Fontes Historiae Daco-Romanae) and Bulgarian (ГИБИ) source collections excerpt these chroniclers only for regional history, not Alexander.
verification.source_text:
All three are public domain in Bekker's CSHB volumes.

1. Kedrenos: Georgius Cedrenus, ed. I. Bekker, vol. I, Bonn 1838.
   - Main Alexander chapter: c. pp. 264–273 (birth via Nectanebo; Diodorus cited; Porus; Candace; Brahmans; founding of Alexandria; death; Diadochi).
   - Visit to Jerusalem and the high priest (Josephus tradition): pp. 340–342.
   - Danielic exegesis: further on in the volume.
   - Online: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_WM0GAAAAQAAJ (also Google Books WM0GAAAAQAAJ).
   - Check readings against Tartaglia 2016 (copyrighted).
2. Glykas: Michaelis Glycae Annales, ed. Bekker, Bonn 1836, Pars II, pp. 267–271. https://archive.org/details/michaelisglycae01glycgoog (also PG 158).
3. Joel: Ioelis Chronographia compendiaria, ed. Bekker, Bonn 1836. The Alexander material is a single paragraph of about 100 words. https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_cmPMxX3yNZ0C
   - Iadevaia 1979 has a better text and an Italian translation, but is copyrighted.

For a synopsis of shared sources, George the Monk, ed. C. de Boor, Teubner 1904, is public domain.
verification.recommendation: This is a reasonable but secondary candidate. The RU/EN gap is real, but the Brahman core is close to George the Monk (already in English in Stoneman), and Joel's Italian translation and the Australian Kedrenos project reduce how novel it is. Start with Kedrenos's Alexander dossier (Bekker I 264–273 plus 340–342, c. 3,000 Greek words), set side by side with Glykas pp. 267–271 and George the Monk, with Joel's paragraph as an appendix. Greek expertise is enough to verify it; no extra languages are needed.

verification.title: Alexander-history papyri: Prandi's corpus of ten anepigraphic fragments (CPGL A.2.9, 2010). Sources: BMCR 2011.04.35 (Straus), Histos 5 (2011) review by Capponi, CEDOPAL MP3 2195–2201.01
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of any of the ten papyri, either complete or partial. WebSearch was unavailable because the session's 200-search budget was used up, and DuckDuckGo and Yandex returned CAPTCHAs, which I did not bypass. The Russian checks were therefore done another way, and a negative result is weaker evidence than usual.
(1) ru.wikipedia API searches for «Эфемериды Александра Македонского», «папирус история Александра Македонского», «Оксиринхские папирусы» and «Птолемей Сотер сочинение об Александре фрагменты». I also grepped the full texts of the articles Александр Македонский, Птолемей I Сотер, Страттис Олинфский and Смерть Александра Македонского. None mentions P.Oxy. 1798 or any Alexander-history papyrus.
(2) The ancientrome.ru antlitr index, including «Анонимные греческие авторы». The only Oxyrhynchus text there is P.Oxy. 842 (Hellenica Oxyrhynchia, tr. Лурье). The Arrian index has nothing on the papyri.
(3) The xlegio.ru sources index: nothing.
(4) CyberLeninka API queries («папирус Александр», «Эфемериды Александра», «оксиринхский папирус Александр», «историки Александра фрагменты перевод») all returned 0 hits. That is unreliable, probably an API or bot block.
(5) vdi.igh.ru (ВДИ) could not be reached.
Not checked: ВДИ back issues (Soviet ВДИ sometimes printed papyrus translations) and Russian Alexander monographs such as Шофман. RU 'none' is probable but not proven.
verification.en_found:
The colleague's claim is partly refuted. English coverage is much broader than the sweep said, and the largest papyrus, P.Oxy. 1798, has a complete English translation.

1. P.Oxy. XV 1798 (FGrHist/BNJ 148)
- COMPLETE: Brill's New Jacoby 148, 'Anonymous on Alexander (P. Ox. 1798)', by Luisa Prandi, published 1 April 2015 (8,084 words). The table of contents lists F 1–54 (with joins to P.Oxy. 2081g and new fragments), each with a 'Translation' section. Evidence: Wayback snapshot of referenceworks.brillonline.com/entries/brill-s-new-jacoby/anonymous-on-alexander-p-ox-1798-148-a148 (2016). Crossref also has a BNJ second-edition English translation record, DOI 10.1163/1873-5363_fgrh.0148.bnjo-2-tr1-eng. Subscription access.
- PARTIAL, public domain: Grenfell & Hunt, P.Oxy. XV (1922), pp. 122ff. The commentary translates Fr. 44 col. i 1–16 (Philip the physician), col. iii 1–19 (the rout at Issus) and col. iv 1–17 (the bread anecdote and the casualty figures). Read in archive.org 'oxyrhynchuspapyrunse_79'.
- PARTIAL: Hammond, GRBS 19 (1978) 331–350, ''Philip's Tomb' in Historical Context', §IV re-edits and discusses Fr. 1 (Philip's death). Open access at grbs.library.duke.edu article 7331.
- PROBABLE, not inspected: C. A. Robinson, The History of Alexander the Great I (Brown 1953; Kraus repr. 1977), pp. 262–263. CEDOPAL cites it, and the volume is a collection of translated fragments.

2. P.Brit.Libr. inv. 3085v (commentary in the manner of the Ephemerides; Illyrian campaign)
- English translation in the editio princeps: Clarysse & Schepens, 'A Ptolemaic Fragment of an Alexander History', CdÉ 60 (1985) 30–47, DOI 10.1484/J.CDE.2.308671.
- A new English translation: Hammond, 'A Papyrus Commentary on Alexander's Balkan Campaign', GRBS 28 (1987) 331–347. Open access under CC BY: https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/view/4701. Hammond says 'In my translation I italicise…'.

3. P.Berol. 21258v (BKT IX 162; three chreiai on Philip, Alexander and Olympias)
- Hock & O'Neil, The Chreia and Ancient Rhetoric: Classroom Exercises (Atlanta 2002), no. 5. Cited in CEDOPAL MP3 2195.01. The series prints text with translation, so an English translation is very likely there; I did not inspect it.

4. P.Cair. JE 49653 (Indian operations, Craterus)
- Roisman, CQ 34 (1984) 373–385 (DOI 10.1017/S0009838800031001) discusses it. Whether it includes a translation is unverified.

No English translation found for: P.Hamb. II 130 (Granicus and Cleitus), P.Oxy. IV 679, P.Oxy. LVI 3823 and 3824, P.Lond. V 1815, P.Laur. IV 138. For 3823/3824 it is unknown whether the P.Oxy. LVI (1989) editio princeps translates.

BNJ 151 (Fragmentum Sabbaiticum) and BNJ 153 (Bearzot 2017) also have English translations, but they are not part of Prandi's corpus. BNJ 153 F 1 is P.Oxy. I 13, which Prandi excluded.
Not verified: Heckel–Yardley, Alexander the Great: Historical Sources in Translation (2004).
verification.other_found:
ITALIAN, complete: Prandi 2010 translates all ten 'where possible', as both BMCR 2011.04.35 and Capponi (Histos 5, 2011, DOI 10.29173/histos213) confirm. Capponi notes that translations are 'a rare thing to be found in the first editions of fragmentary papyri', which suggests most editiones principes have none.
ITALIAN, partial:
- Foraboschi, PapLup 9 (2000) 171–178, on P.Laur. IV 138. Translation not verified.
- CPF II.2 CHR 1 for P.Berol. 21258v. Probably has an Italian translation; not verified.
- Denuzzo, PapLup 12 (2003) 71–96, a survey of all ten. Translations not verified.
GERMAN: The P.Hamb. II 130 editio princeps (1954) and Gronewald, ZPE 115 (1997) on P.Berol. 21258v may include German translations; not verified.
FRENCH: J. Auberger, Historiens d'Alexandre (Les Belles Lettres 2001/2005) may include FGrHist 148; not verified.

CORRECTIONS to the candidate record:
- The siglum is P.Hamb. II 130 (inv. 652), not 'IV 130'. Per CEDOPAL MP3 2196, BMCR also misprints it.
- Since Prandi's book, Maltomini & Messeri, ZPE 202 (2017) 48–61, have joined P.Cair. JE 49653 and P.Oxy. LVI 3824 into one roll, tentatively attributed to Ptolemy Soter (CEDOPAL MP3 2197). The corpus is now effectively nine texts, and any new translation must use the 2017 text.
- The P.Oxy. IV 679 original was lost in WWI, so only the 1904 editio princeps survives.
verification.source_text:
There is no single openly licensed edition of the whole corpus.

PUBLIC DOMAIN:
- Grenfell–Hunt, P.Oxy. IV (1904) no. 679: archive.org/details/oxyrhynchuspapyr0004unse.
- Grenfell–Hunt, P.Oxy. XV (1922) no. 1798: archive.org/details/oxyrhynchuspapyrunse_79.

OPEN ACCESS, CC BY: Hammond, GRBS 28 (1987), with text and translation of P.Brit.Libr. 3085v (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/view/4701).

IN COPYRIGHT:
- P.Hamb. II (1954).
- P.Oxy. LVI (1989); images are on portal.sds.ox.ac.uk, also in copyright.
- BKT IX (1996).
- P.Laur. IV (1983) and Luppe–Pintaudi, ZPE 38 (1980).
- Clarysse–Schepens 1985.
- Maltomini–Messeri, ZPE 202 (2017).
- Prandi 2010 (Fabrizio Serra), the reference edition. Note that Italian law (art. 85-quater, L. 633/1941) gives critical editions a 20-year related right, so a reuse of Prandi's text needs checking until about 2030.
verification.recommendation: A good candidate for Russian, where nothing exists, as one dossier of nine or ten short texts with commentary. It is a weaker candidate for English. P.Oxy. 1798 is already fully in English (BNJ 148) and P.Brit.Libr. 3085v twice. The English value lies in the untranslated pieces: P.Hamb. II 130, the P.Cair. 49653 + P.Oxy. 3824 join (Maltomini–Messeri 2017), P.Oxy. 3823, P.Oxy. 679, P.Lond. V 1815 and P.Laur. IV 138. I would start with P.Hamb. II 130 and the P.Cair. + P.Oxy. 3824 roll. Verification needs Greek papyrological expertise, not oriental languages: the texts are very gappy, and restorations must be marked strictly.

verification.title: Letters of Alexander quoted by Plutarch, Arrian and others (literary corpus) / «Письма Александра Македонского» (корпус)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian corpus edition, anthology, dissertation or article that collects these letters. The "untranslated" claim still fails in substance, because almost every letter-passage already exists in Russian inside full translations of the authors who quote it:
(a) Plutarch, Alexander. Full Russian translations of the Lives exist. It is also appended to Arrian, «Поход Александра», tr. М. Е. Сергеенко (Moscow–Leningrad: AN SSSR, 1962; repr. Миф 1993), together with Diodorus XVII. This was checked on ru.wikipedia «Анабасис Александра», which also lists Н. Кореньков's Arrian translation (Tashkent 1912).
(b) Plutarch, De Alexandri fortuna aut virtute I–II, tr. Я. М. Боровский, and Regum et imperatorum apophthegmata, tr. М. Л. Гаспаров. Both are listed on ancientrome.ru/antlitr/plutarch/index.htm. These cover Monti's F5a, F11a/b and others.
(c) Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae: complete Russian translation by Н. Т. Голинкевич (Наука, «Литпамятники», 2003 and 2010), confirmed via ru.wikipedia «Пир мудрецов». This covers the letters to the satraps at 11.784a.
(d) Curtius, Justin and Gellius 20.5 (the letter to Aristotle, which is also at Plut. Alex. 7) have Russian translations. I did not re-check these in this pass.
Peripheral finds:
(e) simposium.ru/ru/node/9734, «Письма Александра Великого» (translator "Агностик", 2012). This is an amateur Russian translation made from the French of remacle.org. It covers the Romance letter to Olympias and Aristotle (Ps.-Call. II.23–41 type, late recension, Land of Darkness episode) in two manuscript versions. It is Romance material, not the historiographical corpus.
(f) М. М. Холод, «К истории Хиоса второй половины IV в. до н. э.» (2012, cyberleninka) quotes Russian renderings of a few lines of Alexander's inscribed letters to Chios (RO 84A ll. 15–17; 84B ll. 15–16, 24–25). These are fragments only.
Searches run: ru.wikipedia API (3 queries plus Придик), CyberLeninka API (4 queries), simposium.ru (taxonomy pages and search), ancientrome.ru indexes. General web search engines were unavailable: the WebSearch budget was exhausted and the other engines returned CAPTCHAs.
verification.en_found:
Giustina Monti, ed., Alexander the Great. Letters: A Selection (Aris & Phillips Classical Texts; Liverpool UP, 2023), xiii + 256 pp., ISBN 978-1-80034-862-2, DOI 10.2307/j.ctv33b9w5q (verified via CrossRef).
- Content: 43 passages numbered as fragments FF1–34, in chronological order. Each has a critical Greek or Latin text with apparatus, a facing English translation and a full historical commentary, including an authenticity discussion for every letter.
- Scope: only letters Monti thinks may be authentic, plus the spurious letter(s) to Aristotle. The sources include Plutarch's Alexander and Moralia, Arrian, Pliny and others.
- Excluded: the Romance letters and the inscribed letters (Chios, Priene, Eresos/GHI 83).
- Reviews: J. Arthur-Montagne, Histos 19 (2025) I–VIII (open access, CC BY-NC-ND), which gives the 43 passages, FF1–34, and the selection principle quoted from p. ix; B. Antela-Bernárdez, Karanos 8 (2025) 145–46; Degen, Historische Zeitschrift 2025 (DOI 10.1515/hzhz-2025-1008).
Every letter Monti leaves out is still available in English, in Loeb or other translations of Plutarch, Arrian, Curtius, Diodorus, Justin, Athenaeus and Gellius. So the colleague's "partial" understates the coverage. The corpus has a dedicated, complete bilingual English edition of its authentic core, and everything else exists in English inside the host authors.
verification.other_found:
ITALIAN translation (refutes the sweep's "none"): Pietro Citati, Alessandro; con i diari e le lettere a cura di Francesco Sisti (Milano: Rizzoli, «La Scala», 1974, 141 pp.; OCLC 1868921). Reprinted as Alessandro: con i diari e le lettere (Milano: Mondadori, Oscar saggi 479, 1996; ISBN 8804415932). Verified via Open Library edition records. Monti, Histos 10 (2016) 17–33, bibliography, cites it as F. Sisti, «I diari e le lettere», in P. Citati, Alessandro (Milan 1974) 65–122: an Italian translation of the Ephemerides and the letters.
Also: G. Monti, L'epistolario di Alessandro (PhD thesis, Università di Bari, 2009). It is unpublished, and I could not check whether it contains translations.
Older studies and collections, all public domain and written in Latin, with no translation:
- M. Adler, De Alexandri Magni epistularum commercio (Leipzig 1891). I did not find a scan.
- Eugen Pridik (Е. М. Придик, 1865–1935), De Alexandri Magni epistularum commercio (Dorpat: C. Mattiesen, 1893), vi + 168 pp. Scan: archive.org/details/dealexandrimagni00prid. It is an analytical catalogue of 114 letters: nos. 1–71 written by Alexander (to Greek cities including Priene, Chios and Eresos; to Darius; to his generals; to Olympias, Aristotle, Leonidas and others), and nos. 72–114 written to him (by Antipater, Parmenion, Darius, Olympias, Aristotle, Theopompus, Porus, Calanus and others).
- A. M. Zumetikos, De Alexandri Olympiadisque epistularum fontibus et reliquiis (Berlin diss., 1894), 148 pp. Scan: archive.org/details/dealexandriolym00zumegoog (marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). It quotes the Greek text of the surviving letters by addressee and source, and covers the Ps.-Callisthenes and Julius Valerius letters.
- Related studies: Hansen, Philologus 39 (1880); Kaerst, Philologus 51 (1892); Pearson, Historia 3 (1954/55); Hamilton, PACA 4 (1961).
No French, German or Spanish collection or translation turned up in theses.fr, HAL, the German National Library catalogue or CrossRef.
verification.source_text:
There is no single public-domain edition of the corpus. Monti 2023 (Liverpool UP; copyrighted) is the modern critical text and should supply the numbering (FF1–34). For a freely usable Greek or Latin text, take each letter from the host authors' public-domain editions, available as digital texts on Perseus/Scaife (First1KGreek) under open licences, which need checking text by text:
- Plutarch, Lives: Perrin, Loeb 1919
- Plutarch, Moralia: Nachstädt/Babbitt
- Arrian: Roos, Teubner 1907
- Athenaeus: Kaibel 1887–90
- Curtius, Diodorus, Justin and Gellius: the standard 19th- and early 20th-century editions
Public-domain inventories with Greek quotations: Zumetikos 1894 (https://archive.org/details/dealexandriolym00zumegoog) and Pridik 1893 (https://archive.org/details/dealexandrimagni00prid; the author died in 1935). Both are useful for mapping the full corpus, genuine and spurious, beyond Monti's selection.
verification.recommendation: This is a poor Neoscholia candidate, so I recommend dropping it as a "never translated" text. Nearly every letter is already in Russian inside the host-author translations (Сергеенко, Боровский, Гаспаров, Голинкевич), English has a recent complete bilingual edition with commentary (Monti 2023), and Italian has Sisti 1974. A Russian annotated dossier of Monti's FF1–34 could still be made as a derivative study aid, but that is not a new translation. That is not what this platform is for.

- Paton, IG XII 2, 526 (1899), Eresos; Dittenberger, OGIS 1, 8 and Syll.3 283 (also public domain).
Openly licensed: the Axon 2018 Priene texts (CC BY 4.0).
Free but not openly licensed: Bosch-Puche 2008 for the Bahariya altar.
Corrections to the sweep: Tod II (1948) is not public domain in life+70 jurisdictions (Tod died 1974). R-O 2003 and the second Chios letter (SEG 22.506) are in copyright. The Philippi letter (SEG 34.664; Hatzopoulos, Macedonian Institutions II no. 6) has no public-domain edition.
verification.recommendation: Not a candidate under the "never translated" rule: English coverage is full and repeated, and there are also Italian, German and French versions. The gap is only in Russian, where a complete annotated Russian dossier would still be new. If done at all, it should be a low-priority unit of R-O 83, 84A–B and 86 plus the Priene dedication (about 1.5–2.5k Greek words, Greek-only checking, from Hicks–Hill and IG/OGIS). Leave out the Bahariya altar unless an Egyptologist is involved, since its hieroglyphic text needs that expertise.

verification.title: Heidelberg Epitome (FGrHist/BNJ 155; Cod. Pal. gr. 129, ff. 137v–138r, autograph of Nikephoros Gregoras) — «Гейдельбергская эпитома»
verification.ru_found: No Russian translation found, full or partial. The Russian web search for «Гейдельбергская эпитома диадохи перевод» found nothing relevant (only general articles on the Diadochi). The ru.wikipedia articles «Филипп III Арридей» (raw source checked) and «Гиероним Кардийский» do not cite the Epitome at all. The Arridaeus article discusses the epilepsy hypothesis via Worthington, Schachermeyr and Shofman 1984, with no Russian rendering of BNJ 155 F1.2. Caveat: the session's WebSearch budget ran out after this one Russian query, so the required four Russian searches (cyberleninka, elibrary, ВДИ, ancientrome.ru) could not be done. A passage quoted in Russian Diadochi scholarship (for example F1.2 on Arridaeus' epilepsy) cannot be ruled out. Status: none found, confidence medium.
verification.en_found: The full text (all four excerpts) has been translated into English several times. (1) J. C. Yardley, in Yardley, Wheatley and Heckel, Justin: Epitome of the Philippic History of Pompeius Trogus, vol. II, Books 13–15 (Clarendon Ancient History, OUP 2011), appendix. BMCR 2013.04.08 confirms that the appendices include 'the Heidelberg epitome' in translation (http://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2013/2013-04-08.html). (2) P. Wheatley, 'The Heidelberg Epitome: a Neglected Diadoch Source', in Alonso Troncoso and Anson (eds.), After Alexander (Oxbow 2013), 17–29. Per BMCR 2013.08.24 it gives 'a copy of the text with translation'; a search summary said Wheatley reuses Yardley's 2011 version, but the article page itself could not be opened. (3) Brill's New Jacoby 155: Greek text with facing English translation and commentary. Correction to the sweep: Leon 2026 cites it as 'BNJ 155 with Meeus's commentary', so the BNJ editor is A. Meeus, not Wheatley (I could not open the Brill page itself). (4) A free online translation, sections [1]–[4] covering 323–316 BC, at attalus.org/translate/fgh.html. No translator is named on the page; it is part of the site's selection from FGrHist. (5) Partial: D. W. Leon, 'Arrhidaeus and the Desire to Diagnose: A New Approach to the Heidelberg Epitome', GRBS 66.2 (2026) 194–214, CC-BY. It prints and translates F1.2 only (https://grbs.library.duke.edu/index.php/grbs/article/view/17039). The sweep's 'EN full' is confirmed.
verification.other_found: GERMAN, full, and missing from the sweep: Georg Bauer, Die Heidelberger Epitome. Eine Quelle zur Diadochengeschichte (Leipzig: Dieterich/Weicher 1914; also a Leipzig dissertation), Kap. I 'Text und Übersetzung'. It gives the Greek text checked against the MS (pp. 2–4, with notes on the erasures and later additions) and a complete German translation (pp. 4–6). Bauer then analyses the sources (Hieronymus, Diodorus, Justin, Curtius and others). Public domain: https://archive.org/details/dieheidelbergere00baueuoft (verified from the OCR text). The editio princeps, R. Reitzenstein, Poimandres (Leipzig 1904) 308–315 (Beigabe V), gives the text with a short commentary linking it to the Alexander Romance. Per Bauer there is no translation there. ITALIAN, SPANISH, FRENCH: none found, status unknown (could not be searched after the budget ran out). Relevant related scholarship: I. Ševčenko 1964 and A. Biedl 1948 on the codex as Gregoras' notebook; Giacomelli 2014 and Pérez Martín 1993 on its sources.
verification.source_text: Public domain: G. Bauer 1914, Greek text plus German translation, archive.org/details/dieheidelbergere00baueuoft; Reitzenstein, Poimandres 1904, pp. 308–315. Manuscript: Cod. Pal. gr. 129, ff. 137v–138r, digitised by Heidelberg UB, https://doi.org/10.11588/diglit.4105 (good for checking erasures and marginal corrections against Bauer). Reference editions under copyright: Jacoby, FGrHist IIB 155 (1929); Meeus, BNJ 155. The whole text is about two manuscript pages, roughly 550–650 Greek words.
verification.recommendation: Only a weak candidate on its own: it is untranslated in Russian, but it has several full English translations (Yardley 2011, BNJ/Meeus, attalus.org), a full public-domain German one (Bauer 1914), and is tiny. Do it as one quick Russian unit (all four excerpts, from Bauer's text checked against the Heidelberg scans, Greek only, no extra language expertise needed). Better still, put it in a Russian dossier of minor Diadochi and Alexander's-death sources (with the Metz Epitome/Liber de morte), with commentary drawing on Leon 2026's Gregoras attribution.

verification.title: Arrian, Ta meta Alexandron: non-Photian fragments (Vatican palimpsest Vat. gr. 495 ff. 230/235; Göteborg palimpsest ms Graec 1 ff. 72/73; PSI XII 1284) / Арриан, «События после Александра»: фрагменты
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of any of the three non-Photian fragments. Method caveat: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) was already used up before this task began, so I could not run the 4 Russian searches the task asked for. I checked with direct page fetches instead. ru.wikipedia "Флавий Арриан" mentions the lost 10-book Τὰ μετ' Ἀλέξανδρον and lists Russian translations of Arrian (Anabasis: Коренькова 1912, Сергеенко 1962; Indica: Бухарин 2002, Таронян 2007 partial, anonymous 1940; Tactica: Нефёдкин 2010; Cynegeticus: Козаржевский 1961; Acies contra Alanos: Перевалов 2001). It lists nothing for the fragments. ancientrome.ru's Arrian index has only the Indica (Кондратьев) and the Periplus (Прозоров). The only Russian text I know of is Photius cod. 92, from the sweep (Мещанский, azbyka.ru); I did not re-check it. Not checked because search was blocked: cyberleninka/elibrary dissertations on Eumenes or the Diadochi, simposium.ru, facetia.ru. A partial translation inside a Russian Diadochi study therefore cannot be ruled out completely.
verification.en_found: The "EN unknown" claim is refuted. attalus.org (Fragments of the Greek Historians page, https://www.attalus.org/translate/fgh.html#156.0, section "Events after the death of Alexander") has an unsigned English translation of all three non-Photian fragments, alongside Freese's translation of Photius cod. 92 (F 1, 9, 11). (1) F 10 = Vatican palimpsest, "[COD.RESCR.VATIC.]", about 1,200 words. It runs from the desertion of Arrhidaeus to Ptolemy with Alexander's body, through Attalus and Polemon, to Docimus taking over Babylon on Perdiccas' orders. (2) "F 181" = PSI 1284, about 150 words: the cavalry and javelin action and Eumenes' speech to the Macedonians. (3) "F 182" = Göteborg palimpsest, about 800 words, linked to Dreyer's ZPE 125 PDF: Eumenes' plundering raid, the contempt for Antipater, and the embassies to Alcetas, Attalus, Polemon and Docimus. The page notes "Another two fragments have been discovered since the time of Jacoby". Probable but not verified (I could not search): W. J. Goralski, "Arrian's Events after Alexander: Summary of Photius and Selected Fragments", Ancient World 19 (1989) 81–108. Dreyer 1999 cites it as "Goralski, Anc. World 19, 1989, passim". Its "selected fragments" likely include the Vatican palimpsest and PSI 1284. Also likely: Dreyer 2007, "The Arrian Parchment in Gothenburg", in Heckel–Tritle–Wheatley (eds.), Alexander's Empire, 245–263, probably with an English rendering. BNJ 156 could not be checked (Brill returned 403). livius.org has only Freese's Photius excerpt and none of the palimpsests.
verification.other_found: ITALIAN, all three fragments: A. Simonetti Agostinetti, Flavio Arriano, Gli eventi dopo Alessandro (Monografie CERDAC 15; Roma: L'Erma di Bretschneider, 1993; ISBN 88-7062-824-8). It gives the Greek text with a facing Italian translation and a historical commentary. The Greek is reproduced from Jacoby for Photius and Vat. gr. 495, from Bartoletti for PSI 1284 and from Noret for the Göteborg leaf (J. A. Straus's review, AC 64 (1995) 303–304, https://www.persee.fr/doc/antiq_0770-2817_1995_num_64_1_1237_t1_0303_0000_2; also listed on de.wikipedia "Arrian"). FRENCH, Göteborg leaf: J. Noret, "Un fragment du dixième livre de la Succession d'Alexandre par Arrien retrouvé dans un palimpseste de Gothenbourg", L'Antiquité Classique 52 (1983) 235–242 (https://www.persee.fr/doc/antiq_0770-2817_1983_num_52_1_2097). It has a diplomatic transcription, a normalized edition and a French translation (confirmed by Dreyer 1999: 41). GERMAN, Göteborg leaf: B. Dreyer, "Zum ersten Diadochenkrieg. Der Göteborger Arrian-Palimpsest (ms Graec 1)", ZPE 125 (1999) 39–60. §4 is a diplomatic transcription, §6 a normalized transcription and §7 a German translation (pp. 59–60), with lines 5–14 left untranslated as too fragmentary; it also has plates I–VIII, including the Reitzenstein leaves. Dreyer also quotes German renderings from St. Schröder, ZPE 71 (1988) 75–90, so a further partial German translation probably exists there. For PSI 1284, German and English discussion only, not translations as far as I could see: Latte, Kleine Schriften 1968 (1950) 595–599; Wirth, Klio 46 (1965) 283–288; Bosworth, GRBS 19 (1978) 227–237; Thompson, CE 59 (1984) 113ff. No Spanish translation found (not searchable).
verification.source_text: Vatican palimpsest (Vat. gr. 495, ff. 230 and 235): R. Reitzenstein, Arriani τῶν μετ' Ἀλέξανδρον libri septimi fragmenta e codice Vaticano rescripto nuper iteratis curis lecto (Breslauer philologische Abhandlungen 3.3; Breslau 1888). This edition is public domain: https://archive.org/details/arrianitnmetale00reitgoog. The text is also in Jacoby, FGrHist 156 F 10, and Roos–Wirth, Arrianus II (Teubner 1967/68), around p. 277ff.; both are under copyright. Göteborg palimpsest (Universitetsbiblioteket ms Graec 1, ff. 72/73): the best freely readable text is Dreyer, ZPE 125 (1999) 39–60. It is an open PDF, though under copyright, and includes plates: http://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/zpe/downloads/1999/125pdf/125039.pdf. Improved readings from digital imaging are in Dreyer 2007; Noret 1983 is free to read on Persée. PSI XII 1284: V. Bartoletti, PSI XII (Firenze 1951) 158–168. I found no public-domain or openly licensed text for the Göteborg leaf or for PSI 1284. Only the Vatican leaves have a public-domain edition, and Reitzenstein's 1888 readings are outdated.
verification.recommendation: Weak Neoscholia candidate. The whole corpus is about 2,200 words of lacunose Greek. English (attalus.org) and Italian (Simonetti Agostinetti 1993) translations cover all three fragments, and French and German translations exist for the Göteborg leaf, so it fails priority 2. It is also tied to Alexander only at the edges (the diversion of his body to Egypt). If it is used at all, the right unit is a small Russian-only dossier: the three fragments together with Photius cod. 92, translated from Reitzenstein / Roos–Wirth / Bartoletti / Dreyer 1999 and 2007. The Greek can be verified without extra languages, but the lacunae need a papyrologically trained reviewer.

name: Non-Greek ancient perspectives on Alexander: Babylonian, Egyptian, Aramaic, Iranian/Zoroastrian, Jewish-Hellenistic
overview: Russian coverage of this strand is thin and uneven. Russian Egyptology and Iranian studies have translated the big set pieces: the Satrap Stela (Ladynin 2022, full, with hieroglyphic text), the Demotic Chronicle (Panov 2024), and the Arda Wiraz Namag, Bundahishn, Menog i Xrad and Karnamag (Chunakova 1987–2001). Josephus, Ant. XI is also in Russian, and one rabbinic passage (Yoma 69a) appears in an Eshkolot anthology (2011). Searches in Russian and English found no Russian translation of: the Babylonian Astronomical Diaries and chronicles about Alexander (BCHP 1–4, 6), the Dynastic Prophecy, the Bactrian Aramaic documents, Nectanebo's Dream, the Potter's Oracle, the Oracle of the Lamb, Tamid 31b–32b and most other rabbinic Alexander stories, the Alexander passages in the Denkard and the Letter of Tansar, the Samaritan chronicles, and the Alexander chapters of Josippon. English coverage, by contrast, is nearly complete but scattered: livius.org and attalus.org, SBL WAW 44 (2025), Naveh–Shaked 2012, Sefaria, Boyce 1968 and Bowman 2023. The one real gap in English is the Luxor sanctuary texts, which exist only in German (Abd el-Raziq 1984). So the opportunity is a Russian-first collection, organized around Alexander and cross-referenced to the Greek and Latin sources and the Romance, rather than first translations of these texts into any language. Caveat: the web-search budget ran out mid-sweep. Still unverified: Russian status of the Samaritan chronicles; whether Frug's «Агада» (1910) includes the Alexander stories; the contents of Panov's «Египетские тексты» XII/XVIII/XX (his catalogue, vol. XVI 2021, is the place to check); and the ADAB document numbers.
already_translated_ru: Satrap Stela, Cairo CG 22182: full hieroglyphic text, translation and commentary (И. А. Ладынин, 2022, Труды истфака МГУ 198). Demotic Chronicle: in М. В. Панов, «Египетские тексты» XXII (2024); the source is a search snippet, not checked directly. Somtutefnakht's Naples stela: studied by Ladynin (Восток 2014); whether a Russian translation exists is unverified. Arda Wiraz Namag (О. М. Чунакова 2001); Bundahishn and Menog i Xrad («Зороастрийские тексты», 1997); Karnamag i Ardaxshir (1987). Josephus, Ant. XI (Г. Генкель); 1 Maccabees and Daniel (Synodal). Yoma 69a: Eshkolot anthology (Shinan, 2011). Josippon: Table of nations only (Петрухин and Эйдelькинд 1994). Outside this strand: al-Makin's Alexander chapter fragment (philosophers' sayings at the bier), «История философии» 18 (IPhRAS).

verification.title: Alexander through Near-Eastern Eyes: a dossier of non-Greek sources / «Александр глазами Востока: досье негреческих источников»
verification.ru_found:
The Russian 'partial' verdict holds, but Russian coverage is wider than the sweep said. The search budget ran out after 4 Russian searches and 1 English search, so most of the checks below were made by reading known pages directly.

NEW FINDINGS, CONFIRMED FROM THE PAGES THEMSELVES:
(1) Letter of Tansar. The sweep found no Russian. In fact a short Russian excerpt exists in «Хрестоматия по истории средних веков», т. 1 (М., 1961). No translator is named. It covers only Minovi 1932, pp. 12–14 (the four estates passage) and is reproduced at vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/Persien/VI/540-560/Name-i-Tansar/text.phtml?id=7515. Alexander does not appear in it, so the Alexander passages of Tansar still seem to have no Russian translation.
(2) Shahrestaniha-i Eran («Города Ирана»). Full Russian translation by Э. Хуршудян, «Иран-наме» № 3(15), 2010, on vostlit (Persien/VII/640-660/Goroda_Irana). It has 3 Alexander passages: «проклятый Сокандар» burns the Avesta; Merv and Herat founded by «проклятый Сокандар ромеец»; Gay/Isfahan built by «проклятым Александром, сыном Филиппа».
(3) Karnamag-i Ardashir. Full Russian translation by О. М. Чунакова, «Книга Ардашира сына Папака» (М.: Наука, 1987), on vostlit. Alexander appears in I.1 («после смерти Александра Румийского ... 240 удельных правителей»), in the Sasan episode, and later beside Dahag and Frasiyag as a tyrant.

ITEMS THE SWEEP LISTED AS EXISTING (NOT RE-CHECKED):
- Satrap Stela: Ладынин 2022
- Demotic Chronicle: Панов 2024
- Arda Wiraz Namag: Чунакова 2001
- Bundahishn: 1997. Whether the Greater Bundahishn ch. 33 Alexander passage is included needs checking.
- Yoma 69a: Eshkolot 2011
- Josephus, Ant. XI: Генкель 1900, public domain

LIKELY ARTICLE-LEVEL RUSSIAN TRANSLATIONS (found in bibliographies; contents not seen):
- И. А. Ладынин, «Памятники Александра Великого в Египте: опыт интерпретации» (ДВАМ 1, 1998, 32–49) and «Египетская царская титулатура Александра Великого» (Вестник МГУ, сер. 8, 1999, № 2, 85–97); also his 1998 dissertation «Александр Македонский и Египет». These probably render the Luxor bark-shrine and titulary texts in Russian. Source: egyptology.ru/personal/bibl-ladynin.htm.
- К. В. Кузьмин, MSU dissertation 2017 on «Оракул ягненка» and «Оракул горшечника» (abstract at ivran.ru/f/Kuzmin_avtoreferat.pdf), plus his articles in Aegyptiaca Rossica 2 (2014) and 4 (2016) and ДВАМ 9 (2017). These may include Russian versions of the Potter's Oracle and the Oracle of the Lamb. Also В. В. Струве 1925, «Папирус 1116 B recto и пророческая литература Египта».
- Possibly the Russian «Агада» (Бялик–Равницкий, tr. С. Г. Фруг), which may carry the Alexander tales of Tamid 31b–32b. Not verified.

NO RUSSIAN FOUND for: the cuneiform items (ADART −330/−322, BCHP 1 and 3, Dynastic Prophecy), the Bactrian Aramaic documents, the Dream of Nectanebo, Tamid 31b–32b, the Denkard passages, the Alexander sections of Tansar, and the Samaritan chronicles. Because Russian searching was cut short, article-level translations in ВДИ, Aegyptiaca Rossica or Иран-наме cannot be ruled out.
verification.en_found:
I give English 'partial' only because no anthology exists and a few minor items may lack English. Item by item, English coverage is close to complete; I could not show a single core component to be untranslated.

CONFIRMED:
- Samaritan Book of Joshua: O. T. Crane, 'The Samaritan Chronicle or The Book of Joshua the Son of Nun' (New York: J. B. Alden, 1890), ch. XLVI 'The history of el-Iskandar (Alexander the Great)'. Public domain: archive.org/details/samaritanchronic00cran.
- Alexander Chronicle (BCHP 1): English at livius.org/sources/content/mesopotamian-chronicles-content/bchp-1-alexander-chronicle/ (© Livius, all rights reserved).
- The claim that no English collection exists holds up:
  - Heckel & Yardley, 'Alexander the Great: Historical Sources in Translation' (Blackwell 2004), has only Greek and Latin texts. The BMCR 2004.02.13 review (J. Lendering) criticises it for omitting the Astronomical Diaries, the Dynastic Prophecy, the Babylonian chronicles and all Egyptian sources, naming for example Somtutefnakht's Naples stela.
  - Bagnall & Derow, 'The Hellenistic Period' (2004), has Greek documents only. Checked from the PDF table of contents.

CARRIED OVER FROM THE SWEEP, NOT RE-CHECKED: English for each remaining item (Kuhrt 2007 corpus, Sachs–Hunger, Naveh–Shaked 2012, Sefaria, Boyce 1968 for Tansar, Haug–West 1872 and Vahman 1986 for the Arda Wiraz Namag, West SBE for Denkard VIII, Shaki 1981 for Denkard IV, Stenhouse 1985 for Abu'l-Fath). The last chapter of Kuhrt 2007 is the nearest thing to a partial English collection.

POSSIBLE GAPS:
- Full texts of Alexander's Luxor bark shrine. As far as found, these are complete only in German (Abd el-Raziq 1984).
- Denkard III, if included, appears to exist only in French (de Menasce 1973).

POSSIBLE EXTRA ITEM: the Naples stela of Somtutefnakhte (English in Lichtheim, AEL III).

- Dream of Nectanebo: Wilcken, UPZ I 81 (1927); Wilcken died in 1944, so this is public domain in the EU.
- Potter's Oracle: Wessely 1893 and Wilcken 1897 (Hermes) for P.Rainer. Koenen's ZPE 2 (1968) is still under copyright but is the standard text.
- Arda Wiraz Namag: Haug–West–Hoshangji 1872.
- Denkard: Madan 1911.
- Greater Bundahishn: Anklesaria's 1908 facsimile of TD2.
- Tansar: Darmesteter 1894.
- Talmud (Yoma 69a, Tamid 31b–32b): Vilna edition, and Sefaria under CC licences.
- Josephus: Niese.
- Samaritan Book of Joshua: Juynboll 1848, and Crane 1890 (archive.org/details/samaritanchronic00cran).

Still under copyright:
- Cuneiform: Sachs–Hunger ADART I (1988); BCHP editions (Finkel–van der Spek; livius.org preliminary editions, all rights reserved); Grayson 1975 for the Dynastic Prophecy.
- Bactrian: Naveh–Shaked 2012.
- Luxor: Abd el-Raziq 1984.
- Lamb: Thissen 2002.
For these, Neoscholia would translate from the ancient text and cite the editions. The transliterations themselves are largely factual, but check reuse rights.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong Russian-first flagship: a Near Eastern Alexander dossier does not exist in any language. Its English value lies in the compilation and commentary, not in new translations. Start with the Greek-language Egyptian unit: the Dream of Nectanebo (UPZ I 81, public domain) plus the Potter's Oracle. Both fit the Romance's Nectanebo complex and can be checked with Greek alone. Before committing, rule out Kuzmin 2017 and Ladynin 1998–99 as existing Russian versions. Do the cuneiform and Bactrian items second; they need an Assyriologist and an Aramaist reviewer. The Middle Persian items need an Iranist, and several already exist in Russian (Karnamag, Shahrestaniha, the Arda Wiraz Namag).
