verification.title: Nectanebo's Dream (UPZ I 81 = P.Leiden U; Demotic P.Carlsberg 562, 424+499), Potter's Oracle (P.Graf, P.Rainer G 19813, P.Oxy. XXII 2332 + PSI VIII 982 etc.), Oracle of the Lamb (P.Vindob. D 10000) / «Сон Нектанеба», «Оракул горшечника», «Оракул (Пророчество) ягнёнка/агнца»
verification.ru_found:
I found no complete published Russian translation of any of the three texts, but the sweep's "none" (and its "no Russian Wikipedia articles") is too strong. Found so far:
(1) Lamb: B.A. Turaev, История Древнего Востока II (1936; ru.wikisource), a short paraphrase only. It still follows Krall's old readings ("34 г. Августа", "азиаты и Ниневия", 900 years). Turaev, Египетская литература I (М., 1920), pp. 273–275, discusses the Potter (and per Kinzhalov p. 273 the Dream). The rusneb scan (viewer.rusneb.ru/ru/000199_000009_008635623?page=287) would not render, so I could not see whether these pages translate or paraphrase.
(2) Potter: V.V. Struve, «Папирус 1116 B recto и пророческая литература Египта», Записки коллегии востоковедов I (1925), pp. 226–227. I read the PDF on orientalstudies.ru: it has a one-sentence paraphrase and no translation. Struve's «Zum Töpferorakel» (Raccolta Lumbroso, 1925) is in German.
(3) Dream: V.V. Struve, «У истоков романа об Александре», Восточные записки I (Л., 1927), pp. 131–146; the Dream is treated on pp. 139–141. Its contents are known to me only through Kinzhalov's citations: a retelling plus Struve's reconstruction of the lost ending. I have not seen it, and it should be checked for a partial or full translation. R.V. Kinzhalov, «Легенда о Нектанебе в повести "Жизнь и деяния Александра Македонского"», in Древний мир (Festschrift Struve, 1962), pp. 537–544, online at ancientrome.ru/publik/article.htm?a=1366712104. I read it: it only summarises the Dream.
(4) NEW, not in the sweep: Russian Wikipedia now has an article «Оракул горшечника» (created 6 Jan 2024 by NeoEuripides). It contains a summary and bibliography and explicitly cites no Russian translation. The ru.wiki article «Нектанеб II» gives a detailed retelling of the Greek Dream, including a Russian rendering of Onuris' whole speech to Isis. That rendering is unattributed and apparently secondhand via a modern popular work ("как поясняет переводчик"). So for the Dream, a Russian partial excerpt does exist online.
(5) NEW and most important: K.V. Kuzmin, «Древнеегипетские представления об исторических циклах в пропагандистских текстах эллинистического времени (на материале "Оракула ягненка" и "Оракула горшечника")», кандидатская диссертация, МГУ (supervisor I.A. Ladynin), defended at ИВ РАН in 2017, 335 pp. The автореферат is at ivran.ru/f/Kuzmin_avtoreferat.pdf. Its appendix holds only illustrations, but the chapters almost certainly contain extensive Russian working translations of passages. I could not reach the full text. Related articles by Kuzmin: Aegyptiaca Rossica 2 (2014), pp. 166–175; «"Запускающий гончарный круг": солнечный бог в "Оракуле горшечника"», Aegyptiaca Rossica 4 (2016), pp. 150–164; Уч. зап. Казан. ун-та 158:6 (2016), pp. 1423–1431, on PA Hyb in the Lamb; Древний Восток и античный мир 9 (2017).
Not checked, because the search budget ran out: Panov's «Египетские тексты» series, Ladynin's publications on Nectanebo II, Soviet chrestomathies (Хрестоматия по истории древнего мира, Струве ред.; Хрестоматия по истории Древнего Востока 1980), and Ranovich/Zelin/Pavlovskaya on Ptolemaic social movements, which may quote the Potter. Bottom line: no full Russian translation is known, but a "first Russian translation" claim for the Lamb and Potter must first be checked against Kuzmin's dissertation.
verification.en_found:
The EN "full" claim is confirmed for all three texts, as far as each survives.
Dream (Greek UPZ I 81): N. Lewis, The Interpretation of Dreams and Portents in Antiquity (1996), p. 51, reproduced on attalus.org/egypt/nectanebo.html.
Dream (Demotic): K. Ryholt, "A Demotic Version of Nectanebos' Dream (P. Carlsberg 562)", ZPE 122 (1998); and Ryholt, Narrative Literature from the Tebtunis Temple Library (2012), p. 164, for P.Carlsberg 424+499. Both are on attalus.
Potter: L. Koenen's English translation of P.Rainer G 19813 (attalus.org/egypt/potters_oracle.html, via Dollinger). A. Kerkeslager, "The Apology of the Potter: A Translation of the Potter's Oracle", Jerusalem Studies in Egyptology (ÄAT 40, 1998), a synoptic translation of all papyri, reused on philipharland.com (2023). S.M. Burstein, The Hellenistic Age from the Battle of Ipsos to the Death of Kleopatra VII (Translated Documents of Greece and Rome 3, Cambridge 1985), pp. 136–139.
Lamb: R.K. Ritner, in W.K. Simpson (ed.), The Literature of Ancient Egypt (3rd ed. 2003), pp. 445–449 (attalus.org/egypt/lamb_oracle.html; philipharland.com).
From memory and not re-verified this run: Koenen, "The Dream of Nektanebos", BASP 22 (1985), with an English translation. There may also be versions in Hansen's Anthology of Ancient Greek Popular Literature or Stoneman's Penguin appendix; these are unverified, so I do not assert them.
verification.other_found:
German:
- Potter: H. Gressmann, Altorientalische Texte und Bilder zum AT (1909), pp. 207–210 (cited by ru.wiki). L. Koenen, ZPE 2 (1968), pp. 178–209, the edition with German translation. Koenen, "Die Apologie des Töpfers an König Amenophis oder das Töpferorakel", in Blasius & Schipper (eds.), Apokalyptik und Ägypten (OLA 107, 2002); per Kuzmin, this added two new manuscripts.
- Lamb: J. Krall, Vom König Bokchoris (Festgabe Büdinger, 1898), the editio princeps. H.-J. Thissen, "Das Lamm des Bokchoris", in the same OLA 107 volume (2002). J.F. Quack, a new translation in 2007, presumably in Hoffmann & Quack, Anthologie der demotischen Literatur (Kuzmin's abstract confirms only that Quack published a new translation in 2007, not where).
- Dream: Wilcken 1905 (Mélanges Nicole) and UPZ I 81 (1927), with German commentary.
Spanish: a study of the Dream from Univ. Huelva (per the sweep; not re-verified).
French and Italian: nothing verified this run.
Latin: S. Witkowski, «In somnium Nectonabi», Eos 14 (1908), a study rather than a translation.
In sum, all three texts are well covered in English and German scholarship. Only Russian has no full version.
verification.source_text:
- Dream, Greek: U. Wilcken, Urkunden der Ptolemäerzeit I (Berlin 1927), no. 81, pp. 369 ff. This is public domain (Wilcken d. 1944). Also Wilcken, "Der Traum des Königs Nektonabos", Mélanges Nicole (Genève 1905), pp. 579–595, likewise public domain. A digital text is in papyri.info DDbDP (upz;1;81); I did not verify its licence, because papyri.info is now behind bot protection.
- Potter: C. Wessely, Denkschriften Wien 42 (1893), pp. 3–6, editio princeps of P.Rainer and P.Graf, public domain, archive.org (denkschriftende12klasgoog). U. Wilcken, Aegyptiaca (Festschrift Ebers, 1897), pp. 142–152, and Hermes 40 (1905), pp. 544–560, both public domain on archive.org. The current text is papyri.info DCLP 64149, building on Koenen 1968/1974/2002 (copyrighted). Images of P.Oxy. XXII 2332 are on the Oxford POxy portal.
- Lamb (Demotic): Krall 1898 is public domain but outdated; the reliable modern texts (Thissen 2002, Quack 2007) are copyrighted.
- Demotic Dream: Ryholt, ZPE 122 (1998) and 2012, copyrighted.
verification.recommendation: This is a good Russian-only candidate, not an EN gap: all three texts are fully available in English and German, and Russian has only paraphrases and scattered excerpts. Start with the Greek Dream of Nectanebo (UPZ I 81, public domain). It is short and closely tied to the Alexander Romance (AR I.1–14, I.34), and Greek alone is enough to check it. Next do the Greek Potter's Oracle as a synopsis of all the papyri, from DCLP and Koenen. Defer the Lamb and the Demotic Carlsberg versions: they need a Demotist (Kuzmin or Ladynin would be natural reviewers), and Kuzmin's 2017 dissertation must be checked before claiming a "first Russian translation" of the Lamb or Potter.

verification.ru_found:
There is no complete Russian translation of any text in the dossier. That part of the claim holds. But the "none" status is refuted by partial scholarly translations.
(1) E. M. Berzon, «Деятельность и полномочия соправителя царя в Селевкидской Вавилонии: пример Антиоха I», Восток (Oriens) 2020, № 3 (DOI 10.31857/S086919080009907-4; https://vostokoriens.jes.su/s086919080009907-4-1/). It gives Russian renderings of BCHP 6 (Ruin of Esagila), selected lines only (obv. 4'–7', 9': «(Антиох) жертвоприношение на руинах Эсагилы [соверш]ил… по обычаю эллинскому»). She also renders lines of BCHP 5, 7 and 8, which are outside the Alexander dossier. She works from the van der Spek and Finkel transliterations on livius.
(2) E. M. Berzon, «Антиох — наследник и соправитель Великого царя Антиоха», Проблемы истории, филологии, культуры, 2015 (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/antioh-naslednik-i-sopravitel-velikogo-tsarya-antioha). It translates two lines of the Hellenistic King List (BM 35603 rev. 4–5, the Antiochus III lines), not the Alexander section.
(3) Probable but unverified: the Russian translation of P. Briant, «Дарий в тени Александра» (пер. А. Н. Степановой; М.: Вече, 2007, 448 с.; cited in ru.wikipedia «Дарий III»). The French original discusses the AD −330 and the Dynastic Prophecy, so it likely carries short Russian quotations. I could not check the Russian text.
Negative checks, all with no translation found:
- WebSearch: «Династическое пророчество», «Хроника диадохов», the astronomical diary for Gaugamela, and Hellenistic chronicles in Russian.
- CyberLeninka API (about 20 queries). Hits were only paraphrases or citations: Сивкина–Кривощекова 2023; Сивкина–Гусева 2024; Стоянов 2016; Смирнов, «Государство Селевка I» (2013); Немировский (HSE chapter «Что такое теос?», which quotes Seleucid-era diaries, not Alexander texts).
- Internet Archive full-text search. Kuzishchin, «История Древнего Востока. Тексты и документы» (2002), has no Hellenistic chronicles. Бенгтсон, «Правители эпохи эллинизма» (1982), paraphrases the Diadochi Chronicle. The commentary of the Литпамятники Curtius (2023) only mentions cuneiform evidence.
- ru.wikipedia: «Смерть Александра Македонского», «Битва при Гавгамелах» and «Дарий III» only paraphrase the diaries and link to livius. There are no articles on the texts themselves.
Not searchable: elibrary.ru and VDI back issues.
verification.en_found:
The claim is confirmed; English coverage is complete and repeated many times over.
- livius.org (van der Spek / Finkel, preliminary text and translation) covers BCHP 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6, the Dynastic Prophecy (translation by van der Spek) and the King List CM 4 (translation by van der Spek, full). The AD −330 and AD −322 extracts are at /sources/content/oriental-varia/a-contemporary-account-of-the-battle-of-gaugamela/ and …-death-of-alexander/. Copyright: "All rights reserved".
- Finkel, van der Spek, Pirngruber (and Stevens), Babylonian Chronographic Texts from the Hellenistic Period (SBL WAW 44, 2025). Chronicles pp. 13–164; Astronomical Diaries pp. 165–536; King Lists pp. 961–988. Closed access per Unpaywall; JSTOR DOI 10.2307/jj.31106783.
- Sachs–Hunger, ADART I (1988), for −330 and −322. attalus.org/docs/diaries.html links the English translations of the 331/0, 330/29 and 323/2 diaries hosted by Edition Topoi (repository.edition-topoi.org, BDIA collection), which currently returns a database error.
- Grayson, ABC (1975): BCHP 1 = ABC 8; BCHP 3 = ABC 10. Grayson, BHLT (1975), ch. 3: the Dynastic Prophecy.
- Glassner, Mesopotamian Chronicles (WAW 19, 2004): CM 29 = BCHP 1, CM 30 = BCHP 3, CM 4 = King List.
- Sachs & Wiseman, Iraq 16 (1954): the King List.
- S. Smith, Babylonian Historical Texts (1924): the Diadochi Chronicle.
- van der Spek, "Darius III, Alexander the Great and Babylonian scholarship", Achaemenid History XIII (2003) 289–346 (on archive.org). It gives a new text and translation of the Dynastic Prophecy and discusses the AD −330.
- The Dynastic Prophecy is also in: Kuhrt, The Persian Empire (2007), p. 462, no. A41; Context of Scripture 1.150 (Longman); Neujahr, JNES 64 (2005) and Predicting the Past (2012).
BCHP 2, 4 and 6 were first published in English, online on livius and then in WAW 44.

verification.source_text:
There is no public-domain or openly licensed critical text of the full dossier.
- Standard edition: Finkel, van der Spek, Pirngruber, Stevens, BCHP (SBL WAW 44, 2025; copyrighted, closed access). It covers transliteration, translation and commentary for BCHP 1–6, the AD −330 and −322 and the King Lists.
- Free to read but under copyright: the livius.org preliminary transliterations and translations ("All rights reserved"), and van der Spek 2003 for the Dynastic Prophecy (author-shared PDF; archive.org item DariusIiiAlexanderTheGreatAndBabylonianScholarship2003).
- Possibly open: ORACC "Astronomical Diaries Digital" (ADsD), adart1 corpus (https://oracc.museum.upenn.edu/adsd/adart1/corpus, linked from en.wikipedia). ORACC projects are usually CC BY-SA, but the server was unreachable and I could not confirm the licence. The Edition Topoi BDIA repository is also down.
- Public domain (US) for the Diadochi Chronicle only: S. Smith, Babylonian Historical Texts (London 1924).
- Photographs of the British Museum tablets (BM 36304 for BCHP 1, BM 41080 for BCHP 2, BM 40623 for the Dynastic Prophecy, BM 35603 for the King List) are in BM Collection Online under BM image terms.
verification.recommendation: This is a fair Russian-only candidate, not an English one. Nothing in the dossier has a complete Russian translation; the only Russian renderings are scattered lines (Berzon 2020 for BCHP 6, Berzon 2015 for the King List) and probably short quotations in Briant 2007 RU. English, French and Italian translations exist in full, so an English version would be redundant. If you take it on, start with a compact Russian annotated dossier: AD −330 (historical section), BCHP 1, the Alexander lines of the King List, the Dynastic Prophecy col. v (the Darius/Alexander section) and the AD −322 death note. Translate from van der Spek's published transliterations (WAW 44 / livius, cited, not reproduced). This needs an Assyriologist who reads Late Babylonian, well beyond Greek/Latin, and LLM reliability on fragmentary Late Babylonian is low.

Yona: Alexander rises until the world looks like a ball and the sea like a dish). The translation is free. In his note 14 Orshansky says he moved away from the Talmud's text in the order of the last dialogue, and he trims some details.
(2) «Эйн Яаков», tr. Арье Ольман, ed. Яков Синичкин (Книжники, series «Библиотека еврейских текстов»), 7 vols, 2011–2024, 'все тексты публикуются по-русски впервые'. Vol. 2 (2011) covers the aggadah of Shabbat, Eruvin, Pesachim and Yoma, so it includes Yoma 69a. M. Курляндский (lechaim.ru) instead cites «Эйн Яаков», Книжники 2012, т. 3, с. 644 for this passage; the volume number differs. Vol. 6 (2016) covers Sanhedrin, Makkot, Shevuot and Horayot, so it includes 91a. Vol. 7 (2024, 736 pp.) covers Kodashim and Tohorot (chitai-gorod.ru). Ein Yaakov's Tamid section ends with the Alexander/eye passage (checked on Sefaria, Ein Yaakov, Tamid), so vol. 7 almost certainly contains a full Russian Tamid 31b–32b. This is a strong inference; I did not see the volume itself.
(3) «Мидраш раба (Великий мидраш). Берешит раба», 2 vols, tr. Я. Синичкин (Книжники, 2012–), a complete Russian Genesis Rabbah. It therefore includes 33:1 (Alexander and King Katzia).
(4) Retellings: ЕЭБЕ «Александр Великий» (Israel Lévi; ru.wikisource) summarises Tamid, Yoma, Sanhedrin, Megillat Ta'anit, Gen. R. 33, Lev. R. 27 and Pesikta 9; ja-tora.com «Золотые хлеба и суд царя Кации» paraphrases Gen. R. 33:1; lechaim.ru (Курляндский) quotes excerpts of Yoma 69a, Sanhedrin 91a and Tamid.
(5) Per the sweep, not re-verified: the Eshkolot anthology (A. Shinan, Moscow 2011) has Yoma 69a, and Фруг's «Агада» (1910) may have extracts.
Still apparently untranslated into Russian (not verified): PRK 9, which is a parallel of Lev. R. 27; y. AZ 3:1 in its own Yerushalmi form, although the Num. R. parallel is covered; Lev. R. 27:1 in a modern translation; and the Alexander pieces of the Megillat Ta'anit scholion.
Search limits: I ran only 2 Russian and 2 English web searches before the session's search budget ran out. Everything else was verified by fetching specific pages directly (kroraina, lechaim, toldot, chitai-gorod, labirint, ru.wikisource).

verification.title: 'Gizistag Aleksandar' in Pahlavi and Sasanian tradition: Denkard III.420 and IV (history of the Avesta), the Alexander passages of the Letter of Tansar, with Arda Wiraz Namag 1 and Greater Bundahishn 33 as context
verification.ru_found:
I could not run the planned searches. After 1 Russian and 1 English WebSearch the session's search limit (200/200) was used up. I did not work around the limit. Everything below comes from fetching the pages directly.

Russian translations that do exist, and are more than the sweep reported:
(1) Letter of Tansar, an excerpt in Russian: «Из „Письма Тансара“ („Намэ-и Тансар“)» in «Хрестоматия по истории средних веков», т. 1, М. 1961. The translator is not named (vostlit shows «пер. ??»). It is translated from Minovi, Намэ-и Тансар, Тегеран 1932, pp. 12–14, and from Iqbal's Tarikh-i Tabaristan I, pp. 19–20. It covers only the passage on the four estates (sources [175]–[176]) and contains no Alexander passage. Online at https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/Persien/VI/540-560/Name-i-Tansar/text.phtml?id=7515 (also on drevlit.ru). The sweep said there was no Russian translation of Tansar; that is refuted, though not for the Alexander passages.
(2) Denkard IV, the history of the Avesta: the Alexander-related passage exists in Russian at second hand. It is in М. Бойс, «Зороастрийцы. Верования и обычаи», translated by И. М. Стеблин-Каменский (Boyce's preface to the Russian edition is dated June 1985; Наука 1987/88, with later reprints). The book renders Madan 412.5–11 (the Valakhsh passage, «рассеянное из-за разорения и разрушения Александра и из-за грабежа и разбоя македонцев»), Madan 412.11–17 (Ardashir and Tansar), Madan 652.9–17 (Tansar), and Bailey's passage on Wēh-Šābuhr and the 21 nasks. The Russian is made from Zaehner's English, not from the Pahlavi. The same book quotes Arda Wiraz Namag 1.9 and Greater Bundahishn XXXIII.14 («погасил много огней»), and paraphrases Tansar on Alexander's destruction. Chapters online at https://history.wikireading.ru/202682, /202690 and /202699. The sweep said there was no Russian for Denkard IV; that is refuted as an excerpt.
(3) Arda Wiraz Namag in full, including chapter 1: О. М. Чунакова, «Пехлевийская божественная комедия», ПППВ CXXVI, М. 2001. Front matter checked: https://www.orientalstudies.ru/rus/images/pdf/b_chunakova_2001.pdf. It contains no Denkard texts; the companion texts are Ayadgar i Zareran, Draxt i asurig, Wizarishn i chatrang, Khusraw ud redag and Oshnar.
(4) Bundahishn in Чунакова, «Зороастрийские тексты», ПППВ CXIV, М. 1997 (https://www.orientalstudies.ru/rus/images/pdf/b_chunakova_1997.pdf). The English summary says this is a Pazend manuscript of the short "Indian" Bundahishn from West's legacy. So Greater (Iranian) Bundahishn chapter 33 is NOT translated into Russian there. Only the single line quoted in Boyce exists. The sweep's evidence needs correcting on this point.

Gaps I found no Russian for: Denkard III.420 (Madan 405–406) and Denkard IV translated directly from Pahlavi. I also found none for the Alexander passages of the Letter of Tansar (the burning of the books at Istakhr, Alexander's division of Iran), apart from Boyce's paraphrase. Not checked because of the search limit: И. Рак, «Мифы древнего и раннесредневекового Ирана» (1998); Е. Э. Бертельс, «Роман об Александре» (1948); А. И. Колесников (1970, cited on ru.wiki for Ibn Isfandiyar). Any of these may contain more excerpts.
verification.en_found:
Every component of the dossier has an English translation.
Denkard III.420: translated in full in P. B. Sanjana, The Dinkard vol. 9 (Bombay 1900, public domain), English by R. E. Kohiyar. Online at https://www.avesta.org/denkard/dk3s414.html#chap420. It includes "When king Alexander of evil fame came to the country of Iran…", the burning of the Dez-i Napesht copy, and the Ganj-i Shaspigan copy passing to the Arumans and being translated into Greek.
Denkard IV: translated in full in Sanjana 1900 (Madan pp. 409 ff.), with notes from Zaehner and Shaki. Online at https://www.avesta.org/denkard/dk4.html. There are also partial English versions of the Avesta-history section: E. W. West, SBE 37 (1892), per ru.wiki; H. W. Bailey, Zoroastrian Problems (1943); R. C. Zaehner, Zurvan (1955); M. Shaki, Archiv Orientální 49 (1981) 114–125; and M. Boyce, Textual Sources (1984) p. 114, as avesta.org notes.
Letter of Tansar: M. Boyce, The Letter of Tansar (Rome, IsMEO 1968), a full translation from Ibn Isfandiyar's Persian.
Arda Wiraz Namag: Haug and West 1872 (public domain), at https://www.avesta.org/mp/viraf.html. Also F. Vahman 1986.
Greater Bundahishn: B. T. Anklesaria 1956, at https://www.avesta.org/mp/grb.htm. Also Agostini and Thrope (OUP 2020).
Correction to the sweep: livius.org has no translation of Denkard IV. It has only an article on the Avesta and a mention of Arda Wiraz.
verification.other_found:
French: J. Darmesteter, «Lettre de Tansar au roi de Tabaristan», Journal asiatique 9e sér. 3 (1894) 185–250 and 502–555. This is the first critical translation, with the Persian text, and is in the public domain. J. de Menasce, Le troisième livre du Dēnkart (Paris 1973), a complete Book III including ch. 420. Not about Alexander, but Book V also exists in French (Amouzgar & Tafazzoli 2000).
Persian: the Tansar text in Minovi 1932 and in Iqbal's edition of the Tarikh-i Tabaristan.
I could not check Italian, German or Spanish versions, or modern Persian translations of Denkard III and IV, because of the search limit.
verification.source_text:
Denkard III and IV: D. M. Madan, The Complete Text of the Pahlavi Dinkard (Bombay 1911), public domain; Book IV is Madan pp. 409 ff. and III.420 is Madan pp. 405–406. I did not confirm an archive.org URL for it this session. P. B. Sanjana's Dinkard vol. 9 (1900, public domain) gives the Pahlavi text with English. Its English is online at avesta.org/denkard/dk3s414.html and dk4.html.
Letter of Tansar: Darmesteter, JA 1894 (Persian text plus French, public domain), is the safest public-domain base. Minovi, Nāma-ye Tansar (Tehran 1932; Boyce and Minovi 1968) is the better edition, but its rights status is unclear.
Context texts: Arda Wiraz Namag in Haug and West 1872 (public domain). Greater Bundahishn: Anklesaria's 1908 facsimile of TD2 and his 1956 transcription.
verification.recommendation: A weak candidate. All the core passages already exist in English, mostly in public-domain versions, and the Russian already covers Arda Wiraz in full, part of Denkard IV (via Boyce), and an excerpt of Tansar. The only real gap is a Russian, annotated dossier translated directly from Pahlavi. If that is wanted, start with Denkard III.420 together with the Avesta-history section of Denkard IV (Madan 405–406 and 411–415, about 3–4 pages). Checking it needs Book Pahlavi expertise, plus New Persian for Tansar, which is beyond Greek and Latin.

verification.en_found:
Full: J. Naveh & S. Shaked, Aramaic Documents from Ancient Bactria (Fourth Century BCE) from the Khalili Collections (London: Khalili Family Trust, 2012; ISBN 978-1-874780-74-8). It gives the text, English translation, commentary and glossary for all 30 leather documents and 18 tallies. C4 is at pp. 198–212 (per the Khalili IA 17 page). Reviewed by E. D. Reymond, JAOS 136.3 (2016).
Numbering verified:
- C1 = Khalili IA 21, 'List of supplies for Bayasa (Bessus)', dated Kislev, year 1 of 'Artaxerxes'. Its dating is contested. Shaked 2003 and 2004 and Naveh–Shaked 2012, 180 read Artaxerxes V = Bessus (330 BCE). Lane Fox 2007 and Briant 2009 objected. In the addenda (Naveh–Shaked 2012, 259), following Tavernier, Shaked revised this to Artaxerxes IV (Arses). Source: Hyland, Arta 2013.002, n. 2. So the label 'Bessus-Artaxerxes list' is misleading.
- C4 = Khalili IA 17, 'A long list of supplies disbursed', beginning 15 Sivan, year 7 of Alexander (8 June 324 BCE) and running about three months. It spells the name Lksndrs.
- Note: the Khalili site's English description of C1 still gives the Artaxerxes V / 330 BCE dating.
Partial EN elsewhere:
- The Khalili Collections item pages give English summaries/excerpts (e.g. the C1 commodity list).
- J. Hyland, 'Vishtaspa krny', Arta 2013.002 (open access, Achemenet) translates passages of C2 and discusses C1 and C4.
- Kuhrt, The Persian Empire: A Corpus of Sources (2007) may contain pre-publication renderings; not verified.
Only 1 dedicated English search was possible before the search budget ran out.

It is in copyright, not openly licensed; a free PDF is offered after registration (email, name, institution) at https://www.khalilicollections.org/portfolio/aramaic-documents-from-ancient-bactria-fourth-century-bce/. No public-domain or openly licensed edition exists. The Khalili item pages (IA 17: https://www.khalilicollections.org/collections/aramaic-documents/khalili-collection-aramaic-documents-a-long-list-of-supplies-disbursed-ia17/ ; IA 21: …list-of-supplies-for-bayasa-ia21/) give images and descriptions but no full transcriptions. A full English translation exists (Naveh–Shaked 2012) and French partial translations exist (Shaked 2004), so it only qualifies under criterion (1), no Russian translation. It is also documentary rather than Alexander literature. If pursued, start with a Russian translation and commentary of C4 (IA 17, year 7 of Alexander), plus C1 (IA 21), flagging that C1's 'Artaxerxes' dating is disputed (V vs IV). The A1–A6 Akhvamazda letters are an optional second unit. (1) Abu'l-Fath was translated into Russian: А. С. Жамкочян (Арутюн Сизефрович; Haroutun Jamgotchian), «Самаритянская хроника Абу-л-Фатха из собрания Российской национальной библиотеки: введение, перевод и комментарии». Москва: РАН, Институт востоковедения, 1995, 219 pp., ISBN 5726202031. Sources: Library of Congress record LCCN 96119553, DS129.A23 Z48 1995, with alternative title "Kitab al-Tarikh of Abu 'L-Fath" (via Open Library OL540451M). There is also a 200-page variant subtitled «введение, перевод, дешифровка, разночтения, примечания к тексту и комментарии» (Columbia record, OCLC 34643180).
- It is cited in the Православная энциклопедия article «Самаритяне» by К. А. Битнер (pravenc.ru/text/2663528.html).
- Zhamkochyan's 2003 monograph (full scan: archive.org/details/JamgotchianChronicles) refers to "её [Хроники] русскому переводу" and calls the Chronicle the first Arabic-Samaritan work translated into Russian from the original. It cites the translation as АФ, with the text at АФ 30 n. 17 and translated colophons at АФ 183–186. That points to a translation of the whole chronicle, which would include the Alexander section (Vilmar c. pp. 85–92).
- I have not seen a copy, so I cannot confirm page by page that the Alexander section is in it.

(2) Book of Joshua: the same 2003 monograph, «Древнейшие фрагменты арабо-самаритянских хроник из собрания РНБ» (М., 2003, 218 pp.), translates into Russian only a "newly published introductory part" of the Book of Joshua (pp. 96–135). It does not translate ch. XLVI. I found no Russian translation of ch. XLVI.

(3) Russian Wikipedia now has an article, «Самаритянская книга Иисуса Навина». The sweep said there was none. The article mentions no Russian translation.

(4) Chronicle Adler: I found no Russian translation.

(5) Checked with no Samaritan texts found: vostlit.info author indexes (А, С, К, И, Х) and the pravenc article «Иисуса Навина книга». The Senderov article on Alexander legends (berkovich-zametki 2023) uses only Jewish sources.

(6) Zhamkochyan's 2003 bibliography also lists: «Иисус Христос в документах истории» (сост. Б. Г. Деревенский, СПб. 1998, pp. 381–383), probably a Samaritan passage about Jesus, not Alexander (content not checked); and his 1999 article on an apocryphal motif in the Samaritan Book of Joshua (Арабские страны Западной Азии и Северной Африки III, pp. 132–142), which is not about Alexander as far as the title shows.
verification.en_found:
(1) Book of Joshua ch. XLVI: complete English in O. T. Crane, "The Samaritan Chronicle or the Book of Joshua the Son of Nun" (New York 1890), pp. 116–120, with notes 95–98. It is public domain. I checked it in the full text at archive.org/details/samaritanchronic00cran, which shows all of ch. XLVI. It is also on en.wikisource ("The Samaritan Chronicle") and sacred-texts.com/jud/sam/. Crane says he translated from Juynboll's Arabic and consulted the British Museum manuscript. Contents: the angel in the high priest's form appears to Alexander before the war with Darius; Alexander bows before the chief imam near Nablus; the journey into the land of darkness, where dust turns into rubies and pearls; the eagle-drawn car; the founding of Alexandria; Mount Gerizim; and the order to set up statues, evaded by naming the boys Alexander.

(2) Abu'l-Fath: P. Stenhouse, "The Kitāb al-Tarīkh of Abu 'l-Fath", Sydney: Mandelbaum Trust, 1985. It is the first complete English translation, with 55 chapters and 1219 notes, based on Stenhouse's 1980 Sydney doctoral text (confirmed in Zhamkochyan 2003, pp. 22–23, and the NLI and WorldCat records). Copyrighted.

(3) Montgomery, "The Samaritans" (1907): an English paraphrase of Joshua ch. 46 only.

(4) Chronicle Adler: I found no English translation. This was not searched thoroughly.
verification.other_found:
Latin:
- Juynboll, "Chronicon Samaritanum… cui titulus est Liber Josuae" (Leiden 1848): Arabic text with a full Latin translation. Public domain.
- Vilmar, "Abulfathi Annales Samaritani" (Gotha 1865): Arabic text only, plus a Latin paraphrase of the Alexander section in the prolegomena, pp. LXI–LXII. It covers Hizqia meeting Alexander, the land of darkness, the eagle throne, Alexandria, the children named Alexander, Gerizim, the high priest teaching him kingship, poisoning by Antipater, the letter to his mother entrusted to "Philemon", and the philosophers' praises at the funeral, two of them Samaritans.

French:
- E. N. Adler and M. Seligsohn, «Une nouvelle chronique samaritaine», REJ 44–46 (1902–03): Hebrew text with a complete French translation. The Alexander passage (Hizqia; Alexander's dream; siege of Tyre; Ptolemy "the philosopher" as Alexander's brother) is in REJ 45 (1902), c. pp. 73–74. Verified in the scan at archive.org/details/revuedestudesjui45soci.
- A. Neubauer published the Tolidah with a French translation (JA 1869); it is only marginal for Alexander.

Hebrew:
- A 19th-century Samaritan Hebrew translation of Abu'l-Fath by Ya'qub b. Harun (Rylands Sam. 256), noted in Zhamkochyan 2003 p. 22.
- Samaritan Hebrew versions of the Book of Joshua (Gaster, ZDMG 62, 1908).

German: none found.
verification.source_text:
Book of Joshua ch. XLVI: Juynboll 1848, Arabic with Latin, public domain (archive.org/details/AAlexandrina-164708). Caveat from Zhamkochyan 2003, pp. 33–37 (Oglavlenie) and the codicological section: Juynboll printed a single Leiden (Scaliger) manuscript, and the end of ch. 46 falls in a later supplemented part of it. The New York manuscript (JTS, Adler collection) and BL Add. 19956 have a different recension, and the New York copy has lost the first third of ch. 46. A new translation should take this into account.

Abu'l-Fath: Vilmar 1865, public domain (archive.org/details/abulfathiannales00abal and abulfathiannale00vilmgoog). The Alexander section is c. pp. 85–92 (Antipater at p. 89.15; Hizqia after Alexander's death at p. 92 ff.). Stenhouse's fuller 1980 text is unpublished.

Chronicle Adler: REJ 45 (1902), Hebrew with French, public domain (archive.org/details/revuedestudesjui45soci).
verification.recommendation: This is a weak candidate as a cluster. Abu'l-Fath already has a Russian translation (Zhamkochyan 1995) and a complete English one (Stenhouse 1985), and Joshua ch. XLVI has had English (Crane 1890) and Latin (Juynboll 1848) translations for a long time. The only real gap is Russian for Joshua ch. XLVI, about 4 printed pages, plus the short Hebrew paragraph in Chronicle Adler. That suits a small "Samaritan Alexander" dossier set beside Josephus, AJ 11.302–347, rather than a main project. Checking it needs Samaritan Arabic, plus Samaritan Hebrew for Chronicle Adler. Before going ahead, check a physical copy of Zhamkochyan 1995 to confirm it covers the Alexander section.

candidates.title: Hieroglyphic inscriptions of Alexander as pharaoh: the Luxor barque sanctuary, the Bahariya Amun temple, Philip Arrhidaeus at Karnak; Petosiris biography excerpts / «Иероглифические надписи Александра-фараона»
candidates.author: Theban and Hermopolitan priestly scribes
candidates.size: Luxor captions about 2,000 words; Bahariya about 300; Petosiris excerpt about 800
candidates.edition: Abd el-Raziq, Die Darstellungen und Texte des Sanktuars Alexanders des Großen im Tempel von Luxor (1984); Lefebvre, Le tombeau de Petosiris (1923–24, US public domain)
candidates.ru_evidence: Ladynin's articles treat the Bahariya 'altar' titulary, a Petosiris fragment and Theban building work. No full Russian translation of the Luxor texts found.
candidates.en_evidence: Luxor: German only (Abd el-Raziq 1984); no English found. Petosiris: English by Lichtheim (attalus.org).
candidates.value: Shows how Egyptian priests framed Alexander through titulary, sonship of Amun and the Opet rites: the Egyptian substrate of the Siwa sonship and the Romance's Nectanebo paternity. The Luxor texts are the one real English gap in this strand.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Low. Hieroglyphic epigraphy; an LLM can work only from published transliterations or German translations, and an Egyptologist is essential.
candidates.pilot_unit: Luxor barque-sanctuary dedication and titulary (about 600 words).

verification.title: Hieroglyphic inscriptions of Alexander as pharaoh (Luxor barque shrine; Bahariya 'altar'; Philip Arrhidaeus at Karnak/Hermopolis; Petosiris excerpts) / «Иероглифические надписи Александра-фараона»
verification.ru_found:
The 'partial' claim holds, but the gaps sit in different places than the sweep said. The Bahariya part is already fully translated.

(1) BAHARIYA, FULLY TRANSLATED INTO RUSSIAN: I.A. Ladynin, «"Алтарь" из храма Амона в оазисе Бахария с египетской царской титулатурой Александра Великого. I. Надписи памятника», ВДИ 2014, № 2 (289), pp. 3–12. Per the abstract, it gives a full Russian translation with commentary of the hieroglyphic inscription (the only complete five-part titulary of Alexander) and also of the Greek dedication (http://ancienthist.ru/issues/73/articles/1236). Part II, «Интерпретация и датировка», is in ВДИ 2014, № 3 (290), pp. 3–20 (TOC at http://ancienthist.ru/issues/84). Bahariya is therefore not untranslated in Russian.

(2) TITULARY AND MONUMENT STUDIES, PARTIAL: Ladynin's bibliography (http://www.egyptology.ru/personal/bibl-ladynin.htm) lists four relevant items. I could not open any of them, so how much text each translates is unverified:
- «Памятники Александра Великого в Египте: опыт интерпретации», Древний Восток и античный мир 1 (1998), 32–49
- «Египетская царская титулатура Александра Великого», Вестник МГУ сер. 8, 1999, № 2, 85–97
- «"Palin archei Aigyptos" (Ps.-Call. C II 27.3): Ещё раз о египетской царской титулатуре…», Фроловский сборник, СПб. 2008, 245–259
- «Строительная программа Аргеадов в Египте в контексте храмового строительства XXIX–XXX династий», Труды Эрмитажа XXXV (2007), 86–100
These deal with the royal names and the building programme, not with the full texts of the Luxor or Karnak shrines.

(3) LUXOR BARQUE SHRINE, FULL TEXTS: I found no Russian translation of the scene captions, speeches of the gods or bandeaux. At most the dedication formula and the names appear inside Ladynin's articles.

(4) PETOSIRIS: The egyptology.ru bibliography of Russian translations of Egyptian texts (Late Period autobiographies section, http://www.egyptology.ru/thematic/bibl-literature.htm) lists Udjahorresnet, Petiese and two Turaev 1915 items, but no Petosiris. Ladynin & Kolobova, «The Graeco-Egyptian Interaction… The Case of the Tomb of Petosiris» (Cultural Heritage of Egypt and Christian Orient 3, 2006, 27–42) is in English. In Russian I found only popular, unsourced quotations, e.g. an essay by Е. Сикирич on newacropol.ru. Petosiris therefore has, as far as I can find, no scholarly Russian translation.

(5) Ankh-pa-hered building inscription (Luxor, 320 BC): no Russian translation found.

Searches in Russian: Ладынин + Бахария/титулатура; Петосирис + перевод; Ладынин + ВДИ/алтарь; Петосирис + хрестоматия. I also ran a scan of ВДИ issue tables of contents and checked ru.wikipedia, which has no article on Petosiris. The WebSearch budget ran out after the minimum set of searches, so Ladynin's post-2008 output (2015 onward) was checked only through the ВДИ tables of contents.
verification.en_found:
The 'partial' claim holds. English translations exist for some parts, but there is no complete English translation of the Luxor shrine.

(1) LUXOR: The dedication bandeau ("He has created the great chamber anew in white and beautiful sandstone… Nebmaatre… Amenhotep, Ruler of Thebes") circulates in English without attribution, e.g. NILE Magazine 2017 (https://www.nilemagazine.com.au/2017-april/2017/4/9/alexander-the-great-packed-a-lot-into-his-whirlwind-tour-of-egypt). Alexander's names in the shrine are translated in F. Bosch-Puche, «Alexander the Great's Egyptian Names in the Barque Shrine at Luxor Temple» (Academia.edu 3060105; my recollection is Grieb–Nawotka–Wojciechowska (eds.), Alexander the Great and Egypt, Philippika 74, Wiesbaden 2014; please verify). This covers names, not the full ritual texts. I found no complete English translation of the scenes and speeches.

(2) TITULARY CORPUS: Bosch-Puche, «The Egyptian Royal Titulary of Alexander the Great I», JEA 99 (2013) 131–154 (doi:10.1177/030751331309900106), and «II: Personal Name, Empty Cartouches, Final Remarks, and Appendix», JEA 100 (2014) 89–109 (doi:10.1177/030751331410000106). Together they translate the Bahariya titulary and the names attested at Luxor, Karnak, Hermopolis and elsewhere.

(3) ANKH-PA-HERED: This builder's inscription, carved on the outer wall of the Forecourt of Amenophis III in Luxor temple, dates the work in the 'gold house of Amenope' at Luxor to Alexander's year 1, Thoth 1, and the work at Karnak to Philip's year 3. Since it names Alexander, it most likely records the barque shrine itself. A full English translation, adapted from Jansen-Winkeln's German, is at https://www.attalus.org/egypt/luxor.html.

(4) PETOSIRIS: Lichtheim, AEL III (1980), gives selected biographical inscriptions; these are reproduced at https://www.attalus.org/egypt/petosiris.html. The children's speeches (insc. 58a–d) are adapted into English from Otto 1954 and Lefebvre at https://www.attalus.org/egypt/tehen.html.

(5) Philip Arrhidaeus barque shrine at Karnak: I found no English translation of the full text corpus. Its status is unknown within the search budget.
verification.other_found:
GERMAN:
- Luxor: M. Abd el-Raziq, Die Darstellungen und Texte des Sanktuars Alexanders des Großen im Tempel von Luxor (AV DAI Kairo 16, Mainz 1984). This is the full edition with translation, under copyright. Reviews: Goedicke, JARCE 22 (1985), doi:10.2307/40000425; Winter, JEA 74 (1988).
- Ankh-pa-hered: complete German translation by K. Jansen-Winkeln, «Eine Bau- und Bittinschrift am Tempel von Luxor».
- Petosiris: biographical texts in E. Otto, Die biographischen Inschriften der ägyptischen Spätzeit (1954).

FRENCH:
- Petosiris: complete edition and translation in G. Lefebvre, Le tombeau de Petosiris I–III (Cairo 1923–24).
- Bahariya: F. Bosch-Puche, «L'"autel" du temple d'Alexandre le Grand à Bahariya retrouvé», BIFAO 108 (2008) 29–44. The text is edited and translated; the IFAO journal is openly available.
- Ankh-pa-hered: partial translation in G. Gorre, Les relations du clergé égyptien et des Lagides (Peeters 2009).

ITALIAN: Petosiris excerpts very probably appear in E. Bresciani, Letteratura e poesia dell'antico Egitto (Einaudi). This is from memory and was not verified.

FURTHER LITERATURE:
- Karnak: «Thutmosis, Alexander – und Nektanebos? … "sanctuaire du faucon de calcaire" in Karnak», in Legacy of the East and Legacy of Alexander (Harrassowitz 2023), doi:10.13173/9783447121323.285
- D. Schäfer, Makedonische Pharaonen und hieroglyphische Stelen (Studia Hellenistica 50, 2011)
- E. Winter, «Alexander der Grosse als Pharao in ägyptischen Tempeln» (2006)
- Bosch-Puche & Moje, JEA 101 (2015), on Alexander's name in Demotic sources
verification.source_text:
LUXOR AND PHILIP ARRHIDAEUS DEDICATIONS (public domain):
- K. Sethe, Urkunden II, Heft 1: Hieroglyphische Urkunden der griechisch-römischen Zeit I. Historisch-biographische Urkunden aus den Zeiten der makedonischen Könige… (Leipzig 1904), https://archive.org/details/hieroglyphische-urkunden-der-griechisch-romischen-zeit.-i
- Contents relevant here: the Naples stele of Somtutefnakht; 'Inschriften Alexanders d. Gr. in Luxor' ('Alexander als Erneuerer dieses Sanktuars', the exterior wall inscriptions, after Lepsius, Denkmäler); 'Inschriften des Philippus Arrhidäus in Hermopolis, Karnak'; and later the Satrap stele.
- These are hand-drawn hieroglyphic copies only, without translation.
- Lepsius, Denkmäler aus Aegypten und Aethiopien, Abth. IV, also public domain: https://edoc3.bibliothek.uni-halle.de/lepsius/

LUXOR, FULL SHRINE TEXT: available only in Abd el-Raziq 1984, which is under copyright. Fresh transcription from it or from photographs would be needed.

BAHARIYA: Bosch-Puche, BIFAO 108 (2008), open access.

PETOSIRIS: Lefebvre, Le tombeau de Petosiris (1923–24), all three parts (Description; Les textes; Vocabulaire et planches), https://archive.org/details/letombeaudepetos00lefeuoft. Archive.org flags it NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT; it is public domain in the US. Lefebvre died in 1957, so EU protection may run to the end of 2027.
verification.recommendation: As bundled, this is a weak candidate, because Bahariya is already fully translated into Russian (Ladynin, ВДИ 2014) and into English and French via Bosch-Puche. The best unit is the full text of the Luxor barque shrine, with the Ankh-pa-hered building inscription and Sethe's Urk. II Alexander/Philip dedications as a companion: no full Russian or English translation of these was found, though they exist in German (Abd el-Raziq; Jansen-Winkeln). Petosiris, which has no Russian translation, is better treated as a separate project: its Alexander link is indirect and it is large. Every part needs an expert in Late Period/Ptolemaic hieroglyphic (well beyond Greek/Latin), and the AI drafts should be built from transliteration and checked against the German and French translations.

candidates.title: Sefer Yosippon, Alexander chapters (Alexander in Jerusalem; the Romance interpolation in the Mantua and Constantinople redactions) / «Иосиппон»: главы об Александре
candidates.author: Anonymous (southern Italy); redactors including Judah ibn Moskoni
candidates.size: Flusser-text Alexander chapters about 3,000 words; Romance interpolation about 15,000 words
candidates.edition: Flusser 1978–80 (critical); Mantua 1476 and Constantinople 1510 (public domain); Bowman 2023
candidates.ru_evidence: Only the 'Table of nations' (ch. 1) is in Russian (Petrukhin and Eidelkind, 1994), according to Russian Wikipedia. No Russian of the Alexander chapters found.
candidates.en_evidence: Bowman, Sepher Yosippon (Wayne State UP 2023), critical edition with English translation (English Wikipedia).
candidates.other_translations: Latin: Münster 1541, Gagnier 1706. Early modern Yiddish.
candidates.value: A major Hebrew vehicle of Alexander lore: the Josephan Jerusalem visit fused with Romance material (via Leo's Nativitas). It shaped later Hebrew Alexander books and chronographic reception.
candidates.ai_feasibility: High. Biblicizing Hebrew; a Hebraist should review.
candidates.pilot_unit: Alexander's visit to Jerusalem chapter (about 1,500 words).

verification.title: Sefer Yosippon, Alexander chapters (ch. 10 "Alexander in Jerusalem" + the Alexander-Romance interpolation of the Mantua and Constantinople/Venice redactions) / «Иосиппон»: главы об Александре
verification.ru_found: I partly refuted the "RU none" claim. (1) Э. Сендеров, «История преданий об Александре Македонском в Иерусалиме», Заметки по еврейской истории (ред. Е. Беркович) 2023, №2, https://s.berkovich-zametki.com/y2023/nomer2/senderov/. He gives a long continuous Russian rendering of Yosippon ch. 10: the dream, the procession, Alexander's proskynesis before the high priest, the Temple tour, the statue request, the naming of priests' sons "Alexander" and the Urim/Thummim consultation. He says himself that he works from Bowman's 2023 English, so this is an indirect translation, not one from the Hebrew. The fetch summary put the length at about 1,500-2,000 words; I did not count it myself. He does not translate the Romance interpolation (Nectanebo birth legend, Darius, Porus, Candace, Amazons, death); he only discusses it. (2) П. В. Петрухин & Я. Д. Эйделькинд 1994 (from Flusser 1978, pp. 3-9; vostlit.info/Texts/Dokumenty/Russ/X/Kniga_Iossipon/text.htm) covers only the Table of Nations (ch. 1). It has no Alexander material. The vostlit page refused my connection; its contents come from the Russian Wikipedia link label. (3) The Электронная еврейская энциклопедия ОРТ (eleven.co.il/jewish-literature/in-hebrew/11824/) says there were later translations "в том числе на русском языке" but names none. It also claims the Alexander-in-Jerusalem story appears in the ПВЛ "без указания источника". Both claims are unverified and the second looks doubtful. (4) Nothing on vostlit's И and Jewish-sources index pages or on facetia.ru. No Russian translation of the Mantua/Constantinople Romance interpolation was found. Limit: my WebSearch budget ran out after one Russian-language search, so the required four Russian searches were not done. The rest of the Russian check used direct fetches of known pages.
verification.en_found: Confirmed, and there is more than the sweep listed. (1) S. Bowman, Sepher Yosippon: A Tenth-Century History of Ancient Israel (Wayne State UP 2023), translated from Flusser's text. Ch. 10 "Alexander in Jerusalem" is pp. 51-56. The appendix "Gesta Alexandros" (pp. 447-500, with a translator's note at pp. 447-452) has 14 sections: Death of Philipos, Beginning of his wars, War with Darius, Alexandros in Yavan, Spying on Darius and Darius' death, Travels in the lands of marvels, War with Poros, Sages of Hodu, Marvels of Hodu, Alexandros chez Kandaki, Journeys of marvel, Death of Alexandros, From Alexandros to Augustos, and a fragment on Hodu with a Talmud passage. Source: TOC on Project MUSE, muse.jhu.edu/book/118841. I did not verify which Hebrew text the Gesta translates, nor whether the Nectanebo birth legend is in it; no section title names it. (2) L. H. Rubenstein, "The Josippon of Joseph ben Gorion: A Translation of Part I", HUC-JIR New York, rabbinic MA thesis, 1965. It is unpublished but freely online at library.huc.edu/pdf/theses/Rubenstein_Laurence_Henry-NY-Rab-1965%20Jossipon%20Part%201-Searchable.pdf and also on archive.org as "josippon-1-1-180-lh-rubinstein". It translates the Mantua text from Günzburg's Berdichev reprint, cols. 1-180. That includes the whole Alexander block: the rise (cols. 60-65), the birth legend with Nectanebo ("Neketnebor") and Olympias ("Nabiarash") (cols. 65-78), the kingship (cols. 78-112: Darius, Porus, Candace, Amazons, poisoning) and the death and division of the empire (cols. 112-118). Its companions are Patz (Part II) and Zoll (Part III), 1965. Supervisor M. A. Cohen called the three together the first full English translation of any version of Yosippon. (3) Bowman, "Alexander and the Mysteries of India", Journal of Indo-Judaic Studies 2 (1999) 71-111. It probably contains translated passages, but I did not check. (4) P. Morwyng's English of 1558 and later is made from Münster's Latin, which is only partial. I did not verify whether it includes Alexander.
verification.other_found: Latin, full and public domain, both including the Alexander book (lib. II): (a) J. Gagnier, Josippon sive Josephi Ben-Gorionis Historiae Judaicae libri sex, Oxford 1706, archive.org "bim_eighteenth-century_yosippon-josippon-siv_1706". It prints the Latin of the Hebrew ("Hebr. Jos. Gorion.") beside the matching Latin Historia Alexandri (Historia de preliis), from the Nectanebo episode onward. (b) J. F. Breithaupt, Josephus Hebraicus, Gotha-Leipzig 1707, reissued 1710, archive.org "bub_gb_VUdl5MmuvhAC". It gives the Hebrew text of the Venice edition with a Latin translation, collated with the Constantinople print, and includes lib. 2 (e.g. cap. 19, Candace). Münster's Latin (Basel 1541, archive.org "bib_fict_4102659") is partial and "a captivitate Babylonica"; its OCR failed, so I could not check its Alexander coverage. Early-modern Yiddish (Zürich 1546, Amsterdam 1743) as the sweep said. Arabic Kitab Yusifus and Ethiopic Zena Ayhud both have Alexander chapters that merge Josephus with the Romance (Y. Binyam, UCLA lecture 2022). An English translation of the Ethiopic Josippon was uploaded to archive.org (item "Josippon", 2025); I did not check its Alexander coverage. German/French/Italian/Spanish modern translations of the Alexander chapters were not found, but that is unverified because the search budget had run out.
verification.source_text: Mantua redaction: the Abraham Conat print (Mantua c. 1476-80), and D. Günzburg's column reprint (Berdichev 1896-1913, public domain), cols. 60-118. Constantinople/Venice redaction (ibn Moskoni line): Constantinople 1510 and Venice 1544, the Hebrew of which is printed with a Latin translation in Breithaupt, Gotha 1707/1710 (archive.org bub_gb_VUdl5MmuvhAC). Gagnier, Oxford 1706 (archive.org bim_eighteenth-century_yosippon-josippon-siv_1706) has the Latin and the Historia de preliis parallels. Flusser's critical edition (Jerusalem 1978-80) and Hominer's are under copyright and should be used only as references.
verification.recommendation: Ch. 10 is already well covered (English by Bowman and Rubenstein, Russian at second hand from Senderov 2023), so it is not a good unit. The Mantua Romance interpolation (Günzburg cols. 60-118, starting with the Nectanebo birth legend, cols. 65-78) has no Russian translation and is a good Russian-only candidate, translated from the Hebrew with Gagnier/Breithaupt and the Historia de preliis as controls. Verification needs a medieval-Hebrew reader, which goes beyond Greek and Latin.

name: Greek Alexander Romance recensions and the Byzantine/post-Byzantine Greek Alexander tradition, incl. Greek folklore
overview: No Greek recension has a complete Russian translation. The only modern Russian text is Egunov's α excerpt (I.15–26, 30–41; «Поздняя греческая проза», 1961). Russian readers otherwise rely on the Slavonic Alexandrias. English covers α (Haight 1955), L (Dowden 1989; Stoneman 1991) and the Phyllada (Stoneman, I.B. Tauris c. 2010–12). Nothing was found in any language for ε, λ, ζ, the Byzantine Poem (Aerts 2014 gives the Greek text with an English commentary, not a translation) or the Rimada (Holton 1974/2002 is an edition only). Zuwiyya 2011 lists γ as 'Translation: none'. Since then γ has appeared complete in French (Jouanno 2009, confirmed as γ in her 2010 bibliography). The Valla edition (Stoneman–Gargiulo) covers Books I–II of α, β, γ and Julius Valerius; vol. III is still 'in preparazione'. Rights: Teubner and Hain editions from 1959–83 probably fall under the 25-year German term for scholarly editions (§70 UrhG); check with a lawyer. Kroll 1926, Müller 1846, Wagner 1881, the Venetian prints and Politis are public domain. Caveat: the web-search budget ran out mid-sweep. Still unverified: the Russian status of the Byzantine chroniclers; Greek Ps.-Methodius (EN Garstad 2012 from memory); Basilakes and Libanius progymnasmata (EN DOML 2016 / Gibson 2008, from memory); Karagiozis scripts (rights unclear); Kazantzakis' 1940 Alexander novel (EN Vasils 1982; EU copyright until 2028). Raabe's 1896 Greek retroversion of the Armenian is a tool for reconstruction, not something to translate.
already_translated_ru:

Carried over from the previous sweep, not re-checked here: Palladius' De gentibus Indiae (Taronyan 2007); Gorelov 2006 (Latin texts); the Armenian version (Дарбинян-Меликян 1986).

verification.title: Anonymi Byzantini Vita Alexandri regis Macedonum (recension ε) / Byzantine Life of Alexander / «Византийское Житие Александра (редакция ε)»
verification.ru_found:
The sweep's "RU none" is REFUTED in part. A published Russian excerpt exists, and so does an unpublished complete translation.
(1) Н. М. Ботвинник, «Псевдо-Каллисфен. Роман об Александре (главы 44, 2–46, 6). Перевод с древнегреческого и вступительная заметка» // Абарис. Журнал друзей Санкт-Петербургской классической гимназии. №8 (2007). С. 47–50. I checked the PDF myself (http://610.ru/rest/abaris/8/abaris8.pdf; issue page https://www.610.ru/rest/abaris/8/). Her note says she translated "трех заключительных глав редакции [ε], в которых описывается смерть Александра", using "Anonymi Byzantini Vita Alexandri regis Macedonum / Ed. J. Trumpf. Stuttgart, 1974". The excerpt is complete apart from one marked cut <...>. It runs from the poisoning through Alexander's letter to Olympias (which includes the enclosed nations and Candace), the division of the realm, Charmides' lament, Bucephalus killing the slave, and the burial in Alexandria. The note also states that, apart from Egunov's α excerpt, no Greek recension had been translated into modern Russian.
(2) Е. В. Желтова, «Наталья Марковна Ботвинник» // Philologia Classica, 2011 (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/natalya-markovna-botvinnik). It reports that Botvinnik translated the whole of ε into Russian but never published it ("весь перевод, к сожалению, так и не вышел в свет"). She read single chapters at department meetings. Her candidate dissertation (ЛГУ, 1989) was «Редакция ε "Романа об Александре", ее место в традиции и жанровая природа».
(3) Ботвинник Н. М., «Персидские посольства к Александру Македонскому в новой редакции "Романа об Александре"» // Античный мир и археология 4 (Саратов, 1979), с. 26–31 (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/persidskie-posolstva-k-aleksandru-makedonskomu-v-novoy-redaktsii-romana-ob-aleksandre). It paraphrases ε §10 and quotes several sentences in Russian (10.1, 10.4, 10.5, 10.6), plus a phrase from §38.1–4.
(4) Not checked: her Pseudo-Callisthenes entry in «Хрестоматия по литературе Древней Греции», т. 2 (сост. М. Позднев, СПб., [2011]), shared with Xenophon. I could not tell which recension it uses. It may contain more ε, so it should be checked.
(5) Also not checked: her other ε studies in conference abstracts and articles (Нектанеб 1976; ε as source of the Middle Greek Alexandria, 1980; Philologia Classica 2, 1982 and 3, 1987; МОУСЕЙОН 1997, pp. 174–189; Византинороссика 2, 2003; Буцефал 2004). These may also quote ε in translation.
Negative results: facetia.ru lists only Egunov's α excerpt. vostlit.info's А and П indexes have no Alexander Romance entry. ru.wikipedia (Роман об Александре; Псевдо-Каллисфен) gives nothing for ε.
Related item that is not a translation of ε: the Serbian Alexandria (Литпамятники 1965). Botvinnik derives it from ε.
verification.en_found:
No English translation of ε, complete or partial, was found.
- Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994): contains no ε. Its contents per BMCR 1995.08.06 are the Letter to Aristotle, Wonders of the East, George the Monk, Palladius, Alexander–Dindimus, Iter ad Paradisum, and the appendix texts.
- BMCR checked with no ε translation found: Nawotka's α commentary (2017; BMCR 2018.04.47) and Monti's Letters (2023; BMCR 2024.10.31).
- Possible exception, unverified: Ory Amitay, Alexander the Great in Jerusalem: Myth and History (OUP 2025; BMCR 2026.01.36). Its ch. 1 treats the ε Jerusalem episode, and an appendix covers the gates against the northern nations. It probably quotes or translates those ε passages, but the review does not say so, and I could not reach the OUP table of contents.
- I have not checked Stoneman's Penguin Greek Alexander Romance (1991, β with supplements) for ε-derived passages. I found only a pirate upload of it, which I did not use.
- Caveat: the WebSearch budget for this session was used up before this task started (200/200 calls). Instead of general web searches I used site and catalogue searches: BMCR ×3, archive.org advancedsearch ×2, Open Library, Persée, and the CyberLeninka API ×4 (Russian). So the "none" for English rests on these targeted checks, not on open web searching.
verification.other_found:
FRENCH (most important): Corinne Jouanno, Histoire merveilleuse du roi Alexandre maître du monde (Toulouse: Anacharsis, 2009; 333 pp.; ISBN 978-2-914777-50-6). Per BMCR 2010.01.52 (A. Primo), this is a translation of recension γ, made from Lauenstein/Engelmann/Parthe. γ is itself built on ε + β, so much of ε's distinctive content (Jerusalem, the enclosed nations, the Christianized ending) reaches French readers through γ. Primo also says Jouanno prints in an appendix "les variantes" to γ from MS A and from recensions β, λ and ε. So there is partial direct ε material in French, of unknown extent; it should be checked in the book.
Reviews: O. Delouis in REByz 68 (2010) (the Persée PDF is behind an ALTCHA bot check, so I did not read it).
ITALIAN: the Valla Romanzo di Alessandro (Stoneman–Gargiulo) prints and translates α, β and γ plus Julius Valerius, but not ε (BMCR 2014.05.09 on vol. II).
GERMAN: de.wikipedia (Alexanderroman) gives no German translation of ε. Trumpf's 1974 edition has no translation.
Studies, not translations: Jouanno, Naissance et métamorphoses (2002).
Not checked: Modern Greek translations (the el.wikipedia page returned 404) and Spanish (García Gual 1977 is α-based).
verification.source_text:
Edition: J. Trumpf, Anonymi Byzantini Vita Alexandri regis Macedonum (Stuttgart: Teubner, 1974; xxvi + 205 pp.). This is still the only edition. Botvinnik's 2007 excerpt suggests the text runs to 46 chapters (she calls 44.2–46.6 the three final chapters).
Online copies:
- Free full scan uploaded to archive.org on 4 Jan 2026: https://archive.org/details/20260104_20260104_1127 (PDF plus OCR; "opensource" collection). The uploader labels it CC BY-ND 4.0, but the uploader is not the rights holder, so that label is not reliable.
- Controlled-lending copy: https://archive.org/details/anonymibyzantini0000unse
Rights:
- In Germany, §70 UrhG protection for scholarly editions lasted 25 years, i.e. until the end of 1999. The Greek constituted text is therefore free there.
- Trumpf's Latin praefatio is a separately protected work.
- US status is less clear: the URAA may have restored copyright. Translating the constituted text is low-risk, but do not republish the scan or the apparatus.
Manuscript: Bodl. Barocci 17 is the unique full witness. Sources date it differently (13th c. in the sweep; 14th c. in de.wikipedia). I could not confirm that Digital Bodleian has it digitized: medieval.bodleian returned 403 and the search page did not render.
verification.recommendation: Still a strong Neoscholia candidate. There is no complete published translation in any modern language. Russian has only Botvinnik's 2007 excerpt (chs. 44.2–46.6) and quotations in her articles, and English has none found. It is Greek-only, so no extra language expertise is needed. Start with the opening section (Nectanebo through the Persian embassies, §§1–10) or with the Jerusalem and enclosed-nations chapters. Avoid making 44–46 the first unit, since that is the Russian excerpt that already exists. Two points to handle: credit Botvinnik's published excerpt and her unpublished complete translation, perhaps by contacting the SPbU classical philology department or E. V. Zheltova about her archive; and check the extent of the ε appendix in Jouanno 2009 and Amitay 2025 before calling it "untranslated" in English or French.

candidates.title: Byzantine Alexander Poem (Διήγησις Ἀλεξάνδρου, Marc. gr. 408) / «Византийская поэма об Александре» — pilot section, then the whole poem
candidates.author: Anonymous
candidates.date: Colophon 1388. Composition dated either to 1388 (Gonzato, Trumpf, Matzukis) or to the late 13th c. (Mitsakis, Aerts).
candidates.language: Late Byzantine Greek, mixed learned/vernacular; 15-syllable political verse
candidates.size: 6,130 verses (about 45–50k words)
candidates.edition: Wagner, Trois poèmes grecs du moyen-âge (Berlin 1881; public domain; digitized at phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:588); Reichmann 1963; Aerts 2014 (De Gruyter; critical text with English introduction and commentary).
candidates.ru_evidence: Russian searches («византийская поэма об Александре», Marcianus 408) found nothing. Not on facetia.ru.
candidates.en_evidence: Aerts 2014 is described as the Greek text with 'introduction and commentary in English', with no translation. The 'bilingual Marc. 408' book (ISBN 9602868392) covers a chronicle on ff. 1–13v, not this poem.
candidates.value: Verse fusion of α and β: Alexander is still pagan and there is no Gog/Magog. Adds five interpolations from George the Monk (4) and Zonaras (1), and claims Onesicritus as its source. Key evidence for how chronicle and romance merged in late Byzantium. Untranslated anywhere.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Medium: a long, corrupt single-MS text in vernacular-tinged verse. Needs a Byzantinist with late medieval Greek; Aerts' commentary is essential.
candidates.pilot_unit: Proem (vv. 1–31, Onesicritus) plus birth/Nectanebo section (about vv. 1–600), or the five chronicle interpolations as a dossier.

verification.title: Byzantine Alexander Poem (Διήγησις Ἀλεξάνδρου / «Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ βασιλεύς», Marc. gr. 408, ff. 16–142; c. 6120 political verses; colophon 1388)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the poem, either full or partial.

What I checked:
- CyberLeninka API, 8 Russian queries: «поэма об Александре», «византийская поэма Александр», «Александрия византийская», «Псевдо-Каллисфен», «роман об Александре византийский», «поэма об Александре 1388», etc. Nothing on Marc. gr. 408. The only Byzantine Alexander item was Degg 2023, a review of Kaldellis's article on Alexander in Byzantine tradition. It is not a translation.
- facetia.ru searches («Александрия», «византийская поэма», «1388», «Костюхин», «Попова Александр»). Nothing.
- vostlit.info author/title indices А and В, grepped. No Alexander poem.
- ru.wikipedia «Роман об Александре». No mention of the poem.

Near-miss you should know about: «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XV веков», ed. Л. А. Фрейберг (М.: Наука; facetia gives 1968, the volume is often cited as 1969). It contains «Повесть о подвигах Александра» (XIII–XIV вв.), translated by Т. В. Попова: О том, как Александр покорил пустынные земли; О посещении Александром Трои; О письме … в Иерусалим; О сходке, созванной пророком Иеремией (https://facetia.ru/node/4796, text at https://facetia.ru/node/4804).
- This is NOT the 1388 poem. The note gives the source as А. Н. Веселовский, «Из истории романа и повести», вып. 1 (СПб., 1886).
- It is a prose text. The Troy and Jeremiah episodes point to the Byzantine prose tradition related to the Serbian Alexandria.

Yandex is CAPTCHA-blocked and mail.ru redirects to a login page, so I could not run a general Russian web search.
verification.en_found:
I found no English translation, full or partial.

- Aerts, The Byzantine Alexander Poem (De Gruyter 2014; doi 10.1515/9781614513070). Crossref's chapter list shows the structure:
  - vol. 1: Introduction (pp. 1–32), Greek text Books I–III (pp. 33–232), index of names, index of neologisms;
  - vol. 2: Synopsis (pp. 253–266), Commentary parts 1–2 (pp. 267–612), indices, bibliography.
  - So there is an English introduction, a 14-page English synopsis and a commentary, but no translation. The commentary probably renders individual lines, but I could not check that because the De Gruyter PDFs are bot-blocked.
- Related articles have abstracts only, no translations: Aerts, Quaerendo 41 (2011) 46–56 (doi 10.1163/001495211x572067; he counts 6130 verses and argues 1388 is not the date of composition); Matzukis, BZ 80 (1987) and BZ 99 (2006) 109–117 (doi 10.1515/byzs.2006.109).
- There may be scattered translated quotations in secondary literature (e.g. Jouanno, 'The Persians in Late Byzantine Alexander Romances', in Alexander Romance in Persia and the East, 2012; Moennig in Cupane–Krönung, Brill 2016). I did not verify these; at most they would be excerpts.
- Not in Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library. No BMCR review of Aerts 2014.
- Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great: I found no evidence it includes the poem; Open Library describes it only as translations of Greek and Latin texts.
verification.other_found:
I found no translation into any other language.

- German: Reichmann 1963 (Beiträge zur klassischen Philologie 13; Erlangen dissertation) is Greek text, apparatus and German introduction only. I checked the full OCR: no Übersetzung. The archive.org item is a Leiden University thesis scan, freely downloadable since August 2026: https://archive.org/details/IA41536505_0041.
- Partial editions, also without translation (per Reichmann): Kapp 1872 (vv. 1–199, 5569–5813, 6093–6118, plus the lemmata) and Legrand, Bibliothèque grecque vulgaire II (1881), vv. 1–772.
- Italian: Gonzato, BZ 56 (1963), is a dating study, not a translation.
- French near-miss: Jouanno, Histoire merveilleuse du roi Alexandre maître du monde (Anacharsis 2009, 336 pp.). It is a full French translation of recension γ (Lauenstein/Engelmann/Parthe), not this poem (BMCR 2010.01.52). This is also a correction to the sweep's view of γ: a full French translation exists, though γ still has no Russian one.
- Modern Greek: I found nothing. The Greek dissertation archive (didaktorika.gr) search returned no relevant hits.
- Search limits: the WebSearch budget was used up and DuckDuckGo, Yandex, scholar.archive.org and Brave were blocked by CAPTCHA or rate limits. I used Crossref, Open Library, BMCR, archive.org, CyberLeninka, facetia and vostlit directly instead.
verification.source_text:
- Best public-domain text: W. Wagner (ed., posthumously by D. Bikelas), Trois poèmes grecs du moyen-âge inédits (Berlin: S. Calvary 1881), pp. 56–241. The PDF is at https://phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:588 under CC BY 2.0 AT. The volume also contains the Achilleid and Libistros.
- Caveat (Reichmann): Wagner has no apparatus, unmarked conjectures, normalised vernacular forms and omitted verses.
- Use for collation: Reichmann 1963 (critical apparatus; freely downloadable at https://archive.org/details/IA41536505_0041, though still in copyright) and Aerts 2014 (De Gruyter; the current critical text, in copyright).
- Recommended workflow: translate from Wagner and record Reichmann's and Aerts's readings in the notes.
verification.recommendation: A strong candidate: I found no translation of the poem in any modern language, and it is the main Late Byzantine verse reworking of Ps.-Callisthenes (β with α and γ/L contamination; Christensen 1897). Start with the proem and Nectanebo section (vv. 1–772, Legrand's portion), or with the ending and colophon (vv. 5569–6120, which carry the 1388 vs. late-13th-c. dating debate). Checking it needs a Byzantinist who reads medieval vernacular Greek, but no language beyond Greek.

verification.title: Pseudo-Callisthenes, recension γ, Book III (Greek Alexander Romance γ III; «Роман об Александре», ред. γ, кн. III)
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of γ, for any book. The WebSearch budget was used up, so I searched directly instead: the ru.wikipedia full-text API (queries: «Псевдо-Каллисфен перевод», «Псевдо-Каллисфен редакция», «"Роман об Александре" Псевдо-Каллисфен»; I also read «История Александра Великого», «Гог и Магог» and «Ботвинник, Н. М.»), the facetia.ru site search («Каллисфен», «Александрия»), Crossref (RU query) and the ancientrome.ru index. The only Russian rendering of the Greek romance that turned up is Egunov's α excerpt: «Поздняя греческая проза», М. 1960, pp. 397–416, from Book I. Near misses: (1) N. M. Botvinnik worked on the recensions, e.g. «Жанровая природа позднегреческой переработки „Романа об Александре“» (1997) and «Средства художественной выразительности в трех основных редакциях…» (Philologia Classica 3). She also published a translation, «Псевдо-Каллисфен. Роман об Александре. Гл. 44, 46» (Абарис. Журнал друзей СПб классической гимназии, № 8, 2007, pp. 47–50), and a Ps.-Callisthenes excerpt in «Хрестоматия по литературе Древней Греции», т. 2 (2011). The recension and book for both are unverified; they are probably α / Book I, but neither could be accessed, so neither is a confirmed γ III translation. (2) Indirect overlap: Tvorogov's Russian translation of the Serbian Alexandria (Литпамятники 1965) shares ε-derived material. γ III's Brahman section is Palladius, De gentibus Indiae; the sweep reported a Russian translation of it (Taronyan 2007), which I did not re-check.
verification.en_found: No English translation of γ as a text exists, but the 'none' claim is partly refuted by excerpts. (1) R. Stoneman, The Greek Alexander Romance (Penguin 1991; a 2006 Penguin extract is 'The Legendary Adventures of Alexander the Great'). It translates β but includes the γ Book III episode not found in β: Alexander puts to flight the Belsyrians, then encloses the 22 unclean nations, including 'Goth and Magoth', behind the Breasts of the North (pp. 185–187). En.wikipedia's 'Gog and Magog' and 'Alexander Romance' articles cite these pages for the γ passage. I could not check the Penguin text myself because Google Books/archive.org search-inside were blocked by CAPTCHA/restrictions. (2) A. R. Anderson, Alexander's Gate, Gog and Magog, and the Inclosed Nations (1932), pp. 35–37, treats the same passage (Müller's codex C). (3) Content overlap: the β-shared narrative of γ III (Porus, Candace, Amazons, death/testament) is in Stoneman 1991, translated from β, and the Brahman section (γ III, from Palladius) has independent English translations, e.g. Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994). That last point is from memory, not re-verified. (4) Trahoulias, The Greek Alexander Romance: Venice Hellenic Institute Codex Gr. 5 (Athens: Exandas 1997) is a facsimile of MS D. Its introduction and captions are in English and Modern Greek, but it has no translation of the text (Open Library record). Risk: BMCR 2014.05.09 reports Stoneman's promise that 'an English edition will one day appear from Oxford'.
verification.other_found: FRENCH, complete: C. Jouanno, Histoire merveilleuse du roi Alexandre maître du monde (Anacharsis, coll. Famagouste, April 2009, 336 pp., ISBN 978-2-914777-50-6). Confirmed as recension γ, translated from Lauenstein–Engelmann–Parthe 1962–69 and described as the first French translation (O. Delouis, REB 68, 2010, 254–256, Persée; A. Primo, BMCR 2010.01.52). It includes a translated appendix of α/β/λ/ε variants (pp. 257–324) and a concordance with Müller's numbering (pp. 329–332). ITALIAN, partial: Stoneman–Gargiulo, Il Romanzo di Alessandro (Fondazione Valla), vol. I (2007) and vol. II (2012). Each volume prints one book of α, β and γ separately, with Gargiulo's facing Italian translation (BMCR 2014.05.09; en.wikipedia), so γ Books I–II exist in Italian. Vol. III (Book III) is still 'in preparazione' (it.wikipedia, Scrittori greci e latini) and is not in the fondazionevalla.it catalogue. LATIN, partial: C. Müller, Didot 1846 (Arriani Anabasis et Indica…). His mixed A/B/C text has a facing Latin version and takes some codex C (γ) chapters into the text, e.g. III.26 on Eurymithres, Gog and Magog (index, pp. 138–139). GERMAN, summaries only: H. Weismann, Alexander (1850), vol. 2, the 'vollständige Übersetzung des Pseudo-Kallisthenes' from Müller's text. In Book III, C's divergences appear only as short parenthetical summaries, and he explicitly skips the chapters Müller added from A/C at the end (testament etc.); I checked the archive.org OCR. RELATED: an ε French translation by Ch. Sempéré (thesis, Montpellier III, 2005), cited by Delouis, covers the ε material inside γ. Other modern Romances (Tallet-Bonvalot α 1994; Bounoure–Serret L 1992; Centanni L 1988/1991; Nawotka, Polish, 2014; García Gual, Spanish, Gredos) are not γ. I have not checked whether any covers γ passages.
verification.source_text: There is no public-domain critical text of γ III. The standard edition is F. Parthe, Der griechische Alexanderroman, Rezension Γ, Buch III (Beiträge zur klassischen Philologie 33; Meisenheim am Glan: Hain, 1969). It is in copyright, although under German §70 UrhG the 25-year protection of scholarly editions has lapsed for the constituted Greek text; the introduction and apparatus are still protected, so get a legal check. An uploaded scan is on archive.org (id gamma_buch3, 'S. 330–463'). It is not openly licensed and should not be used as a licensed source. The public-domain fallback is C. Müller's Pseudo-Callisthenes in Arriani Anabasis et Indica (Paris: Didot, 1846), archive.org/details/arrianianabasis00arrigoog. It is only a mixed A/B/C text with Latin and covers γ only partially. Manuscripts: C = Paris, BnF suppl. gr. 113 (Gallica digitisation not found); R = Oxford, Barocci 20; D = Venice, Hellenic Institute gr. 5 (Exandas facsimile, 1997).
verification.recommendation: A good Russian-first candidate, but not truly untranslated: there is no Russian translation and English has only excerpts, while a complete French translation exists (Jouanno 2009), and an Italian translation (Valla III) and a possible English one (Stoneman's promised Oxford edition) are pending. Start with the Book III material that is only in γ: the Eurymithres/Belsyrians and 22-unclean-nations chapters and γ's narrative recasting of the marvels letter (use Jouanno's concordance for the chapter numbers). Then do the full book from Parthe. Checking it needs only Byzantine Greek.
