verification.title: Pseudo-Callisthenes, Historia Alexandri Magni, recensio vetusta (α), Books II–III (Kroll 1926; MS A = Paris. gr. 1711)
verification.ru_found:
I confirmed the "partial" verdict, but Russian coverage of α Books II–III is much larger than the sweep found. Books II–III are not untranslated in Russian.
(1) Egunov, «История Александра Великого», in «Поздняя греческая проза» (М.: ГИХЛ, 1960/61, pp. 397–416). This covers only α I.15–26 and 30–41. Facetia, which reproduces it (https://facetia.ru/pseudo-callisthenes-alexander-romance), states: "фрагмент книги I, главы 15-26 и 30-41, редакция α". It contains nothing from Books II or III. The same page also gives a Russian plot summary of all three books, based on Kroll.
(2) NEW, and this partly refutes the claim: «Письма Александра Великого», compiled and with commentary by Б. Г. Деревенский, translated from the ancient Greek by Р. А. Гимадеев (СПб.: Алетейя, 2022 [2023 on Litres], 400 pp., series «Новая античная библиотека. Источники», ISBN 978-5-00165-511-4). Section VII is titled «Псевдоэпиграфы в „Жизни Александра Македонского“ (Псевдо-Каллисфен, редакция Α)». It contains these letters:
- nos. 123–134: to the Tyrians; the four letters of Darius and Alexander's replies; to the Athenians and to the Lacedaemonians; to the satraps; to the Persians
- nos. 135–136: to Statira and Rodogune; to Roxane
- nos. 137–138: Porus and Alexander, with the Metz Epitome parallel
- no. 139: to Aristotle (= α III.17)
- nos. 140–143: the Amazon correspondence (= III.25–26)
- no. 144: to his mother
Section VIII, no. 145, is «Завещание Александра (Псевдо-Каллисфен А)» (= III.33). By my own (unchecked) mapping, the letters fall roughly in α II.1, 6, 10–11, 17, 21–22 and III.2, 17, 25–28, 33, so most epistolary chapters of Books II–III already exist in Russian. Full table of contents: https://esxatos.com/pisma-aleksandra-velikogo. Bibliographic record: https://www.litres.ru/book/boris-georgievich-derevenskiy/pisma-aleksandra-velikogo-68739183/
(3) α III.7–16 is Palladius' De gentibus Indiae et Bragmanibus, which MS A incorporates into Book III. A Russian translation from Greek exists: Г. А. Таронян, «Древний Восток в античной и раннехристианской традиции» (М.: Ладомир, 2007), no. 44, «Палладий. О народах Индии и брагманах», made from Berghoff's 1967 edition. It includes the Dandamis dialogue and the Theban scholasticus story (https://azbyka.ru/otechnik/Istorija_Tserkvi/drevnij-vostok-v-antichnoj-i-rannehristianskoj-traditsii-indija-kitaj-yugo-vostochnaja-azija/45). Gorelov 2006 covers the same material in its Latin form (Commonitorium Palladii).
(4) Not α: an amateur online Russian version of the two β/γ letters to Olympias and Aristotle, made from Berger de Xivrey's 1836 French (facetia.ru/node/2732, simposium.ru, a VK repost by «Агностик» 2024). The Serbian Alexandria translation (1965) also belongs to another tradition.
(5) Unverified: the reported Russian translation of the Armenian version by Дарбинян-Меликян (1986). Searches on Bing, Wikipedia and vostlit found no record of it.
Still apparently without any Russian translation:
- Book II narrative: Plataea, the Athenian debate speeches (II.2–5), Alexander as his own envoy (II.13–15), battles, death of Darius (II.20)
- III.1–6: Porus battle, gymnosophists
- III.18–24: Candace
- III.29–32 and 34–35: portents, death narrative, burial, foundation list
verification.en_found: Full. E. H. Haight, The Life of Alexander of Macedon by Pseudo-Callisthenes (New York: Longmans, 1955; xi+159 pp.). It translates Kroll's α text, all three books. It is listed on the Online Books Page as free at HathiTrust (https://babel.hathitrust.org/cgi/pt?id=mdp.39015046413939). An online English version of α Books 1–3 is on attalus.org (https://www.attalus.org/info/alexander.html). It combines Haight 1955 with Wolohojian's Armenian (1969) and Budge's Syriac (1889) in parallel columns, with Armenian-only sentences marked. Other relevant English: Wolohojian 1969 (Armenian, the closest witness to α; PDF on archive.org); Stoneman 1991 (Penguin; β-based composite); Dowden 1989 (β); Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994/2012), which includes Palladius' 'On the Life of the Brahmans' (= α III.7–16 material). Nawotka's Brill commentary on α (2017) gives detailed summaries, not a translation (BMCR 2018.04.47).
verification.other_found:
IT: Stoneman–Gargiulo, Il Romanzo di Alessandro (Fondazione Valla). Vol. I (2007) covers Book I. Vol. II (2012) covers Book II and prints α, β and γ separately with translation (BMCR 2014.05.09). Vol. III (Book III) was announced; I found no evidence it has appeared. Centanni, Il romanzo di Alessandro (Einaudi 1991; reissued 2018, 2025) has the Greek facing; its recension base is reportedly α but I did not verify it. Franco, Vita di Alessandro il Macedone (Sellerio 2001).
FR: Tallet-Bonvalot, Le roman d'Alexandre: vie d'Alexandre de Macédoine (GF 788, 1994; the subtitle matches A's Βίος Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος, but the base is unverified). Bounoure–Serret (Belles Lettres 1992) is L-based.
PL: Pseudo-Kallistenes, Romans o Aleksandrze / Historia Alexandri Magni, translated with introduction and commentary by K. Nawotka (Poznań, Fontes Historiae Antiquae, 2010, 336 pp.); α by its title.
ES: García Gual (Gredos 1977; RBA 2008; Siruela) translates L (van Thiel) plus A-only passages. This is confirmed from his prologue: "sobre la versión del manuscrito L … editada por H. van Thiel".
DE: Ausfeld, Der griechische Alexanderroman (ed. Kroll, Teubner 1907, pp. 29–127). This is a German reconstructed translation of the original romance from A, Armenian and Julius Valerius, covering all three books. It is public domain at archive.org/details/dergriechischea00ausfgoog.
Side findings for other candidates:
- ε recension: Н. М. Ботвинник translated it completely. Only chs. 44 and 46 were published (gymnasium journal «Абарис»); the full translation is unpublished (Желтова, Philologia Classica 2011, cyberleninka). This qualifies the sweep's claim that ε is untranslated anywhere.
- Metz Epitome: Gorelov 2006 includes the Metz Epitome's gymnosophist episode (facetia.ru/node/2861). This qualifies the sweep's claim that the Metz Epitome has no Russian translation.
verification.source_text: W. Kroll, Historia Alexandri Magni (Pseudo-Callisthenes), vol. I: Recensio vetusta (Berlin: Weidmann, 1926). It is public domain in the EU (Kroll d. 1939) and in the US (published 1926, PD since 2022). Open scan: https://archive.org/details/historiaalexandr00pseu (UIUC Classics Library, not access-restricted). Supporting PD texts: Ausfeld 1907 (German reconstruction, archive.org/details/dergriechischea00ausfgoog); Müller 1846 Didot (B-based hybrid text with A variants, archive.org/details/arrianianabasis00arrigoog); Wolohojian 1969 (Armenian in English, archive.org/details/TalesAlexanderWolohojianTrans, copyright status unclear). For control, use the Valla vol. II α text for Book II (in copyright).
verification.recommendation: This is a weaker candidate than claimed. English is full and free (Haight 1955 via HathiTrust and attalus.org), and Russian already covers α III.7–16 (Taronyan 2007) and nearly all the embedded letters and the Testament (Derevensky–Gimadeev 2022). If pursued, present it as the first complete Russian α with commentary, not as an untranslated text. Start with the uncovered narrative block III.18–24 (Candace) plus III.29–35 (portents, death, burial, minus the Testament III.33), and check the corrupt MS A against the Armenian (via Wolohojian) and Julius Valerius; no Armenian expertise is needed beyond Wolohojian.

candidates.author: Anonymous

verification.title: Recension ζ (*ζ) of the Alexander Romance: late Byzantine / post-Byzantine vernacular prose versions F (Laur. Ashb. 1444, copied 1521) and E (Eton College 163, 16th c.); «Поздневизантийская прозаическая Александрия (ред. ζ)»
verification.ru_found:
No Russian translation of the Greek F, E, V or *ζ text, in full or in part, turned up. Checked: CyberLeninka API (about 10 Russian queries: Сербская Александрия, Псевдо-Каллисфен, византийская/среднегреческая Александрия, перевод с греческого, Филлада and others), facetia.ru (Alexander literature), Russian Wikipedia, and every author/source index on vostlit.info (no Pseudo-Callisthenes material there). Yandex showed a CAPTCHA, which I did not bypass. elibrary was not searched.

Indirect coverage you should know about:
(1) The Slavonic descendant has a modern Russian translation. The Serbian Alexandria, in its Russian redaction, was translated by O. V. Tvorogov in «Александрия. Роман об Александре Македонском по русской рукописи XV в.» (Литпамятники, 1965). Its contents (facetia.ru/node/3045) contain no Greek text or translation. Istrin (1899) says the Greek Iviron copy matches the Slavonic translation closely in content, so Russian readers already have an indirect version.
(2) 19th-century Russian scholarship printed or quoted the Greek, without translating it. Veselovsky, «Из истории романа и повести» I (1886; archive.org/details/izistoriromanai01vesegoog), edited the Greek V text (Vind. theol. gr. 244) in an appendix and retold episodes in Russian alongside the Slavonic. V. Istrin, «Иверский список среднегреческой Александрии», ВВ 6 (1899) 97–130 (archive.org/details/vizantskvremenn02sssrgoog), prints Greek excerpts from Iviron 162 (17th c.) next to the Slavonic. Both are quotations and paraphrase, not translations.
verification.en_found:
No English translation of F, E, V or *ζ was found.
- The Lolos/Konstantinopulos edition prints the Greek text only, with the introduction in German (K10plus record: "Text griech., Einl. u. Vorw. dt").
- Stoneman's Penguin Greek Alexander Romance (1991) translates L and supplements it from A and γ, with nothing from ζ. I confirmed this from the note on the text in the OCR at archive.org.
- Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great (1994/2012) contains no ζ material (contents checked, archive.org/details/legendsofalexand0000unse).

Caveats that weaken "untranslated" for English readers:
(a) Stoneman, The Book of Alexander the Great: A Life of the Conqueror (I.B. Tauris 2012, ISBN 9781848852938) is a full English translation of the Phyllada. Konstantinopulos (ed. vol. II, pp. 2–4) calls the Phyllada a reworking of exactly this text. He also lists 31 passages that F has and the Phyllada lacks, plus content differences: the Poros duel trap, the Amazon embassy, and whether Bryonusis poisons Alexander alone or with five conspirators.
(b) Jouanno, "Herodotean Material in a Late Version of the Alexander Romance," in Reading the Late Byzantine Romance (CUP 2018), doi:10.1017/9781108163767.010, studies a 15th-c. version on the basis of Lolos/Konstantinopulos, Veloudis and Moennig. It probably quotes the troop-review episode in English, but I did not check this. Her 2012 chapter on Persians in late Byzantine Alexander romances may also contain short English excerpts (not checked).
(c) The WebSearch budget was exhausted, so the English-side checks relied on the K10plus union catalogue, the Crossref, archive.org and Wikipedia APIs, and Cambridge Core.
verification.other_found:
No translation of the Greek F, E, V or *ζ text into German, French, Italian or Spanish was found. Related material:
- Phyllada (the 17th-c. reworking): French by J. Lacarrière, «Alexandre le Grand: la vie légendaire» (1993), translated from the Phyllada; German, G. Veloudis, «Alexander der Grosse: ein alter Neugrieche» (1969), which may contain extracts (not checked).
- Paraphrase of V: H. J. Gleixner, «Das Alexanderbild der Byzantiner» (Diss. München 1961), in German, according to Lolos.
- Serbian descendant: German, D. Christians, «Die serbische Alexandreis» (1991), text and translation, with a contribution on the Greek texts by E. Trapp (it may include Greek parallels; not checked). Partial Dutch in van den Berk (1970). Polish excerpts in Usakiewicz/Falski, Colloquia Humanistica 2014.
- Partial Greek texts from the 19th century: Veselovsky, Archiv f. slav. Philologie 11 (1888) 324–343, prints the "Wunderepisode" from F.

Corrections and cross-checks for the earlier sweep (outside this candidate):
- ε does have a translation: C. Sempéré, «La recension epsilon du Roman d'Alexandre, traduction et commentaire» (Diss. Montpellier 2005, French).
- Jouanno, «Histoire merveilleuse du roi Alexandre» (Anacharsis 2009) is a full French translation, probably of γ: the publisher dates the text to the 10th–14th c.
- Aerts, The Byzantine Alexander Poem (De Gruyter 2014) gives text and commentary only, with no translation listed.
- Moennig's survey chapter "A Hero Without Borders 1" is in Cupane & Krönung (eds.), Fictional Storytelling (Brill 2016), doi:10.1163/9789004307728_008.
verification.source_text:
Main edition: A. Lolos (vol. I, F and E in parallel for Books I–II.23/24) and V. L. Konstantinopulos (vol. II, II.24 to the end), «Ps.-Kallisthenes: Zwei mittelgriechische Prosa-Fassungen des Alexanderromans» (Beiträge zur klass. Philologie 141, 150; Königstein: Hain 1983). F is Laur. Ashb. 1444, copied 1521 by Michael Kyriakopoulos. E is Eton College 163, 16th c., and according to Lolos the fullest witness.

Copyright: the edition is © Hain, "alle Rechte vorbehalten". A user upload on archive.org (archive.org/details/20260104_20260104_1637) carries a CC BY-ND label, which is almost certainly not authorised, so do not rely on it. A lending scan of vol. I is at archive.org/details/pskallistheneszw0001pseu. German §70 UrhG protects scholarly editions for only 25 years from publication, so protection of the edited text itself has probably lapsed (2008). The introductions remain protected. This needs a legal check.

Public-domain alternatives, all partial or lacunose and for related witnesses rather than F/E:
- Veselovsky 1886 appendix: Greek text of V (archive.org/details/izistoriromanai01vesegoog).
- Veselovsky 1888, Archiv f. slav. Phil. 11: 324–343: the F "Wunderepisode".
- Istrin 1899, ВВ 6: 97–130: Iviron excerpts.

Reference works: Moennig, «Die spätbyzantinische Rezension *ζ des Alexanderromans» (Köln: Romiosini 1992, Neograeca Medii Aevi 6), a study of *ζ. Mitsakis 1967 covers V.
verification.recommendation: This is a sound candidate: no Russian or English translation of the Greek F/E text exists. Russian and English readers already have close relatives, though: Tvorogov's 1965 translation of the Serbian Alexandria and Stoneman's 2012 Phyllada. So the case rests on presenting the Greek original behind the Slavonic Alexandria, annotated against both. Start with the self-contained ending in Konstantinopulos vol. II (≈pp. 186–204: Bryonusis' plot and poisoning, the farewell, the transfer of the body, and the laments of Olympias and Roxane), or Book I in Lolos' F/E parallel text. Verification needs experts in late-medieval vernacular Greek (the Kriaras lexicon) and Church Slavonic, beyond classical Greek.

verification.en_found: I found no English translation of the 1889 essay. I checked the full texts of the likely English sources. (a) J. C. Lawson, Modern Greek Folklore and Ancient Greek Religion (1910), pp. 184–185 (archive.org moderngreekfolkl00laws): a close English paraphrase of the Gorgon motif. The Gorgon grabs the bows and asks 'Is king Alexander living?'; the answer is 'he lives and reigns'; she calms the sea and sings to her lyre, or else she capsizes the ship or raises a storm with her laments. This matches the essay's p. 38 paragraph, but Lawson's source is Politis' earlier article in Parnassos 2 (1878), pp. 259ff, not the 1889 essay. Lawson is a paraphrase, not a translation. (b) R. Rodd, The Customs and Lore of Modern Greece (1892), p. 173: one sentence alluding to Alexander's sisters as Nereids. (c) Stoneman, The Greek Alexander Romance (Penguin 1991), introduction: passing allusions to the mermaid and 'lord of storms', no translated text. (d) Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994; rev. 2012). I checked the table of contents on IA (legendsofalexand0000unse): Letter to Aristotle, Pharasmanes, George the Monk excerpt, Palladius, Collatio, Iter ad Paradisum, two papyri, and Middle English excerpts. There is no Modern Greek folk material. (e) G. F. Abbott, Macedonian Folklore (1903), ch. 'Alexander and Philip in Folk-Tradition': retells the Phyllada and other material; no Politis translation. (f) L. Garnett, Greek Folk Poesy (1896): has Alexander and Water-of-Life allusions in other tales; no Politis translation. One possible exception I could not verify: R. M. Dawkins, 'Alexander and the Water of Life', Medium Ævum 6 (1937) (Crossref DOI 10.2307/43626046). It probably gives English versions of Modern Greek water-of-life and sister-mermaid variants, possibly including Politis' Fellos/Kalavryta text or Paradoseis items. JSTOR could not be reached, so this needs a manual check. Dawkins' Modern Greek Folktales (1953) and More Greek Folktales (1955) are lending-only on IA and could not be searched.
verification.other_found: None found. The French Wikisource author page for Politis lists only 'Les Jeux Olympiques 776–1896' (1896). The Greek Wikisource author page lists the 1889 essay with no translator field. I found no French, German or Italian translation of the essay. There is related German scholarship, which I did not verify in this pass: G. Veloudis, Der neugriechische Alexander (1968). It is a study, not a translation.
verification.source_text: The 1889 essay is public domain (Politis d. 1921). The best source is the proofread transcription on el.wikisource (pagequality level 3), with page scans from Ἐτήσιον Ἡμερολόγιον τοῦ ἔτους 1889 (ed. K. F. Skokos), pp. 37–40: https://el.wikisource.org/wiki/Ετήσιον_Ημερολόγιον_του_Έτους_1889/Αλέξανδρος_ο_Μέγας_κατά_τας_δημώδεις_παραδόσεις (index 'Ημερολόγιο Σκόκου (1889)', pages 037–040). It is about 1,060 words. The text runs as follows. (1) An opening on why Alexander alone among kings survives in folk memory; it sets him against the Marble King / Constantine Palaiologos. (2) Folk sayings and storm charms: the Kyra Kalo, queen of the Nereids, as Alexander's sister; the Macedonian charm «Ζῇ καὶ βασιλεύει»; the Gorgon, daughter of Alexander and the Sea. (3) A demotic Peloponnesian text from Fellos (Kalavryta), sent to Politis by Dr Ch. P. Korryllos of Patras: the immortal water, the sisters bathing and becoming Nereids, and how the hen and the squill (μπότσικας) got their share. (4) A short survey of the line from Ps.-Callisthenes to the Phyllada, Julius Valerius, the Arabic and Slavonic versions, ending with a contemporary Macedonian-Question framing. Παραδόσεις I–II (Μελέται περὶ τοῦ βίου καὶ τῆς γλώσσης τοῦ ἑλληνικοῦ λαοῦ, Athens 1904) is also public domain, but it is not transcribed on el.wikisource and has no copy on the Internet Archive (both checked). The previous sweep said scans exist on Anemi (Univ. of Crete) and Google Books; I could not confirm a URL in this pass.
verification.recommendation: This is a reasonable small candidate with no translation found, but the essay alone is very short (about 1,060 words). Its most valuable part is the demotic Fellos/Kalavryta legend, and it is reception rather than antiquity. Start with a dossier: the 1889 essay plus the Alexander items from Παραδόσεις 1904 (Gorgon, immortal water, the Nereids as Alexander's sisters), with commentary tying them to the Romance's water-of-life episode and the Phyllada. Translation needs checking by someone who reads Modern Greek, both katharevousa and Peloponnesian dialect. First check Dawkins, Medium Ævum 6 (1937) for overlap.

verification.title: Φυλλάδα τοῦ Μεγαλέξαντρου / Phyllada (Διήγησις Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος) / «Филлада о Мегалександре»
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation, either full or partial. One limitation: the WebSearch budget for this session had already run out (200 of 200), so I could not run general Russian web searches. I checked these specific sources instead:
- facetia.ru site search: no hits for «Филлада» or «новогреческ». The «Каллисфен» and «Александрия» hits are all Slavonic or Latin material.
- Gorelov's anthology (Азбука-классика 2006, https://www.facetia.ru/povest-o-rozhdenii-i-pobedah-aleksandra-velikogo): it contains only Latin and Old French texts (Leo/Bamberg, Dindimus, Epistola, Iter ad Paradisum and others). No Modern Greek material.
- ru.wikipedia search for «Мегалександр», «Фюллада», «Филлада» and «Псевдо-Каллисфен новогреческ»: 0 hits. The article «Александрия (роман)» does not mention the Phyllada.
- ru.wikisource: only dictionary hits for the mineral «филлад».
- vostlit.info: the alphabetical indexes have no relevant entry.
- CyberLeninka (API returned 0 even for control queries, so this check is inconclusive), rusneb.ru (403) and eLibrary: not usable.
Stoneman 2012 (p. xi) notes only that the Russian and Bulgarian Alexandrias derive from ε, with material from the Serbian (*ζ) version. That is a Slavonic adaptation, not a translation of the Phyllada. Verdict: none found, with medium confidence because no general Russian web search was possible.
verification.en_found:
The colleague's claim is confirmed: there is a complete English translation.
- Richard Stoneman (tr. and introd.), The Book of Alexander the Great: A Life of the Conqueror. London/New York: I.B. Tauris, 2012. xxix + 178 pp. ISBN 9781848852938 / 9781848852945; ebook Bloomsbury, Google Books id bRKJDwAAQBAJ.
- The publisher's blurb says the Phyllada "has never been translated into English" until this book.
- Stoneman's own note (p. 163) gives the source text: "This translation follows Veloudis' edition, though I have retained the more numerous chapter headings from Pallis' edition."
- It is a full translation. It even includes the printer's preface dated "Venice, 1670" (p. xxix) and has a commentary section (pp. 163–170).
- Sources: https://books.google.de/books?id=bRKJDwAAQBAJ (in-book snippets on pp. vii, viii, x, xxix, 163), https://www.goodreads.com/book/isbn/9781848852938, https://openlibrary.org/works/OL22748627W.
- Not in Stoneman's earlier anthology Legends of Alexander the Great (1994). BMCR 1995.08.06 lists its contents and there is no Phyllada material.
- Patrick Leigh Fermor's Mani (1958, p. 187) retells the mermaid episode; this is a paraphrase, not a translation.
verification.other_found:
The sweep said no other translations exist. That is wrong; I found these:
(1) POLISH, excerpts. Krzysztof Usakiewicz, 'The Greek Phyllada and the Old Serbian Alexander Romance', Colloquia Humanistica 2 (2013) 257–289, DOI 10.11649/ch.2013.012, CC BY 3.0. It prints the Greek text with a Polish translation of four excerpts: Alexander's birth (Olympias and Nectanebo, here 'Ektenabos'), the sack of Athens, Alexander in Jerusalem, and the Island of the Blessed. It also has facsimile pages of the 1750 edition. URL: https://journals.ispan.edu.pl/index.php/ch/article/view/ch.2013.012. The companion article (Colloquia Humanistica 3, 2014, DOI 10.11649/ch.2014.011) gives the parallel Old Serbian excerpts, translated by Maciej Falski.
(2) TURKISH (Karamanlidika), a historical full translation. Agapios Papazoglou, Constantinople 1843, 336 pp. Studied by Artemis Papatheodorou, 'A Greco-Turkish Alexander the Great: The Karamanli Phyllada from 1843', Anatolian Studies 76 (2026) 161–176, DOI 10.1017/S0066154626100714.
(3) ARABIC, of the source text only. Stoneman 2012 (p. x) says the 'Middle Greek' prose version (*ζ, the Phyllada's source) was translated into Arabic by Yusuf ibn Suwaydan of Mt Sinai in 1671.
(4) GERMAN, possible excerpts, not verified. Veloudis wrote two German books on the Phyllada: Der neugriechische Alexander (Miscellanea Byzantina Monacensia 8, München 1968; a study) and Alexander der Grosse: Ein alter Neugrieche (München: Heimeran, Tusculum-Schriften, 1969, 95 pp.). Both are confirmed in the DNB catalogue; I could not check whether either contains translated passages.
No French, Italian or Spanish translation turned up in the BnF, Dialnet or DNB catalogue queries.
SIDE FINDING, outside this candidate but relevant to the earlier sweep. In the notes to Stoneman 2012 (p. 164), a reference that probably concerns ε reads "translated into French by Corinne Jouanno 2009", i.e. Histoire merveilleuse du roi Alexandre maître du monde (Paris: Anacharsis, 2009). The previous sweep said ε is "apparently untranslated anywhere"; that should be re-checked.
verification.source_text:
The standard critical text is G. Veloudis, Ἡ Φυλλάδα τοῦ Μεγαλέξαντρου. Διήγησις Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος (1977; repr. Athens: Βιβλιοπωλεῖον τῆς Ἑστίας, 1989), based on the 1750 Venice edition preserved at Hilandar. It is in copyright. A. Pallis' edition (Athens 1935) uses a 19th-century text and is probably also still in copyright.

The sweep's description of the source needs correcting. No 1680 print survives: according to Usakiewicz, following Veloudis, the two oldest editions are lost. Stoneman (p. vii) dates the first edition to Venice 1670 and says the earliest surviving copy is from 1699. So "Venetian prints from 1680 (public domain)" is not a usable source.

Public-domain witnesses I could confirm online:
(a) Athens 1897 print, Ἱστορία τοῦ Μεγάλου Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος, βίος, πόλεμοι καὶ θάνατος αὐτοῦ, N. Michalopoulos. https://archive.org/details/historiatoumegal00mich (Columbia microfilm, 62 images). Its OCR is unusable, so it would need re-keying, and it is a late and probably modernized text.
(b) Greek Wikipedia links a Venice 1838 print (St George press) at Google Books id jHFZAAAAcAAJ. The Google metadata for that id says 1858 and 16 pp., which does not fit, so the link is unverified.
(c) Usakiewicz 2013 (CC BY 3.0) prints openly licensed Greek passages and facsimiles from the 1750 edition.
The best route would be an Ottoman-era Venetian print, ideally the 1750 edition or another 18th-century one. The Anemi digital library (University of Crete) probably holds such prints, but the site failed with a certificate error, so I could not confirm.
verification.recommendation: For English this is not a good candidate: Stoneman's complete 2012 translation of Veloudis' text already exists. It is a possible Russian-only project but low priority, because it is an early-modern reception text rather than an ancient one and the standard edition is still in copyright. If pursued, start with one self-contained episode from a public-domain 18th–19th-century print, such as the Island of the Blessed or the Water of Life and Thessalonike's turning into a mermaid. Checking it needs someone who reads early modern demotic Greek of the Ottoman period, not just classical Greek or Latin.

verification.title: Διήγησις τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου, rhymed version (Rimada): «Γέννησις, κατορθώματα καὶ θάνατος Ἀλεξάνδρου τοῦ Μακεδόνος διὰ στίχου» (Venice 1529); «Рифмованная повесть об Александре»
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, whether full, partial or excerpted. Searches run: Bing for «Римада Александр новогреческая поэма 1529», «рифмованная Александрия новогреческая Венеция политический стих» and «Фюллада Александра Македонского перевод новогреческая Александрия»; Yahoo for «Римада Александр Македонский новогреческая», «"Фюллада" Александр», «новогреческая рифмованная повесть об Александре 1529 Венеция», «стихотворная греческая Александрия 1529 Венеция Зинос» and «греческая народная книга об Александре Македонском Венеция печатная»; two full-text searches through the ru.wikipedia API. The CyberLeninka search API returned 0 even for control queries, so it told me nothing. I found no trace in the Литпамятники or Gorelov 2006 material. verification.en_found: I found no English translation, full or partial. (1) I checked Holton's own edition from the OCR of the 1974 volume (archive.org/details/holton-d.-the-tale-of-alexander.-the-rhymed-version-thessalonica-1974). Its contents are: an English introduction in 7 chapters, a Greek summary («Περίληψη τῆς Εἰσαγωγῆς»), the text, an English commentary, a glossary, an index, and an appendix listing Rimada elements not found in α/β. There is no translation. The MIET page for the 2nd edition (2002, xx+297 pp., ISBN 960-250-245-2; https://www.miet.gr/book-list/book-Dihghsis-toy-Alejandroy) also describes only a critical edition. The reviews (REB 34, 1976, Persée; Scriptorium 31, 1977, Persée; Jeffreys, MÆ 1977) describe it as an edition. (2) Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994/2012), contains the Letter to Aristotle, the Wonders of the East, an excerpt of George the Monk, Palladius, Alexander–Dindimus, the Journey to Paradise and an appendix of fragments. It has no Modern Greek texts (TOC checked via ebin.pub/dokumen.pub). (3) Zuwiyya (ed.), A Companion to Alexander Literature in the Middle Ages (Brill 2011): I grepped the full OCR on archive.org and it never mentions the Rimada, the Phyllada or Holton. (4) The Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library list of Byzantine Greek volumes (domedieval.org/volumes/byzantine-greek/) has no Alexander volume. (5) Bing and Yahoo searches for "Rimada of Alexander", "Tale of Alexander" "rhymed version" translated, "Rimada" "translated by", and Rimada with Holton or Moennig turned up only the edition, its reviews and bookshop listings. One caveat: I could not search inside Stoneman, Alexander the Great: A Life in Legend (2008), or Trypanis, Penguin Book of Greek Verse (1971); both are restricted on archive.org. Either could quote a few lines in English. That would be an excerpt, not a translation.
verification.other_found: I found no translation into any language. Searches in Modern Greek («Ριμάδα Αλεξάνδρου μετάφραση», «Ριμάδα του Αλεξάνδρου», «Ριμάδα Μεγαλέξαντρος Ζήνος μετάφραση»), Italian (Rimada Alessandro Magno 1529 traduzione), French (Rimada Alexandre le Grand grec 1529 traduction), Spanish (Rimada Alejandro Magno traducción) and German (Rimada Alexander Übersetzung neugriechisch) found nothing beyond the Holton edition. Related items that are not translations of the Rimada: (a) an article (2015) on ResearchGate that prints selected fragments of the Phyllada (the prose text, not the Rimada) with a Polish translation (researchgate.net/publication/307763844); (b) Papathomas 2022, on the Pseudo-Callisthenes tradition, in the Venice Hellenic Institute Codex 5 facsimile volume, which discusses the Rimada as partly derived from α*; (c) the Rimada has an entry in the index of Perspectives médiévales 39 (2018), which refers to Gaullier-Bougassas (ed.), La fascination pour Alexandre le Grand, II (Brepols 2014). I could not open that entry (bot-check page), so French paraphrase or excerpts there or in Jouanno's Naissance et métamorphoses (2002) cannot be ruled out. They would at most be excerpts.
verification.source_text: Facts from the OCR of Holton 1974: the poem has 2,948 rhymed fifteen-syllable verses in couplets. It survives in 14 Venetian editions (1529, 1553, 1600, 1603/08, 1620, 1654, 1690, 1729, 1738, 1747, 1778, 1794, 1804, 1805) and one manuscript, which is a copy of the editio princeps and of no textual value. The editio princeps is Ὁ Ἀλέξανδρος ὁ Μακεδών (Venice: Giovanni Antonio & fratelli da Sabbio, at the instance of Damiano di Santa Maria, Sept. 1529), ed. Demetrios Zenos, who was only the editor; the versifier is an anonymous Zakynthian, c. 1490–1520. Copies are in the British Museum/BL and the Bodleian (Mason, Bywater). Best freely available public-domain witness: the 1553 Venice reprint (Rampazetto for Damiano di Santa Maria), digitized at the BSB/MDZ, shelfmark Rar. 467#Beibd.1, https://www.digitale-sammlungen.de/en/view/bsb10857896. Holton says it follows the 1529 text closely. I did not find a digitized 1529 print online. Anemi (Univ. of Crete) may hold later editions, but its search was not machine-accessible. The critical text is Holton, Διήγησις τοῦ Ἀλεξάνδρου. The Tale of Alexander. The Rhymed Version (Βυζαντινή και Νεοελληνική Βιβλιοθήκη 1, Thessaloniki 1974; 2nd ed. MIET, Athens 2002). It is in copyright. It is based exclusively on the 1529 print, with orthography normalized. The archive.org copy (uploaded 2026 by a user) carries a CC0 tag, but that is the uploader's claim, not a licence from Holton or MIET, so it should not be relied on for republishing. Recommended setup: translate against Holton's verse numbering, and publish the Greek only from a fresh transcription of the public-domain prints, or seek MIET permission.
verification.recommendation: A strong candidate: I found no Russian or English translation, or translation in any language, and the poem is a manageable length (2,948 verses). It also matters for scholarship on the Alexander Romance: Holton derives it from a lost Greek recension between α and β, closer to α, via a vernacular prose intermediary. Start with vv. 1 to about 400 (the prologue on Egyptian wisdom, Nectanebo and Alexander's birth), which can be checked directly against α/Kroll and Julius Valerius; then go through the rest in roughly 500-line blocks. Flag: checking the translation needs expertise in early modern vernacular Greek (Zakynthian/Ionian dialect features, Venetian loanwords, archaizing 'barbarisms'), not only Classical Greek.

verification.title: Pseudo-Callisthenes, recension β, II.23–44 (Letter to Olympias and Aristotle / wonders; Land of Darkness and Land of the Blessed)
verification.ru_found:
REFUTED: the claim that there is no Russian translation is wrong. Three Russian versions exist.
(1) Directly from the Greek: Б. Г. Деревенский (авт.-сост.), «Письма Александра Великого», пер. с др.-греч. Р. А. Гимадеева. СПб.: Алетейя, 2022, 400 с. (Новая античная библиотека. Источники), ISBN 978-5-00165-511-4. Its table of contents (esxatos.com/pisma-aleksandra-velikogo; publisher listing aletheia.spb.ru) has a Section IX, «Позднеантичные и средневековые фабрикации». It contains no. 147 «Письмо к Олимпиаде и Аристотелю [1] (Псевдо-Каллисфен Β)», no. 148 the same letter in its Г (γ) version, no. 151 «Утешительное письмо к матери (Псевдо-Каллисфен Β)» (= III.33), and no. 149 «Послание к иерусалимлянам (Λ)». No. 147 is almost certainly the β letter II.23–41, because it is the only β letter addressed to both Olympias and Aristotle. I could not check whether it is complete or abridged, or which edition was used (Bergson?). Section VII separately translates the α letters.
(2) Indirectly, via French: «Письма Александра Великого», facetia.ru/node/2732. It is credited «Перевод с французского: simposium.ru», with no translator named. The French source is Berger de Xivrey 1836 (see Other translations). There are two letters, about 4,500–5,000 words together. One of them gives the 24-cubit giants, the Ochlotes, the Land of the Blessed, the birds speaking Greek, the revived salted fish and the punished cook. That matches β II.32–41.
(3) Indirectly, via Old Russian: the Хронографическая Александрия (Slavonic, translated from a Greek β-family text no later than the mid-13th c.) in modern Russian by О. В. Творогов, in «Изборник» (М.: Худож. лит., 1969); text at facetia.ru/node/2756. It includes the letter episode: 24-cubit giants, «земля блаженных», the revived fish and the cook. Its exact Greek affiliation (β, L or γ) is debated and I did not verify it.
Also: Egunov 1960/61 (α I.15–26, 30–41) does not cover this passage, which facetia.ru/pseudo-callisthenes-alexander-romance confirms. The α parallel of the letter reaches Russian through the Armenian version (Дарбинян-Меликян 1986), not β.
Searches I could not run: yandex.ru (CAPTCHA). ancientrome.ru and simposium.ru failed (connection reset / expired certificate).
verification.en_found:
Bergson's constituted β text has never been translated into English as such. However, the content of II.23–44 is fully available in English through L, the fullest β manuscript.
(a) R. Stoneman, The Greek Alexander Romance (Penguin 1991). I checked the OCR text at archive.org/details/the-greek-alexander-romance-pseudo-callisthenes. Stoneman says he translated the whole of L as the fullest β version, adding material from A and γ. He notes that L's letter to Olympias (II.38–41) is much expanded, and that L is the only β version with the diving bell and the flight.
(b) K. Dowden, 'Pseudo-Callisthenes: The Alexander Romance', in B. P. Reardon (ed.), Collected Ancient Greek Novels (Berkeley 1989), pp. 650–735. Garstad (DOP 72, 2018, archive.org/details/DOP72_03_Garstad) describes it as a translation of 'the L MS of the β recension'.
(c) The α parallel of the letter is in English in E. H. Haight 1955 (from Kroll), and the Armenian in Wolohojian 1969.
Garstad 2018 also gives his own English translation from Bergson of another β passage (III.28, the Lysos episode). In practice, an English reader already has II.23–44 in a β-family text; what is missing is only Bergson's constituted text, with B-specific readings.
verification.other_found:
- French, 1836: J. Berger de Xivrey, Traditions tératologiques (Paris: Impr. royale, 1836), pp. 333ff. It gives the Greek text and a French translation of the letter to Olympias and Aristotle from Paris. suppl. gr. 113 (C, γ). For comparison it adds the same letter from Paris. gr. 1685 (= Codex B, a core β manuscript). Online: archive.org/details/b29340664; French text at remacle.org/bloodwolf/philosophes/callisthene/alexandre.htm.
- French, 1992: G. Bounoure & B. Serret, Le Roman d'Alexandre (Les Belles Lettres, La Roue à livres 13). Translated from L (van Thiel 1974), with episodes from other versions in an appendix.
- German: H. van Thiel, Leben und Taten Alexanders von Makedonien. Der griechische Alexanderroman nach der Handschrift L (Darmstadt 1974), Greek–German, from L. Also cited by the Belles Lettres blurb.
- Italian: R. Stoneman (ed.) / T. Gargiulo, Il Romanzo di Alessandro, vol. II (Fondazione Valla / Mondadori, 2012). Composite Greek text with Italian translation, including β/L material.
- Latin: C. Müller's Didot edition (Paris 1846, appended to Arrian) gives a composite A/B/C text with a Latin translation.
- Spanish (García Gual, Gredos 1977) and French (Tallet-Bonvalot, GF 1994): I could not verify their base text or whether they include β II.23–44.
verification.source_text:
- Critical edition: L. Bergson, Der griechische Alexanderroman. Rezension β (Stockholm: Almqvist & Wiksell, 1965). Still in copyright; on archive.org only as a restricted lending item (archive.org/details/dergriechischeal0000pseu).
- Public domain, β letter: Berger de Xivrey 1836, Greek of codex B's letter (Paris. gr. 1685) plus γ codex C, with French (archive.org/details/b29340664).
- Public domain, composite: C. Müller, Pseudo-Callisthenes in Arriani Anabasis et Indica (Paris: Didot, 1846), Greek A/B/C with Latin (archive.org/details/arrianianabasis00dbgoog; also bub_gb_LNYWAAAAQAAJ).
- Public domain, L: H. Meusel, Pseudocallisthenes nach der Leidener Handschrift (1871) (archive.org/details/bub_gb_Rf0ZjonQaKIC).
For a faithful β translation, Bergson is needed. Bergson's text could be the reference, with the public-domain B/L texts for checking. Verifying the translation needs only Greek.
verification.recommendation: Weak, low-priority candidate. This letter is the most-translated part of β: it is in Russian from the Greek (Gimadeev 2022, plus indirect versions via Berger de Xivrey's French and the Chronographic Alexandria), and in English, German, French and Italian through L. If the platform still wants it, the defensible unit is a complete Russian translation of Bergson's β with commentary, not the II.23–44 excerpt. Otherwise it should move to genuinely untranslated material such as ε (Trumpf 1974) or a full γ.

verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of any λ material, full or partial. WebSearch had run out of budget, so I searched through other routes. (1) CyberLeninka API, 9 Russian queries: «Псевдо-Каллисфен», «Псевдо-Каллисфена перевод», «редакция лямбда Псевдо-Каллисфена», «греческий роман об Александре рукописи редакции», «роман об Александре Македонском перевод», «Мефодий Патарский Гог Магог Александр», «Откровение Мефодия Патарского перевод», «Псевдо-Мефодий Александр нечистые народы», «апофтегмы Александра Македонского». They returned work on the Serbian and Chronograph Alexandrias and on Pseudo-Methodius in Slavonic. None of it touches λ. (2) vostlit.info: I grepped the author/source indexes for А, Д, Е, Ж, И, К, Л, М, О, П, Р, С (incl. В). They have no entry for Ps.-Callisthenes, the Alexander Romance or Pseudo-Methodius. (3) ancientrome.ru/antlitr: no Ps.-Callisthenes. (4) ru.wikipedia «Псевдо-Каллисфен» and «Роман об Александре»: λ is not mentioned. Yandex returned a CAPTCHA, which I did not bypass. The only Russian translations of the Greek Romance I could confirm are Egunov's α excerpts (from the sweep) and N.M. Botvinnik, «Персидские посольства к Александру Македонскому в новой редакции „Романа об Александре"» (1979; cyberleninka.ru/article/n/persidskie-posolstva-k-aleksandru-makedonskomu-v-novoy-redaktsii-romana-ob-aleksandre). That article translates passages of ε §10, not λ. I did not verify whether a modern Russian translation of the Greek Pseudo-Methodius exists. That text is the source of λ's Gog and Magog insertion.
verification.en_found: I found no English translation of the λ Greek text. Checks: (a) Stoneman, The Greek Alexander Romance (Penguin 1991). By the archive.org OCR of its introduction, it is based on L, with insertions from A, γ and ε; λ is not mentioned. (b) en.wikipedia Alexander Romance: lists van Thiel 1959 only, no translation. (c) Crossref search for "Alexander Romance λ" found a new edition the sweep missed: Caterina Franchi, Alexander Romance λ III: Introduction, critical edition and commentary (Bologna: Pàtron, Eikasmos Studi 33, 2021; DOI 10.2307/jj.29787152). The subtitle and the publisher's page (patroneditore.com/volumi/9788855535427) describe a synoptic edition of 7 manuscripts, an introduction, a palaeographical study and a commentary, with no translation. The English commentary on III 5–6, III 8 (apophthegmata), III 15–16 (Gog and Magog) and III 30–35 may translate quoted lines; I could not inspect it. Near-equivalents, not λ itself: (i) Garstad, Apocalypse of Pseudo-Methodius (Dumbarton Oaks Medieval Library 14, 2012) translates the Greek 1st redaction; per van Thiel, λ follows the 2nd redaction (Istrin). (ii) A.R. Anderson, Alexander's Gate (1932), pp. 38ff., paraphrases the β-family (B/M/Byz.) III.29 enclosure, which van Thiel says closely matches λ's second version. (iii) The λ form of III.17 matches Leo's J version (Merkelbach), whose Latin is in Pritchard 1992 (J1). (iv) Not checked: Bonura, "A Forgotten Translation of Pseudo-Methodius in Eighth-Century Constantinople" (Brill 2016, pp. 260–276; abstract not accessible) may concern λ's Greek Pseudo-Methodius text and may quote it in English. His A Prophecy of Empire (UC Press 2025), App. B "Early Interpolations in the Greek Pseudo-Methodius" (pp. 307–310), is also unchecked.
verification.other_found: Italian: none. The Fondazione Valla catalogue (fondazionevalla.it) lists only vol. I (2007) and vol. II (2012) of Il Romanzo di Alessandro; vol. III, which would cover Book III where most λ material sits, is not listed. German: van Thiel 1959 is an edition with no translation, and his 1974 Leben und Taten Alexanders translates L, not λ. French, Spanish and Modern Greek: none found. Jouanno, Naissance et métamorphoses (2002), discusses λ but I did not check it for translated passages. Also relevant: Bodl. Auct. T.5.21 (λ only in Book III; dated 1516) is itself a medieval vernacular Greek rendering. Side finding for the sweep: Botvinnik 1979 partly translates ε into Russian, which weakens the sweep's claim that ε is untranslated anywhere.
verification.source_text: 1) The best full text is Franchi 2021 (Pàtron, Eikasmos Studi 33; ISBN 9788855535427, e-book 9788855582827; DOI 10.2307/jj.29787152). It is a synoptic critical edition of λ Book III from all seven manuscripts, with the text on pp. 53–182. It is in copyright: the Italian protection for critical editions (art. 85-quater, 20 years) runs to about 2041. Use it to collate and translate from, but do not republish its Greek. 2) Van Thiel, Die Rezension λ des Pseudo-Kallisthenes (Bonn: Habelt 1959, 79 pp.) prints only the divergent passages: the apophthegmata, the λ III.17 letter, the Ps.-Methodian enclosure, and the letter with the second Candace version. App. I gives the apophthegm collections in V and δ; App. II the Ps.-Methodius text. Scan: https://archive.org/details/helmut_van_thiel_lambda (community upload). Germany's 25-year right in scholarly editions (§70 UrhG) ended in 1984, so the edited Greek is reusable; the introduction and apparatus prose are not. 3) Public domain: Meusel 1871 (Jahrb. f. class. Phil. Suppl. 5, 701–816) prints L and a synoptic III.17 from manuscripts O, P, Q, R, C, including the λ manuscripts O and P: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_qMkIAQAAMAAJ (Public Domain Mark). Istrin 1897 has the Ps.-Methodius redactions. Manuscripts (Pinakes, recension 494): Bodl. Barocci 23 (Pinakes s. XIII¹; van Thiel s. XIV); Vat. gr. 171 (s. XVI); Bodl. Holkham gr. 99 (s. XV); Ambros. O 117 sup. (s. XV–XVI, a copy of H); Bodl. Auct. T.5.21 (= van Thiel's 'misc. 283', AD 1516; λ in Book III only, vernacularised); Iviron 165 and Marc. gr. II.91 (both s. XV–XVI).
verification.recommendation: This is a good candidate: no Russian or English translation is verified. First unit: λ's Book III additions in van Thiel pp. ~39–66 / Franchi III 15–16ff., i.e. the Ps.-Methodian Gog and Magog insertion plus Alexander's letter to Olympias with the unique second Candace version. Pilot on the 7-saying apophthegm series at III.18. Greek alone suffices for review, though the text mixes late and vernacular forms. Get Franchi 2021 for collation, and ideally check Bonura 2016 before claiming 'never translated'.

verification.title: Alexander in Byzantine chronicles and scholarship (George the Monk; Zonaras IV; Kedrenos; Glykas; Manasses; Tzetzes, Chiliades; also Malalas VIII) / «Александр у византийских хронистов»
verification.ru_found:
The claim of "no Russian dossier" is refuted for part of the material. Method note: the WebSearch budget was used up (200/200), and DuckDuckGo, Google, Qwant and Startpage returned captchas. Everything below was checked directly against vostlit indexes and pages, the Russian Wikipedia API, Crossref and archive.org.
(1) GEORGE THE MONK, Alexander section: a modern Russian translation EXISTS, made indirectly from the Old Russian «Временник» (11th c.) and checked against de Boor's Greek, with omissions and additions marked: В. А. Матвеенко, Л. И. Щеголева, «Временник Георгия Монаха (Хроника Георгия Амартола)», М.: Богородский печатник, 2000. It is online in full at vostlit (https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/rus16/Amartol/text1.phtml). Its Book 1, ch. 22–26 contains: Alexander's birth via Nectanebo; Stratigion and Chrysopolis; Jaddus and Jerusalem; Issus; the Kandake episode; Alexandria; "worlds innumerable"; Darius' daughters; the Brahman island and the Palladius material. Separately, Т. А. Сенина (2012) translated only the Leo V section, not Alexander.
(2) MALALAS VIII (not in the core list): a Russian translation exists by Н. Н. Болгов, «Мир поздней античности. Документы и материалы», вып. 6–7, Белгород: БелГУ, 2015–2016. It is on vostlit as Texts/rus15/Malalas_2/text8.phtml and Malalas_3/text3.htm, and covers Alexander, Kandake and Addous. В. Н. Талах (2013) also translated excerpts of VIII.11, 13, 15.
(3) ZONARAS: the only modern Russian is XII.15–XIII.19, translated from the English of Banchich–Lane by А. Игнатьев in 2023 (vostlit Texts/rus17/Zonaras). «Паралипомен Зонарин» (ed. О. Бодянский, 1847) is the Church Slavonic version, not modern Russian. No Russian of Book IV was found.
(4) MANASSES: Russian exists only in fragments, none on Alexander. О. В. Смыка 2012 covers vv. 1–143, 2546–54 and 6722–33. О. В. Бычков 1989 gives 20 lines; Д. Е. Афиногенов 1999 gives vv. 4805–30. Д. Полывяный 1990 («Родник златоструйный», on vostlit rus6/Manassia) renders Middle Bulgarian extracts; I checked these, and their "Alexander" is Tsar Ivan Alexander. The Slavonic text is edited in Дуйчев/Лихачёв 1988.
(5) KEDRENOS: И. И. Сидоровский made a Russian translation in 1794 (2nd ed. 1820), titled «Деяния церковные и гражданские, от Рождества Христова…». Going by the title, it starts at the Nativity, so the Alexander section is excluded. I could not open the rusneb record (403).
(6) GLYKAS: only the prison poem has been translated (Грабарь-Пассек, ПВЛ IX–XIV, 1969). Vostlit has notes only.
(7) TZETZES: Russian has only «отрывки» in «Памятники византийской литературы IX–XIV вв.» (1969), pp. 252–259 (Т. В. Попова). I could not check whether these include any Alexander histories. There is no complete Russian Chiliades.
verification.en_found:
TZETZES, CHILIADES: a FULL English translation is on theoi.com (https://www.theoi.com/Text/TzetzesChiliades1.html ... 13.html). Translators: A. Untila (I), G. Berkowitz (II–IV), K. Ramiotis (V–VI), V. Dogani (VII–VIII), J. Alexander (IX–X), M. S. Fadhlurrahman (XI), N. Giallousis (XII–XIII). I checked all 13 books; Alexander material is concentrated in Books VI–VIII.
MANASSES: FULL English by Linda Yuretich, «The Chronicle of Constantine Manasses», Liverpool UP 2018 (ISBN 9781786941510), from the Greek and Slavonic versions; verified via the en.wikipedia bibliography.
GEORGE THE MONK: an English excerpt exists, contrary to the sweep. Stoneman's «Legends of Alexander the Great» (Everyman 1994; I.B. Tauris 2012) has ch. 3, "Excerpt from The Chronicle of George the Monk" (DOI 10.5040/9780755625741.ch-003; contents confirmed in archive.org item legendsofalexand0000unse). It sits next to Palladius and the Alexander–Dindimus correspondence. I could not see the exact span, but it at least covers the Brahman/India material.
MALALAS VIII: full English in Jeffreys, Jeffreys & Scott (Byzantina Australiensia 4, 1986). A free English translation of Books VIII–IX is also on attalus.org (http://www.attalus.org/translate/malalas.html).
NOT FOUND in English: Zonaras Book IV (Banchich & Lane 2009 covers only XII.15–XIII.19; Crossref chapter list checked); the Alexander section of Kedrenos (no English of the early Kedrenos is known); Glykas, Annales. These rest on absence of evidence, because the search engines were blocked.

Scholarship to use for the commentary: C. Jouanno, "Byzantine Views on Alexander the Great" (Brill's Companion to the Reception of Alexander, 2018); C. Jouanno, "Alexander Romance and Byzantine world chronicles" (in The Alexander Romance, 2018); C. Jouanno, "The Alexander historians in Byzantium" (2019); A. Kaldellis, "Alexander the Great in Byzantine Tradition" (CUP 2022); W. Adler, "Byzantine Chronicles and Antiquity" (Companion to Byzantine Chronicles, Brill 2024).
verification.source_text:
All of these are public domain and on archive.org:
- Zonaras (Greek only): L. Dindorf, Teubner vol. 1, 1868 (Books I–V incl. Book IV); archive.org cuaioanniszonara01zona or iannoytoyznapae01canggoog.
- Zonaras (Greek with Wolf's Latin): M. Pinder, CSHB 1841; archive.org ioanniszonaraea0Xpindgoog series; I did not check which scan is vol. 1.
- George the Monk: C. de Boor, Teubner 1904; archive.org georgiimonachic00boorgoog. The corrected reprint by P. Wirth (1978) is in copyright, but the 1904 text is public domain.
- Kedrenos: I. Bekker, CSHB 1838 vol. 1; archive.org georgiuscedrenu00bekkgoog. A newer edition by L. Tartaglia (2016) is from memory and in copyright.
- Glykas: I. Bekker, CSHB 1836 / PG 158; no archive.org identifier was found.
- Manasses: I. Bekker, CSHB 1837 (archive.org breviariumhisto00bekkgoog). Lampsidis' CFHB 36 (1996) is the critical edition but in copyright.
- Tzetzes: Kiessling 1826 (archive.org historiarumvari00kiesgoog). Leone's 1968/2007 edition is in copyright.
verification.recommendation: As a whole dossier this is weaker than claimed. George the Monk's Alexander section already exists in Russian (Матвеенко–Щеголева 2000, via the Slavonic, on vostlit) and has an English excerpt in Stoneman's «Legends». Tzetzes and Manasses have full English translations, and Malalas VIII has full English plus Russian (Болгов 2016). The good candidate is a narrowed unit: the Alexander chapters of Zonaras, Epitome IV (Dindorf 1868 / Pinder 1841, public domain), which have no Russian or English translation that I could find and only 16th-c. Italian and Latin versions. Kedrenos' and Glykas' Alexander sections could follow as a second unit; all are Greek only, so no extra language expertise is needed.

name: Latin and Western medieval Alexander tradition (late antique Latin to vernacular romances)
overview: The Latin and Western strand has big Russian gaps. Of the late antique and early medieval Latin core, only one group exists in modern Russian: N. Gorelov's 2006 volume. It translates Leo's Nativitas (Bamberg MS), the Brahman dossier, the Epistola, and short excerpts of later Latin legend. Nothing else has a Russian version: no Julius Valerius, no Zacher Epitome, no Itinerarium, no Historia de preliis J2/J3, no Quilichinus. Walter's Alexandreis exists in Russian only as Gasparov's excerpts (1972, about 10 pp.). In English, the core is covered: Leo and J1 (Kratz 1991, Pritchard 1992), the Epistola, Iter ad Paradisum and the Alexandreis (Townsend 1996). But Julius Valerius has only the birth episode (DeAngeli 1982), and there is no English for the Zacher Epitome or Quilichinus (Bernardinello's Italian, c. 2024, is the first in any modern language). The Old French tradition is the largest gap in English. Arlima lists no English translation of Alexandre de Paris (FR 1994, IT 2014) or Thomas of Kent (FR 2003), and no modern translation at all of the Prose Alexander or the Voeux du Paon. No Russian versions of the Western vernacular romances turned up. NOT VERIFIED in this sweep (the search budget ran out): Russian and English status of Alexanders saga, Scéla Alaxandair, the Old Czech Alexandreis (originally about 8,500 lines, about two-fifths survive), Maerlant, Rudolf von Ems, Ulrich von Etzenbach, the Italian cantari, Libro de Alexandre (English reportedly Such–Rabone 2009) and Kyng Alisaunder/Wars. The Metz Epitome and Liber de morte belong to the historiography strand.
already_translated_ru:
N. Gorelov, «Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого» (Азбука-классика 2006), translated from Latin and Old French. Contents:
- Leo's Nativitas et victoria from the Bamberg MS (prologue and Books I–III).
- «Александр Македонский и брахманы»: the Commonitorium Palladii and the Alexander–Dindimus correspondence.
- The Epistola Alexandri ad Aristotelem.
- Part 3, «Средневековые истории об Александре»: the journey to Paradise (probably Iter ad Paradisum), the sky and sea ascents, Jerusalem, Gog and Magog, the basilisk, the poison maiden, the Book of Stones, the ten gymnosophists, parables and sayings.

Gasparov translated excerpts of Walter's Alexandreis («Памятники средневековой латинской литературы X–XII вв.», 1972, pp. 449–459).

Outside this strand: «Александрия» (Литпамятники 1965), and T. A. Isachenko's commented translation of the Chronographic Alexandria (Лицевой летописный свод apparatus, 2008).

verification.title: Iulius Valerius Alexander Polemius, Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis translatae ex Aesopo graeco, Book III (Юлий Валерий, «Деяния Александра Македонского», кн. III)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of any part of JV, Book III included. Note on method: the session's WebSearch budget was used up, so I searched through Yahoo results fetched with curl, plus direct site and API queries. I ran more than 10 Russian queries, including «Юлий Валерий Александр Полемий перевод», «"Юлий Валерий" "Деяния Александра"», «"Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis" перевод на русский», «латинский роман об Александре Юлий Валерий русский перевод», and site: queries on ancientrome.ru, vostlit.info and simposium.ru. I also queried the CyberLeninka API for «"Юлий Валерий"» and «"Юлия Валерия"» (0 hits) and searched ru.wikipedia. Results:
- ancientrome.ru «Античные писатели» (1999): the JV entry is only a cross-reference to «Роман об Александре».
- facetia.ru (/pseudo-callisthenes-alexander-romance, /alexander-romances): JV is described but not translated.
- Gorelov 2006 («Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого», Азбука-классика) covers the Leo/Bamberg corpus, not JV.
- O. N. Bleskina, «Латинские "Александрии": истоки и версии» (кандидатская диссертация, СПб., 2000; the abstract and table of contents are on dissercat/cheloveknauka) is a codicological study of manuscripts in Russian libraries, with no JV translation.
- Egunov's 1960/61 excerpt translates Greek α (I.15–26, 30–41), not JV and not Book III.
- The ru.wikipedia "List of surviving works of classical Latin literature" ("Список сохранившихся произведений классической латинской литературы") and the article on the Alexander Romance ("История Александра Великого") mention JV only descriptively.
I could not run a full-text search of elibrary.ru, because it needs a login.
verification.en_found:
The only published English translation is an excerpt from Book I:
- E. S. DeAngeli, "Julius Valerius' Account of the Birth of Alexander: Text and Translation", in P. G. Beidler (ed.), John Gower's Literary Transformations in the Confessio Amantis, Washington DC: University Press of America, 1982, pp. 119–41. It is facing-page Latin/English of the Nectanebo and birth episode (https://gower.lib.utsa.edu/items/show/9086).
- Nothing from Book III has been published in English. Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great (1994/2012) includes no JV; I checked its table of contents (dandelon PDF): Letter to Aristotle (Latin Epistola), Wonders of the East, George the Monk, Palladius, Alexander and Dindimus, Journey to Paradise, plus appendices. McCrindle's Ancient India (1901) translates Palladius from the Greek, not JV.
- New finding that refutes "no English version exists" in the strict sense: C. T. Djurslev, in H. Wulfram (ed.), Der lateinische 'Alexanderroman' des Iulius Valerius (De Gruyter, Millennium-Studien 101, 2023, open access), p. 175 n. 5, reports via Gavin Kelly an UNPUBLISHED English translation of Julius Valerius made for Cecil Rhodes in the 1890s. It is held at Groote Schuur, Cape Town, and he mentions an initiative to digitise it. I found no online copy and no publication, and its completeness is not stated.
- Short passages are quoted and translated in English-language studies (e.g. Wulfram 2018; the English chapters in Wulfram 2023). These are quotations, not translations.
- The colleague's EN "partial" should be downgraded to "excerpts only": one Book I episode in print, nothing from Book III.
verification.other_found:
Wulfram 2023 (Einleitung, p. 3 and n. 10; open access PDF at archive.org/details/oapen-20.500.12657-63846) counts exactly four published first translations: three French and one Italian. That implies no complete German, English or Spanish translation as of 2023.

FRENCH (all complete):
- I. Brenez, Julius Valérius et le corpus alexandrin du IVe siècle: présentation et traduction, unpublished doctoral thesis, Metz 2003, translation at pp. 45–417 (theses.fr/2003METZ014L).
- J.-P. Callu, Julius Valère, Roman d'Alexandre, Brepols 2010 (Recherches sur les rhétoriques religieuses 12), Latin and French; translation at pp. 40–217.
- F. Foubert, La geste d'Alexandre le Grand. Version latine de Julius Valerius, Peeters, Leuven/Paris/Walpole MA 2014; translation at pp. 31–166.

- T. Gargiulo in R. Stoneman and T. Gargiulo, Il Romanzo di Alessandro, Fondazione Valla/Mondadori. Vol. I (2007) gives JV Book I at pp. 356–463; vol. II (2012) gives Book II at pp. 300–373. The Valla catalogue pages say each volume pairs the Greek recensions with the parallel Latin text of Giulio Valerio.
- Vol. III, which would contain Book III, is still unpublished. The Valla catalogue (2026) lists only vols. I–II, and the Stoneman obituary in Karanos 8/2025 calls vol. III "still forthcoming". Stoneman died in 2025.

GERMAN: no translation. Bohmhammel's Berlin dissertation (2008) is a study, not a translation. Wulfram 2023 contains German chapters that quote and translate short passages of Book III (Steinmann on III.17; Schöffberger on Candace, III.18–24).

SPANISH: none found. Conde Salazar's work is linguistic.
verification.source_text:
Best open text: digilibLT DLT000319 (https://digiliblt.uniupo.it/teidocs/idno/DLT000319; TEI-XML at /teidocs/idno/DLT000319/format/xml). It is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 3.0 IT and follows M. Rosellini, Iuli Valeri Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis translatae ex Aesopo Graeco, adhibitis schedis R. Calderan, editio correctior cum addendis, Munich and Leipzig: Saur 2004 (first edition Teubner 1993; DOI 10.1515/9783110956207). I checked that it contains all of Book III (Porus, Candace and so on).

Public-domain fallback for control and quotation: B. Kübler, Leipzig: Teubner 1888.
- archive.org/details/iulivalerialexan00vale
- archive.org/details/iulivalerialexa00kbgoog
- archive.org/details/iulivalerialexa00valegoog
- HathiTrust record 001810318
Cite by Kroll book and chapter, plus Rosellini's line numbers within each book. Rosellini 2004 is the standard critical text; Kübler's is outdated.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate. Book III has no Russian or English translation and no published Italian one, since Valla vol. III is still forthcoming; only the three French versions exist. Start with III.17, the long Letter to Aristotle about India (much fuller than ms. A of the Greek, and directly relevant to the Epistola and Armenian traditions), or with the Candace episode III.18–24. The death and testament section, III.30–35, can follow. Verification needs only Latin and Greek, with Kroll's α, the Armenian version in Wolohojian's English, and Callu's and Foubert's French as controls. Two caveats: JV's mannered late Latin will need close human review, and the unpublished Rhodes English typescript and Valla vol. III should be watched.

verification.title: Iulii Valerii Epitome ('Zacher Epitome'; Эпитома Юлия Валерия / Эпитома Цахера), anonymous Latin abridgement of Julius Valerius' Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis, 9th century or earlier
verification.ru_found: I could not refute the "none" claim and found no Russian translation, whole or partial. Searches I ran: «Эпитома Юлия Валерия» (exact phrase, no results); «Юлий Валерий эпитома Александр перевод»; «"Юлия Валерия" александрия латинская извлечение»; «эпитома Цахера Александр»; «"Юлий Валерий" "Res gestae Alexandri" перевод»; site:facetia.ru Юлий Валерий; and a check of Gorelov 2006. What I checked: (1) facetia.ru/alexander-romances: it describes the epitome (9th c. or earlier, more widely read than the full Julius Valerius) but gives no Russian translation; facetia.ru/historia-de-preliis-alexandri-magni mentions Julius Valerius only as the earlier translator. (2) Gorelov's «Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого» (СПб.: Азбука-классика, 2006), per facetia.ru/povest-o-rozhdenii-i-pobedah-aleksandra-velikogo: Leo's Nativitas from the Bamberg manuscript, the Brahman texts (Commonitorium Palladii, Collatio), the Epistola ad Aristotelem and later medieval episodes. It contains no Julius Valerius and no Epitome. (3) О.Н. Блескина, «Латинские "Александрии": истоки и версии (по материалам российских книгохранилищ)», кандидатская диссертация, СПбГУ, 2000 (summary at cheloveknauka.com/latinskie-aleksandrii-istoki-i-versii). It names Julius Valerius and the 9th-century Epitome as sources and cites Zacher 1867, but contains no translation. The only Russian translation of a Latin Alexander text it lists is Kopievsky's early-18th-c. Curtius. (4) No hits on cyberleninka or ru.wikisource either. A Ukrainian hit (Lakhmotova, Kharkiv) turned out to be a false match on the patronymic «Юлия Валериевна».
verification.en_found: There is no real English translation. One item looks like a counter-example but is not. Arlima (arlima.net/il/julii_valerii_epitome.html, updated 2 Apr 2022) lists under "Traductions modernes – en anglais": Robert Steele, The Story of Alexander, drawn by Fred Mason (London: David Nutt, 1894). I read it (archive.org/details/storyofalexander00steeuoft). It is a free retelling for a child, framed as "An Open Letter" to "My dear Gracie", and names no source. Its chapters include material that is not in the Zacher Epitome: the visit to Jerusalem, the 'Foray of Kadesh' (= Fuerre de Gadres), Gog and Magog, the flight into the air and the dive under the sea, the Trees of the Sun and Moon, and 'Candoyl's wife'. That puts it in the Historia de preliis / medieval-romance tradition, so it is not a translation of the Epitome, and Arlima's listing is misleading. Other English anthologies checked: (1) Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (I.B. Tauris, contents page via dandelon). It has the Epistola ad Aristotelem, Pharasmanes, an excerpt from George the Monk, Palladius, the Alexander–Dindimus correspondence, the Iter ad Paradisum, two papyri and Middle English excerpts. No Epitome. (2) Kratz, The Romances of Alexander (Garland 1991; Open Library OL1865368M). It has HdP J1 complete, J2/J3 excerpts, the Epistola, the Iter and Leo of Naples. No Epitome. (3) Siemoneit 2023 (open-access chapter, see other_found) describes the Epitome as "von der modernen Forschung bislang weitgehend vernachlässigt" and cites no translation. English searches run: "Zacher" epitome "Julius Valerius" translation; "Zacher Epitome" translated; "Julii Valerii epitome" English; "Epitome of Julius Valerius" translation/thesis; plus searches for the Kratz and Stoneman contents. The only hits were Zacher 1867 reprints and scans, the Wikipedia redirect to Res gestae Alexandri Macedonis, and the Siemoneit chapter.
verification.other_found: No modern translation into French, German, Italian or Spanish found. Searches: German "Zacher-Epitome" Übersetzung; Italian epitome "Giulio Valerio" traduzione Zacher; French "épitomé de Julius Valerius" traduction. A Dialnet hit was only an index entry for Siemoneit's chapter. Fondazione Valla, Callu 2010 and Rosellini 2004 cover Julius Valerius, not the Epitome. There is one medieval vernacular translation: the Middle French prose L'ystoire du fort roy Alexandre (probably 15th c.). Per Arlima (/eh/fort_roy_alexandre_ystoire_du.html) it translates the Epitome together with the Epistola ad Aristotelem, survives in a single manuscript (Brussels, KBR 11104-11105), and has no edition and no modern translation. Main recent study: J. Gabriel Siemoneit, "Die Zacher-Epitome. Änderungen, Erweiterungen, Auslassungen", in H. Wulfram (ed.), Der lateinische ›Alexanderroman‹ des Iulius Valerius (De Gruyter 2023), pp. 199–219, DOI 10.1515/9783111091679-012, open access under CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. Points from it: Ross 1956 and Voorbij 1984 count 80 manuscripts, not the ~67 given in the sweep; Arlima also lists 80. The oldest manuscript is early 9th c. The related Oxford Epitome is edited by Cillié 1905 and the Montpellier Epitome by Hilka, RF 29 (1911). Zacher's manuscripts never call the text an epitome. Siemoneit compares it with Rosellini's text of Julius Valerius. Sweep corrections: the manuscript count is 80; Steele 1894 is a retelling, not a translation; the Middle French translation should be added.
verification.source_text: Base text: Julii Valerii epitome, zum ersten Mal herausgegeben von Julius Zacher (Halle: Waisenhaus, 1867). Public domain. Scans: archive.org/details/juliivaleriiepi00zachgoog; HathiTrust; Phaidra Belgrade, phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:583 (CC BY 2.0 AT, 6.1 MB PDF). Best working text: a CC0 XML/TEI transcription of Zacher 1867 by Gabriel Siemoneit (2023), github.com/qlat/zacher-epitome (file julii_valerii_epitome.xml, about 70 KB). It is in three books of about 45 numbered chapters and has no apparatus. My rough estimate from the file size is about 8–10k Latin words; a quick automated check gave a much higher figure, so the length needs a proper count. Supporting texts: Rosellini's Julius Valerius (Teubner 1993/2004, under copyright) to show what the epitomator changed; Kübler 1888 for a public-domain Julius Valerius. There is still no modern critical edition of the Epitome, so Zacher's text rests on a few of the 80 manuscripts; flag this in the commentary.
verification.recommendation: A strong candidate: the most widely copied Latin Alexander text before the 12th century (80 MSS), with no Russian and no real English translation (Steele 1894 is a children's retelling, not a translation). It has a CC0 TEI text, needs only Latin, and is short. Start with Book I (Nectanebo to Alexander's accession), printed side by side with the matching Julius Valerius passages and noting the epitomator's changes as Siemoneit 2023 does.

verification.ru_found: The colleague's RU "none" claim is REFUTED in part, for one excerpt. Roman Hautala's anthology prints the Latin original of one fragment with a Russian translation and commentary: Р. Хаутала, «От "Давида, царя Индий" до "ненавистного плебса сатаны". Антология ранних латинских сведений о татаро-монголах» (Казань: Институт истории им. Ш. Марджани АН РТ, серия «Язма Мирас / Textual Heritage», вып. 2, 2015, 496 с.), pp. ~150–152. XIII века» (2020, cyberleninka.ru/article/n/mongolskie-zavoevateli-glazami-evropeytsev-30-40-h-gg-xiii-veka) cites this fragment by title and page in its source list. (2) Гиниятуллина Л.С., review in «Золотоордынское обозрение» 2016 №1, pp. 229–232 (cyberleninka.ru/article/n/novaya-kniga-roman-hautala-...), confirms that each of the anthology's 91 fragments comes with its Latin text and a Russian translation with commentary. I did not see the book itself. No other Russian translation was found. Searches with no hits: CyberLeninka for Квиликин / Квиличино / Квиликино / Квилихин / Кюиликин / «Сполето Александр»; facetia.ru for Квиликин / Квиликино / Квиличино / Quilichinus (its Historia de preliis page has only Gorelov's Leo translation and Blëskina's 2003 survey); vostlit.info K-index (no Kvilikino entry); ru.wikipedia (no article). Russian name forms used in the literature: «Квиликино из Сполето» or «Квиликин Сполетский».
verification.en_found: No English translation of the work, full or partial, was found. Evidence for "none": (1) Pacini's blurb for Bernardinello's 2021 Italian calls it "the first translation in a modern language" (pacinieditore.it/prodotto/quilichino-spoleto-storia-di-alessandro-magno/). (2) ARLIMA (arlima.net/qt/quilichino_da_spoleto/historia_alexandri_magni.html, updated 15 July 2026) lists "Traductions modernes: ∅"; it even misses Bernardinello, so its silence is weak evidence. (3) English scholarship found through archive.org full-text search discusses or quotes the poem without translating it: Cary, The Medieval Alexander (1956); Stoneman's survey chapters in Alexander the Great (2008) and in Zuwiyya ed., A Companion to Alexander Literature in the Middle Ages (2011); Latin Fiction (1999); P. Jackson, The Mongols and the West (2005/2018), which only says Quilichinus was the first to use 'Tartars'. Hautala's English articles in Golden Horde Review (2015, 2019) paraphrase the passage. A.R. Anderson, Alexander's Gate, Gog and Magog, and the Inclosed Nations (1932), pp. 74–78, quotes the Latin of the Tartars passage ('Gentes immundas, quae Tartara turba vocatur, / Post hoc rex magnus clausit in arta loca…'). The archive.org copy is restricted, so I could not check whether Anderson also translates it. Related but not this text: Kratz, The Romances of Alexander (Garland 1991; Routledge reissue 2025, DOI 10.4324/9781003682912) translates J1 in full plus excerpts of J2 and of the prose J3, Quilichinus' source. This also corrects the earlier sweep's 'Kratz = J1 only'. Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great does not include Quilichinus.
verification.other_found: Italian: Lorenzo Bernardinello, «Quilichino da Spoleto. Storia di Alessandro Magno» (Pisa/Ospedaletto: Pacini, «Scrittori latini dell'Europa medioevale» 15, 2021, 328 pp., ISBN 978-88-6995-938-7), Latin with facing Italian translation, introduction and notes. The year is 2021, not c. 2024 as the sweep had it. It is the only complete modern translation found; not open access. Medieval adaptations (not modern translations): Domenico Scolari, Istoria di Alessandro Magno (Italian ottava rima, 1355); 'Der Grosse Alexander' / Wernigerode Alexander (German verse, late 14th c.), ed. G. Guth, DTM 13, Berlin: Weidmann 1908 (public domain, archive.org: dergrossealexan00guthgoog / DerGrosseAlexanderGuthDTM13), studied by Neuling 1884/1885. German and French: no modern translation found. Kirsch's edition is Latin only. German scholarship (Pfister 1911/12; Schmieder, Europa und die Fremden, p. 259 n. 327, cited by Jackson) quotes the Latin; I did not check whether Schmieder gives a German rendering. Spanish: nothing found. Scholarship: Pfister, 'Die Historia de preliis und das Alexanderepos des Quilichinus', Münchener Museum 1 (1911/12) 249–301; Kirsch, 'Quilichinus oder Terrisius?', Philologus 117 (1973); Gärtner, RHT 30 (2000) 263–276; Ferri 1936/1957; Thomson, Speculum 10 (1935) on the Preconia (now given to Terrisio di Atina); entry 'Quilichinus Spoletinus' in the Encyclopedia of the Medieval Chronicle.
verification.source_text: No complete public-domain text exists. (1) The only full critical edition is W. Kirsch, Quilichinus de Spoleto, Historia Alexandri Magni, nebst dem Text der Zwickauer Handschrift der Historia de preliis, Rezension I3 (Skopje: Živa antika, Posebni izdanija 4, 1971). ARLIMA gives lxiii + 337 pp.; the LC/Open Library record says 256 pp. It is not online. The edited Latin text may no longer be protected under the short terms for scholarly editions (DE §70 UrhG: 25 years; IT art. 85-quater: 20 years), but the introduction and apparatus are protected, and the place of publication (Skopje) complicates things, so get a rights check before using it. (2) Bernardinello 2021 (Pacini) prints Latin with facing Italian; it is under copyright, but useful as a cross-check. (3) Public-domain partial sources: Pfister 1911/12 in Münchener Museum f. Philol. d. MA 1, 249–301, which has extensive Latin excerpts from the Heidelberg MS (archive.org/details/MuenchenerMuseum1, full text open), and Endlicher 1832 (Jahrbücher der Literatur 57). (4) ARLIMA lists 20 manuscripts (e.g. Heidelberg Sal. 8,29b; Vat. Pal. lat. 327; BnF lat. 8501; Cambridge UL Gg.1.34; Bodl. 496/844; Berlin lat. qu. 518). Some are probably digitized (Heidelberg/Palatina, Gallica), but bot-protection pages stopped me from confirming which. A text built afresh from a digitized manuscript checked against Kirsch would be the cleanest legal route. The J3 prose source is in Kirsch 1971 (Zwickau MS) and Steffens 1975.
verification.recommendation: A strong candidate: no English translation, only one short Russian excerpt (Hautala 2015), a manageable c. 3,914-verse Latin poem, and verification needs only medieval Latin, with Bernardinello's Italian as a check. Start with the prologue (the four kingdoms and Maccabees frame) plus the Gog-Magog/'Tartara turba' section and the closing 'De dictatore' sphragis with its Frederick II/Cortenuova revision, since these are what historians most need. Settle the rights question for the Kirsch 1971 text first, or build the text from a digitized manuscript.
