verification.title: Historia de preliis Alexandri Magni, recension J2 ("Orosius recension"), with J3 interpolations / «История битв (сражений) Александра Великого», ред. J2
verification.ru_found:
No complete or substantial Russian translation of J2 or J3 turned up. The only Russian material is three short episodes in N. Gorelov (ed. and trans.), «Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого» (СПб.: Азбука-классика, 2006), Part 3, «Средневековые истории об Александре Великом», online at facetia.ru:
(a) «Александр достигает высот неба и глубин моря», about 1,100 words. No recension is named, but a footnote says the animals-under-water detail «содержится в одном из списков версии J2» (https://facetia.ru/node/2837).
(b) «Александр и города Сирии», about 1,400 words: the siege of Tyre, the floating tower and Jaddus. No source is given. Gorelov's introduction credits J3 with adding the capture of Tyre and Sidon, so this is probably J3 (same page).
(c) «Александр и василиск» quotes an HdP passage of about 1,100 words. It is explicitly credited to «История сражений Александра Великого. XIII в.», the «новая, дополненная редакция», i.e. J3 (https://facetia.ru/node/3721).
Correction to the sweep: Gorelov's «Александр и племена Гога и Магога» does not come from the HdP. It is Peter Comestor's Historia scholastica (Esther, ch. 5) plus the Latin Pseudo-Methodius (https://facetia.ru/node/3722). No separate HdP Jerusalem piece was found on facetia either. The main HdP text in Gorelov is Leo's Nativitas from the Bamberg MS, not J2 (https://facetia.ru/historia-de-preliis-alexandri-magni).
Also checked, with nothing found: vostlit.info author indexes (А, Л), ru.wikisource and ru.wikipedia searches, and facetia site searches («preliis», «Гог Магог», «Иерусалима», «первосвященник», «города Сирии»). The Russian «Александрии» (Serbian and Chronograph) come from the Greek. Per ru.wikipedia, the Polish HdP derivatives were translated from Czech versions and did not significantly influence the Russian tradition.
verification.en_found:
The only English J2/J3 material is in Dennis M. Kratz, The Romances of Alexander (Garland 1991). It was reissued by Routledge in 2016 (DOI 10.4324/9781315056494) and again in 2025 (ISBN 9781003682912). Crossref chapter metadata for the 2025 reissue gives:
- J1 recension, complete: pp. 1–82 (10.4324/9781003682912-2)
- "Historia de Preliis: J2 (Excerpts)": only pp. 83–88 (10.4324/9781003682912-3)
- "Historia de Preliis: J3 (Excerpts)": pp. 89–106 (10.4324/9781003682912-4)
- Also the Epistola ad Aristotelem and the Iter ad Paradisum.
R. Telfryn Pritchard, The History of Alexander's Battles: Historia de preliis, the J1 Version (Toronto: PIMS, 1992; archive.org/details/historyofalexand0000leoa) is J1 only.
Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (2012; Crossref chapter list) has no HdP. It contains the Letter to Aristotle, Wonders of the East, George the Monk, Palladius, Dindimus and the Journey to Paradise.
The base narrative that J2 and J3 share is therefore available in English twice through J1. What is missing is J2's Orosian restructuring and inserts (6 pp. of excerpts) and most of the J3 additions (18 pp.). The Middle English Wars of Alexander (ed. Skeat 1886) is a medieval adaptation, not a modern translation.
verification.other_found:
GERMAN (the main risk to the "untranslated" claim): Wolfgang Kirsch, «Historie von Alexander dem Großen», «aus dem Mittellateinischen», Reclam Leipzig (RUB 625). The first edition is 1975, not 1978 as the sweep said; reprints followed in 1978, 1981 and 1984, plus a Röderberg licensed edition (Frankfurt, 1984). The same translation was reissued as «Das Buch von Alexander, dem edlen und weisen König von Makedonien. Mit den Miniaturen der Leipziger Handschrift» (Reclam Leipzig / Büchergilde, 1991). It was then republished as «Der mittellateinische Alexanderroman. Die Geschichte der Kämpfe Alexanders des Großen. Lateinisch/Deutsch», newly revised by Lennart Gilhaus (Hiersemann, Mittellateinische Bibliothek, 2020; XII+248 pp.; TOC d-nb.info/1214661335/04: Books I–III complete).
Recension NOT verified. The catalogue note says "translation of Leo's Latin... and various versions and interpolations which appeared in the 11th–13th centuries". One indication points to J2: the 1991 miniatures come from Leipzig Rep. II 4° 143, which Hilka 1920 lists as J2 MS "L" ("Zahlreiche Miniaturen italienischen Ursprungs"). Jan Cölln reviewed the 2020 edition in Editionen in der Kritik 12 (2024); I could not access it. Check this before claiming that no modern-language translation exists.
ITALIAN: Boitani, Bologna, Cipolla and Liborio (eds.), Alessandro nel Medioevo occidentale (Fondazione Valla/Mondadori, 1997) is an anthology with Italian translations. It possibly includes HdP excerpts, but I could not get its contents list.
FRENCH, SPANISH: no modern translation found. The Old French prose Roman d'Alexandre (ed. Hilka 1920), the Italian volgarizzamenti, the Czech Kronika and the Polish Historyja (1510) are medieval or early-modern vernacular adaptations.

verification.source_text:
Public domain, J2: Alfons Hilka, Der altfranzösische Prosa-Alexanderroman nach der Berliner Bilderhandschrift nebst dem lateinischen Original der Historia de preliis (Rezension J2), Halle: Niemeyer, 1920 (archive.org/details/deraltfranzsis00pseuuoft; US public domain).
- It gives "den bloßen Text von J2" without the variant apparatus, mainly from M1 (Munich), with ten MSS listed, including L = Leipzig Rep. II 4° 143.
- According to the AI summary of the scanned introduction (the scan was not read directly), Hilka places the "Gogh et Machgogh" (gentes inclusae) passage only in the expanded Breslau MS Br4. Check this, because the candidate description treats Gog–Magog as a core J2 episode.
Critical edition (in copyright): Hilka, Historia Alexandri Magni (Historia de preliis), Rezension J2 (Orosius-Rezension), Teil 1, ed. H.-J. Bergmeister (Meisenheim: Hain, 1976, 217 pp.) and Teil 2, ed. R. Grossmann (1977, XVII+201 pp.).
J3 (in copyright): K. Steffens, Die Historia de preliis Alexandri Magni, Rezension J3 (1975; archive.org lending copy only, diehistoriadepre0000leoa); W. Kirsch 1971 (Zwickau MS of J3, printed with Quilichinus).
Synopsis: Bergmeister 1975 (Books I–II).
Not useful as a J2 base: Zingerle 1885 (archive.org/details/diequellenzumalexanderde, public domain) prints the Graz MS, which is normally classed as J1. A public-domain J3 would need an incunable or MS facsimile; not verified.
verification.recommendation: A good candidate for Russian and nearly untranslated in English: Russian has only about 3,600 words of Gorelov excerpts (mostly J3), and English has 6 pp. of J2 and 18 pp. of J3 in Kratz. Before publishing, check what Kirsch's German (1975; Latin/German 2020) actually translates. Start with J2 Book I from Hilka 1920, prioritising the Orosius-derived inserts; that needs Latin expertise only.

verification.en_found:
The "full" claim holds.
1) Full translation: Iolo Davies, "Alexander's Itinerary (Itinerarium Alexandri): An English Translation", Ancient History Bulletin 12 (1998), pp. 29–54. I confirmed it in AHB's own back-issue list, which sells it as a $1 PDF (https://ancienthistorybulletin.org/volume-11-15-purchases/). The German and English Wikipedia bibliographies cite it the same way. I found no free online copy.
2) An extra find the sweep missed: a public-domain partial translation. J. W. McCrindle, "Ancient India as Described in Classical Literature" (Westminster 1901), Section VII, "The Itinerary of Alexander the Great". It translates only the Indian chapters, c. 103/104–117 in Mai/Müller numbering (the first number is printed "108", apparently a typo). It runs from the recrossing of the Hindu Kush to the return to Babylon, with notes. Full text: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/Ancient_India_as_Described_in_Classical_Literature/Section_7
3) Possible excerpts I could not confirm:
- Dodgeon & Lieu, "The Roman Eastern Frontier and the Persian Wars AD 226–363" (1991), p. 385. English Wikipedia cites this page for the text, probably for the preface to Constantius. Google Books showed no text.
- Heckel & Yardley, "Alexander the Great: Historical Sources in Translation" (2004), p. xxvi. This looks like a discussion of the source in the introduction, not a translated excerpt; Google Books blocked access behind a CAPTCHA.
4) Stoneman, "Legends of Alexander the Great" (1994/2012) does not include it. I checked the table of contents in the Internet Archive record legendsofalexand0000unse.
verification.other_found:
- Italian, full: Raffaella Tabacco, "Itinerarium Alexandri. Testo, apparato critico, introduzione, traduzione e commento" (Firenze: Olschki, 2000; Univ. di Torino, Fondo di studi Parini-Chirio, Filologia n.s. 1). LIV + 270 pp., ISBN 88-222-4920-8. The Italian and German Wikipedia records confirm the translation is included. Tabacco's preparatory studies: Bollettino di Studi Latini 17 (1987) 77–120; "Per una nuova edizione dell'Itinerarium Alexandri" (Bologna 1992); a 1996 paper on the sententiae.
- French: none found. Persée has 33 hits, all studies, e.g. H. Tonnet, Revue d'Histoire des Textes 9 (1979) 243–254, and J.-P. Callu, Littérales 2 (1999) 33–50.
- German: none found. There is H.-J. Hausmann's critical edition (Köln dissertation, 1970), with no translation evident; M. Fuhrmann covers the text in HLL 5 (1989) §540.2.
- Spanish: none found on Dialnet.
- Not checked: Regesta Imperii OPAC (blocked by bot protection); Google Books for Heckel–Yardley (CAPTCHA).
verification.source_text:
The text survives in a single manuscript, Ambrosianus P 49 sup. (11th c.), which also contains Julius Valerius; the Itinerarium breaks off at the end.
Best public-domain edition: D. Volkmann, "Itinerarium Alexandri" (Einladungsprogramm Schulpforta, Naumburg: H. Sieling, 1871). It is based on Studemund's complete new collation of the Ambrosianus. Scan, PDF and OCR text: https://archive.org/details/itinerariumalexa00unse
Supplementary notes: "Ad Itinerarium Alexandri" (Naumburg 1877), https://archive.org/details/aditinerariumale00unse
Other public-domain editions:
- A. Mai's editio princeps (Milan 1817): https://archive.org/details/itinerarivmalex00alexgoog
- Frankfurt 1818 reprint: https://archive.org/details/itinerariumalexa00maiauoft
- C. Müller's appendix to the Dübner Arrian (Paris: Didot 1846/1865), using Mai/Müller chapter numbering: https://archive.org/details/anabasisetindica00arri
The current critical edition is Tabacco 2000, which is under copyright. Use it only to check readings, and base the translation on Volkmann.
verification.recommendation: A good Russian-first candidate: the text is short (about 32 pp. in Volkmann), in late-antique Latin only, so no extra language expertise is needed beyond Arrian's Greek for the parallel commentary. Its value for English readers is limited, because full English (Davies 1998) and Italian (Tabacco 2000) translations already exist, plus McCrindle's public-domain Indian chapters. Translate the whole text from Volkmann 1871, starting with a pilot unit: the dedicatory preface to Constantius II and the opening chapters, paired with an Arrian parallel commentary.

verification.source_text:
- **Public domain:** F. A. W. Mueldener (Müldener), M. Philippi Gualtheri ab Insulis dicti de Castellione Alexandreis. Leipzig: Teubner, 1863. Archive.org scans: https://archive.org/details/walterofchatillonalexandreised.mueldener1863 (Public Domain Mark 1.0); also alexandreisadfi00waltgoog and bub_gb_ayfxmVkdnlkC. Migne's PL 209 (1855) is also public domain but a weaker text.

- **Most recent text (in copyright):** M. Lehmann, De Gruyter / Sammlung Tusculum, 2023.

- The Latin Library has only Walter's lyric poems, not the Alexandreis.
verification.recommendation: A weak candidate under priority 2, but it does fill a real Russian gap. Full translations already exist in English (Pritchard 1986 prose; Townsend 1996 verse; Jolly's 1968 dissertation), German (Streckenbach 1990/2012; Lehmann 2023), Spanish (Pejenaute Rubio 1998) and Italian (Bernardinello 2019). Russian has only the 1972 excerpts of about 370 lines. "Books I and X" is the worst possible starting unit: the 1972 Russian selection comes almost entirely from those two books, so starting there would largely re-translate it. If the project takes this on, plan a complete Russian Alexandreis and start with a book the 1972 selection does not touch (any of Books II–IX, each about 450–550 lines). Checking requires only Latin.

verification.title: Le Roman d'Alexandre en prose (Old French Prose Alexander, 13th c.; vernacular rendering of Historia de preliis J2)
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, either full or partial. I could not run any new web searches (the search budget was used up). I checked ru.wikipedia instead: the article «Роман об Александре» only names the Old Russian Alexandria (Литпамятники 1965), and searches for «Historia de preliis» and «Александре в прозе» turned up nothing relevant. I also checked facetia.ru: the searches «Александрия» and «Александре» list only Slavic versions, Pseudo-Callisthenes, Alexandre de Paris, Lamprecht and Gorelov. Gorelov, «Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого» (Азбука-классика 2006), needs a caveat. Its appendix «Средневековые истории об Александре Великом» (facetia.ru/node/2837) contains Russian versions of two episodes that the Prose Alexander also tells. One is the griffin flight and diving bell, with a note citing a J2 manuscript. The other is the Syria–Tyre–Gaza sequence: Meleager's foraging raid, Sarison, «Битурий», «Валаам», the grape dream. Gorelov presents these as Latin (Historia de preliis / J3) material. The only Old French in the book is Lambert le Tort's verse prologue, quoted in the introduction. So the book overlaps in content with the Prose Alexander but does not translate it.
verification.en_found: I found no English translation. ARLIMA (https://www.arlima.net/eh/historia_de_proeliis_alexandri_magni/fr_roman_d_alexandre_en_prose.html) lists «Traductions modernes: ∅». The English Wikipedia article 'Roman d'Alexandre en prose' lists only the Hilka 1920 and Otaka et al. 2003/2008 editions. Open Library and archive.org show only unrelated works: the Thornton Middle English Prose Alexander, which derives from Latin J3 (Chappell 1992), and Magoun 1926. Limitation: I could not run web searches, and Crossref, OpenAlex and Google Books were rate-limited or unavailable. Short English excerpts in studies, exhibition catalogues or BL blog posts therefore cannot be ruled out.

verification.source_text: A. Hilka, Der altfranzösische Prosa-Alexanderroman nach der Berliner Bilderhandschrift nebst dem lateinischen Original der Historia de Preliis (Rezension J2), Halle: Niemeyer 1920 (Slatkine reprint 1974). There is no Russian or English translation, and the only full modern translation is Japanese (2008), of the Royal 15 E VI version rather than Hilka's Berlin text, so a RU+EN translation of Hilka's text would be a first in any European language. Start with a self-contained block of Hilka 1920: Book I (Nectanebus to youth), or the J2 Syria–Tyre–Jerusalem section, printed against Hilka's Latin J2. Flag that checking the translation needs Old French expertise, not just Greek and Latin.

verification.ru_found:
"RU none" is refuted, but only for short excerpts from other branches. Nothing from Branch IV was found in Russian.
(1) facetia.ru, «Александр Парижский. Роман об Александре» (https://facetia.ru/alexandre-de-bernay-romance-of-alexander): a facing-text line-by-line Russian translation by Марина Лущенко of Branch III, vv. 422–499 (Alexander's descent into the sea in the glass barrel). The OF text and translation are given laisse by laisse. The page credits russianplanet.ru/filolog as its source (Cloudflare blocked access, so I could not see the original). It looks like amateur or student work.
(2) N. Горелов (ed./tr.), «Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого», СПб.: Азбука-классика, 2006 («Пер. с лат. и ст.-фр.»). The introduction has a Russian prose rendering of the OF prologue laisse that lists the poem's episodes and names «клирик из Шастиодуна Ламберт ли Тор» (https://facetia.ru/povest-o-rozhdenii-i-pobedah-aleksandra-velikogo). This is presumably the opening of Branch I in the vulgate; I identified it from content, not checked against Armstrong. I checked the rest of the anthology: its sky and sea episodes are from Latin HdP (J2 is cited), and the Aristotle story is from Jacques de Vitry. So nothing else in it comes from the French poem.
Russian scholarship discusses the poem without translating it: А. Д. Михайлов, «Французский рыцарский роман» (1976), ch. 1 (facetia.ru/node/3644); Грабарь-Пассек 1966, ch. 8 (facetia.ru/node/3654); ru.wikipedia «Роман об Александре». I checked all three: paraphrase only, no translated passages.
Caveat: the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so I could not check Пуришев's «Хрестоматия по зарубежной литературе средних веков» or dissertations on elibrary.ru. The CyberLeninka API returned nothing relevant.
verification.en_found:
"EN none" is refuted. There is an abridged English translation of the whole poem: Alexandre de Paris, "The Romance of Alexander", translated by David Favager, Kindle edition (self-published), 30 March 2021, 457 pp., ASIN B091FQD8HV (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B091FQD8HV). Amazon lists Favager as "Translator". The blurb covers "the king's birth ... the campaign in India and his death in Babylon" and says: "For the first time an abridged translation of this important work is made available to English readers." So Branch IV is almost certainly covered in abridged form. Its source text, method (prose or verse) and accuracy are unknown, and it is not a scholarly translation. Favager's other listing is a modernisation of Lydgate's Troy Book, which suggests an independent non-academic translator. en.wikipedia "Roman d'Alexandre" also cites it: "Abbreviated translation into English: Favager, D.J. The Romance of Alexander Kindle (2021)".
Related but not the poem itself: Nigel Bryant (tr.), Jehan Wauquelin, "The Medieval Romance of Alexander: The Deeds and Conquests of Alexander the Great" (Boydell, 2019). This translates the 1448 prose reworking based largely on Alexandre de Paris. Arlima lists no English translation. I found no complete scholarly EN translation and no separate EN translation of Branch IV.

verification.source_text:
Public domain, full poem including Branch IV: H. Michelant (ed.), «Li romans d'Alixandre par Lambert li Tors et Alexandre de Bernay», Stuttgart: Bibliothek des Litterarischen Vereins 13, 1846. Archive.org: https://archive.org/details/liromansdalixand00lamb (also liromansdalixan00michgoog, bub_gb_kbELAAAAIAAJ). I checked the OCR: it includes the Antipater/Divinuspater poisoning. It is a non-critical text, so the numbering does not match Armstrong.
Standard critical text: E. C. Armstrong, D. L. Buffum, B. Edwards, L. F. H. Lowe, «The Medieval French Roman d'Alexandre», vol. II: «Version of Alexandre de Paris: Text», Princeton (Elliott Monographs 37), 1937. Notes to Branches III–IV are in vol. VII (A. Foulet, 1976). I could not verify the 1937 volume's US copyright status (renewal unknown), and I found no scan of vol. II on archive.org. Community uploads exist for vols III, IV/VI/VII and VI (archive.org ids "the-medieval-french-roman-dalexandre-iii", "mfra-v-vii", "mfra-vi"), but their rights status is unclear.

verification.recommendation: Still a good candidate for Russian: no Russian version of Branch IV exists, and the whole poem has only two short excerpts in Russian (Branch III 422–499 and the prologue). The English case is weaker, because Favager's 2021 self-published abridged Kindle version exists, though English still has no scholarly or complete translation. Start with Branch IV (Mort Alixandre, the shortest branch, roughly 1,600–1,700 lines; I did not verify the exact count). Note that its source is the anonymous Mort Alixandre, not Lambert le Tort or Eustache as the candidate entry says: Lambert le Tort is the source of Branch III and Eustache of Branch II. Verification needs Old French expertise, which goes beyond Greek and Latin.

verification.en_found: REFUTES "none". The source is Nigel Bryant (trans.), The Medieval Romance of Alexander: Jehan Wauquelin's The Deeds and Conquests of Alexander the Great (Woodbridge: D. S. (a) Appendix 3, "Jacques de Longuyon's excursus on the Nine Worthies [from Les Voeux du Paon], c.1310" (pp. 305–6), translated directly from the verse poem into English prose (https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/medieval-romance-of-alexander/jacques-de-longuyons-excursus-on-the-nine-worthies-from-les-voeux-du-paon-the-vows-of-the-peacock-c1310/3FDE41B85961D2389F1804FBB63254E1). That redaction is indirect and condensed, but it gives the whole plot in English: the killing of the peacock, the vows and their fulfilment. No complete English translation of the verse poem was found. Arlima's 'Traductions modernes' field is empty (∅), which confirms there is no full modern translation.
verification.other_found:
Modern: no published modern French, German, Italian or Spanish translation found. Searches covered French ("traduction", "français moderne"), German ("Übersetzung") and Italian ("Voti del pavone" traduzione). Hélène Bellon-Méguelle (Geneva) lists a critical edition for CFMA (Champion) as "en préparation" (her UNIGE page); it had an FNS grant 2010–12 and is unpublished. Medieval translations and adaptations (Arlima):
- Middle Scots: the Buik of Alexander (1438, attributed to Barbour) and Gilbert Hay's Buik of King Alexander, which includes the Avowis
- Middle Dutch: Roman van Cassamus
- Latin prose translation: Vatican, Archivio di San Pietro E 36 (Bellon-Méguelle & Châtelain 2013)
- French prose: Jean Wauquelin, Les fais et concquestes d'Alexandre (mid-15th c.), which is what Bryant 2012 translates
Other editions:
- Casey 1956: Columbia PhD, P redaction
- Magill 1964: Columbia PhD, Part I, MSS S–S6
- Cropp 2002: Romania 120, Neuf Preux verses
- M. R. James 1933: facsimile of Bodley 264
- fragment editions by Ham, La Du, Veneziale (2022) and Lebsanft (2024)
The manuscript tradition is large: Arlima lists 51 witnesses including fragments.
verification.source_text: R. L. Graeme Ritchie (ed.), The Buik of Alexander … together with the French originals ("Li fuerres de Gadres" and "Les voeux du paon") collated with numerous MSS, 4 vols, Scottish Text Society (Edinburgh & London: Blackwood, 1921–1929). The volumes are vol. I 1925, II 1921, III 1927, IV 1929. Archive.org scans uploaded by Arlima carry the Public Domain Mark: https://archive.org/details/thebuikofalexanderritchie1 (also …ritchie2, …ritchie3, …ritchie4). Ritchie lived 1880–1954, so the edition is public domain in the US (published before 1931) and in life+70 jurisdictions since 1 Jan 2025. The Old French text is printed facing the Scots and has a variant apparatus. Cropp 2002 (Romania 120, on Persée) is useful as a control text for the Neuf Preux stanzas, but it is not public domain. Casey 1956 (the P redaction) is useful for collation, also not public domain.
verification.recommendation: It is still a viable candidate, mainly for Russian. The only Russian rendering is an unpublished verse excerpt of the Nine Worthies stanzas, and no full translation of the verse poem exists in any modern language. EN status must be downgraded from "none" to "partial" because of Bryant 2012. Start with the peacock-killing and vow-banquet sequence from Ritchie's public-domain text rather than the Nine Worthies excursus, which is already in English (Bryant) and Russian (Ворошень). It is a medieval reception text, not antique, and checking it needs Old French expertise with Lorraine/Picard scripta, beyond Greek and Latin.

Kinzel, 'Lamprechts Alexander nach den drei Texten mit dem Fragment des Alberic von Besançon und den lateinischen Quellen' (Germanistische Handbibliothek 6, Halle: Waisenhaus, 1884, 636 pp.) is the best public-domain source. It is public domain and downloadable as PDF and text from archive.org: https://archive.org/details/lamprechtsalexan00lampuoft (also lamprechtsalexa00lampgoog and lamprechtsalexa00kinzgoog). - V: J. Diemer, 'Deutsche Gedichte des XI. und XII. Jahrhunderts', Wien 1849.
- S: H. F. Massmann, 'Deutsche Gedichte des zwölften Jahrhunderts', Quedlinburg 1837. This is effectively the only witness for S, because the Strasbourg manuscript was destroyed in 1870 (stated from memory, not checked in this session).
- B: R. M. Werner, 'Die Basler Bearbeitung von Lambrechts Alexander', BLVS 154, Tübingen 1881, at https://archive.org/details/diebaslerbearbe00werngoog.

The best first unit is a Russian translation of the Vorauer Alexander (1,532 vv., from Kinzel 1884 checked against Diemer). A possible next unit is the untranslated Basler Alexander (Werner 1881), if no translation of it turns up later. Checking either one needs a Middle High German specialist; Greek or Latin expertise alone is not enough.

verification.ru_found: No Russian translation found, not even an excerpt. I also searched the full text of ru.wikipedia. The only hit was alphapedia.ru, a machine-translated mirror of the English Wikipedia stub. Михайлов, «Французский рыцарский роман», 1976) for a short quoted passage. Those would at most be quotations, not a translation.
verification.en_found:
This refutes the sweep's 'EN none': an English excerpt does exist, although there is still no complete or substantial English translation.
(1) The prologue is published with facing English translation in J. Wogan-Browne, T. Fenster and D. W. Russell (eds.), Vernacular Literary Theory from the French of Medieval England: Texts and Translations, c.1120–c.1450 (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 2016; pb 2018). It is item 28, 'Thomas of Kent, Le Roman de toute chevalerie / Romance of the Best Chivalry (Alexander the Great)' [Dean 165], pp. 277ff., from Paris BnF fr. 24364. Appendix 7 of the same book covers the Kyng Alisaunder reflex of the prologue. I confirmed this from the publisher's preview PDF (api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781782048718_A42902621/…) and the UWA catalogue record.
(2) Scholarly studies quote passages in translation: Charles Russell Stone, The Roman de toute chevalerie: Reading Alexander Romance in Late Medieval England (University of Toronto Press, 2019), and Mary Franklin-Brown, 'The Monstrous Birth of Alexander the Great', JMEMS 49.3 (2019), which is open access in the Cambridge Apollo repository. I could not open either text, so I have not checked how much each one translates.
(3) There is no FRETS volume. The Online Medieval Sources Bibliography (medievalsourcesbibliography.org/sources.php?id=2146114644) lists no translation, and the French of England teaching bibliography lists only the ANTS edition.
(4) Arlima lists the Middle English Kyng Alisaunder (c.1300) under 'English translation'. That is a medieval adaptation, not a modern translation.
English searches: four general Bing queries ('… English translation', '"translated by"', excerpt/Candace, thesis/dissertation), plus targeted searches for FRETS, C. R. Stone, Vernacular Literary Theory and Stoneman. Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great (Everyman 1994) contains only Greek and Latin texts, so Thomas is not in it. The WebSearch tool was out of budget, so all searching went through the browser and Bing.

Matsumura in ZrP 2005). Arlima confirms it, and it is also in SUDOC and the National Library of Israel catalogue. I have not checked whether it prints the ANTS text on facing pages.
German, Italian, Spanish: no translation found. A combined search was uninformative because Bing returned translator-tool pages. The German items are source studies only, all on archive.org: J. verification.source_text:
The critical edition is The Anglo-Norman Alexander (Le Roman de toute chevalerie) by Thomas of Kent, ed. B. Foster with the assistance of I. Short, ANTS 29–33 (London, 1976–77). Vol. I is the text with variants; vol. II is introduction, notes and glossary. It is still in copyright. The Anglo-Norman Dictionary textbase (anglo-norman.net/textbase-browse/alexander) has it digitised, with ANTS permission covering browsing and searching only: 'Any other use … requires the prior written permission'. A full Neoscholia translation on this base would need ANTS permission; the archive.org copy (anglonormanalexa0000thom) is lending-only.
Public-domain alternatives:
(a) P. Meyer, Alexandre le Grand dans la littérature française du moyen âge, vol. I (Paris, 1886; archive.org id alexandrelegrand01meyeuoft), pp. c.177–235. This gives the table of rubrics from the Durham MS and 'Extraits d'après le ms. de Paris', which I checked in the archive.org OCR: the prologue, the mid-poem prologue where the poet names himself ('Thomas ai non de Kent'), and the death-of-Alexander finale, with the first lines of later laisses and concordances.
(b) The manuscripts: Paris BnF fr. 24364 (Gallica digitisation seen in image results, ark not checked); Cambridge Trinity College O.9.34; Durham Cathedral C.IV.27B; fragments in BL Add. 46701 and Bodl. Lat. misc. b.17.
Length per Arlima: 8,054 dodecasyllables in 546 monorhymed laisses.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong Russian-first candidate. There is no Russian translation at all and no full or substantial English one (only the prologue in Vernacular Literary Theory, 2016, plus quotations in studies), so an English version would also be new except for the prologue. The catch is the base text: the ANTS edition is copyrighted, so either ask ANTS for permission or start from a public-domain unit. I suggest starting with the Nectanabus/conception section that follows the prologue (Durham rubrics iii–viii), or with the Indian/Ethiopian marvels block that uses climate theory, transcribed from BnF fr. 24364 and checked against Meyer 1886. Verification needs an Anglo-Norman/Old French philologist, not a Greek or Latin one, and the Champion 2003 French translation can serve as a control.

name: Syriac, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Georgian, Hebrew/Jewish and Slavonic Alexander traditions
overview:
This strand is well covered in English and almost entirely missing in Russian. English has Budge's Syriac volume (1889: Romance, Legend and Song), his Ethiopic volume (1896), Wolohojian's Armenian (1969), several Hebrew versions (Gaster 1897, Kazis 1962, Reich 1972, van Bekkum 1992 and 1994) and Bowman's Josippon (2022). The Coptic fragments exist only in Lemm's German (1903) and an indirect amateur English web version (Colavito 2026). In French there is Debié's Syriac volume (2024).

Russian coverage is strong only for the Slavonic texts: the Serbian Alexandria (1965 and 2003), the Chronographic Alexandria (Tvorogov 1969 excerpts; Isachenko 2008 full commented translation) and «Тайная тайных» (Bulanin). Outside Slavonic there are a few isolated pieces: the Syriac Legend (Pigulevskaya 1958, full; confirmed from the scan), Harkavy's Hebrew Damascus version, and Orshansky's Talmudic legends (1867).

No Russian translation was found for: the Syriac Romance, the Song of Alexander, the Coptic fragments, the Armenian History (including the kafas), the Ethiopic texts, the Syriac original of Ps.-Methodius, the Alexander chapters of Josippon, Bonfils, the Old Czech Alexandreis, or the Georgian Aleksandriani.

The earlier lead "Darbinyan-Melikyan 1986" for the Armenian could not be confirmed. Her published Russian translations are other Armenian works, including Drasxanakertc'i (1984/1986); no Alexander title appears in her bibliography. Topchyan (2026) lists only Armenian editions and Wolohojian's English. A new Armenian critical edition appeared in 2025 (Muradyan and Topchyan, Matenadaran).

Caveat: the shared web-search quota ran out partway through. The later checks used direct reads of Wikipedia (ru/en/hy/ka/cs), facetia.ru, CyberLeninka, archive.org, OpenLibrary and phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs. Treat any "none" as "none found".

Hebrew "popular" Damascus Alexandria: A.Ya. Garkavi (Harkavy), 19th c.; reprinted in Косолобова (сост.), «Александр Великий в легендах и исследованиях Востока и Запада» (2000); facetia.ru/node/2964.

Talmudic legends: I.G. Orshansky, 1867.

Chronographic Alexandria (2nd redaction): Tvorogov, «Изборник» 1969 (abridged); T.A. Isachenko 2008, commented translation in the apparatus to the Лицевой летописный свод facsimile (ll. 587–797).

candidates.title: Tašʿītā d-Aleksandrōs: Syriac Alexander Romance / Сирийская версия «Романа об Александре» Псевдо-Каллисфена. Unit: Book I (chs. 1–47)
candidates.author: Anonymous Syriac translator from Greek (attributed to East Syrian Christian circles)
candidates.date: Early 7th c. (Debié 2024); 6th–7th c. in older scholarship
candidates.size: 3 books, 85 chs. (47+14+24); Budge's English runs pp. 1–143 (about 45–50k words, estimate). Book I is about 18k words (estimate).
candidates.edition: Budge 1889, Syriac text with English, public domain: archive.org/details/BudgeSyriacAlexander; phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:727. No newer critical edition found; Debié 2024 is a French translation and study.
candidates.ru_evidence: Pigulevskaya (Палестинский сборник 3(66), 1958, p. 76) only summarizes the Romance; her translation (pp. 88–97) is of the Legend alone. No Russian translation found on CyberLeninka or facetia.
candidates.en_evidence: E.A.W. Budge, The History of Alexander the Great, Being the Syriac Version (Cambridge 1889), pp. 1–143; reprinted Gorgias 2003. Reproduced online by J. Colavito.
candidates.other_translations: French: M. Debié, Alexandre le Grand en syriaque (Les Belles Lettres 2024). Nöldeke 1890 and Ciancaglini 2001 are studies, not translations.
candidates.value: Witness to the lost Greek δ* recension, translated directly from Greek (Ciancaglini 2001, now the consensus). Parent of the Arabic, Ethiopic and Persian lines, with Iranian place names. Needed for the stemma. A first Russian translation would anchor the whole Oriental branch.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Medium-high. The Syriac prose is plain, and Budge's English plus Debié's French allow cross-checking. Needs a Syriacist for verification.
candidates.pilot_unit: Book I (Nectanebo to the Darius correspondence), about 18k words (estimate), checked against Kroll's α and Bergson's β.

verification.title: Syriac Alexander Romance (Syriac Pseudo-Callisthenes, recension *δ), Book I (chs. 1–47 in Budge's division) / Сирийская версия «Романа об Александре» Псевдо-Каллисфена, кн. I
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of any book of the Syriac Romance, so the claim of RU "none" could not be refuted. A caveat on method: the WebSearch budget was already used up (200/200), so I ran no open web searches in either language. All checks were catalogue or site-specific queries.
(1) facetia.ru, site search "сирийская". Its Pseudo-Callisthenes page (https://facetia.ru/pseudo-callisthenes-alexander-romance) mentions the Syriac prose version only in its overview of the tradition. The only Russian text on it is Egunov's Greek α excerpt (I.15–26, 30–41; «Поздняя греческая проза», 1960/61), not the Syriac.
(2) vostlit.info letter indexes П, С, И, Р, Л, К (https://www.vostlit.info/haupt-Dateien/index-Dateien/S.phtml?id=2058, etc.). Under С it lists only the Сирийская анонимная хроника 1234 г. and the хроника о времени Сасанидов. It has no Псевдо-Каллисфен, Сирийская Александрия or Искандер entry.
(3) ru.wikipedia, «История Александра Великого» (redirect from Псевдо-Каллисфен) and «Роман об Александре». Both mention only that a Syriac translation exists, with no Russian rendering.
(4) CyberLeninka API, five Russian queries: «сирийская версия романа об Александре», «Псевдо-Каллисфен сирийский», «Александр Македонский сирийская литература», «сирийский роман об Александре перевод», «Александр Двурогий сирийская легенда». The only relevant hit is the 2013 article on the philosophers' sayings over Alexander's coffin in al-Makin, which is Arabic material. There is nothing on the Romance.
(5) Pigulevskaya 1958 (Палестинский сборник 3(66)). I could not open the article to re-check it. Per the sweep it only summarises the Romance and translates the Christian Legend (Neṣḥānā), not the Romance; this is unverified here.
(6) Avoid a false positive: Darbinyan-Melikyan 1986 is the Armenian version, and Gorelov 2006 covers Latin texts. Neither is Syriac.
verification.en_found:
The English claim of "full" is confirmed, and there is also an earlier partial English version.
(a) Budge, E. A. W., The History of Alexander the Great, being the Syriac Version, edited from five manuscripts, of the Pseudo-Callisthenes (Cambridge UP 1889). The English translation covers Book I at pp. 1–63, Book II at pp. 64–86 and Book III at pp. 87–143, with the Syriac text separately paginated 1–275. Budge describes the books as having 47, 14 and 24 chapters, with a lacuna of about 8 chapters in Book II (I checked this in the archive.org djvu text). Reprints: APA-Philo Press, Amsterdam 1976; Gorgias 2003; Cambridge Library Collection (CUP) 2013 (per Open Library). The full Budge English is online on Colavito's site: https://www.jasoncolavito.com/the-syriac-alexander-romance.html.
(b) Partial earlier English, not in the sweep: Justin Perkins' English translation, made from an Urmia manuscript. It was never published in full; T. D. Woolsey printed extracts in "Notice of a Life of Alexander the Great, translated from the Syriac by Rev. Dr. Justin Perkins … with extracts from the same", JAOS 4 (1853–54), 357–440 (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.55127). Extract I is the founding of Alexandria from Book I, fuller than A and V. Extracts II–IV include the letter to Aristotle and matter not found in the Greek.
(c) Not in the anthologies. Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994/2012) contains the Letter to Aristotle, Pharasmanes, George the Monk, Palladius, Collatio and Iter ad Paradisum, but nothing Syriac (TOC checked on archive.org). The e-GEDSH entry "Alexander Cycle" (Brock 2011) cites only Budge's English for the Romance.
verification.other_found:
French: M. Debié, Alexandre le Grand en syriaque. Maître des lieux, des savoirs et des temps (Les Belles Lettres, Bibliothèque de l'Orient chrétien 7, 16 Feb 2024, 656 pp.; https://www.lesbelleslettres.com/livre/9782251454900/alexandre-le-grand-en-syriaque). This is PARTIAL, not a full translation, which corrects the sweep. Per the BMCR review by C. Jouanno (https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2024/2024.09.05/), it gives "un bref passage du livre I, évoquant la naissance et l'éducation d'Alexandre" and the whole of Book III. Part II adds further extracts from the Romance: the young Alexander's wisdom, rhetorical exempla, and Nectanebo's magic and astrology. Those extracts may overlap the Book I unit, so they should be checked against the book before translation. The publisher's table of contents for Part I reads "Le portrait d'Alexandre / L'épitomé du Roman / Le voyage en Orient (livre III)". The edition is French only, not bilingual. Most of Book I in French therefore remains untranslated (Bucephalus, the games, Pausanias, the western campaign, Darius' letters, Tyre); the founding of Alexandria is probably also absent, but I have not confirmed that.
German: Nöldeke, Beiträge zur Geschichte des Alexanderromans (Denkschriften Wien 38, 1890) is a study. His preface says the German translations he gives are of a few Arabic pieces, not the Syriac Romance (archive.org beitrgezurgesch00nlgoog). Ciancaglini, Le Muséon 114 (2001) is a study.
Italian/Spanish: I found no translation of the Syriac. Google Books returned errors (rate limit), so Spanish and Italian could not be properly checked.
Other: e-GEDSH notes "There is also a Modern Syriac version", a Neo-Aramaic reworking or translation that I did not identify further. Arabic, Persian and Turkish modern translations: unknown, not checked.
verification.source_text: Budge 1889, the only edition. It is public domain but not critical: it rests on five late East-Syriac (Urmia/Alqosh) manuscripts, the oldest c. 1708, and B is dated 1844 (Budge's preface). The chapters are arranged to match Müller's Greek order. Scans: https://archive.org/details/BudgeSyriacAlexander (683-page PDF compiled by R. Bedrosian, plus djvu text) and https://archive.org/details/bub_gb__14LmFqhc8QC (Google scan). The djvu OCR reads the English acceptably, but the Syriac comes out as garbage, so the Syriac must be re-keyed or put through a Syriac OCR. The phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:727 copy was not re-checked. I found no newer critical edition; Debié 2024 is a translation only and adds no text. Dating caveat for the dossier: the candidate's "early 7th c. (Debié 2024)" conflicts with BMCR's summary of Debié. That summary says the version was made from Greek *δ "sans doute … avant la fin du VIe siècle", and Debié argues the dragon and China episodes come from the lost Greek recension.
verification.recommendation: This is a valid candidate for RU, since no Russian translation turned up, but not for EN: Budge's full 1889 English exists, with Perkins/Woolsey extracts from 1854. Its Neoscholia value is a first Russian version plus a new English one against an outdated Budge, and verification needs a Syriacist. For the pilot, consider Book III (~24 chapters; China, dragon, Samarkand), the most distinctive part, with Budge and Debié's full French available as controls. Keep Book I (~63 Budge pages) only if the aim is a synoptic comparison with Egunov's Russian α excerpt and with Julius Valerius, and first check Debié's Book I extracts for overlap.

candidates.title: Coptic (Sahidic) Alexander Romance fragments / Коптский «Роман об Александре». Unit: all 9 fragments as edited by Lemm
candidates.author: Anonymous
candidates.date: c. 6th–9th c. (codex from the White Monastery, Sohag)
candidates.size: 9 fragments of one codex (originally about 220 pp.); roughly 4–6k words (estimate)
candidates.edition: O. von Lemm, Der Alexanderroman bei den Kopten (St Petersburg 1903): text, German translation and notes. Public domain; open PDF at phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:556 (CC BY).
candidates.ru_evidence: Lemm, a Russian Coptologist, published only in German. CyberLeninka query «коптский роман об Александре» returns no translation; nothing on facetia or vostlit.
candidates.en_evidence: Only J. Colavito's 2026 web translation, made from Lemm's German. It is indirect and non-scholarly; no English translation from the Coptic was found.
candidates.value: The only version of the Romance in Egypt's native language. It has episodes absent from the Greek: Alexander disguised as an envoy or captive, Eleazar 'elder of the Persians', the sack of the Elamite city. Alexander is styled 'pharaoh'. Relevant to the Copto-Arabic (Quzman) line.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Medium. The text is full of gaps and restorations; Lemm's German is a control. Needs a Coptologist for verification.
candidates.pilot_unit: All fragments with Lemm's restorations, as a first Russian translation with commentary (about 5k words).

verification.title: Coptic (Sahidic) Alexander Romance: the White Monastery paper-codex fragments (Lemm 1903, 9 leaves, 18 pp.), plus the Moscow papyrus scrap Pushkin Museum I.1.b.685
verification.ru_found:
REFUTED: the sweep's RU status of "none" is wrong. Two of the nine leaves have been published in complete Russian translations made directly from the Coptic, both by A.L. Khosroev:
(1) Fr. 6, recto and verso (the end of Selpharios' testament to his son Philias, then Alexander's tears). Хосроев А.Л., «Коптский роман об Александре и ближневосточная литературная традиция», ВДИ 1982, № 4, с. 125–130. It has notes and an English summary. Open PDF: https://elib.gsu.by/bitstream/123456789/16276/1/ (file «Хосроев А.Л._Вестник древней истории_1982_№ 4.pdf»).
(2) Fr. 9, recto and verso (Antipater's plot and the poisoning; close to α III.31). Хосроев А.Л., «Из истории коптского романа об Александре», Палестинский сборник 28 (91), Л., 1986, с. 153–157. It has textual notes against Kroll. PDF: https://www.orientalstudies.ru/rus/images/pdf/journals/PPS_28_91_1986_19_khosroyev.pdf
(3) Unpublished: Хосроев, канд. дисс. «Роман об Александре на Ближнем Востоке (Коптская версия)», Л., 1983, 139 с. (автореферат 15 с.; rusneb.ru, disscat.com). It probably holds a Russian version of all fragments, but I could not check this.
(4) Studies that give only short quotations: Хосроев, «О происхождении коптского романа об Александре» and «К проблеме историчности персонажей коптского романа об Александре: Менандр», both in ППиПИКНВ XVII, ч. 2, М. 1983, с. 52–55 and 55–60 (PDFs on orientalstudies.ru). Ернштедт П.В., «К коптскому тексту романа об Александре», ВВ 10 (1956) 178–180, a note on one phrase of fr. 6 (vremennik.biz/sites/all/files/BB10_10.pdf).
FALSE LEAD: one search-engine summary claimed that A.I. Elanskaya published a Russian translation in 1993. I checked and it is false. Her «Изречения египетских отцов» (1993; 2nd ed. 2001) only mentions that the Romance existed. The only romance it translates is the «Фрагмент Романа о Камбизе».
Nothing in Stoneman's Legends, Gorelov 2006, facetia.ru or ru.wikipedia.
Result: fragments 1–5, 7 and 8 have no published Russian translation.
verification.en_found:
The EN status of "full" holds, but not on the sweep's evidence. Colavito is not the only English version.
(1) Maspero, Popular Stories of Ancient Egypt, trans. Mrs C.H.W. Johns (London: Grevel, 1915), pp. 290–303, "Fragments of the Theban-Coptic Version of the Romance of Alexander". Maspero states his translation "is founded on the text established by" Lemm, in Lemm's order. All continuous text is translated, the illegible Brahman leaf (fr. 8) is summarised, and fr. 9 is given in full. Public domain: archive.org/details/cu31924091207393. Reissued as ed. Hasan El-Shamy (ABC-CLIO 2002; OUP 2004, chapter DOI 10.1093/oso/9780195173352.003.0024). This is indirect: Coptic, then Maspero's French, then English.
(2) Partial, made directly from the Coptic: W.E. Crum, "Another Fragment of the Story of Alexander", PSBA 14 (June 1892) 473–482. It gives the text and an English translation of BL Or. 3367, the Land of Darkness leaf (= Lemm fr. 7). Archive.org: proceedingssoci04archgoog.
(3) J. Colavito, 2026 web translation from Lemm's German: jasoncolavito.com/the-coptic-alexander-romance.html. Fragments 1–9, with fr. 8 left untranslated.
(4) Studies: D.L. Selden, "The Coptic Alexander Romance", in Zuwiyya (ed.), Companion (Brill 2011), 133–156; Selden, "Guardians of Chaos: The Coptic Alexander Romance", Journal of Coptic Studies 13 (2011), 39 pp.; L.S.B. MacCoull, "Aspects of Alexander in Coptic Egypt", in Stoneman–Erickson–Netton (eds.) 2012. These may quote passages; I did not check.
No modern scholarly English translation of the whole corpus made directly from the Coptic was found.
verification.other_found:
FRENCH:
- U. Bouriant, "Fragments d'un roman d'Alexandre en dialecte thébain", JA 8e sér. 9 (1887) 1–38 and 10 (1887) 340–349. Text and French translation of the Paris leaves. Archive.org in.gov.ignca.26222 / 26223.
- Maspero, Les contes populaires de l'Égypte ancienne: 2nd ed. 1889, pp. 321–338 (Paris leaves only); 3rd ed. 1905 and 4th ed. 1911 (all fragments, translated from Lemm's text). Public domain, archive.org.
GERMAN:
- Lemm 1903: full edition with German translation and commentary.
- R. Pietschmann, "Zu den Überbleibseln des koptischen Alexanderbuches", Festschrift Wilmanns (Leipzig 1903) 301–312: readings and notes.
ITALIAN:
- G. Lusini, "Osservazioni sulla versione copta del Romanzo di Alessandro", Studi Classici e Orientali 42 (JSTOR 24184101). A philological study; whether it translates passages is unknown.
EXTRA WITNESS, not among Lemm's nine:
- Pushkin Museum, Moscow, I.1.b.685 (Golenishchev): a papyrus scrap of 4×4 cm, 10th–11th c. It carries the names Alexander, Selpharios and Diatrophe on one side and a Coptic alphabet on the other, probably a writing exercise. Edited by Lemm, Koptische Miscellen LIII; catalogued in Elanskaya, Literary Coptic MSS (VigChr Suppl. 18, 1994) 163–164; Würzburg Coptic Magical Papyri KYP T-12.
DATING CORRECTION:
- The "6th–9th c." in the sweep can only describe the translation (Lemm dates it to the 6th c.). The codex itself is paper. Lemm dated it to the 11th c. Maspero put it no earlier than the 13th c. (1915), or the 14th c. (1889, as cited by Khosroev).
REFERENCE ENTRY:
- C.D.G. Müller, "Romances", Coptic Encyclopedia 7 (1991) 2059b–2061a.
verification.source_text: O. von Lemm, Der Alexanderroman bei den Kopten. Ein Beitrag zur Geschichte der Alexandersage im Orient (St. Petersburg 1903). It gives the Coptic text of all 9 leaves, a German translation, commentary and plates. Lemm died in 1918, so the book is public domain. Open PDF (16.6 MB) under CC BY 2.0 AT, verified: https://phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:556. A mirror is linked from arhiva.unilib.rs; the coptica.ch link cited on Wikipedia returns 404. Supplementary sources: Bouriant JA 1887 and Crum PSBA 14 (1892) on archive.org, which provide earlier readings and an independent second set of readings to check Lemm against.
verification.recommendation: Still a reasonable but downgraded candidate. Two leaves (fr. 6 and fr. 9) already have Russian translations, and English has a near-complete public-domain version via Maspero (1915), a direct partial one (Crum 1892) and Colavito's. The added value would be the first complete Russian translation and the first complete translation made directly from the Coptic in both languages, with commentary. Start with Lemm fr. 1–5 (Eleazar and the detained messengers, Antilochos and Chaos in Gedrosia, Menander's dream, the disguised return, Agrikolaos), which have no Russian translation. Then add fr. 7–8 and the Moscow scrap, and use Khosroev 1982/1986 for comparison. Checking the result needs a Sahidic Coptic specialist, not only someone with Greek and Latin.

candidates.title: Patmut'iwn Aleksandri Makedonac'woy: Armenian Alexander Romance / «История Александра Македонского» (древнеармянская версия). Unit: Book I
candidates.author: Anonymous (traditionally attributed to Movses Xorenac'i)
candidates.size: 3 books; whole text about 60k words (estimate), Book I about 20k (estimate). Two complete recensions survive, plus two abridged ones and an oral version.
candidates.edition: T'reanc' (Venice 1842), public domain on archive.org. Critical editions: Simonyan 1989; Muradyan and Topchyan 2025 (Matenadaran). Raabe 1896 Greek retroversion, public domain at phaidrabg o:702.
candidates.ru_evidence: Topchyan 2026 (Shagi/Steps 12.1) lists only Armenian editions and Wolohojian's English. No Alexander title in Darbinyan-Melikyan's bibliography (ru.wiki); the '1986' lead is her Drasxanakertc'i. hy.wiki: not even modern Armenian exists.
candidates.en_evidence: A.M. Wolohojian, The Romance of Alexander the Great by Pseudo-Callisthenes (Columbia UP 1969), translated from the 1842 text. PDF on attalus.org.
candidates.other_translations: Greek retroversion by Raabe (1896). No other modern-language translation found.
candidates.value: The most faithful early witness to α, often better than Greek MS A, and used by Kroll. It shows Armenianizing (Zeus becomes Aramazd). The 2025 critical text makes a new collated translation timely, and the first Russian one.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Medium-high. The Armenian follows the Greek closely, so the α text, Raabe's retroversion and Wolohojian's English all allow checks. Final verification needs an Armenologist (Classical Armenian).
candidates.pilot_unit: Book I (Nectanebo through accession and the western campaign) set against Kroll's α. Use the 1842 text for the open release; collate with the 2025 edition if permission is granted.

verification.title: Patmut'iwn Aghek'sandri Makedonac'woy (Old Armenian Alexander Romance), Book I: Armenian Pseudo-Callisthenes, translated probably in the 480s; attribution to Movses Xorenac'i is traditional
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation, either full or partial, of the Armenian version.

Searches and pages checked:
- Russian web searches.
- facetia.ru: the Alexander literature survey (/alexander-romances) and /node/2730. The latter is Egunov's translation of Greek α from «Поздняя греческая проза» 1960/61. It only says the Old Armenian translation was made «как полагают, в V в.».
- ru.wiki «История Александра Великого». Its only Russian translation is Egunov's (Greek α).
- ru.wiki «Роман об Александре». Its only Russian item is the 1965 Литпамятники «Александрия».
- ru.wiki «Хачатур Кечареци».
- vostlit.info author indexes А, И and П. None has an Alexander or Pseudo-Callisthenes entry.

Russian appears in the scholarship only as metadata. Simonyan's 1989 diplomatic edition carries the Russian parallel title «Повесть об Александре Македонском» (648 pp.). The Russian-language journal Шаги/Steps 12.1 (2026) has Topchyan's article, but it is written in English. I found no Russian text of the romance in either.

One residual risk, not verified: ru.wiki says Xač'atur Keč'arec'i's poems «переведены на русский язык». Some of these may be his kafas interpolated into the A recension (Venice MS 424), and Grigoris Aght'amarc'i's kafas may also exist in Russian anthologies. These are 13th–16th-century verse insertions, not the 5th-century prose of Book I.

A search-engine summary claimed «На русский язык этот текст был переведен». The sources it cited don't support this: they are Egunov's Greek α.
verification.en_found:
Full English translation: A. M. Wolohojian, The Romance of Alexander the Great by Pseudo-Callisthenes, translated from the Armenian version (Records of Civilization LXXXII; Columbia UP, 1969; 196 pp.).
- It translates the T'reanc' 1842 text, which is MS Venice 424 (Keč'arec'i's recension A).
- The 2025 Matenadaran editors confirm the source: «Հայերեն բնագրի այս տարբերակից է արվել նաև Ոլոհոջյանի անգլերեն թարգմանությունը» ("Wolohojian's English translation was also made from this version of the Armenian text").
- PDF: https://www.attalus.org/armenian/Tales_Alexander_Wolohojian_trans.pdf
- Also on archive.org: archive.org/details/TalesAlexanderWolohojianTrans

Partial English (new): A. S. Topchyan, "The translator's and later revisers' additions to the old Armenian version of the Alexander Romance", Шаги/Steps 12.1 (2026), pp. 218–236.
- It is CC BY 4.0: https://steps.ranepa.ru/jour/article/view/1171 (PDF at /1171/363).
- The author says "The English translations, unless indicated otherwise, are mine". It gives his own renderings of passages, for example from chapters 2, 87, 90, 112, 121, 128 and 190.
verification.other_found:
This refutes the sweep's claim that no other modern-language translation exists.

Italian, complete text of MS Venice 424:
- "[Pseudo-Callistene] (2003). La Storia di Alessandro il Macedone: codice armeno miniato del XIV secolo (Venezia, San Lazzaro, 424)", edited by G. Traina with C. Franco, D. Kouymjian and C. Veronese Arslan; Padova: Bottega d'Erasmo / AAGEP Aldo Ausilio Editore. Two volumes: a facsimile, plus a companion volume of studies with Traina's Italian translation.
- This is cited in Topchyan 2026 (that citation is verbatim). It is also cited in the Muradyan–Topchyan 2025 introduction (p. 15: «Այն ընդգրկում է նաև երկի՝ Տրաինայի իտալերեն թարգմանությունը», "It also includes Traina's Italian translation of the work").
- So the sweep's statement that Topchyan lists only Armenian editions and Wolohojian is also wrong.

Other items:
- Greek retroversion: R. Raabe, Ἱστορία Ἀλεξάνδρου: die armenische Übersetzung der sagenhaften Alexander-Biographie (Leipzig: Hinrichs, 1896), based on T'reanc' 1842.
- Readings of the Armenian are transliterated in the apparatus of Bergson's β edition (1965).

Modern Armenian: none. hy.wiki «Ալեքսանդրի վեպը» says «գրաբար տեքստի աշխարհաբար թարգմանություն դեռևս չի կատարվել» ("no modern Armenian translation of the grabar text has been made yet").

I found no French, German or Spanish translation of the Armenian version. This was checked with less search coverage than the Russian and English (see confidence note in the recommendation).
verification.source_text:
Public domain:
- R. T'reanc' (ed.), Patmut'iwn Aghek'sandri Makedonac'woy, Venice: San Lazzaro, 1842. Its base text is MS Venice 424 (14th c., recension A, with Keč'arec'i's kafas).
- Google scan from Michigan: https://archive.org/details/patmutiwnagheks00pseugoog

Openly licensed aids:
- Raabe 1896 Greek retroversion, CC BY 2.0 AT: https://phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:702
- Tašean 1892 study: archive.org/details/TasheanCallisthenesAM5

Critical texts (copyrighted; consult and cite, do not reproduce):
- Simonyan 1989 (Erevan, 648 pp.), with recensions A/B/C.
- G. Muradyan & A. Topchyan, Պատմութիւն Մեծին Աղեքսանդրի Մակեդոնացւոյ, Matenadaran 2025, 368 pp., DOI 10.57155/MFWA8238. It collates A with recension D (Simonyan's "intermediary") to approach the original translation; the text is on pp. 61–345.

Start with Book I from the public-domain 1842 text, recording where the 2025 Muradyan–Topchyan critical text differs. Checking the grabar needs a Classical Armenian specialist, not just Greek and Latin; Raabe's retroversion and Kroll's α / Bergson's β help as controls.

verification.title: Mēmrā on Alexander ('Song of Alexander', Syriac Alexanderlied), Ps.-Jacob of Serugh / «Мемра (Песнь) об Александре» Псевдо-Иакова Серугского
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, full or partial. The search was cut short: only 2 Russian WebSearch queries ran before the session's 200-search limit was reached, so the minimum of 4 Russian searches was not met. Those 2 queries were «Песнь об Александре Иаков Серугский перевод сирийский» and «"Псевдо-Иаков" Александр Гог Магог мемра сирийская поэма». Neither turned up any Russian rendering. After that I checked specific pages directly. (1) The vostlit.info alphabetical indexes for И, П, С, А and Я have no entry for the poem; the only Syriac items listed are the Chronicle of 1234 and the anonymous chronicle on the Sasanian period. (2) The Russian Wikipedia article «Иаков Серугский» names only the «Гимн Богоматери» as known in Russian and does not mention the Alexander poem. (3) The Pravenc (Православная энциклопедия) article «Иаков Саругский» (pravenc.ru/text/200347.html) does not list the poem among Jacob's works. A search-engine summary did tie the poem to A. Weber's German translation (Berlin 1852), which is a bibliographic note and not a Russian translation. Pigulevskaya (1958) translated the prose Neṣḥānā (Syriac Legend), not this poem; that was not re-checked in this run. Not checked: CyberLeninka/eLibrary, and any short quotations inside Russian studies of the Neṣḥānā or of Gog and Magog. Verdict: 'none' still stands, but with medium confidence.
verification.en_found: E. A. W. Budge, The History of Alexander the Great, being the Syriac version of the Pseudo-Callisthenes (Cambridge 1889), pp. 163–200: 'A Discourse composed by Mar Jacob upon Alexander'. It is public domain (archive.org/details/BudgeSyriacAlexander, with OCR text). Budge's own introduction (pp. lxxix ff.) says the translation is 'made chiefly from the very faulty text published by Knös in his Chrestomathia Syriaca, pp. 66–107', with corrupt passages fixed from BL Add. 14624 (9th c.) and variants given in the notes. So it is a full but pre-critical, eclectic English version, essentially Reinink's Recension 1 (the Knös Paris MS) with readings from Recension 2 mixed in. Budge's volume does not print the Syriac of the poem; he edited the London MS separately in ZA 6 (1891). Jason Colavito reprints Budge's translation online (jasoncolavito.com/the-song-of-alexander.html). Partial English: G. S. Reynolds, The Qur'an and the Bible (Yale 2018), pp. 463–465, summarises the water-of-life/cook episode and gives some translation (seen only as a citation in Wikipedia). P. Crone, Collected Studies vol. 3 (Brill 2016), pp. 67–68, discusses the poem; whether it translates anything was not checked. T. Tesei, The Syriac Legend of Alexander's Gate (OUP 2023), is listed under 'Editions' in the Wikipedia article, but I could not confirm that it translates the poem rather than the prose Legend. I found no English translation based on Reinink's critical text, and none of Recension 2 or Recension 3 as separate texts. Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great was not re-checked; I do not believe it contains this poem.
verification.other_found: GERMAN (more than the sweep found). Hunnius 1904 (pp. 2–3) gives the history. (a) A. Weber, Das Mar Yaʿkûb-Gedicht über den gläubigen König Alexander, Berlin 1852: a translation of Knös's text. (b) [P.?] Zingerle, Ein altes Alexanderlied, Brünn 1882: also a translation of Knös's text. (c) C. Hunnius, Das syrische Alexanderlied, Göttingen dissertation 1904 (34 pp., public domain, archive.org/details/dassyrischealex00hunngoog). This is only the introduction and analysis; the rest appeared as C. Hunnius, 'Das syrische Alexanderlied', ZDMG 60 (1906), 169–209, 558–589, 802–821. There Hunnius gives an emended text based on three MSS (Paris syr. 13 = Knös; BL Add. 14624; Paris syr. 243, copied 1610–11 by the Maronite Sergius in Rome, used for the first time) and a full German translation. (d) G. J. Reinink, Das syrische Alexanderlied: die drei Rezensionen, CSCO 454–455 / Syr. 195–196 (Leuven 1983): critical text of all three recensions with German translation. FRENCH (now confirmed): M. Debié, Alexandre le Grand en syriaque (Les Belles Lettres, Bibliothèque de l'Orient chrétien 7, 2024, 656 pp., ISBN 9782251454900), described as 'Traductions, introductions et commentaires'. Part III, ch. 3, has a section 'Le Mimro sur Alexandre' (lesbelleslettres.com/livre/9782251454900). It very probably contains a French translation, but I could not see whether it covers the whole poem or only excerpts, or which recension it uses. ARABIC: a medieval Arabic version survives in 2 MSS (Monferrer-Sala in Zuwiyya, Companion 2011, p. 45). I found no modern Italian or Spanish translation; this was not exhaustively checked.
verification.source_text: Best open (public-domain) texts: (1) C. Hunnius, ZDMG 60 (1906), 169–209, 558–589, 802–821. This is an emended text from 3 MSS (P, L, P2) with German translation, the closest thing to a critical text that is out of copyright. ZDMG 1906 should be digitized (DMG/ULB Halle menadoc, JSTOR); I did not confirm a URL, and the Internet Archive has no 1906 volume. The Göttingen 1904 dissertation part is at archive.org/details/dassyrischealex00hunngoog. (2) G. Knös, Chrestomathia Syriaca (Göttingen 1807), pp. 66–107, Recension 1 from a Paris MS; Budge calls this text 'very faulty'. It is at archive.org/details/ChrestomathiaSyriaca_201705 under a Public Domain Mark. (3) Budge's edition of BL Add. 14624 (9th c.; Recension 2, the oldest witness) in Zeitschrift für Assyriologie 6 (1891); this comes from Hunnius' account, and I did not find a URL. The standard critical edition is Reinink, CSCO 454 (1983), still in copyright; use it as the reference text. Recension 3 (Paris syr. 243) is in print only in Reinink and in Hunnius' apparatus.
verification.recommendation: This is a good candidate for a Russian translation: Russian is confirmed missing, and the poem is important for Gog and Magog, Q 18:83–102 and 7th-c. imperial apocalyptic. English already has a full public-domain version (Budge 1889), so a new English translation is justified only if it is critical and recension-aware, for example the first English translation of Recension 2 (BL Add. 14624) or of Reinink's three recensions in parallel. Start with the whole poem (a manageable length of several hundred dodecasyllabic lines; the exact count was not checked), translating from Hunnius 1906 or Knös and checking against Reinink 1983. Verification needs a Syriac specialist.

verification.title: Kafas (Middle Armenian monorhymed poems) added to the Armenian History of Alexander: Khachatur Kech'arets'i (c.1260–1331), Grigoris Aght'amarts'i (c.1478–c.1550), Zak'aria Gnunets'i (16th c.) / Кафы к «Истории Александра Македонского»
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of any Alexander kafa. Checks:
(1) The full text of «Армянская средневековая лирика», compiled by Л. М. Мкртчян (Библиотека поэта, Л.: Советский писатель, 1972, 2nd ed.; archived at belousenko/imwerden). Khachatur Kech'arets'i is represented only by nos. 127–130: «Бренное тело корила душа», «Господь словам моим свидетель», «Я, смертный, сотворен из праха», «Жизнь на земле подобна морю». The notes say they were "печатаются на русском языке впервые", translated from Авдалбекян 1958. Grigoris is represented by nos. 146–151: «Песнь об одном епископе», «Песнь о розе и соловье» and other love or spiritual songs, some translated by Bryusov. None of these is an Alexander kafa, and the volume has no Alexander or kafa material at all. This refutes the sweep's lead.
(2) Russian Wikipedia articles on Хачатур Кечареци, Григорис Ахтамарци and Закария Гнунеци. They describe the kafas (Grigoris "около 170 кафами"; autographs Venice Mekhitarist 280 of 1526 and Jerusalem St James 473 of 1536). They list Russian translations only of the lyrics in the 1972 anthology.
(3) The КЛЭ entry on Хачатур Кечареци (vol. 8, 1975, by М. Т. Авдалбекян) lists only the 1972 anthology for Russian.
(4) Simonyan's 1979 ИФЖ article on the redactions (hpj.asj-oa.am) is in Armenian. Only its summary is in Russian, and it has no translated kafas.
(5) facetia.ru's Alexander survey and Grabar-Passek ch. 8 have no Armenian material. The vostlit.info alphabetical indices (А, Г, З, И, К, П, Х) and the Кавказ section have no Pseudo-Callisthenes, Хачатур, Григорис or Гнунеци. The Памятники письменности Востока volume list has no Alexander volume (Дарбинян-Меликян there: Нарекаци 1988; Симеон Лехаци and Закарий Канакерци as Дарбинян).
(6) The "Дарбинян-Меликян 1986 Армянская версия" lead could not be confirmed in Open Library or archive.org. Open Library has her only for Pseudo-Shapuh (1971) and a miniature album.
Caveat: the WebSearch budget ran out after one Russian query. I could not check «Армянская классическая лирика» (1977), «Поэзия народов СССР IV–XVIII вв.» (БВЛ 1972) or Yerevan-printed Russian anthologies.
verification.en_found:
Only selections exist, all by one scholar, Alex MacFarlane. There is no complete English translation of any of the three cycles.
- Wolohojian 1969 (Columbia UP; attalus.org PDF) translates the prose from V424 but explicitly omits all kafas. Confirmed by MacFarlane 2020, nn. 45 and 218.
- MacFarlane, A. 2020. "Alexander Re-mapped: Geography and Identity in the Alexander Romance in Armenia", DPhil thesis, Oxford, open access on ORA (uuid:79299f87-5815-4ea9-a2be-5157ea1b7956). It gives original English translations of a selection of kafas by all three poets, mainly the edges-of-the-world episodes and the Letter to Olympias. Ch. 6 covers anthology sets in M3668 (30 kafas attributed to Khachatur), M7726 and M7709.
- MacFarlane 2019. "'This Shocking Lobster'", in Ivanova and Jeffery (eds), Transmitting and Circulating the Late Antique and Byzantine Worlds (Brill), pp. 125–48. Some kafas.
- MacFarlane, Iran and the Caucasus: Part 1, vol. 25.4 (2021), 334–51; Part 2, vol. 26.4 (2022), doi 10.1163/1573384x-20220403; a further installment, vol. 27.3 (2023), doi 10.1163/1573384x-02703002. These give a full translation and commentary of the out-of-sequence Alexander kafas in the talaran MS M7709, which centre on Alexander's death. That is an anthology set, not the Khachatur or Grigoris cycle. The 2023 item is listed in Crossref; I did not read it.
- MacFarlane 2022. Armeniaca 1, 49–62, open access. A linguistic study with sample half-lines and kafas.
- MacFarlane 2023. "'My City Which Is of Bronze'", Brill chapter, doi 10.1163/9789004527607_016.
- Maranci 2003–04 (JSAS 13) is a preliminary English discussion of the kafas. I did not check it for translations.
- Hacikyan et al., Heritage of Armenian Literature II (2002), pp. 569–571, translates part of Khachatur's Lament, not the kafas.
verification.other_found:
ITALIAN (this refutes the sweep's "none found"):
- Traina, G. et al. 2003. La storia di Alessandro il Macedone. Codice miniato armeno del secolo XIV (Venezia, ms. San Lazzaro 424). Padova: Bottega d'Erasmo / Aldo Ausilio. Facsimile plus Italian translation of the prose and of all kafas preserved in V424. MacFarlane calls it "the first significant translation of the kafas into a modern Western European language". V424 is the sole contemporary witness of Khachatur's cycle, about 100 surviving kafas, so his cycle effectively has a complete Italian translation as far as preserved in V424.
- M. Bernardelli, "Alessandro Magno nel Medioevo armeno: quando l'effimero diventa eterno", PhD thesis, Ca' Foscari Venezia, 2004–07. It contains Italian translations of kafas; the BnF blog cites p. 113. Extent and access are unknown.
FRENCH:
- One Nectanebo kafa, rendered via Bernardelli, in V. Desclaux, "Un roman d'Alexandre arménien", manuscripta.hypotheses.org/3815 (2020), on BnF Arm. 291.
- KLÉ cites Tchobanian, La Roseraie d'Arménie (Paris 1923), p. 67, for Khachatur poems. Whether that includes any Alexander kafa is unverified; Gallica was behind a bot check.
ARMENIAN SCHOLARSHIP (editions and studies, not translations):
- Simonyan, Hay mijnadaryan kafaner (1975), pp. 41–134.
- Simonyan 1968, "Grigoris Aght'amarts'i as author of the kafas", Lraber 8, pp. 85–93.
- Avdalbegyan 1958, the Khachatur corpus including the kafas (pp. 184–188 for the M3668 set).
- Avdalbegyan 1963, critical edition of Grigoris' poems.
- N. Akinean 1910 on Zak'aria Gnunets'i.
No German or Spanish translations were found.
verification.source_text:
The standard edition is H. Simonyan, Patmut'iwn Alek'sandri Makedonac'woy. Haykakan xmbagrut'iwnner (Erevan: AN ArmSSR, 1989).
- Text A is the critical text with kafas, based on M5472 (Zak'aria's Rome copy), V424, Kiurdian MS 2 (Grigoris, 1526), J473 (1536) and M10448. It marks Zak'aria's and Grigoris' kafas.
- Text C is the folk version.
- It is in copyright, and I did not verify whether it is online, e.g. at arar.sci.am.
For Khachatur, M. T. Avdalbegyan, Khach'atur Kech'arets'i (Erevan 1958) is also in copyright.
Openly accessible witnesses:
- John Rylands Library, Manchester, Armenian MS 3 (MCR3). Zak'aria Gnunets'i's autograph, Constantinople 1544, fully digitised (Manchester Digital Collections; formerly luna.manchester.ac.uk ...Manchester~91~1~416825~147912). Public-domain manuscript images.
- V424: only six images are on Wikimedia Commons. The full facsimile is Traina 2003, which is in copyright.
The 1842 Venice Mekhitarist edition (based on V424) is in the public domain, but I did not verify whether it prints the kafas.
For practice, the best route is Simonyan 1989 checked against the MCR3 images. For Khachatur, MacFarlane's open-access thesis (ORA) and Armeniaca 2022 (Edizioni Ca' Foscari, open access) quote the Armenian of many kafas.
verification.recommendation: Good RU candidate: I found no Russian translation of any Alexander kafa, and English has only MacFarlane's selections. Khachatur's V424 cycle, however, already has a complete Italian translation (Traina 2003). So start with Grigoris Aght'amarts'i's ~170 kafas from Simonyan 1989 text A, checked against MCR3; they have no full translation in any language. Khachatur could follow as a RU+EN pilot, with the Italian as an external control. Verification needs an Armenologist for Middle Armenian, with its Persian, Arabic and Turkish loanwords and metre-driven forms; Greek and Latin will not suffice, and current LLMs are weak here.

verification.title: Ethiopic 'Christian Romance of Alexander' (Budge) = Zenā ʾƎskǝndǝr, CAe 2616; incipit title Baʾǝnta gǝbru wa-mangǝśtu la-ʾƎskǝndǝr nǝguś, fǝqura ʾƎgziʾabǝḥer («О деяниях и царствовании царя Александра богоизбранного», Chernetsov). Preface + 33 chapters.
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation, either full or partial, so the claim that this text is untranslated in Russian still stands.
(1) Chernetsov, «Эфиопская литература [до конца XVI в.]», История всемирной литературы, т. 3 (1985), FEB text frame at http://feb-web.ru/feb/ivl/vl3/vl3-5462.htm?cmd=2. It names the text as «О деяниях и царствовании царя Александра богоизбранного» and calls it an original Ethiopic reworking in which Alexander is a saint who foresees Christ. It also quotes Turaev on the Synaxarion entry for Alexander. It gives a description only, with no translated excerpt.
(2) vostlit.info: I checked its alphabetical indexes (А, Д, И, З, К, М, П, Р, С, Э). The only Ethiopic items are «Эфиопские хроники» and «Краткая эфиопская хроника». There is nothing on Alexander, Eskender or al-Makin.
(3) facetia.ru/alexander-romances has no Ethiopic entry.
(4) Russian Wikipedia: there is no article on the Ethiopic romance, and nothing came up when I searched it.
(5) Web searches in Russian found nothing: «эфиопский роман об Александре… перевод», «"Христианский роман" Александр эфиопский Будж», «vostlit… Зена Эскендер», «"Александра богоизбранного" эфиопск».
Caveats: my WebSearch budget ran out after 5 searches in this pass (4 Russian, 1 English), so I could not check CyberLeninka, eLibrary, ПППВ or Христианский Восток directly. I also did not re-check the sweep's note that Seleznev 2013 translated only al-Makin's sayings at Alexander's tomb; even if true, that is a different work (CAe 4092/al-Makin, not CAe 2616).
verification.en_found:
There are two complete English translations, both by Budge.
(a) E. A. W. Budge, The Life and Exploits of Alexander the Great (London: C. J. Clay, 1896), vol. II "A Christian Romance of Alexander the Great", pp. 437–553. It is a complete literal translation with notes, and the introduction discusses the text at pp. XLIX–LIII. I confirmed this in the OCR text at https://archive.org/details/cu31924091208573; another copy is https://archive.org/details/lifeandexploits00budggoog (Google/Harvard, marked NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT). Budge's base manuscript is BL Or. 827, with variant readings from BnF éth. 146 (Zotenberg), so this is the one text in the collection he edited from more than one manuscript. The work was reprinted in 1968 (archive.org bwb_Y0-BSX-535_1 / _528_2, lending only).
(b) Budge, The Alexander Book in Ethiopia (Oxford UP, 1933; AMS reprint 1976, archive.org alexanderbookine0000budg, lending only). This is a revised English-only translation, and its subtitle names "a Christian romance of Alexander". Budge died in 1934, so it is public domain in the UK, EU and Russia; in the US it is probably protected until 2029.
Not translations: Sylvia Pankhurst, Ethiopia: A Cultural History (1955), ch. XIV "The Christian Romance of Alexander the Great" (online at https://www.marxists.org/archive/pankhurst-sylvia/1955/ethiopia/ch14.htm), is a retelling that copies long passages from Budge without marking them. Kotar, "The Ethiopic Alexander Romance", in Zuwiyya ed., A Companion to Alexander Literature in the Middle Ages (Brill 2011), pp. 157–176, and Asirvatham, Acta Classica 2014, are studies; I could not check whether they quote excerpts. Beta maṣāḥǝft lists only Budge 1896 as edition and translation.
verification.other_found:
I found no French, German, Italian, Spanish or modern Amharic translation. Beta maṣāḥǝft (https://betamasaheft.eu/works/LIT2616Zenaes/main) lists only Budge, plus Lusini, "Alexander the Great", Encyclopaedia Aethiopica I (2003), p. 195. Cerulli's and Ricci's histories of Ethiopic literature, Littmann 1907, and any Amharic church editions of ዜና፡እስክንድር are unknown: I could not check them because the search budget was gone.
Points that correct the sweep's framing:
(1) Names are easily confused. English Wikipedia uses "Zēnā Eskender" for the Ethiopic Pseudo-Callisthenes, which Beta maṣāḥǝft catalogues separately as CAe 1670 Ḥuratu la-ʾƎskǝndǝr (BL Or. 826, single manuscript). Beta maṣāḥǝft gives "Zenā ʾƎskǝndǝr" to the Christian Romance, CAe 2616.
(2) The sweep's "only critical edition / no variant readings" comes from that Wikipedia article and refers to the Pseudo-Callisthenes. The Christian Romance has 7 known manuscripts: BL Or. 827; BnF éth. 146; BL Or. 818; BnF éth. 159; Lincei Conti Rossini 5; ʾƎndā Māryām Qorrār (ESemq012); and partial content in BL Or. 826. Budge used only the first two.
(3) Origin is disputed. Budge (pref. p. ix; intro p. XLIX) thought it "probably an original Ethiopian work". Beta maṣāḥǝft describes a 14th-century loose translation from a lost Christian Arabic source.
verification.source_text: Budge 1896, vol. I: The Ethiopic Text, Introduction, etc. (privately printed, 250 copies; Drugulin, Leipzig), Christian Romance at pp. 259–353. Public domain. A scan is at https://archive.org/details/india.history.resource.77280 (PDF 77280.pdf), but archive.org's OCR does not read Ge'ez, so the text needs new Ge'ez OCR or transcription. Budge's English, vol. II pp. 437–553 (https://archive.org/details/cu31924091208573), is public domain and can serve as a control text. Beta maṣāḥǝft LIT2616Zenaes has no transcribed text, and I did not check whether BnF éth. 146 or 159 are digitised on Gallica.
verification.recommendation: This is a good candidate for a Russian translation only: there is no Russian version, but English is fully covered by Budge's literal 1896 translation and his revised 1933 one, so a new English version is low priority. Start with the preface plus a block of chapters, for example the Gog and Magog, brass citadel, Enoch and Elijah, and Water of Life episodes, or the closing dialogues on Alexander's death. Translate from the Ge'ez with Budge as the control text. Checking the translation needs a Ge'ez specialist, which goes beyond Greek and Latin, and the Ge'ez text must be digitised first.

verification.source_text:
There is no public-domain printed edition of the Syriac Pseudo-Methodius.
- Standard critical text: G. J. Reinink, Die syrische Apokalypse des Pseudo-Methodius, CSCO 540 (Scriptores Syri 220), Peeters, Leuven 1993. It is in copyright; the German translation is in CSCO 541.
- Alternative: Martinez 1985 dissertation (Syriac text and English, on ProQuest; copyright).
- Main manuscript: Vat. syr. 58, fols 118v–136v. Other witnesses: Yale Beinecke Syr. 10, fols 225–236, and the Mardin manuscripts (syriaca.org/work/1779). I could not confirm a DigiVatLib digitization (its record search returned no match).
Public-domain comparison texts:
- Greek: Istrin 1897 (ЧОИДР).
- Latin: Sackur, Sibyllinische Texte und Forschungen (1898).
- Edessene Fragment: Nau, JA 1917, https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.70967.
In practice a translation would have to be made from Reinink's text. The editorial-rights status of that 1993 Belgian edition should be checked; the ancient text itself is not protected.
verification.recommendation: Weak candidate on the "untranslated" criterion. English has three complete translations (Alexander 1985, Martinez 1985, Bonura 2025) and German has Reinink's. Only Russian lacks one: no translation from the Syriac exists, only Derevensky's partial Greek-based version and the Slavonic. If pursued as a first Russian version from the Syriac, take ch. VIII–IX of Reinink's division (Philip/Kushyat, enclosure of the nations of the north, the Kushyat–Byzas–Rome line) plus the release passage in ch. XIII. It is short, but it needs a reviewer who reads Syriac and Reinink's CSCO 540 text.
