Bowman, Sepher Yosippon: A Tenth-Century History of Ancient Israel (Wayne State UP, Nov. 2022; https://wsupress.wayne.edu/9780814349441/). It translates Flusser's whole text. I could not confirm whether Bowman also renders the Alexander Romance interpolations in an appendix. (2) Romance layer, which the sweep missed: Laurence Henry Rubinstein, "The Josippon of Joseph ben Gorion: A Translation of Part I with an Introduction and Source Analysis" (HUC-JIR New York rabbinic/MAHL thesis, 1965, adviser Martin A. Cohen). It translates cols. 1–180 of the Günzburg Berdichev reprint (1896–1913) of the Mantua print, including all the Alexander material: rise (cols. 60–65), birth legend with Nectanebo ("Neketnebor") (65–78), kingship (78–112), with Bucephalus, Nikolaos, the letter to Aristotle (100–103) and Queen Candace ("Kandiki"), then Antipater's poison and the death (to col. 118). It is unpublished, but full and freely online: http://library.huc.edu/pdf/theses/Rubenstein_Laurence_Henry-NY-Rab-1965%20Jossipon%20Part%201-Searchable.pdf and archive.org/details/josippon-1-1-180-lh-rubinstein. Cohen's referee report notes mistranslations and calls it not ready for publication. Companion theses: Patz (Part II, Hasmoneans to Herod) and Zoll (Part III). (3) Peter Morwyng's 1558 English (reprinted 1561–1688; archive.org EEBO copy of the 1669 edition) follows Münster and opens with Alexander's death. It has no Alexander chapters.
verification.other_found: LATIN: J. F. Breithaupt, Josephus Gorionides sive Josephus Hebraicus (Gotha 1707; reissued 1710). Hebrew text after the Venice 1544 print (the Constantinople recension) with a full Latin translation, including the Alexander Romance material (Nectanebus, Candace). Breithaupt says he first meant to follow Münster in leaving out most of the fabulous Alexander deeds, but in the end translated them in place. Public domain on archive.org: bub_gb_VUdl5MmuvhAC. Münster (Basel 1541, from the Constantinople exemplar) has only "Gesta quaedam Alexandri Magni"; Breithaupt says Münster omitted most of the Alexander deeds. Gagnier (Oxford 1706) is a Latin translation of books I–VI; I did not check its Alexander content. GERMAN: Dagmar Börner-Klein and Beat Zuber, Josippon. Jüdische Geschichte vom Anfang der Welt bis zum Ende des ersten Aufstands gegen Rom (Wiesbaden: Marix, 2010; XIV + 912 pp.). Hebrew with German facing, following Flusser's chapter division. Ch. 10 "Alexander in Jerusalem" is at pp. 142–151. The table of contents lists no Alexander Romance appendix (DNB 1002673445; ToC at d-nb.info/1002673445/04). Also "Josippi Jüdische Historien" (1530), an early German version not checked for Alexander content. Ge'ez Zēnā Ayhud: Ge'ez text with German translation by Murad Kamil (New York: J. J. Augustin, 1937; 333 pp.). ENGLISH FROM AMHARIC: anonymous, archive.org/details/Josippon (2025). This Ethiopian derivative includes a summary of Alexander's birth (Philip, the seduction, Pharas/Nikolaos) and his reign. YIDDISH: Michael Adam (Zürich 1546). JUDEO-SPANISH: Libro de Ben Guryon (1901). JUDEO-ARABIC/ARABIC: Shulamit Sela, Sefer Yosef ben Guryon ha-ʿArvi (Ben-Zvi Institute and Tel Aviv University, 2009). ITALIAN/FRENCH/SPANISH: none found, but the search budget was exhausted before these could be checked.
verification.source_text: Flusser, Sefer Yosippon (Jerusalem: Bialik, 1978–80; vocalized edition 2009) is the critical text of ch. 10 and is in copyright. Public-domain options: (a) the Mantua editio princeps (Abraham Conat, c. 1476–80), as reprinted with column numbers by D. Günzburg and A. Kahana, Yosipon ke-fi defus Mantova (Berdichev 1896–1913). This is the text Rubinstein translated; the Alexander sections are cols. 60–118. (b) The Constantinople 1510 print (Tam ibn Yahya, Judah ibn Moskoni's recension) and Venice 1544, which carry the longer Alexander Romance interpolation. (c) Breithaupt's Gotha 1707/1710 Hebrew–Latin edition after the Venice print, which gives a Latin crib for checking. Archive.org: https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_VUdl5MmuvhAC (public-domain mark). I did not verify a digitized copy of the Berdichev edition; HebrewBooks or the National Library of Israel probably have one.
verification.recommendation: Not a strong candidate, because English is full for both layers: Bowman 2022 for ch. 10 and Rubinstein's 1965 HUC thesis, freely online, for the Mantua-recension Alexander Romance. Latin (Breithaupt 1707) and German (2010, ch. 10) also exist. If pursued for Russian, the right unit is the Alexander Romance interpolation (Mantua/Berdichev cols. 60–118, or the longer Constantinople 1510 text), translated directly from the Hebrew, which nobody has yet done in Russian. Checking it needs a Medieval Hebrew specialist, beyond Greek and Latin.

verification.en_found:
The claim holds. Israel J. Kazis, The Book of the Gests of Alexander of Macedon. Sefer Toledot Alexandros ha-Makdoni. A Mediaeval Hebrew Version of the Alexander Romance by Immanuel ben Jacob Bonfils (Cambridge, MA: Mediaeval Academy of America, Publication no. 75, 1962), xi + 227 pp. + Hebrew section. I downloaded and read the PDF.
- The English translation (pp. 59–176) is complete. It covers all three parts: (1) the Romance, from Nectanebus to the burial in Alexandria; (2) the [Apothegms], from Sefer Musre ha-Philosophim; (3) the [Chronicle], from Alexander's death to Pompey.
- The 47 Hebrew picture captions, which record the illustrations of the lost illuminated Latin model, are translated in the footnotes.
- Kazis divides the text by the paragraph numbers of Zingerle 1885 (I1) and Hilka 1920 (I2).
- Notes and appendices: II (Hebrew expansions), III (differences from the Latin), IV (transliterations).
- Free PDF from the Mediaeval Academy: https://cdn.ymaws.com/sites/www.medievalacademy.org/resource/resmgr/maa_books_online/kazis_0075_bkmrkdpdf.pdf (also on Scribd).
- Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (1994; rev. 2012), does not include it. I checked its contents list on archive.org: Letter to Aristotle, Pharasmanes, George the Monk, Palladius, Dindimus, Iter ad Paradisum, plus appendices.
verification.other_found: I found no translation into French, German, Italian, Spanish or modern Hebrew; given the limited searching, treat this as unconfirmed rather than proven. One partial PD item: Israel Lévi, "Les traductions hébraïques de l'histoire d'Alexandre," REJ 3 (1881), 238–275, at pp. 245–246, printed an excerpt from the first folio of the Turin manuscript (Peyron 1880, Cod. CCXVIII.A.VII.6). That folio carries Bonfils' title, attribution and preface. Kazis says the Turin manuscript was later destroyed by fire (the 1904 Turin library fire). I did not check whether Lévi gives a French rendering of the excerpt. Lévi's other publications do not concern this text: Toledot Alexander (1886/87) and Sefer Alexandros Mokdon (Steinschneider Festschrift 1896) cover the Arabic-derived Paris and Modena-type versions. Van Bekkum's books (1992, London Jews' College MS 145; 1994, Paris héb. 671.5) also treat other Hebrew versions, not Bonfils. I could not open Dönitz's chapter in Zuwiyya's Companion (Brill 2011) to check its list of translations.
verification.source_text:
Best edition: Kazis 1962, Hebrew text with apparatus, edited from a photostat of the only copy, Paris BnF hébr. 750(3). The text runs on ff. 80–90v and then 24–79v (65 folios); the first folio is lost; it was copied by Hayyim and his grandfather Yehosef, completed Elul 1428. Kazis emends the Hebrew from Zingerle (I1) and Hilka (I2).
- Access: free PDF from the Mediaeval Academy (URL above).
- Copyright: © 1962 Mediaeval Academy of America. I could not check whether it was renewed: the Stanford renewal database blocked automated access. The MAA's terms page returned 403, so I could not read its licence. Treat it as freely available but not openly licensed.
- The medieval text itself is public domain. A fresh transcription from the manuscript would avoid the editorial-rights question. I could not confirm a digitization of hébr. 750 on Gallica; Vajda's catalogue notes on hébr. 750–752 are there (https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/btv1b8530164d). Ktiv/IMHM microfilm is likely but not verified.
- Public-domain extras: Lévi, REJ 3 (1881), 245–246, for the lost Turin preface. For the Latin side: Zingerle 1885 and Hilka 1920, both PD.
verification.recommendation: Eligible only as a Russian project of moderate priority: there is no Russian translation, but a complete English one with facing Hebrew is free online. Most of the text is a straight rendering of the Historia de preliis (I1/I2), which itself has no Russian translation. The distinctively Jewish material is the place to start: Bonfils' Turin preface (from Lévi 1881), the Yosippon and Musre ha-Philosophim insertions, the 47 picture captions, and Parts II (Apothegms) and III (Chronicle). Checking the Russian will need a Medieval Hebrew specialist, beyond Greek and Latin.

verification.title: Old Czech Alexandreis (Staročeská Alexandreida), St Vitus fragment (Svatovítský zlomek, AlexV, early 15th-c. copy, 2,460 vv.)
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation, either full or in excerpts. I ran four Russian searches: «Староческая Александреида перевод»; «"Александреида" староческая поэма XIII век чешская литература»; «чешская "Александреида" перевод на русский фрагмент»; and «"Александреида" хрестоматия по зарубежной литературе средних веков чешская литература». They returned only reference-work mentions: Brockhaus-Efron "Александрида" (ru.wikisource ЭСБЕ), the ru.wikipedia article on the Old Russian Alexandria, which mentions the two Czech versions (verse and prose), and booksite.ru "Чешская литература". None of them offers a Russian text. facetia.ru/node/2257 (Walter of Châtillon, with Grabar-Passek excerpts) does not mention the Czech poem. I could not check two places: the Czech section of Purishev's Хрестоматия (1975; the dokumen.pub copy was down for maintenance) and quotations in Soviet histories of Czech literature (e.g. АН СССР 1959). Short quoted lines in such surveys cannot be ruled out, but I found no evidence of an actual translation.
verification.en_found: This overturns the sweep's "EN none". Walter Schamschula, An Anthology of Czech Literature, 1st Period: From the Beginnings until 1410 (Westslavische Beiträge; Frankfurt a.M.–Bern–New York–Paris: Peter Lang, 1991), pp. 117–136. It prints the Old Czech text with an English interlinear translation. Schamschula's translation is reproduced online, with his permission, by Charles University's MECZ project: https://mecz.kreas.ff.cuni.cz/publication/the-alexandreis/ . It has 549 verses: 381 from the St Vitus fragment and 168 from the Budějovice-Museum fragment. The St Vitus passages are, in Vážný's numbering, vv. 1–68, 202–300, 935–1103, 1937–1953 and 2241–2258 (by my count about 371 of 2,460 lines, roughly 15%). I found no complete English translation. Zdeněk Salzmann's survey "Czech Literature Before Hus" (1961, en.wikisource) discusses the poem but translates no passages. My fifth English search hit the session's web-search cap (200/200), so I could not run a final query for post-2020 English work (theses, a full translation).
verification.other_found: German: Reinhold Trautmann, Die alttschechische Alexandreis, mit Einleitung und Glossar (Heidelberg: Winter, 1916; Sammlung slavischer Lehr- und Handbücher). It is an edition with a German introduction and glossary, not a translation. I found no German translation. Czech: Staročeská Alexandreida, prepared by Václav Vážný with an introduction co-written with Albert Pražák (Praha: ELK, 1949, Národní klenotnice). This is the text put into modern spelling, not a modern-Czech translation. Vážný's critical edition (ČSAV, 1963) is the line-numbering standard cited by MECZ. Česká čítanka/cs.wikisource has transcriptions of all nine fragments. Fragments, per cs.wikipedia: St Vitus 2,460 vv.; Jindřichův Hradec 492; Budějovice 342; Budějovice-Museum 346; Museum 124; Šafařík 118; Vienna 109; Esztergom 82; Budějovice II 6 couplets. That makes 4,140 lines in all, of which 3,449 are unique. I did not verify whether any full modern-Czech, Polish or other translation exists.
verification.source_text: The Old Czech text is public domain. (1) cs.wikisource, "Alexandreis/Zlomek Svatovítský": the full St Vitus fragment in normalised transcription, taken from citanka.cz and tagged PD-old-70, but without line numbers (https://cs.wikisource.org/wiki/Alexandreis/Zlomek_Svatovítský; index of all fragments at https://cs.wikisource.org/wiki/Alexandreis). (2) Trautmann 1916, digitised at https://archive.org/details/diealttschechisc00trauuoft . Trautmann died in 1951, so the edition is PD in the EU since 2022 and in the US as a 1916 publication; it is the best fully open scholarly base text. (3) For line numbering and cross-checking, use Vážný's critical edition (1949 ELK / 1963 ČSAV), scanned in the Czech Academy of Sciences' Czech language institute (ÚJČ) online Vokabulář webový (http://147.231.53.91/src/index.php?s=v&cat=47&bookid=887&page=1). The text is PD, but the apparatus is still under copyright (Vážný died in 1966).
verification.recommendation: A good Neoscholia candidate for Russian: I found no translation of any kind, so it would be a first. It is also worth doing in English, since the only English version is Schamschula's 1991 interlinear excerpt of about 15% of the St Vitus fragment. Start with the St Vitus fragment (2,460 vv.) in roughly 400–500-line instalments keyed to Vážný's numbering, beginning with sections Schamschula did not cover (e.g. vv. 301–934). Two caveats: this is medieval reception rather than the antique core, and checking the translation needs an Old Czech specialist (a Bohemist), beyond Greek/Latin, with comparison against Walter's Latin and Ulrich von Etzenbach's German.

candidates.title: Aleksandriani (ალექსანდრიანი): Georgian Alexandria / «Грузинская Александрия». Archil II's prose and Petre Chkhataraisdze's verse and prose versions
candidates.author: King Archil II (prose, 1700–1713); Petre Chkhataraisdze (verse and prose reworking, 1713–1724)
candidates.date: Early 18th c. (an older Georgian translation, before the 11th c., is lost)
candidates.tradition: Reception and romance; Georgian, from the Russian Serbian Alexandria
candidates.size: Full-length romance; extent unknown
candidates.edition: Manuscripts only, as far as found: Central Archive No. 123; Institute of Manuscripts H-105, Q-736, H-1204, S-1514 (ka.wiki). Khakhanov's 1893 Russian study is open at phaidrabg o:558.
candidates.ru_evidence: Khakhanov 1893 («Грузинская повесть об Александре Македонском и сербская Александрия») may contain excerpts; no full Russian translation found.
candidates.en_evidence: No English translation found; en.wikipedia notes that the early Georgian versions are lost.
candidates.value: Low value for antiquity (it derives from the Serbian Alexandria). Chkhataraisdze adds Persianate Georgian heroes (Vepkhistqaosani, Visramiani) and an anti-Muslim slant, which is of interest only as reception.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Low. No confirmed printed edition, and 18th-c. Georgian; needs a Kartvelologist.
candidates.pilot_unit: Not recommended until an edition is located.

verification.title: Aleksandriani (ალექსანდრიანი), the Georgian Alexandria: King Archil II's prose translation (1700–1713, made from a Russian text of the Serbian Alexandria) and Petre Chkhataraisdze's verse and prose reworkings (1713–1724)
verification.en_found: No English translation or excerpt was found. en.wikipedia "Alexander Romance" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Romance) only records that the early Georgian versions are lost and that an 18th-century version by Archil II, from a Serbian or Russian source, survives. Open Library, Harvard LibraryCloud and archive.org metadata searches for Aleksandriani, Alekʻsandriani, Chkhataraisdze / Čxataraisże and "Georgian Alexander romance" turned up only the 1980 Georgian edition and no translation. Caveat: the WebSearch budget for the session ran out after one English web search, so English-language articles (for example in Rayfield's literary history or the Ancient Narrative / Brill Alexander volumes) were not checked by search. They are unlikely to contain more than brief quotations.
verification.other_found:
No French, German, Italian or Spanish translation was found. Points that are new compared with the sweep:
(a) Archil's version has a published critical edition: Arčʻili, ალექსანდრიანი / Alekʻsandriani, "tekʻsti gamosacʻemad moamzada, damokvleva, komentarebi, lekʻsikoni da sażiebeli daurtʻo Revaz Mirianašvilma". Tbilisi: Mecʻniereba, 1980, 201 pp., Rustaveli Institute of Georgian Literature. Russian added title «Александрия», Russian summary, catalogued as "In Georgian, translated from Russian". OCLC 32782774, LC PK9169.A72 A8 1980, held at Harvard; Open Library OL57869831M.
(b) For Petre Chkhataraisdze's verse version (Q-736) and his prose reworking (H-1204, S-1514), I found no edition. ka.wikipedia (https://ka.wikipedia.org/wiki/ალექსანდრიანი and https://ka.wikipedia.org/wiki/პეტრე_ჩხატარაისძე) lists manuscripts only. The 1928 Georgian anthology of 16th–18th c. secular literature (vol. II) may include an excerpt. It is in Georgian only and I could not check it, because the NPLG server returned 410/404.
(c) Khakhanov (1893, p. 251) also mentions a further prose Alexandria translated into Georgian c. 1850–60 by a Georgian Catholic priest called Petros, probably from Latin, which he says is lost. In the same place he cites a piece on Alexander in Georgian folk literature in СМОМПК вып. X, отд. III, pp. 37–44, which I did not check.
verification.source_text: Archil's prose: R. Mirianashvili (ed.), ალექსანდრიანი (Tbilisi: Metsniereba 1980), OCLC 32782774. This is the only printed critical text. It is not public domain or openly licensed, since the edited text and apparatus are from 1980, and I found no online scan. The underlying manuscripts are in the Central State Archive of Georgia (No. 123) and the K. Kekelidze National Centre of Manuscripts (H-105). Petre Chkhataraisdze's verse (NCM Q-736) and prose (NCM H-1204, S-1514) versions survive in manuscripts only, and I found no open digital facsimiles. Openly licensed secondary source: Khakhanov 1893, ЖМНП, CC BY 2.0 AT scan at https://phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/o:558 (download: https://phaidrabg.bg.ac.rs/download/o:558). For comparison, the Russian-tradition model text of the Serbian Alexandria is available in the Литпамятники 1965 volume.
verification.recommendation: This is a weak candidate. Archil's text is a close Georgian rendering of the Russian Serbian Alexandria, which Russian readers already have, and its only edition (Mirianashvili 1980) is neither open nor online. The original-value material is Petre Chkhataraisdze's verse and prose reworkings, but these are unpublished manuscripts, so work would need a Georgian philologist for transcription and checking and is not feasible with an LLM alone. If pursued, start with the prologue and the Roxane wedding episode of Petre's verse version (Q-736), compared against Archil.

name: Arabic, Persian, Turkic, Malay and other Islamicate Alexander (Dhu l-Qarnayn / Iskandar) traditions
already_translated_ru:
Russian translations exist for:
- **Nizami, Iskandar-nāma**: complete Soviet translations (Lipskerov 1953; not re-checked).
- **Firdawsi, Alexander section of the Shahnameh**: Литпамятники «Шахнаме» (Бану-Лахути et al.).
- **Navoi, «Стена Искандара»**: in «Поэмы», БВЛ 1972 (Державин, Пеньковский, Липкин); may be abridged.
- **Tarsusi, Dārābnāma (mostly about Alexander)**: Russian by N. B. Кондырева (Moscow 2000), cited in Venetis's review in Iranian Studies 39 (2006).
- **Biruni, al-Āthār al-bāqiya**: М. А. Салье, 1957 (not re-checked).
- **Sirr al-asrār**: only indirectly, through the Old Russian «Тайная тайных» (from Hebrew), with modern Russian in БЛДР т. 9.

Tabari, Dinawari and Mas'udi in Russian are excerpts (vostlit) and do not cover Alexander.

English-only (no Russian found):
- prose Iskandarnāma (Venetis 2017/18 complete);
- Qiṣṣat Dhulqarnayn (Zuwiyya 2001);
- Tabari's Taʾrīkh, Alexander part (SUNY vol. 4);
- Thaʿlabī (Brinner 2002).

candidates.title: Rasāʾil Arisṭāṭālīs ilā l-Iskandar (Arabic epistolary novel) / The Correspondence of Aristotle and Alexander / «Переписка Аристотеля и Александра»; unit: the biographical letters
candidates.author: Anonymous; Arabic version attributed to Sālim Abū l-ʿAlāʾ, secretary of Caliph Hishām
candidates.date: Greek original c. 6th c. (Maróth); Arabic c. 724–743
candidates.tradition: wisdom / epistolary romance / mirror for princes; Graeco-Arabic
candidates.size: Arabic text about 149 pp. (Maróth 2006). Ch. 8 (a proto-Sirr al-asrār, 59 pp.) makes up about one third of it. The biographical letters run about 30–45 pp.
candidates.edition: Maróth, The Correspondence… (Piliscsaba: AIMES 2006), from two Süleymaniye MSS, not openly licensed. His full study is open: Acta Antiqua 45 (2005) 231–315, real.mtak.hu/45844
candidates.ru_evidence: No Russian translation found on the Russian web or vostlit. The only related Russian text is the Old Russian «Тайная тайных» (from a Hebrew Sirr al-asrār), with modern Russian in БЛДР т. 9.
candidates.en_evidence: Maróth 2006 is Arabic text plus English introduction and commentary, with no translation (checked the 2005 study's structure). S. M. Stern, Aristotle on the World State (1968), translates one inserted treatise (siyāsat al-mudun).
candidates.other_translations: French studies and partial renderings by Grignaschi (1965–67); Bielawski–Plezia 1970 (French) of the letter on governing cities.
candidates.value: Possibly the last Greek epistolary novel and the first Arabic prose book. Includes letters on Alexander's birth and Persian war, and on the killing of the Persian nobles (Aristotle dissuades). Matrix of the Sirr al-asrār / Secretum secretorum mirror tradition.
candidates.ai_feasibility: Medium: archaic Umayyad Arabic, only two MSS, edition rights needed from AIMES. Needs an Arabist reviewer; Greek epistolography helps.
candidates.pilot_unit: Opening letter with the birth narrative, plus chs. 11–12 (the Persian nobles), about 15–20 pp. Arabic.

verification.title: Rasāʾil Arisṭāṭālīs ilā l-Iskandar / «Переписка Аристотеля и Александра». This is the Arabic epistolary cycle attributed to Sālim Abū l-ʿAlāʾ (under Hishām, 724–743). Maróth's own title is Aḥwāl al-ḥukamāʾ fī ayyām al-Iskandar; Gutas calls it "The Epistolary Cycle between Aristotle and Alexander". Unit assessed: the biographical/narrative letters, without the four inserted treatises.
verification.ru_found:
I ran 8 Russian searches through Google, including the vostlit.info site, plus Russian Wikipedia and a specialist Russian bibliography. None of them turned up a Russian translation of the cycle or of any biographical letter. What exists in Russian:

(1) G. A. Koshelenko, «Аристотель и Александр (к вопросу о подлинности „Письма Аристотеля к Александру о политике по отношению к городам")», ВДИ 1974, № 1, 22–44 (http://ancienthist.ru/issues/261/articles/6167?locale=ru). This is a study of the inserted Peri basileias letter only (Gutas's Letter 9). The full text is not online, so I could not check whether it quotes passages in Russian. At most it would give excerpts of that treatise, not of the biographical letters. It is cited in Marinovich's «Источниковедение Древней Греции (эпоха эллинизма)» (annales.info/greece/istved/idg2_02.htm), which mentions no Russian translation.

(2) A. A. Ignatenko, doctoral dissertation abstract (автореферат), 1989 (cheloveknauka.com/obschestvenno-politicheskie-vzglyady-arabo-islamskih-filosofov-srednevekovya-ix-xv-vv). It only mentions the Peri basileias letter and the "многие небольшие послания Стагирита Александру"; it contains no translation.

(3) M. A. Solopova, «Античная философия и Восток. Избранная библиография. Ч. III», Историко-философский ежегодник 2018 (https://iphras.ru/uplfile/histph/2018/386-418-greece-east3.pdf). Under this text it lists only Maróth 2006. It has no Russian translation and no Koshelenko entry. Its introduction calls the Aristotle–Alexander correspondence probably the first Aristotelian text put into Arabic under the Umayyads.

(4) A related but different text: the Old Russian «Тайная тайных», made from a Hebrew Sirr al-asrār, with a modern Russian version in БЛДР т. 9 (D. M. Bulanin; Russian Wikipedia s.v. Secretum Secretorum). The Sirr grew out of Letter 7 (as-Siyāsa al-ʿāmmiyya) of the cycle, but it is not the cycle. There is no modern Russian translation of the Arabic Sirr.

(5) Letters on the Persian nobles: Stern and Maróth note that the exchange about killing the Persian nobles (Grignaschi's chapters 11–12) is also known as the introduction to the Letter of Tansar. Russian works only mention «Письмо Тансара»; I found no Russian translation of it. One possible indirect excerpt is the Russian version of Stoneman's «Александр Великий: жизнь в легенде», ch. 10 (simposium.ru), which discusses the Tansar letter. I did not check whether it quotes the exchange.
verification.en_found:
There is no complete English translation, and the biographical letters exist in English only as short quotations and summaries.

(1) Maróth 2006 (Piliscsaba: AIMES, Documenta et Monographiae V). The publisher's page gives 112 pp. English + 149 pp. Arabic, languages "angol, arab": https://avicenna-kkki.hu/documenta-et-monographiae/the-correspondence-between-aristotle-and-alexander-the-great/. Gutas's review confirms "112 pp. (English text); i–v, 149 pp. (Arabic text)". The English part is the study, not a translation.

(2) D. Gutas, "On Graeco-Arabic Epistolary 'Novels'", Middle Eastern Literatures 12.1 (2009) 59–70, DOI 10.1080/14752620902760590. He states explicitly that before Maróth the cycle "was neither published nor translated" and that "there is no complete translation". He gives a section-by-section English synopsis with Maróth's page numbers: summaries, not translation.

(3) Maróth, Acta Antiqua 45 (2005) 231–315 (open access: https://real.mtak.hu/45844/1/aant.45.2005.2-3.11.pdf). It contains English paraphrases and a few short quoted sentences, e.g. the opening of Alexander's letter to Darius (p. 47 of the edition).

(4) S. M. Stern, Aristotle on the World State (1968). It translates material from the inserted Peri basileias / Risāla fī siyāsat al-mudun letter only. I did not re-check how much.

(5) A. S. Fulton's English translation of the later Arabic Sirr al-asrār (in Steele, Opera hactenus inedita Rogeri Baconi V, 1920). This is the derivative treatise, not Letter 7 itself.

(6) M. Boyce, The Letter of Tansar (Rome 1968). It renders the Persian (Ibn Isfandiyār) version, whose introduction parallels the exchange about the Persian nobles. It is a parallel, not this text.

(7) Recent studies whose contents I could not inspect (possible short excerpts): E. Cottrell, "An Early Mirror for Princes and Manual for Secretaries: The Epistolary Novel of Aristotle and Alexander", in Nawotka–Wojciechowska (eds.), Alexander the Great and the East (2016); R. Forster, "The Arabic Secretum secretorum and the So-Called 'Epistolary Novel': Reading Pseudo-Aristotelian Letters in Arabic", in Donato–Scrofani–Dorandi (eds.), Thinking through Letters (Brill).

(8) Excluded: L. Marlow, Medieval Muslim Mirrors for Princes (CUP 2023). It anthologises texts of the 10th–12th c. and only refers to the cycle in footnotes.
verification.other_found:
French:
- J. Bielawski & M. Plezia, Lettre d'Aristote à Alexandre sur la politique envers les cités (Wrocław 1970). Critical edition with a full French translation and commentary, but of Letter 9 (Peri basileias) only (confirmed by Gutas and Maróth).
- M. Grignaschi, "La Siyâsatu-l-ʿâmmiyya et l'influence iranienne sur la pensée politique islamique", Monumentum H. S. Nyberg III (Acta Iranica 6, 1975) 33–287. Edition of Letter 7 with study and "Notes au texte arabe". I saw no running French translation. The same article states that the biographical pieces (his I, II, III, VI, VII, IX, XIII, XV) were still unpublished in 1975 and remained so until Maróth 2006.
- Grignaschi, BEO 19 (1965–66) 7–83, and Le Muséon 80 (1967) 211–264. Studies with partial French renderings; I could not verify how much.
- J. Bielawski, "Lettres d'Aristote à Alexandre le Grand en version arabe", Rocznik Orientalistyczny 28 (1964) 7–34. A description; I could not check whether it translates anything.
- P. Carlier, Ktèma 5 (1980), reprinted by UN@ 2022 (https://una-editions.fr/etude-sur-la-pretendue-lettre-d-aristote/). Study only, no translation.
- Darmesteter, JA 1894: French translation of the Letter of Tansar, a parallel to the Persian-nobles exchange.

German, Italian, Spanish: no translation of the cycle found. Spanish only has the medieval Poridat/Bocados lines, which descend from the Sirr and from Mubashshir, not from this text.

Scholarly debate: Maróth argues for a 6th-c. Greek original. Grignaschi dates a Greek "roman épistolaire classique" to the 5th c., with Persian and Hermetic additions by Sālim's circle. Stern judged it a compilation put together in Islamic times. Gutas (2009) rejects the "Greek novel" label. Present the framing as contested, not as fact.
verification.source_text:
Only edition of the whole cycle: M. Maróth, The Correspondence between Aristotle and Alexander the Great: An Anonymous Greek Novel in Letters in Arabic Translation (Piliscsaba: Avicenna Institute of Middle Eastern Studies, 2006; ISBN 963-86359-7-5; Arabic text i–v + 149 pp.). It is based on Istanbul, Süleymaniye, Fatih 5323 and Ayasofya 4260, both late 11th c. and by the same scribe. It is in copyright and not openly licensed, so translate from it, cite its page numbers, and do not reproduce the Arabic.

Maróth's companion study is open access: Acta Antiqua 45 (2005) 231–315, https://real.mtak.hu/45844/1/aant.45.2005.2-3.11.pdf.

Public-domain editions cover only the inserted treatises, not the biographical letters:
- J. Lippert, De epistula pseudaristotelica περὶ βασιλείας (Halle 1891): Letter 9.
- L. Cheikho in Malouf–Eddé–Cheikho, Traités inédits d'anciens philosophes arabes (Beirut 1911) 36–49: the Admonitions and Letter 9.

For the biographical unit, Maróth 2006 is therefore the only usable text. Gutas 2009 gives a page map of the edition.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate. There is no Russian translation and no translation in any language of the biographical letters; only the inserted treatises have been translated (Letter 9 in full into French, parts of it into English). Start with the opening block, Narrative 1 to Narrative 3 (Maróth pp. 3–12): Philip, Aristotle and Alexander's education. Then do Letters 5–6 and the exchange about the Persian nobles, alongside its Letter of Tansar parallel. Checking the translation needs an Arabist who knows early Umayyad chancery prose and its Syriac and Greek calques, which is beyond Greek and Latin.

candidates.title: Akhbār al-Iskandar, the Alexander chapter of Mukhtār al-ḥikam wa-maḥāsin al-kalim / The Life and Sayings of Alexander / «Известия об Искандаре» из «Избранных изречений»
candidates.author: al-Mubashshir ibn Fātik
candidates.tradition: romance-derived biography and wisdom (sayings, laments at the coffin); Fatimid Egypt
candidates.size: About 25–30 pp. of Arabic (estimate)
candidates.edition: Meissner, ZDMG 49 (1895), the Alexander section only, public domain (ZDMG digitised on MENAdoc); complete work ed. Badawi, Madrid 1958.
candidates.ru_evidence: No Russian translation of Mukhtār al-ḥikam or its Alexander chapter found (Russian web; no vostlit index entry).
candidates.en_evidence: No modern English from the Arabic found. Only the Middle English 'Dicts and Sayings' via Latin/French (Scrope c. 1450; Woodville/Caxton 1477), per Wikipedia.
candidates.other_translations: Medieval Spanish Bocados de oro; Latin Liber philosophorum moralium antiquorum; Meissner 1895 (German translation not verified).
candidates.value: Compressed Arabic Pseudo-Callisthenes biography, the earliest datable Arabic witness, which Cottrell links to α. Includes sayings and death laments. Links the Greek Romance to the European 'Dicts' tradition.
candidates.ai_feasibility: High: plain classical Arabic, public-domain text, and Latin/Spanish/Middle English parallels for checking. Needs an Arabist reviewer.
candidates.pilot_unit: The whole Alexander chapter (about 25 pp.).

verification.title: al-Mubashshir ibn Fātik, Mukhtār al-ḥikam wa-maḥāsin al-kalim (1048–49), ch. 14: Akhbār al-Iskandar plus Ādāb al-Iskandar wa-mawāʿiẓuhu (narrative, coffin laments, Olympias' lament, then a separate block of Alexander's sayings)
verification.ru_found: I partly refuted the "none" claim: a Russian selection of maxims exists, and it has a section on Alexander. The translation is А. В. Сагадеев, «Абу-ль-Вафа ал-Мубашшир Ибн Фатик. Изысканные афоризмы и изящные речения», with an introduction («Арабский Диоген Лаэртий») and commentary by В. Марков. It first appeared in Вестник Восточного института № 1(7), т. 4 (СПб., 1998), pp. 18–52. Two sources cite it: Yu. Arzhanov, Христианский Восток 6 (XII), 2013, p. 311 n. 2 (archive.org item xb-1.1-2-1912, file "6-12,-2013"), and Е. Ю. Гончаров in «Оригинал и повторение» (2014), p. 113 n. 2. It was reprinted in «Средневековая арабо-мусульманская философия в переводах А. В. Сагадеева», т. 3 (М.: ИД Марджани, 2010; Bibliotheca Islamica), pp. 300–324. I checked the volume's table of contents in the free LitRes preview (https://www.litres.ru/book/nur-serikovich-kirab/srednevekovaya-arabo-musulmanskaya-filosofiya-v-perev-17145738/). It runs: Гермес, Саб, Гомер, Солон, Зенон, Гиппократ, Пифагор, Диоген, Сократ, Платон, Аристотель (310), «Александр Македонский» (pp. 316–318), Птолемей, Лукман, Медаргис, Василий, Гален, anonymous sayings. So about 2 pages, set against roughly 28 pages for the whole chapter in the Turkish bilingual. I could not see the content of pp. 316–318. Given the title, it is most likely a selection of sayings, not the narrative Akhbār. I found no complete Russian translation of the chapter. Searches on archive.org full text and DuckDuckGo («Мубашшир», «Ибн Фатик», «Изысканные афоризмы и изящные речения», «Сагадеев Мубашшир», «Мубашшир Искандар», «аль-Мубашшир Александр Македонский перевод») turned up nothing else. vostlit.info timed out, so I could not re-check it. Separately, Arzhanov 2013 discusses the coffin laments but does not translate them.
verification.en_found: There is no modern complete English translation from the Arabic, but there are excerpts, so "none" does not hold. (1) E. Cottrell, "Al-Mubaššir ibn Fātik and the α Version of the Alexander Romance", in Stoneman, Erickson and Netton (eds), The Alexander Romance in Persia and the East (Ancient Narrative Suppl. 15, Barkhuis 2012), pp. 233–253 (DOI 10.2307/j.ctt13wwxb1.16). I read the OCR on archive.org. It gives short English translations of passages: the one-sentence summary of the Letter to Aristotle (Badawi p. 236) and the China episode, set in a table against the Syriac. It also calls Meissner's edition and translation "incomplete". (2) The Middle English Dicts and Sayings is a full but indirect medieval version (Arabic > Old Spanish > Latin > French > English). It includes the Alexander chapter: Scrope c. 1450 and Woodville/Caxton 1477, ed. Bühler, EETS 211, 1941. Knust 1879, pp. 415ff., prints the Alexander biography in its Spanish, Latin, French and English versions (Meissner p. 585 n. 1). (3) Related but not Mubashshir: Brock, JSS 15 (1970), translates the Syriac laments, and Seleznyov, Scrinium 10 (2014), edits and translates al-Makīn's laments. Searches I ran: "Mubashshir Alexander Mukhtar al-hikam English translation", "Choicest Maxims Alexander Mubashshir translation", "Mubashshir Alexander laments philosophers translation", "Akhbar al-Iskandar Mubashshir" (no results), plus archive.org full-text, OpenAlex/Crossref and BMCR 2012.11.08. None turned up a complete English version.
verification.other_found: GERMAN, verified: B. Meissner, "Mubaššir's Aḫbār el-Iskender", ZDMG 49 (1895), pp. 583–627. The sweep had not checked this. It contains the Arabic text (pp. 586–603), a full German translation of the narrative part, "Die Geschichte Alexanders" (pp. 604–620), and an analysis (pp. 620–627). The translation runs from Philip's murder through the coffin laments and Olympias' banquet to the physical description. It stops before the section of Alexander's own sayings (Ādāb wa-mawāʿiẓ), which is the gap Cottrell means by "incomplete". TURKISH, complete and verified: Mübeşşir İbn Fâtik, Muhtâru'l-Hikem ve Mehâsinu'l-Kelim / Hikmetli Sözler, Arabic text with Turkish translation by Osman Güman, ed. Abdulkadir Coşkun (Türkiye Yazma Eserler Kurumu, İstanbul 2013, 2nd ed. later), based on Topkapı Ahmed III 3249 (dated 1259), 3206 and 2598. Ch. 14 "İskender'in Haberleri" runs pp. 418–454 and "İskender'in Âdâbı ve Öğütleri" pp. 454–473. A free official PDF is at https://ekitap.yek.gov.tr/Uploads/ProductsFiles/64962e4f-fcf5-401c-810a-51b6144546d9.pdf. FRENCH: Cottrell's unpublished EPHE thesis (2004, pp. 220–240) translates al-Shahrazūrī's Alexander chapter, whose first part copies Ibn Fātik, so it is an indirect partial translation. The ALIENTO database (aliento.eu) also holds individual Mukhtār maxims; I did not check whether any Alexander items are among them. MEDIEVAL: Old Spanish Bocados de oro (ed. Knust 1879; Crombach 1971); Latin Liber philosophorum moralium antiquorum (ed. Franceschini 1931–32); French, Tignonville's Dits moraulx (ed. Eder 1915); Occitan. Badawi's Arabic edition (Madrid 1958; Beirut 1980²) has a parallel Spanish title only, not a translation. I found no modern Spanish or Italian translation of the chapter.
verification.source_text: Public domain, for the narrative part only: Meissner, ZDMG 49 (1895), pp. 586–603. He uses Leiden Warner 515 and Berlin Or. quart. 785, with al-Shahrazūrī MSS for variants. Digitised at https://archive.org/details/zeitschriftderde0049ewin (also archive.org zeitschrift49deutuoft and MENAdoc Halle); the Arabic OCR is unusable, so work from the page images. The facing German translation (pp. 604–620) serves as a ready control text. The sayings section (Ādāb al-Iskandar) is not in Meissner. For it, use Badawi, Mukhtār al-ḥikam (Madrid 1958; Beirut 1980), still in copyright, or the Arabic text in the 2013 YEK bilingual: free official PDF, all rights reserved, collated from Topkapı Ahmed III 3249/3206/2598. Before publishing the Arabic of that section, check rights or re-establish the text from the manuscripts.
verification.recommendation: Still a good candidate, but it cannot be billed as untranslated. Russian has a roughly 2-page selection (Sagadeev), English has excerpts (Cottrell), German has the whole narrative (Meissner 1895, public domain) and Turkish the whole chapter (Güman 2013). Neoscholia can offer the first complete Russian and English translations made directly from the Arabic. Start with the Akhbār al-Iskandar on Meissner's public-domain text (Philip's murder through coffin laments, Olympias' lament and the portrait), using Meissner's German and the Turkish as checks. Then add the Ādāb section from Badawi or the Topkapı manuscripts, once rights are cleared. Checking the translation needs an Arabist, not Greek or Latin; Syriac helps for comparison with the α tradition.

verification.title: Kitāb al-Tījān fī mulūk Ḥimyar (Ibn Hishām, from Wahb b. Munabbih): the section on al-Ṣaʿb Dhū l-Qarnayn (Malik al-Ṣaʿb Dhī l-Qarnayn)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the al-Ṣaʿb section, either in full or as an excerpt. Three Russian items come close.
(1) С. А. Французов, «Что значит имя? (о происхождении и значении имени Абраха…)», Христианский Восток 2 (VIII), 2000, c. ~105–106 (full text on archive.org, item xb-1.1-2-1912, file "2-8,-2000"). It translates about three sentences of Tījān p. 138 (Sanaa 1979 edition). These are the opening lines of the next section, which say that when Dhū l-Qarnayn al-Ṣaʿb died, his son Abraha Dhū l-Manār succeeded him. They come just after the Ṣaʿb narrative and are not part of it.
(2) М. Б. Пиотровский, «Коранические сказания» (1991). I read the Зу-ль-Карнайн chapter in full on rulit.me (book 543184, p. 67). It mentions in a footnote only that the epithet was sometimes given to "какой-то химйаритский царь Йемена". There is no translation, and it cites only Bertels, Nöldeke and Friedlaender. The book uses the Tījān elsewhere (Sanaa 1979 edition) for ʿĀd and Luqmān.
(3) Piotrovsky, «Предание о химйаритском царе Асʿаде ал-Камиле» (1977). Its full text was not available to me. Its scope is Asʿad, as the sweep said, and the references to it that I found give no sign of a Ṣaʿb translation.
Negative searches: archive.org full-text search for «ат-Тиджан», «ат-тиджан» + Карнайн, «Зу-л-Карнайн» Химйар Са‘б, «ас-Са‘б» Карнайн, «Вахб ибн Мунаббих» + Зу-л-Карнайн/Хидр/Александр; facetia.ru search for «Тиджан» and «Карнайн» (nothing); and the ru.wikipedia article «Зу-ль-Карнайн» (no mention of Tījān or Ṣaʿb). Four sources could not be checked: vostlit.info timed out, and the Wayback index showed no Ibn Hishām or Wahb text there; the CyberLeninka API returned 0 for every query, which suggests it is broken; Bertels 1948 is not available as full text.
verification.en_found:
The colleague's "EN none" is partly refuted. There is no English translation, but there is a detailed English paraphrase, plus summaries and a short translated excerpt.
(1) F. Krenkow, "The Two Oldest Books on Arabic Folklore", Islamic Culture 2 (Hyderabad 1928) 55–89 and 204–236, with the Ṣaʿb section at pp. 64–74 (https://archive.org/details/in.ernet.dli.2015.91802). This is a running English paraphrase of the whole prose narrative, in about 10 pages:
- the four dreams; the march to Jerusalem; Mūsā al-Khiḍr names him Dhū l-Qarnayn;
- the western campaign: the Sand river, the Darkness, the Valley of Rubies, Jirjīs's bones, and Khiḍr at the Spring of Life;
- al-Andalus, the White Castle, Gog and Magog and the wall;
- the Land of the Angels (the grapes and the stone), and the Banū ʿArjān/"Tarjumānīs" dialogue, which is rendered almost verbatim;
- his death at Ḥinw Qurāqir.
Krenkow only summarises the poems, the inscription, the series of heavenly maxims and Ibn Hishām's excursus on al-Iskandar al-Rūmī and the reading of Q 18:86.
(2) Minnie S. Southgate, Iskandarnamah (Columbia University Press, 1978), appendix: "A summary of the al-Tijan follows", pp. ~198–201 (archive.org: southgate-1978-iskandarnamah).
(3) Anna Akasoy, "Geography, History and Prophecy", in Locating Religions (Brill, 2016, open access; archive.org: oapen-20.500.12657-53818), pp. ~23–24. She gives a translated excerpt of about 8 lines from Tījān pp. 96–97 (the dream of the sun rising in the west, the order to go to the Valley of Diamonds).
(4) Summaries or discussion only: B. Wheeler, Moses in the Qur'an and Islamic Exegesis (2002), pp. 16–19, which cites Lidzbarski's text; Z. D. Zuwiyya's chapter in The Alexander Romance in Persia and the East (2012). Doufikar-Aerts, Alexander Magnus Arabicus (2010) was not checked.
Other checks:
- Jayyusi (ed.), Classical Arabic Stories (2010) has Tījān selections (Luqmān, Anmār and others). I found no Ṣaʿb excerpt in it, though this is not fully confirmed.
- Gorgias Press 2009, "The Book of Crowns on the Kings of Himyar" (Kiraz Chronicles Archive 19), is an Arabic-only reprint.
- The "English translation on Wikisource" claimed in the en.wikipedia article is wrong: the infobox links to Arabic Wikisource.
verification.other_found:
German:
- M. Lidzbarski, "Zu den arabischen Alexandergeschichten", ZA 8 (1893) 263–312 (https://archive.org/details/zeitschriftfuras8189deut). This is not a translation. It is an Arabic edition of the Ṣaʿb story at pp. 278–312, made from Berlin MSS Glaser (A) and WE 137 (B), with a German introduction and notes. B leaves out most of the poems. I checked the text and there is no German rendering, so the sweep's "German treatment" means an edition, not a translation.
- I. Friedlaender, Die Chadhirlegende und der Alexanderroman (1913), pp. 192–203 (https://archive.org/details/diechadhirlegend00frie). This is a detailed German paraphrase with sizeable verbatim German translations: the meeting in Jerusalem and the naming, the Spring of Life episode, and the Land of the Angels. He collates Lidzbarski's text with BM Or. 2901 (1622) and with al-Sūrī. Public domain.
- T. Nagel, Alexander der Große in der frühislamischen Volksliteratur (1978), analyses the text at length. I could not check how much of it is translated.
French, Spanish and Italian: no translation found. The 18th-century "Livre des couronnes d'un grand prix" (Silvestre de Sacy, Notices et extraits 4) is a different, Ottoman-period history of Yemen. The Fondazione Valla Detti islamici di Gesù translates only a single Jesus saying from Tījān p. 27.
Turkish and other languages: nothing found.
verification.source_text:
Three Arabic texts are available.
(1) The editio princeps: Kitāb al-Tījān fī mulūk Ḥimyar, ed. Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn al-Mūsawī with F. Krenkow, Hyderabad: Dāʾirat al-Maʿārif al-ʿUthmāniyya 1347/1928. Scan with OCR at https://archive.org/details/al-Tijan. It was published in 1928, so it is public domain in the US since 2024, and Krenkow died in 1953.
(2) Arabic Wikisource, from a PDF of the same edition: https://ar.wikisource.org/wiki/التيجان_في_ملوك_حمير/ملك_الصعب_ذي_القرنين. Page-level transcriptions (صفحة:التيجان في ملوك حمير.pdf/80–140) all exist. The chapter page itself, however, includes only PDF pp. 82–94 (about 3,400 words), while the Ṣaʿb section actually runs to about PDF p. 126, where the chapter on Abraha begins at p. 127.
(3) For variant readings: Lidzbarski, ZA 8 (1893) 278–312, from Berlin MSS A and B (public domain), together with Friedlaender's 1913 collation notes from BM Or. 2901.
The Sanaa 1979 reprint (Markaz al-Dirāsāt, which adds Akhbār ʿUbayd) and the Gorgias 2009 reprint are not public domain; most modern scholarship cites the Sanaa pagination.
verification.recommendation: This is a strong candidate. There is no Russian translation and no full English or other modern translation, only Krenkow's 1928 paraphrase, Friedlaender's 1913 German extracts and short summaries. The Arabic text is public domain and openly transcribed (Hyderabad 1928 plus Lidzbarski's 1893 manuscript-based edition). Start with the opening unit: the dreams, Jerusalem and the naming by Khiḍr, and the western campaign as far as the Spring of Life (Lidzbarski pp. 278–292; Wikisource PDF pp. 82–94, about 3,400 words). Next do the Land of the Angels and the Banū ʿArjān episodes, and leave the poetry-heavy excursus by Ibn Hishām for last. Use Krenkow and Friedlaender as checks. The work needs an Arabist to verify it (corrupt manuscripts, pseudo-Himyarite verse, Qurʾānic exegesis); Greek and Latin expertise is not enough.

verification.title: al-Thaʿālibī (attrib.), Ghurar akhbār mulūk al-Furs wa-siyarihim: the Iskandar chapter (Zotenberg pp. 399–c.456)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the chapter or of the work, so the colleague's "none" holds for any real translation. Only second-hand quotations exist.

(1) P. Briant, «Дарий в тени Александра», tr. А. Н. Степанова (М.: Вече, 2007; ISBN 978-5-9533-1946-1), chapter on Dārā and Iskandar, c. pp. 315–364. It quotes Thaʿālibī in Russian, translated from Zotenberg's French. Example, p. 339: Dārā came to the throne «в той поре молодости, когда не слушают советов…». ru.wikipedia «Дарий III» cites this (sfn Бриан 2007, с. 339).

(2) Correction to the sweep: vostlit does have an entry «АС-СААЛИБИ, АБУ МАНСУР». Under «Избранные сведения о персидских царях» it holds only a «Заметка». That is an article on authorship by С. С. Додобаев, «Об авторстве труда "Гурар ахбар мулук ал-фурс ва сийарухум"», Известия АН Таджикистана, сер. востоковедение, история, филология, 1992, № 1(25). It is not a translation. URL: vostlit.info/Texts/rus17/As_Saalibi/zametka_1992/text.phtml. The same entry has a text of «Книга остроумных сообщений» (Laṭāʾif al-maʿārif), which is irrelevant here.

(3) Other searches found nothing: CyberLeninka (6 queries, including «Саалиби Гурар», «ас-Саалиби Искандар», «Гурар ахбар мулук ал-Фурс», «Избранные сведения о персидских царях»), ru.wikipedia full-text searches, and facetia.ru (Саалиби / Са'алиби / Искандар). The only CyberLeninka hit is Н. Ш. Зохидов, «К вопросу об атрибуции "Гурар ус-сияр"» (Уч. зап. ХГУ, 2014), also about attribution only.

(4) С. Б. Дашков, «Цари царей — Сасаниды» (2008) is a popular Sasanian history and, as far as I could tell, doesn't cover Iskandar. Not checked in full.

(5) Possible lead I could not confirm: Додобаев may also have written a dissertation on the Ghurar that contains Russian fragments.
verification.en_found:
I found no English translation of the chapter or the work, full or partial. Only quotations in secondary literature:

(1) P. Briant, Darius in the Shadow of Alexander, tr. Jane Marie Todd (Harvard UP, 2015), ch. 10 "Dārā and Iskandar" (DOI 10.4159/9780674744608-012). It is the same book as the Russian 2007 edition, so it carries the same Thaʿālibī quotations, translated from Zotenberg's French. This is inferred from the RU/FR editions; I could not open the English chapter, which is paywalled.

(2) Probably further quoted passages in H. Manteghi, Alexander the Great in the Persian Tradition (I.B. Tauris/Bloomsbury 2018), ch. 2 "Alexander the Great and the Legacy of Sasanian Historiography". Also in Manteghi's and Stoneman's chapters "The Persian Alexander (1)/(2)" in Stoneman (ed.), A History of Alexander the Great in World Culture (CUP 2022). Unverified: paywalled.

(3) Searches with no English translation found: Crossref (about 10 queries), Open Library, archive.org metadata, English Wikipedia full text (the "Hushang" and "Barbad" articles cite the Ghurar without any English translation), and the Iranica entries ESKANDAR-NĀMA and ALEXANDER THE GREAT (the latter is the historical-Alexander article). Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great does not contain it.

Search limits: WebSearch was exhausted, and Google Scholar and DuckDuckGo were blocked by bot challenges, so a quotation in an article cannot be fully ruled out. A published English translation is unlikely.
verification.other_found:
The sweep listed only Zotenberg. Several more complete translations exist.

FRENCH (full, Arabic with French): H. Zotenberg, Histoire des rois des Perses (Paris: Imprimerie nationale, 1900). Iskandar section pp. 399–c.456, from "Commencements de l'histoire d'Alexandre" to the philosophers' sayings at the coffin. Reprints: Tehran 1963 (Publications de M. H. Asadi 4, with a Persian preface by M. Minovi, under the title "Tārīkh ghurar al-siyar"); Amsterdam: APA-Oriental Press 1979.

PERSIAN (three full translations of the Persian-kings part, all including Iskandar):
(a) Maḥmūd Hidāyat, Shāhnāma-yi Thaʿālibī dar sharḥ-i aḥwāl-i salāṭīn-i Īrān (Tehran: Chāpkhāna-yi Majlis 1328/1949, 363 pp.; repr. Tehran: Asāṭīr 2006, ISBN 9789643313975).
(b) Muḥammad Faḍāʾilī, Tārīkh-i Thaʿālibī (Ghurar akhbār mulūk al-Furs wa-siyarihim) (Tehran: Nashr-i Nuqra 1368/1989).
(c) Sayyid Muḥammad Rūḥānī, Shāhnāma-yi kuhan: pārsī-yi Tārīkh-i ghurar al-siyar (Mashhad: Dānishgāh-i Firdawsī 1372/1993–94, 436 pp.). Cited in Zohidov 2014.
Also ʿAbbās Parīshrūy, Barābar-nihād-i Shāhnāma-yi Firdawsī va Ghurar al-siyar-i Thaʿālibī (Tehran: Mawqūfāt-i Afshār 1390/2011), a side-by-side comparison with the Shahnameh.

TAJIK (Cyrillic): Taʾrikhi Ghurar us-siyar maʾruf ba "Shohnoma"-i Saolibī, prepared with introduction and commentary by Nizomiddin Zohidov (Dushanbe: Bukhoro, 2014, 441 pp.; series Tojnoma, kitobi 3; ISBN 9789997542024). Open Library and OCLC 919027035 describe it as a "Tajik translation of Arabic text".

AZERBAIJANI: A. Shiraliyeva's 2020 article (archive.org "aytac-sirliyeva-1") is a study only, not a translation.

GERMAN / ITALIAN / SPANISH / TURKISH: none found.

AUTHORSHIP: Zotenberg, Jādir, Dodobaev (1992) and Zohidov (2014) attribute the work to Abū Manṣūr ʿAbd al-Malik al-Thaʿālibī. Brockelmann and Minovi attribute it to Abū Manṣūr al-Ḥusayn b. Muḥammad al-Marghanī.
verification.source_text:
H. Zotenberg (ed. and tr.), Ghurar akhbār mulūk al-Furs wa-siyarihim / Histoire des rois des Perses (Paris: Imprimerie nationale, 1900). Public domain: published 1900, and Zotenberg died in 1914. The Iskandar section is on pp. 399–c.456.

Scans on archive.org:
- archive.org/details/histoiredesroisd00thaluoft (Toronto copy; the French OCR is usable)
- archive.org/details/ghurarakhbrmulka00thaluoft (Arabic-titled Toronto copy)
- archive.org/details/histoiredesroisd00thaa
- archive.org/details/AAlexandrina-028710 (the sweep's copy)

Caveat: the archive.org OCR of the Arabic is unusable. The Arabic would have to be retyped or re-OCRed from the page images; Zotenberg's French makes a reliable aligned crib. The Tehran 1963 photo-reprint is identical to the 1900 text.
verification.recommendation: A strong candidate: no Russian or English translation of the chapter exists, only quotations in Briant (RU 2007, EN 2015). It is an Arabic counterpart to Firdawsi's Iskandar, with material Firdawsi lacks (the ball/racquet/sesame exchange, the temple destruction, the Tibet and China expeditions, the death account close to Eutychius, the philosophers' sayings). Start with the whole Iskandar section, Zotenberg pp. 399–c.456, ideally with the preceding Dārā b. Dārā pages. Checking it needs Arabic (and Persian for the names), not just Greek/Latin; Zotenberg's French and the three Persian translations can serve as cross-checks.

verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of Ṭabarī's tafsīr on Q 18:83–98, either full or excerpted. Method: the WebSearch quota was already used up and Yandex and DuckDuckGo returned captchas, which I did not try to get past. I searched instead through archive.org full-text search, the Crossref API, site checks and a vostlit index saved earlier in this session.

(1) The only Russian translation of the tafsīr I found is a scholarly serial by D. V. Frolov and I. A. Zaripov in «Ислам в современном мире». It covers the Introduction in parts 1–3 (2022; e.g. 18(3):27–42, DOI 10.22311/2074-1529-2022-18-3-27-42) and sūra al-Fātiḥa in parts 1–4 (2023–24; e.g. 19(1):47–72, DOI 10.22311/2074-1529-2023-19-1-47-72; part 4, āyāt 6–7, DOI 10.22311/2074-1529-2023-19-4-67-85). Nothing in it goes past the Fātiḥa, so sūra 18 is not covered. Zaripov also has a 2024 methodological article in Minbar 17(1). This series refutes the sweep's flat claim that no Russian translation of the tafsīr exists at all, but not for this unit.

(2) Every vostlit entry under «АТ-ТАБАРИ» is from «История пророков и царей», i.e. the Taʾrīkh (publications of 1840, 1939, 1958, 1960, 1968, 1986, 1987 and 2003). The index has no tafsīr entry and no Зу-л-Карнайн hits. This confirms the sweep.

(3) quran-online.ru gives only Kuliev, Abu Adel and as-Saʿdī for 18:83; there is no Ṭabarī.

(4) Archive.org full-text searches for «Зу-л-Карнайн» / «Зулькарнайн» / «Зуль-Карнайн» together with Табари or Джарир turned up only reference works and retellings. These are Piotrovsky, «Коранические сказания» (1991), a scholarly retelling; the encyclopedia entries «Ислам: словарь атеиста» (1988) and «Ислам: энциклопедический словарь» (1991); Yurchenko's cosmography volumes (2007); and Topbaş, «Посланники Всевышнего», a popular retelling. None of them translates the tafsīr.

(5) Not checked: whether E. A. Rezvan's «Коран и его толкования» (2000) or his section in «Хрестоматия по исламу» (1994) includes any Ṭabarī excerpt on Q 18. Neither book's table of contents was reachable, so this needs a library check.
verification.en_found:
(1) Cooper's translation (OUP 1987) is the only full-text English version, and it stopped after vol. 1 (Introduction, al-Fātiḥa, Q 2:1–103), so sūra 18 is not covered. This confirms the sweep (en.wikipedia "Tafsir al-Tabari").

(2) The sweep's EN "none" is refuted. Brannon M. Wheeler, Prophets in the Quran: An Introduction to the Quran and Muslim Exegesis (Continuum 2002), has a chapter "Khidr and Dhu al-Qarnayn" (around pp. 224–235) that translates exegetical reports on Q 18:83ff. Archive.org full-text snippets (item prophetsinqurani0000whee) include the Abū l-Ṭufayl/ʿAlī report, the explanations of the name "qarnayn", and the Afrīdūn identification. The book lists Ṭabarī's tafsīr explicitly as a source and quotes "Tabari mentions a report from the Prophet Muhammad that Dhu al-Qarnayn was a young man". These are selected excerpts mixed with other exegetes, not a continuous translation, and isnāds are mostly cut.

(3) Some of the same material is in English in other works, though not as Ṭabarī's tafsīr: the SUNY History of al-Ṭabarī (Taʾrīkh) vols. II–IV, including Khiḍr in the vanguard of Dhū l-Qarnayn the Elder (vol. III, Brinner 1991) and Alexander (vol. IV, Perlmann); the Ibn Isḥāq report "Marzubān b. Mardhaba the Greek" in Guillaume's Life of Muhammad, p. 139; and abridged English Ibn Kathīr, which quotes "Ibn Jarir recorded…".

(4) Secondary studies that paraphrase Ṭabarī's tafsīr on the barrier and on Gog and Magog without translating it: van Donzel & Schmidt, Gog and Magog in Early Eastern Christian and Islamic Sources (Brill 2010), and de Polignac, «L'Homme aux deux cornes» (MEFRA 1984).

(5) I found no complete English translation of the pericope, in print or online; quranx.com, for example, has no Ṭabarī.
verification.other_found:
INDONESIAN (full, isnāds kept): Tafsir Ath-Thabari, Pustaka Azzam, Jakarta (colophon "September 2007"), 26 vols. Q 18:83–98 is in vol. 17 (archive.org item tafsir-ath-thabari-26jilid). Full-text hits include "Berkatalah Dzulqarnain, 'Tiuplah…'" and complete chains such as "Ibnu Humaid menceritakan kepada kami… Salamah… Ibnu Ishaq". The translators are not named in what I saw.

TURKISH: Taberî Tefsiri, trans. Hasan Karakaya and Kerim Aytekin, Hisar Yayınevi, İstanbul, 9 vols (archive.org taberi-tefsiri-1-9-hisar-yayinevi). It covers 18:83ff, with full-text hits on "Zülkarneyn kıssası", 18:87 and 18:89. The 9-volume size suggests an abridgment, but I did not confirm that. There is also a 16-volume Turkish set (Beka Yayınevi; archive.org taberitefsir) and a standalone Turkish "Taberî Tefsiri – Kehf Sûresi" PDF (archive.org kehf-sures, 2024). That PDF is an abridged-looking text without isnāds and with no translator named.

URDU: "Tafseer-e-Tabri", 7 vols on archive.org (tafseer-e-tabri). I did not check the translator or whether it reaches sūra 18.

FRENCH: Pierre Godé's abridgment, Commentaire du Coran (Les Heures Claires 1983–), reissued as "Arcanes du Coran" (2017–18), reaches only sūra 4 in tome 6. I found no French version of sūra 18.

PERSIAN: the Samanid Tarjuma-yi tafsīr-i Ṭabarī (ed. Yaghmāʾī), which is a free translation and adaptation and not the isnād text.

MALAY: early sūras only.

GERMAN, ITALIAN, SPANISH: nothing found.
verification.source_text:
Public domain: the Būlāq / al-Maṭbaʿa al-Kubrā al-Amīriyya edition (Cairo 1321–1330 AH, 30 parts). Q 18:83–98 should fall in part 16 if the parts follow the Qurʾānic ajzāʾ; I did not check this. Scans are on archive.org and the Arabic text is on al-Maktaba al-Shāmila (shamela.ws).

The Shākir edition (Dār al-Maʿārif 1954–69) is no use here because it stops at Q 14:27. The best critical text is ed. ʿAbd Allāh al-Turkī (Hajr, Cairo 2001, 26 vols), but it is in copyright and should be used for checking only.

For a Neoscholia base text: take the Būlāq text, check it against al-Turkī, and mark variant readings. Also compare the open digital texts on shamela.ws and tafsir.app.
verification.recommendation: For Russian this is still a good candidate. I found no Russian version of the pericope, and the only Russian tafsīr translation (Frolov–Zaripov) has not got past the Fātiḥa. For English it is only a moderate one: Wheeler 2002 translates selected excerpts, and a full Indonesian translation and a Turkish one also exist. Start with Ṭabarī ad Q 18:83–98 complete with isnāds, split into 83–91 (identity of Dhū l-Qarnayn, the two journeys) and 92–98 (Gog and Magog, the barrier). Checking it needs an Arabist rather than a Hellenist, especially for the isnāds and Ṭabarī's discussions of qirāʾāt (ḥamiʾa/ḥāmiya, saddayn/suddayn, kharjan/kharājan, dakkan/dakkāʾ).

verification.title: Ḥunayn ibn Isḥāq (attrib.), Nawādir/Ādāb al-falāsifa in al-Anṣārī's abridgement: the Alexander chapter ("Ādāb al-Iskandar b. Fīlifūs … Dhū l-Qarnayn": sayings and anecdotes; two consolation letters to his mother and the banquet; the golden coffin and the philosophers' sayings at Babylon and Alexandria; the mother's lament; Aristotle's letter to Olympias and her reply)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of Ḥunayn's text, either in full or in part.

Where I looked:
- vostlit.info author indexes Х, И, А (from the cached index pages). No Ḥunayn and no Mubashshir; the only Ansari is Muḥammad-Rafīʿ Ansari, an unrelated Persian author.
- The full list of the Памятники письменности Востока series: nothing relevant.
- Russian Wikipedia article «Хунайн ибн Исхак»: no mention of this work.
- CyberLeninka and Google Books Russian queries: «Хунайн … философов … Александр», «гробом Александра» философы, «гроба Искандера мудрецы».

Two near misses, both parallel texts rather than Ḥunayn:
1. N. N. Селезнёв, «Изречения философов над гробом Александра Великого по "Истории" ал-Макина ибн ал-Амида», История философии, 2013. CC BY: https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/izrecheniya-filosofov-nad-grobom-aleksandra-velikogo-po-istorii-al-makina-ibn-al-amida. It gives a critical Arabic text of al-Makīn's funeral sayings (al-Majmūʿ al-mubārak) from 4 MSS, with a Russian translation. Seleznyov cites the Ḥunayn version (Badawī 1985, pp. 98–104) only for comparison. He states that it differs substantially in length and structure from the Eutychius tradition, and that al-Makīn takes his sayings from Ibn al-Rāhib.
2. A 2025 Russian rendering of Budge's Ethiopic Alexander Book: «Жизнь и подвиги Александра Великого. Вторая часть», Google Books y0hOEQAAQBAJ. It contains the Ethiopic sayings at the coffin.

Not covered either: S. A. Моисеева 2017 (Вестник ПСТГУ III) is about Arabic-Christian consolatio (al-Jawharī, Severus, Elias of Nisibis) and does not translate Alexander's letter. Бертельс 1948, «Роман об Александре…», may paraphrase the material, but I could not access it.

On method: the WebSearch quota was already used up, so these checks ran as catalogue and site queries rather than general web searches.
verification.en_found:
There is no full English translation of the Arabic Alexander chapter, but scholarly English excerpts exist. This refutes the colleague's EN "none".

- F. Doufikar-Aerts, chapter in M. Rohde and H. O. Bizzarri (eds.), La mort du roi / Der Tod des Königs, Reichert 2021, doi 10.29091/9783752000719. It quotes the funeral sentences in English, for example: "Today is the end of a most glorious kingship … Alexander's kingdom has become obliterated". I checked this against Badawī's Arabic and it renders the mother's lament at the coffin's arrival in Alexandria, so it comes from Ḥunayn's text.
- Doufikar-Aerts, Alexander Magnus Arabicus (Peeters 2010). The Letters of Consolation are discussed at pp. 120–128 and the funeral sentences at pp. 93–94; probably with partial English quotations, not seen.
- Doufikar-Aerts, "Adab in Early Wisdom Literature and the Role of Aristotle's Letters to Alexander", in L'adab, toujours recommencé (Brill 2023), pp. 289–318, doi 10.1163/9789004526358_010. Closed access.
- Doufikar-Aerts, chapter in M. Stock (ed.), Alexander the Great in the Middle Ages (Toronto 2016). It only refers back to the 2010 book.
- E. J. Cottrell (ed.), Prophets, Viziers and Philosophers (Ancient Narrative Suppl. 28, 2020/21). It includes M. Zakeri on the signet-ring aphorisms of Ps-Ḥunayn's Ādāb al-falāsifa and Zuwiyya on kingship; neither is an Alexander-chapter translation.

English for related but different texts:
- Rosenthal, The Classical Heritage in Islam (1975), translates a parallel version of the coffin scene (apparently al-Thaʿālibī's).
- Brock, JSS 15 (1970), covers the Syriac laments.
- Budge 1896 covers the Ethiopic.
- Caxton's Dicts and Sayings derives from Mubashshir.

Sturm, The Libro de los buenos proverbios (UP Kentucky 1970/71; reprinted 2014/2021) is a critical edition of the Castilian with an English introduction. The Alexander material is in chs. XIV–XXVI, pp. 93–137. The publisher's blurb says "translation", but every other source calls it an edition. I have not checked Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great; my unconfirmed recollection is that it does not include this text.
verification.other_found:
German:
- A. Loewenthal, Honein ibn Ishâk, Sinnsprüche der Philosophen (Berlin 1896). Translated from al-Ḥarizi's Hebrew, not from the Arabic. It includes both consolation letters and the mother's reply ("Cap. II–III"). Public domain; on Google Books (e.g. iZR7bO2o198C).
- The Hebrew edition, Musre ha-filosofim (Frankfurt 1896), is on archive.org (musarehafilosofi00unayuoft, musrehafilosofi00harigoog). Earlier Hebrew printings: Riva di Trento 1562 and Lunéville 1804.
- M. E. Stern, Zur Alexander-Sage (Wien 1861): a German version of the letter from the Hebrew.
- K. Merkle, Die Sittensprüche der Philosophen 'Kitāb ādāb al-falāsifa' … in der Überarbeitung des Muhammed ibn ʿAlī al-Anṣārī (Diss. München 1910; Leipzig 1921, 72 pp.). A study of the Arabic, possibly with partial German renderings; not verified. Badawī reports that Merkle took the consolation letter for al-Anṣārī's addition.
- A. Spitaler, "Die arabische Fassung des Trostbriefs Alexanders an seine Mutter", Studi orientalistici in onore di G. Levi Della Vida II (Rome 1956), pp. 493–508; reprinted in Spitaler, Philologica (1998). It edits the Arabic letter in three recensions (types I–III) from MSS Escorial 760, Munich 651 and Paris. Whether it includes a German translation is not verified.
- Meissner, ZDMG 49 (1895) translates Mubashshir's parallel and cites Ḥunayn from MS München arab. 651, fol. 80ff.

Castilian and Spanish:
- The medieval Libro de los buenos proverbios is the Castilian translation. Editions: Knust, Mittheilungen aus dem Eskurial (1879), Alexander material from p. 36; Sturm 1971.
- Christy Bandak, Libro de los buenos proverbios: estudio y edición crítica de las versiones castellana y árabe (Zaragoza: IEIOP 2007, 381 pp., ISBN 978-84-95736-06-2). A critical edition of the Arabic (al-Anṣārī recension) alongside the Castilian. A modern Spanish translation of the Arabic is not confirmed.
- García Gómez, Un texto árabe occidental de la leyenda de Alejandro (1929), pp. cliv–clviii, studies both letters from MS Escorial ár. 760, fols. 31v–34v. It may include partial Spanish renderings; not verified.

No French, Italian or Turkish translation found.

Related corpora: the laments in the Syriac (Brock 1970), Ethiopic (Budge), Mubashshir, al-Masʿūdī, al-Yaʿqūbī, al-Thaʿālibī, Eutychius and al-Makīn traditions. The Greek original of the second consolation letter is in the L recension (Zacher 1867, p. 190; van Thiel).
verification.source_text:
There is no public-domain Arabic edition.

Base text: ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī (ed.), Ḥunayn b. Isḥāq, Ādāb al-falāsifa, ikhtaṣarahu Muḥammad b. ʿAlī b. Ibrāhīm al-Anṣārī (Kuwait: Maʿhad al-Makhṭūṭāt al-ʿArabiyya, 1985).
- Alexander chapter: about pp. 87–110. The coffin sayings are pp. 98–104 (per Seleznyov 2013).
- Based on MSS Escorial ár. 760, München BSB Cod. arab. 651 and Tehran University Central Library 2103.
- Scans on archive.org, copyrighted but readable: https://archive.org/details/adaab-alfalasifah and the Byblion 2009 reprint https://archive.org/details/nawader-alfalasifah (Alexander section pp. 151–179).

Collate with Bandak 2007, which is copyrighted, and Spitaler 1956 for the letter. Indirect witness: MS Köprülü 1608, Isḥāq b. Ḥunayn's "nawādir falsafiyya", which includes the coffin sayings. I could not confirm whether the Munich MS has been digitised.

Public-domain comparanda: Loewenthal 1896 (Hebrew and German); Knust 1879 (Castilian).
verification.recommendation: A good candidate. There is no Russian translation (only the parallel al-Makīn version by Seleznyov 2013) and English has only scattered excerpts by Doufikar-Aerts, but EN should be recorded as "excerpts_only", not "none". Start with the whole Alexander chapter in Badawī 1985 (about 25 printed pages, from the Ādāb al-Iskandar through the coffin sayings to Aristotle's letter to Olympias), collated with Bandak 2007 and Spitaler 1956. Verification needs an Arabist, not just Greek/Latin, and ideally also Hebrew (al-Ḥarizi) and Old Castilian for the comparison.

verification.title: Āʾīna-yi Iskandarī (The Alexandrine Mirror / «Зерцало Искандара»), Amīr Khusraw Dihlavī, 699 H / 1299–1300, 4th masnavi of his Khamsa, about 4,450 couplets (Wahid Mirza 1935 gives 4,450)
verification.ru_found:
No Russian translation found, either complete or partial. Caveat: the WebSearch budget for this session was already used up (200/200), and all four queries I sent (2 RU, 2 EN) were refused. I therefore could not run the required 4+4 open web searches and checked catalogues and reference pages directly instead.

What I checked:
(1) Russian Wikipedia, «Амир Хосров Дехлеви». Its list of Russian editions has no Āʾīna: gazals tr. Седых 1975 and Алиева 1980; «Восемь райских садов» tr. Ревич 1975/2002 (Hasht Bihisht only); «Лирика» 2001; «Избранное» Ташкент 1980; Гребнев 1968/2005. Wikipedia articles «Хамсе», «Искандер-наме», «Роман об Александре» and «Александрия (роман)» say nothing about Khusraw's poem.
(2) Open Library, Russian-language holdings of Khusraw: only the Moscow critical-text series (Shirin 1961, Majnun 1964/65, Hasht Bihisht 1972, Duval Rani 1975), gazal selections, and «Избранное» (Ташкент, Изд-во ЦК КП Узбекистана, 1980, 120 pp.). That volume was compiled by Ш. Шамухамедов for the series «Избранная лирика Востока», so it is probably lyric. Short masnavi excerpts in it are possible but not checked.
(3) The Mirsaidov edition, «Ойина-йи Искандари» (Moscow, ГРВЛ «Наука», 1977; xxxiii + 313 + 27 pp.; LCCN 79970890; OCLC 22776626), is Persian text with a Russian introduction only, not a translation.
(4) vostlit.info: the author index had no Khusraw entry; its search timed out.
(5) The publisher's blurb for Piemontese 1999 says the poem was translated there "per la prima volta in una lingua europea". That rules out any earlier Russian translation.

Not verified (possible paraphrase, not translation): E. Э. Бертельс, «Роман об Александре и его главные версии на Востоке» (1948), and the Tashkent jubilee volume «Амир Хосров Дехлеви» (ТашГУ, 1975, 158 pp.). Either may retell the poem or quote passages in prose.
verification.en_found:
No English translation found, complete or partial.
- Losensky & Sharma, In the Bazaar of Love (Penguin India, 2011): the introduction discusses the poem (Alexander as explorer and scientist, his marriage to Kanifu). Its narrative-poems section seems to take only from ʿIshqiya and Hasht Bihisht ("The Tale of the Camphor Princess"). I found no Āʾīna excerpt, but could not read the whole book.
- M. Wahid Mirza, The Life and Works of Amir Khusrau (Calcutta, 1935; archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.81771): searched in full text. It gives only a short description (pp. 200–201, 217: composed 699 H, 4,450 couplets), with no translation.
- Mohammad Habib (1927) and Mirza both translated other works, not this one.
- English Wikipedia (Amir Khusrau; Khamsa; Alexander the Great in Islamic tradition, which cites only Casari 2023 in Ashtiany ed., Persian Narrative Poetry in the Classical Era) shows no translation.
- Open Library has no English title for the poem.
- Murty Classical Library of India: no Khusraw volume listed on Wikipedia.

Short verse quotations in secondary literature (Sharma 2005; Casari 2023; Manteghi) are likely but were not checked.
verification.other_found:
This refutes the sweep's "none in Western languages". There is a complete Italian translation:
Amir Khusrau, Lo specchio alessandrino, traduzione dal persiano e introduzione di Angelo M. Piemontese. Soveria Mannelli: Rubbettino, 1999 (Medioevo romanzo e orientale. Testi, 5). 178–188 pp. (records disagree). ISBN 9788872848579.
Sources:
- Open Library OL52473580M, with by-statement and note "Poem".
- Publisher page https://www.store.rubbettinoeditore.it/catalogo/lo-specchio-alessandrino/, whose blurb says it is the first translation of the poem into a European language.
The page count suggests a complete prose translation.

Other languages:
- Uzbek: uz.wikipedia lists Uzbek translators of Khusraw (Vasfiy, Chustiy, Sh. Shamuhamedov, J. Kamol, N. Muhammad, J. Suvanqulov) but does not tie any of them to Oyinai Iskandariy. Unverified.
- Urdu: archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.440523, "Nāma-yi Iskandarī maʿrūf ba Sikandarnāma-yi Khusrawī" (Delhi: Maṭbaʿ-i Qayṣariyya, 1914, 216–222 pp.). The Toronto catalogue record calls it Persian; DLI metadata and the OCR language guess call it Urdu. It may be an Urdu prose rendering. Unresolved.
- German Wikipedia's list of editions and translations has nothing for this poem.
- No French, German or Spanish translation found. Piemontese's French article on the diving-bell episode (in Pand-o Sokhan, 1995) is recalled from memory and not verified.
verification.source_text:
Public domain:
- Āʾīna-yi Iskandarī, ed. (murattaba) Maulana Muhammad Saʿid Ahmad Faruqi, Aligarh: Institute Press, 1917.
- Scan: https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.440512. The OCR is Persian verse but almost unusable, so it would need re-keying or new OCR.
- A second 1917 copy: https://archive.org/details/dli.ernet.434078.
- Published in 1917, so public domain in the US. Indian copyright depends on the editor's death date, which I could not confirm.

Best critical text (not public domain; use for collation):
- Amīr Khusraw Dihlawī, Āʾīna-yi Iskandarī, critical text and introduction by Jamal Mirsaidov. Moscow: Nauka, ГРВЛ, 1977 (Khamsa series vol. 4; xxxiii + 313 + 27 pp.; Persian with Russian introduction; LCCN 79970890).

Also not public domain:
- Khamsa-yi Amīr Khusraw Dihlavī, ed. A. A. Ashrafi, Tehran: Shaqayiq, 1362/1983, 701 pp.

Possibly public domain:
- The Delhi 1914 Qayṣariyya print (archive.org in.ernet.dli.2015.440523). Its language needs checking first.

Ganjoor.net has only Khusraw's Divan, not the Khamsa.
verification.recommendation: Still a strong candidate: no Russian or English translation was found. However, Piemontese's complete Italian translation (1999) must be acknowledged and used as a control. Verification needs a Persianist, which goes beyond Greek and Latin. Start with one self-contained episode of about 300–500 couplets, such as Alexander's descent into the sea in a diving bell or the Kanifu episode. Use the Aligarh 1917 text as base and check it against Mirsaidov 1977.
