verification.title: İskendernâme (Book of Alexander), Tâceddîn Ahmedî. Begun 1390 (792 H), revised to about 1410. Old Anatolian Turkish mesnevî, 8,754 couplets in MS A (İstanbul Üniv. TY 921)
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation of the poem or of any section. The WebSearch budget for this session ran out (200/200), so I searched Russian sources through their own interfaces and APIs.
(1) vostlit.info author index for А: Ашик-паша-заде is listed, Ахмеди is not.
(2) CyberLeninka API, 6 queries ("Ахмеди Искендер-наме", "Ахмеди Искендернаме", "Ахмеди османский поэт", "Ахмеди Дастан-и теварих", etc.). Only secondary literature turned up. N. Arasly, «Особенности восприятия творчества Низами в Турции» (2019), quotes one or two lines in her own Russian, citing the BnF manuscript. E. G. Vartanyan (2020, 2023) gives an overview with no translation.
(3) The KLE entry «Ахмеди» (т. 1, 1962) and Boroлина in ИВЛ т. 3 (1985) list Turkish literature only and no Russian translation.
(4) ru.wikipedia «Искендер-наме (поэма Ахмеди)» and «Ахмеди»: the full bibliographies list no Russian translation. The only Russian scholarship is on manuscripts: А. Х. Нуриахметов, «"Искандарнаме" Ахмади в рукописных собраниях Ленинграда», КСИНА 69 (1965), 136–155; Дмитриева 1980; Васильева 1986; Петросян, Manuscripta Orientalia 1.2 (1995, in English). The verse boxes in the «Ахмеди» article come from «Литература Востока в Средние века» (МГУ 1970, с. 366) and are ghazal lines, not lines from the İskendernâme.
(5) facetia.ru: one passing mention (the mother's name "Rakia") in a commentary on the Yiddish Alexander.
I could not check printed anthologies of Turkish poetry for a stray fragment. Treat the status as none, apart from isolated lines quoted in scholarship.
verification.en_found:
The sweep's claim that no English exists for the Alexander narrative is refuted.
(a) E. J. W. Gibb, A History of Ottoman Poetry, vol. I (London 1900; public domain; archive.org historyofottoman01gibbuoft). pp. 269–285: detailed prose synopsis of the whole romance. pp. 287–294: three verse translations from the Alexander narrative: [40] "Alexander buildeth the Dyke of Gog and Magog", [41] "Alexander seeketh the Fountain of Life", [42] "Alexander is forewarned of his Death by a Tree". The Turkish originals of numbered extracts are printed in vol. VI.
(b) K. Silay, "Aḥmedī's History of the Ottoman Dynasty", Journal of Turkish Studies 16 (1992) 129–200. Expanded as Ahmedi's History of the Kings of the Ottoman Lineage and their Holy Raids against the Infidels, Sources of Oriental Languages and Literatures (Harvard 2004). Critical text and English translation of the Dâstân only, couplets 7537–7870.
(c) Furkan Öztürk, "An Early Ottoman Interpretation of the Alexander Romance: Ahmedî's İskendernâme", Trames 30.1 (2026) 93–114, CC BY 4.0, doi 10.3176/tr.2026.1.05. English renderings of selected couplets: ideal ruler, about 858–877; Gülşah, 1392–1402; medicine, 2759–2768; Rāyij island, 3243–3259. It also has a full section outline in Appendix 1.
(d) Scholarship with short excerpts, extent not checked: Dankoff, "The Romance of İskender and Gülşah", in Turkic Culture: Continuity and Change (Indiana UP 1987) 95–103; Sawyer, "Dove of the soul" (Bern 1996) 135–147; Sawyer, Edebiyât 13.2 (2003) 225–243; Sawyer, "The Seafaring Episode…", JTS 29 (2005) 289–317; Kastritsis 2016 (Ergon) 243–283; Küçükhüseyin 2016; İnalcık on the Kosovo passage (2000).
No complete English translation exists. Öztürk's 2026 bibliography and Dankoff's 2020 bibliography both list none.
verification.other_found:
MODERN TURKISH: the sweep's "selections only" is wrong. Furkan Öztürk (haz.), Ahmedî, İskendernâme (İş Bankası Kültür Yayınları, Hasan Âli Yücel Klasikleri, 2018, 848 pp.) is a complete intralingual translation into modern Turkish (günümüz Türkçesi), not selections. Akdoğan, İskendernâme'den Seçmeler (1988) is a separate, older selection.
GERMAN: J. von Hammer-Purgstall, Geschichte der osmanischen Dichtkunst I (Pesth 1836) 89–104, public domain (archive.org 11687705bsb). He works from the Marciana MS and gives:
- a heading-by-heading summary of all 369 sections;
- German verse translations of the proem and of the candle/moth/censer debate (about 60 lines);
- shorter passages: the seven imams of the divine names, the Iskender = soul / Aristotle = reason allegory, the autumn description, and the epilogue.
He cites an earlier notice of his own in the Jahrbücher der Literatur LVII (Anzeigeblatt).
Kortantamer 1973 (German) covers the Dîvân, not this poem.
FRENCH, ITALIAN, SPANISH, AZERBAIJANI: nothing found. Only encyclopaedia articles, e.g. Mélikoff, EI² "Iskandar nāma".
EDITIONS: Ünver 1983 (TDK) is a facsimile of A with an introduction. Yaşar Akdoğan, Ahmedî: İskender-nâme, is a Ministry of Culture e-book (Kültür Eserleri 411, ISBN 978-975-17-3341-2, 505 pp.). It is a full transliteration with numbered couplets running to about 8,088, not selections. Original listing: ekitap.kulturturizm.gov.tr/TR,78415/ahmedi---iskendername.html. Mirror: archive.org/details/Skender-NNme-Ahmede. Two critical editions exist:
- Akdoğan & Kutsal, İnceleme-Tenkitli Metin (Türkiye Yazma Eserler Kurumu 2019);
- R. Dankoff, İskendernâme: İnceleme–Tenkitli Metin I–II (TÜBA 2020). Study in Turkish and critical text from 8 MSS (A, B, C, D, H, M, Q, Z), 8,754 couplets plus 17 add-ons (eklenti), 66 Marciana images. No translation.
verification.recommendation: A strong candidate. Russian has nothing, and English and German are fragmentary (Gibb 1900, Hammer 1836, Silay for the Dâstân, Öztürk 2026 excerpts). Start with the closing Alexander block, couplets 8315–8678 in Dankoff's numbering, about 360 couplets: Land of Darkness, debate with the Brahmans, Monastery of the first Dhū'l-Qarnayn, Land of Women, Speaking Tree, Alexander's death, letter to his mother, and the laments of 15 philosophers. These episodes match Ps.-Callisthenes, Palladius/Collatio and the Epistola ad Aristotelem directly, and Gibb has only fragments of them in English. Reviewing it needs an Old Anatolian Turkish (Ottoman) specialist with some Persian, which goes beyond Greek and Latin. Öztürk's 2018 modern-Turkish version (in copyright) can serve as a crib for checking.

verification.title: Khiradnāma-yi Iskandarī (Haft Awrang VII) / «Книга мудрости Искандара» — ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Jāmī (c. 1485–87; Persian masnavī, mutaqārib; 78 sections, c. 2,315 bayts)
verification.ru_found:
The claim that it is "unknown"/untranslated is REFUTED. Vladimir Derzhavin made a Russian verse translation (one line per hemistich) that has been published many times:
(1) Standalone edition: Джами А. Книга мудрости Искандара / пер. В. Державина; вступ. ст. и примеч. Л. И. Климовича. Сталинабад: Таджикгосиздат, 1949. 121 [3] с., 17×13 см (Классики таджикской литературы). Sources: NLR Jami bibliography https://expositions.nlr.ru/ex_manus/jami/liter.php; auction lot http://www.auction-imperia.ru/wdate.php?t=booklot&i=100125; http://www.gornitsa.ru/item.php?id=15525339. I could not check how much of the poem it contains. My inference is that it is abridged: a complete text would run to about 4,630 lines, which does not fit in 121 small pages.
(2) Reprinted in Джами. Избранное, translated by Державин and Липкин (М., 1955), as «Книга мудрости Искендера». This is a selection; an e-text is at https://litmir.club/br/?b=827936.
(3) Джами. Избранное: Из книги поэм (М., 1964; сост. М. Занд), listed by NLR.
(4) The Библиотека всемирной литературы anthology «Ирано-таджикская поэзия» (М., 1974; 2nd ed. 1984) has an 8-part excerpt «Из поэмы»: Начало повествования; Арасту's book of precepts; Iskandar's humility; Книга мудрости Арасту; Книга мудрости Сократа; Поход на Чин; Город людей, чистых нравом; Завещание. Sources: https://fantlab.ru/work1174664; http://litena.ru/books/item/f00/s00/z0000069/st539.shtml.
(5) Джами. Избранные произведения (Л.: Советский писатель, 1978; сост. А. Афсахзод), no. 368, is the fullest version I could check. It has about 1,612 lines, roughly 806 of 2,315 bayts (about 35%). Full text: https://facetia.ru/node/6168.
(6) Probably reprinted in Джами. Лирика; Поэмы; Весенний сад (Душанбе, 1989).
Comparing the 1978 text with Ganjoor's 78-section layout, these parts are NOT in Russian: the prologue (§§1–14); the khiradnāmas of Plato, Hippocrates and Hermes (§§21, 25, 31); §45 (Aristotle's pupils); §46 (Alexander in India with the Indian sages); §§49–50; the ten sages' laments at the coffin (§§57–66); the five condolences and the mother's excuse (§§68–73); the epilogue (§§76–78); and about 15 ḥikāyāt. Bertels' studies (Навои и Джами, 1965; Роман об Александре, 1948) are secondary literature; I did not verify whether they contain further excerpts.
verification.en_found:
I found no complete or substantial English translation. What exists:
(a) Short excerpts in scholarship. Casari, "The Alexander Legend in Persian Literature," in Persian Narrative Poetry in the Classical Era (A History of Persian Literature; ed. Ashtiany), I.B. Tauris 2023, pp. 504–510; a 10-line passage on the conquests is quoted from it at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kherad-name. Bürgel, "Ǧāmī's Epic Poem on Alexander the Great: an Introduction," Oriente Moderno 15/76 (1996) 415–438 — an introduction, probably with translated passages, which I did not verify. Toutant, "Evaluating Jāmī's Influence on Navāʾī…" in Jāmī in Regional Contexts (Brill 2018) 602–648 — comparative, with excerpts.
(b) Possible free rhymed excerpts in Paul Smith's self-published anthologies: Jami: Selected Poems (2012), Jami: Life & Poems, and The Book of Jami (2014). Their blurbs promise "a good selection from most of his masnavis" and name the Book of the Wisdom of Alexander, but I could not check whether they actually contain passages from this poem.
(c) N. Karimova's article, Учёные записки ХГУ no. 2 (43), 2015 (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/iz-istorii-perevodov-proizvedeniy-abd-ar-rahmana-dzhami-na-angliyskiy-yazyk), says "Издание Trinity College Кембриджа" published English translations of Laylī u Majnūn and the Khiradnāma. It gives no translator, date or title, I could not corroborate it, and it is probably a confusion.
Iranica (Losensky, JĀMI i, 2008) lists no translation.
verification.other_found:
TURKISH — complete translation (verified). Elif Aydınbaş, "Molla Câmî'nin Hırednâme-i İskenderî'si (İnceleme–Tercüme)," MA thesis, Ankara Üniversitesi SBE, Fars Dili ve Edebiyatı, October 2015 (adviser Hicabi Kırlangıç). It is a prose translation on pp. 79–249, with all 2,315 bayts numbered, based on the Tehran 1999 Mīrāṯ-e Maktūb edition. Open access: https://dspace.ankara.edu.tr/server/api/core/bitstreams/753e7848-7d01-4ef2-af43-0619e6517370/content.
UZBEK. Жомий, «Искандар хирадномаси», Тошкент: Ғафур Ғулом номидаги Адабиёт ва санъат нашриёти, 1978 (record: https://book.iiau.uz/books/iskandar-khiradnomasi-3241). Translator and extent not verified.
TAJIK. Cyrillic-script printings and «Мухтасари хирадномаи Искандарӣ» (an abridgement, nlt.tj/book/409654) are transliterations or abridgements, not translations.
FRENCH. Fouchécour, "Djâmi, conseiller des princes, ou Le Livre de la Sagesse Alexandrine," Kâr-Nâmeh 5 (1999) 11–32. This is a study; it may quote translated passages (not verified).
GERMAN / ITALIAN / SPANISH. Nothing found.
verification.source_text:
Critical text: Джами, Хафт ауранг. Критический текст, т. 1 (poems 3, 4, 7: Тухфат ал-ахрар, Субхат ал-абрар, Хираднама-йи Искандари), ed. Г. А. Тарбият (Ḥusayn Aḥmad Tarbiyat), Moscow: Nauka, 1984 (per the NLR bibliography).
Revised reprint: Masnavī-yi Haft awrang, ed. Aʿlā Khān Afṣaḥzād, J. Dād-ʿAlīshāh, A. Jānfidā, Ẓ. Aḥrārī and Ḥ. A. Tarbiyat, 2 vols., Tehran: Mīrās̱-i Maktūb, 1378/1999, vol. II pp. 415–529. Iranica calls it a revised reprint of the Moscow editions. A scan is at https://archive.org/details/HeftEvrengCami; it is in copyright, not openly licensed.
Older edition: Murtaḍā Mudarris-Gīlānī (Tehran 1337/1958; later printings 1361/1982, 1987, pp. 911–1013). Scans on archive.org: dli.ernet.471849; 198-ketabeerfani, whose PD mark is doubtful.
Freely accessible digital text: Ganjoor, https://ganjoor.net/jami/7ourang/7-7 — 78 sections, 2,316 bayts. Its base edition and licence were not verified.
The 15th-century Persian text is itself in the public domain. In practice: work from Ganjoor and check it against Tarbiyat 1984 / Afṣaḥzād 1999. No modern edition is openly licensed.
verification.recommendation: Weak as a whole-work candidate. A published Russian verse translation exists (Derzhavin; 1949 standalone, ~35% in the 1978 Afsahzod volume), and so does a complete Turkish prose translation (Aydınbaş 2015). Two-thirds of the poem, however, has never appeared in Russian, and there is no English translation. If pursued, start with the untranslated death cycle §§56–73: the ten sages' laments at Alexander's coffin and the five condolences to his mother. These sections continue the late-antique and Arabic gnomic tradition of philosophers speaking at Alexander's coffin. Next would be §46 (Alexander and the Indian sages) and the khiradnāmas of Plato, Hippocrates and Hermes. Checking the translation needs a classical-Persian/Sufi-lexicon expert, not just Greek/Latin.

verification.title: Alexander (al-Iskandar) in early Arabic chronicles: al-Masʿūdī, Murūj al-dhahab, chs. 25–26 (kings of the Yūnān; Alexander's Indian expedition) and ch. 32 (Alexandria), and al-Dīnawarī, al-Akhbār al-ṭiwāl, Iskandar section (ed. Guirgass pp. 31–41)
verification.ru_found:
The "none" claim is partly refuted. Three Russian translations exist, and the core chapters remain untranslated.
(1) D. V. Mikulski, «Ал-Мас‘уди (Х в.) о том, как была основана таинственная и прекрасная Александрия», Восточный курьер 2025, № 4, pp. 73–86, DOI 10.18254/S268684310036859-2, https://oriental-courier.ru/s268684310036859-2-1/. This is an academic, fully annotated Russian translation of the whole of Murūj ch. 32 (Alexander's foundation of Alexandria, the sea monsters, the Pharos; BdM II 420–441; Pellat ed. II 99–109), made from Pellat's text. In footnote 3 Mikulski himself places the main Alexander narrative in chs. 25–26 (BdM II 242–259, 260–278; Pellat II 5–13, 14–23; Cairo 1973 I 285–300). For those chapters he cites only Bertels 1948 and Kostyukhin 1972 as literature, not any Russian translation. That suggests chs. 25–26 had no Russian translation as of Nov. 2025.
(2) A. E. Schmidt (posthumous), «Материалы по истории Средней Азии и Ирана», Учёные записки Института востоковедения 16 (1958), on vostlit: https://www.vostlit.info/Texts/rus5/Dinavari/text.phtml. His Dinawari excerpt begins at Guirgass p. 40: Alexander back from China at Jerusalem, his counsel with Aristotle, the creation of the mulūk al-ṭawāʾif, and his death. So only the last paragraph or so of Dinawari's Iskandar section (pp. 40–41) is in Russian. The 1958 sweep check missed this. His al-Masʿūdī excerpt in the same volume (Ardashir's court and related matters) only mentions Alexander in passing.
(3) Mikulski, «Легендарная египетская царица Клеопатра…», Восточный курьер 2022, № 3, pp. 105–112 (https://oriental-courier.ru/s268684310023721-1-1/). This translates the Cleopatra/Augustus passage from the same Greek-kings section (BdM II 285–291). It is not about Alexander.
Checked, and not about Alexander: every Masʿūdī publication on vostlit (1835; 1939 Материалы по истории туркмен; 1960 Africa; 1987 al-Andalus and the West; 2002 Mikulski, Abbasids; 2009 Slavic sanctuaries); Bolshakov 1970 on Dinawari (begins at Hurmuz IV, Guirgass p. 77); and Alnaddaf's 2018 survey of Russian Masʿūdī translations (CyberLeninka).
Not verified: whether Bertels, «Роман об Александре и его главные версии на Востоке» (1948) contains Russian paraphrases or quotations of Dinawari or Masʿūdī. Also not verified: whether Beilis's Russian Tanbīh, Part I (2021), includes Masʿūdī's Alexander passage from the Tanbīh (a different work).
Net result: no Russian translation was found of Murūj chs. 25–26 or of Dinawari, Guirgass pp. 31–40.
verification.en_found:
Dinawari: there is a complete English translation of the Iskandar section. Michael Richard Jackson Bonner's online translation of the pre-Islamic part of al-Akhbār al-ṭiwāl ("The Book of Lengthy Histories", headed "This translation copyright Michael Richard Jackson Bonner 2012 … may not be used without written permission") includes the sections [Dārā], [Iskandar] (with the Persian birth story: Dārā son of Bahman, Faylafūs's daughter, the sandar herb), [Iskandar's Conquests], [Yājūj and Mājūj] and [The Regional Princes]. These follow Guirgass's page numbers 31–41, about 3,800 English words. The original site (mrjb.ca) has been taken over by another owner; the page survives on Wayback: https://web.archive.org/web/20181111002130/http://www.mrjb.ca/current-projects/abu-hanifah-ahmad-ibn-dawud-al-dinawari. It is not a thesis appendix, as the sweep said. I found no print publication of it.
Masʿūdī: no English translation of chs. 25–26 or ch. 32 was found. Sprenger's 1841 volume (archive.org historicalencycl00masrich) covers only the first part of the work; its chapter list includes "26. The history of Alexander in India", but the volume itself has only incidental Alexander mentions (Porus, the Alexandria canal, Dhū l-Qarnayn's barrier). Lunde & Stone, The Meadows of Gold: The Abbasids (1989; Routledge 2013) is limited to the Abbasid period. It does contain one short anecdote, "An Aphorism on the Death of Alexander" (DOI 10.4324/9780203037997-120).
Possible English paraphrases or short quotations, not checked: Shboul, Al-Mas'udi and his World (1979), pp. 113–119; Manteghi, Alexander the Great in the Persian Tradition (2018), chapter on the legacy of Sasanian historiography; Stoneman, "Alexander the Great in the Arabic Tradition" (2003). Iranica, "Eskandar-nāma" (Hanaway) lists Masʿūdī and Dinawari only as sources; Ṭabarī's Alexander section is in English (SUNY vol. IV, pp. 87–95), but that is a different text.
verification.other_found:
French: complete Masʿūdī. Barbier de Meynard & Pavet de Courteille, Les Prairies d'or, Arabic text with French translation, vol. II (Paris 1863; public domain), on archive.org as lesprairiesdor02masuuoft. Checked in the OCR: ch. XXV on the Greek kings with Alexander (Philip, the golden-egg tribute, Dārā, the meaning of Dhū l-Qarnayn, the death and the philosophers' sayings, Rawshanak, the tomb) at pp. 242–259; ch. XXVI "Histoire abrégée de l'expédition d'Alexandre dans l'Inde" (Porus, Kayd) at 260–278; ch. XXXII on Alexandria at 420–441. Pellat's revised French translation (Société asiatique, 1962–97) is from memory and was not re-verified. For Dinawari, I found no French translation; Krachkovsky's 1912 volume is a preface with variants and indices, not a translation.
Persian: complete Dinawari, per fa.wikipedia «اخبارالطوال». Translations by Ṣādiq Nashʾat (1346 Sh./1967) and by Maḥmūd Mahdavī Dāmghānī (Nashr-e Ney, Tehran 1364 Sh./1985–86). Bonner's archived page also links a Persian PDF, "tarjome-akhbarot-teval.pdf".
German: possible discussion or translation of excerpts in Nöldeke 1890 (Beiträge zur Geschichte des Alexanderromans) and in Spiegel 1851; neither checked. Turkish, Italian, Spanish: none found, not verified.
Method note: the WebSearch budget for the session (200 calls) was used up and the search engines (DuckDuckGo, Bing, Brave, Mojeek, Qwant, Google) were blocked. Verification therefore used direct sources: vostlit indices and texts, the Восточный курьер article pages, Crossref, Wikipedia (ru, en, fa) raw text, archive.org OCR, the Wayback Machine and Iranica. The CyberLeninka API, eLibrary, Google Books and OpenAlex were unavailable. The required 4 + 4 search-engine queries could not be run as such.
verification.source_text:
al-Masʿūdī: Barbier de Meynard & Pavet de Courteille, Maçoudi, Les Prairies d'or, Arabic and French, vol. II (Paris: Société asiatique, 1863), public domain. Chs. 25–26 at pp. 242–278 (ch. 32 at pp. 420–441). https://archive.org/details/lesprairiesdor02masuuoft. Collate with Pellat's revised Arabic edition (Beirut, Publications de l'Université Libanaise, 1966–74, vol. II pp. 5–23), which is under copyright, and with the Cairo text of Muḥyī al-Dīn ʿAbd al-Ḥamīd (repr. Beirut 1973, I 285–300).
al-Dīnawarī: Kitāb al-akhbār al-ṭiwāl, ed. V. Guirgass (Leiden: Brill, 1888), public domain, Iskandar section pp. 31–41. https://archive.org/details/kitabalakhbaralt00ahmauoft. Supplement with I. Krachkovsky, Préface, variantes et index (Leiden 1912): https://archive.org/details/abhanfaaddnawerk00krac.
verification.recommendation: Still a good candidate if narrowed to Masʿūdī, Murūj chs. 25–26 (BdM II 242–278; about 18 Arabic pages): it has no Russian or English translation, the French BdM text (public domain) gives a control, and the story material (the golden-egg tribute, the meaning of Dhū l-Qarnayn, Kayd's four gifts, the philosophers at the bier) is valuable. Drop ch. 32 (Mikulski 2025). Dinawari, Guirgass pp. 31–40, can be added as the first Russian translation, but it is not new in English (Bonner). Verification needs an Arabist, and the Persian names and mulūk al-ṭawāʾif material call for Iranist input, beyond Greek/Latin expertise.

verification.title: Ḥadīth Dhī l-Qarnayn ("Leyenda de Alejandro", «Сказание о Зу-л-Карнайне»): anonymous Andalusi (Aragonese) Middle Arabic Alexander romance, MS Junta XXVII (from the Almonacid de la Sierra find of 1884), copied in the 15th century. Its only edition is García Gómez 1929. Not to be confused with the Qiṣṣat Dhī l-Qarnayn (Zuwiyya 2001) or the aljamiado Rrekontamiento (Nykl 1929).
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation, whole or partial, and no Russian scholarly treatment of this text. Search limits first: the WebSearch quota for this session was used up (200/200), and Google, Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yandex and Brave returned CAPTCHAs or irrelevant results. So the Russian checks were run through the sites' own search engines.
(1) ru.wikipedia full-text search, four queries: «Гарсиа Гомес Александр легенда», «"Зу-ль-Карнайн" андалусский», «об Александре морисков альхамиадо», «Легенда об Александре арабская версия испанский манускрипт». None returned anything relevant.
(2) ru.wikipedia articles «Зу-ль-Карнайн», «Роман об Александре» and «Александрия (роман)». None mentions the Andalusi, aljamiado or Western-Arabic versions.
(3) facetia.ru site search, three queries: «Карнайн», «альхамиадо», «Александр арабский». Only the Pseudo-Callisthenes, Secretum secretorum and Methodius pages came up; nothing on Andalusi or Morisco Alexander texts.
(4) cyberleninka.ru search: the page renders by JavaScript and returned no results. A Yandex query hit a CAPTCHA. vostlit.info has no site search, and the URL I guessed for its Spain index returned 404.
Indirect evidence of absence: Guidotti's 2022 thesis has a full bibliography of the Western-Arabic Alexander tradition. It cites no Russian translation or study of this text.
Confidence for Russian: medium-high. The evidence is negative and the search tools were impaired.
verification.en_found:
I found no English translation, whole or partial. Checks made:
(1) en.wikipedia article "Hadith Dhi'l-Qarnayn" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadith_Dhi'l-Qarnayn). It lists only García Gómez 1929 (Arabic with Spanish translation). The article "Alexander the Great in Arabic tradition" adds nothing.
(2) The sweep's claim about Zuwiyya is confirmed and sharpened. Z. David Zuwiyya, "Islamic Legends Concerning Alexander the Great: Taken from Two Medieval Arabic Manuscripts in Madrid" (Binghamton: Global Publications/SUNY, 2001; ISBN 1586841327 / 1586841785) edits and translates into English a different text, the Qiṣṣat Dhī l-Qarnayn. The two Madrid manuscripts are BNE ms. 5379 (codex optimus) and RAH ms. Gayangos 61. Source: Guidotti 2022, list of abbreviations ("QD … Edizione e traduzione in inglese: Zuwiyya 2001"; "LEY … Edizione e traduzione in castigliano: García Gómez 1929"). Zuwiyya's 2000 Qurṭuba note also calls the Qiṣṣat "La Leyenda de Alejandro". That label is ambiguous, so future sweeps should not be misled by it.
(3) The English-language secondary literature is analysis only, not translation: Guidotti, "The Leyenda de Alejandro: an Islamic and Andalusi Version of the Alexander Romance", Studi Magrebini 18.1 (2020) 48–84, doi:10.1163/2590034x-12340016 (closed access per OpenAlex); Anderson, "The Arabic History of Dulcarnain and the Ethiopian History of Alexander", Speculum 6 (1931) 434–45; Marín, "Legends on Alexander the Great in Moslem Spain", Graeco-Arabica 4 (1991) 71–89; Zuwiyya, Brill Companion 2011, 73–112; Doufikar-Aerts, Alexander Magnus Arabicus (2010). Guidotti 2020 and Anderson 1931 may quote short passages in English. I could not open either, so this is unverified.
(4) Stoneman's "Legends of Alexander the Great" (CrossRef table of contents) does not contain the text.
Related but distinct: the Timbuktu text TAM 25, a sister Western-Arabic version, has a French translation (Bohas, Saguer and Sinno 2012) and possibly an English one (Sukdaven et al., Pretoria 2015, which Guidotti cites without having seen it). Neither is the Leyenda.
verification.other_found:
Spanish, complete: Emilio García Gómez, "Un texto árabe occidental de la Leyenda de Alejandro, según el manuscrito ár. XXVII de la Biblioteca de la Junta para Ampliación de Estudios. Edición, traducción española y estudio preliminar" (Madrid: Instituto de Valencia de Don Juan / Hispanic Society of America, 1929; clxiv + 108 + 72 pp.). The Spanish translation, "Historia de Dulcarnain", runs about 27,000 words in the OCR. I found no other translation in any language.

Italian: Giulia Guidotti's doctoral thesis, "La Qiṣṣat Ḏī l-Qarnayn ('Storia del Bicorne') e la tradizione arabo-occidentale del romanzo di Alessandro" (Cádiz/Naples, 2022; open access at http://hdl.handle.net/10498/28848, 942 pp.). Chapter 6 gives an episode-by-episode Italian synopsis of the whole Leyenda, folio by folio, compared with the other Western-Arabic versions (QD, ABU, TAM, REK), the Greek, the Syriac and the Ethiopic. It quotes the Arabic of LEY verbatim, usually without translating it. This is a synopsis, not a translation. Her MA thesis (Napoli L'Orientale, 2018) is a linguistic study of the text and is unpublished. Picherot's French studies (2013–2015) deal with the aljamiado Rrekontamiento, not this text.

Codicology, from García Gómez 1929, pp. LXXXV–LXXXVIII, and Guidotti 2022:
- The text fills fols. [1]–47v of a 180-folio miscellany and is acephalous. García Gómez says fols. 1–2 are missing with lacunae at fol. 5 and fols. 9–12; Guidotti adds that fol. 1 was also missing.
- The title Ḥadīth Dhī l-Qarnayn is García Gómez's own.
- Fols. 47v–51r carry a separate Dhū l-Qarnayn ma'a l-Khaḍir story. García Gómez left it unedited because it is close to al-Tha'labī.
- The codex has since disappeared from the CSIC library and was never digitized (Marín 1991:71; Corriente, Pereira and Vicente 2015:259 n. 51). The 1929 edition is therefore the only surviving witness.
- Dating: the manuscript is 15th century per Ribera and Asín 1912; García Gómez's date rests on the year 864 in the Gog-and-Magog prophecy.
- Fols. 34r–39r adapt the Christian Syriac Alexander Legend (Ḥarāz/Huns, the gate, the prophecy, the war against Namrāq/Tūbārlāq). This section is unique among the Western-Arabic versions.
- The ending is unusual: Alexander is poisoned by the Amazon queen.
verification.source_text:
The base text is García Gómez's Arabic edition (1929), which is now also the only witness. A free scan is at https://archive.org/details/untextorabeoccid00unse: University of North Carolina copy, scanned 2025, PDF downloadable, no access restriction.

Rights:
- The book was published in 1929, so it has been public domain in the US since 1 January 2025.
- In Spain/EU, García Gómez's Spanish translation and study stay protected until 1 January 2066 (he died in 1995).
- The Arabic text is a transcription of a medieval text that he says he reproduced "tal cual es". Any Spanish editorial right (LPI art. 129) lasted 25 years and has long expired.
- Neoscholia can therefore translate from the Arabic, but must not reuse the Spanish translation's wording.

The OCR of the Arabic (72 pp.) is unusable; the Spanish OCR is good. The Arabic will need to be re-keyed or re-OCRed from the scan, keeping the Maghrebi fā'/qāf. Estimated size is about 18–22k Arabic words, judging from the roughly 27k-word Spanish translation.
verification.recommendation: Strong candidate: there is no Russian or English translation, the only translation is García Gómez's 1929 Spanish, and the manuscript is lost, so the US-public-domain 1929 Arabic edition is the sole witness. Start with fols. 34r–39r (the adaptation of the Syriac Alexander Legend: Ḥarāz/Gog-Magog, the gate, the prophecy dated 864, the war with Namrāq), with Budge's Syriac and Ethiopic and Bohas 2009 as parallels. Then continue with Candace–Amazons–poisoning (fols. 39r–47v). Checking the Arabic needs an Arabist who reads Andalusi Middle Arabic and Maghrebi script, which is beyond Greek/Latin; Guidotti 2022 is the main open-access aid.

verification.title: Hikayat Iskandar Zulkarnain (Classical Malay Alexander romance) / «Повесть об Искандаре Двурогом»
verification.ru_found: REFUTED: the Russian status is not "none". I checked this directly in the book's OCR on archive.org. The anthology is «Сказания о доблестных, влюбленных и мудрых. Антология классической малайской прозы», translated from Malay, compiled and prefaced by В.И. Брагинский, ed. Д.В. Деопик (М.: Наука, ГРВЛ, 1982). It has a section «Повесть об Искандаре Двурогом» on pp. ~101–118: Braginsky's introductory essay (pp. 101–103), then two translated episodes. The first is «Путешествие к Великому водовороту» (Michael and the weather angels, the descent in a chest into the encircling ocean, the fish; about 2,000 words). The second is «Путешествие в страну мрака за живой водой» (Khidr, Ilyas, Aram the Syrian, Israfil's raisin-branch and the ruby weighed against a handful of dust; about 4,700 words). That is roughly 6,700 words in total, about 5–6% of the ~118,000-word text. The commentary (pp. 380–381) says «Перевод по источнику [19]», and [19] in the «Источники» list is P.J. van Leeuwen, De Maleische Alexanderroman (Meppel 1937). So Braginsky translated from van Leeuwen's partial edition, which prints the sea and darkness episodes at pp. 193–231. Scan: https://archive.org/details/1982-202553750807. The intro gives the Russian title used in scholarship, «Повесть об Искандаре Двурогом»; ru.wikipedia «Литература Малайзии» uses the same title. A related overlap: Е.В. Ревуненкова's full Russian translation of the Sulalat al-salatin / Sejarah Melayu from the Krusenstern MS (2008, per ru.wikipedia) contains the opening Iskandar–Raja Kida Hindi marriage. Van Leeuwen (1937, p. 21) shows that passage is copied almost word for word from the Hikayat Iskandar. Braginsky's monograph «История малайской литературы VII–XIX вв.» (1983) discusses the text; I could not check whether it quotes it at length. Nothing relevant on facetia.ru (it has only Ostroumov's article and Persian/Turkic Iskandar texts). vostlit.info timed out. No complete or larger Russian translation was found.
verification.en_found: I found no English translation, complete or of a continuous episode. There are summaries and studies only. R.O. Winstedt, A History of Classical Malay Literature (2nd ed. 1969, pp. 85–86, 92–95) gives a summary (cited by the Malay Concordance Project). English Wikipedia lists no translation. Recent scholarship: Su Fang Ng, "Global Souvenirs: Bridging East and West in the Malay Alexander Romance", Literature Compass 2014 (doi 10.1111/lic3.12154); Ng, Alexander the Great from Britain to Southeast Asia (OUP 2019), ch. "Islamic Alexanders in Southeast Asia" (doi 10.1093/oso/9780198777687.003.0003); Ng, "Candace in the Malay Alexander Romance" in The Intersectional Alexander the Great (Bloomsbury 2026, doi 10.5040/9781350468337.ch-004); Ng 2016 in Alexander the Great in the Middle Ages: Transcultural Perspectives; Braginsky, The Heritage of Traditional Malay Literature (2004). These works probably quote short passages in the authors' own English, but I could not open them; the publisher pages were paywalled or blocked. There is also an Encyclopaedia of Islam THREE entry "Iskandar Zulkarnain, Hikayat" (paywalled). Caveat: the WebSearch budget for this session was used up (200/200). The English check therefore relied on Wikipedia, the Malay Concordance Project bibliography, Crossref and Open Library, not on open web searches.
verification.other_found: Dutch: P.J. van Leeuwen, De Maleische Alexanderroman (Utrecht dissertation, Meppel: B. ten Brink, 1937; archive.org/details/demaleischealexanderroman). It is not a translation. It is a partial critical edition in romanized Malay (text pp. 40–231), collating about 10 manuscripts, with the two manuscript groups y and z printed on facing pages for the opening. It covers under 1/5 of MS H and under 1/7 of MS F: the opening Bahman/Humai/Darab section, the conversion, the journey to the sunset, the Kida Hindi marriage, the Brahmans, Gog and Magog, the heart of the sea, and the Land of Darkness. It adds a detailed ~36-page Dutch summary of the whole romance ("Overzicht van den inhoud", pp. 232–267) and notes with Greek and Arabic parallels. Other Dutch: catalogue summaries by Juynboll (Leiden catalogue, 1899) and Pijnappel (BKI 1870). Indonesian: Siti Chamamah Soeratno, Hikayat Iskandar Zulkarnain: analisis resepsi (Balai Pustaka/UGM, 1989 per Open Library); Perpustakaan Nasional RI, Hikayat Iskandar Zulkarnain & Syair Raja Siak (2002). Modern Malay or Indonesian editions don't really count as translations. I found no French, German, Italian or Spanish translation. Searches in those languages were limited by the exhausted search budget.
verification.source_text: Standard edition: Haji Khalid Muhammad Hussain (ed.), Hikayat Iskandar Zulkarnain, Kuala Lumpur: Dewan Bahasa dan Pustaka, 1967; 2nd ed. 1986 (351 pp., ~118,000 words); reprinted 2020. It is in copyright. It is based on Leiden Cod. Or. 1696 (c. 1830, copied by Muhammad Cing Sa'idullah in the Batavia secretariat). Note that van Leeuwen counts Cod. 1696 (his "B") in a group of manuscripts that stops before the end of the story. The 2nd edition is OCR'd as a searchable concordance in the Malay Concordance Project (http://mcp.anu.edu.au/N/Isk_bib.html); it is not openly licensed. The best freely accessible text is van Leeuwen 1937 on archive.org, with PDF and OCR (https://archive.org/details/demaleischealexanderroman; second copy at /details/de-maleische-alexanderroman). Its public-domain status is unclear: the author's death date is unknown and archive.org gives no rights statement. The manuscripts themselves are public domain: Leiden Cod. Or. 1696 and Cod. 1967; the oldest MS "K" at Leiden, dated 10 Ramadan 1125 AH = 30 Sept 1713 (van Leeuwen p. 28); Berlin Schoemann 11; and Monash Winstedt MSS I–IV. I did not check which of them are digitized.
verification.recommendation: Still a strong candidate. Only about 6% exists in Russian (Braginsky 1982, two episodes), and I found no English translation at all. Start with the opening (the Bahman–Humai–Darab prehistory, Iskandar's birth and conversion; van Leeuwen pp. 40ff.) or with the Brahmans/gymnosophists dialogue plus the Gog and Magog wall, both of which have Pseudo-Callisthenes parallels; avoid simply redoing Braginsky's sea and Land of Darkness episodes. Checking the work needs Classical Malay/Jawi expertise (plus Arabic and Persian for the names), well beyond Greek/Latin, and the only openly accessible text is van Leeuwen's partial 1937 edition.

name: Alexander in wisdom literature, philosophy, letters, rhetoric, apocalyptic and legend motifs (late antique to Byzantine)
overview: This strand is wisdom literature, letters, rhetoric and apocalyptic about Alexander, from late antiquity to Byzantium. Russian coverage is thin outside the Romance texts the previous sweep already found (Gorelov 2006 and Taronyan 2007, not re-checked here). I verified the following Russian translations: Pigulevskaya's 1958 Syriac Christian Legend; Seleznev's Arabic laments of the philosophers in al-Makin; Dio Or. 1 and Or. 62; and Seneca the Elder's Suasoria 6 (2024). I found no Russian translation of: the papyrus letter collection (P.Hamb. 129 and PSI 1285); the gymnosophist papyri (Berlin 13044 and Geneva 271); Dio Or. 2 and 4 (Danilova 2023 says they are untranslated); Seneca's Suasoriae 1 and 4; Libanius' and Ps.-Nicolaus' exercises on Alexander; or the Alexander sayings in the Greek gnomologia. English coverage is good for literary works (Loeb, Gibson 2008, Stoneman's Legends 1994/2012, Garstad 2012, Brock 1970). It is weak or missing for the papyrus letters (one excerpt only), the new Geneva fragments (Willis–Maresch 1988) and the gnomologia (only partly online, SAWS). The best flagship is the papyrus letters: no Russian, almost no English, Greek only, compact. Next come the gymnosophist papyri and Dio Or. 4. The web-search budget ran out partway through. Russian status for Iter ad Paradisum, George the Monk and a modern Russian Ps.-Methodius is therefore 'unknown'. A rabbinic dossier (Tamid 32a–b) was not checked and is left out. Caveat: a Moscow team (Krivolapov and Snedkova) is translating the Suasoriae, so check with them before starting Suasoriae 1 and 4.
already_translated_ru: Verified: the Syriac Christian Legend of Alexander (Neṣḥānā), full Russian translation by N.V. Pigulevskaya, Палестинский сборник 3(66), 1958, from Budge 1889 pp. 255–275. The Arabic laments of the philosophers at Alexander's tomb, from al-Makin's al-Majmuʿ al-mubarak, translated by N.N. Seleznev (edited by D.A. Morozov), История философии 18. Dio Or. 1 (Zvirevich 2012) and Or. 62 (Sidash, Кинические речи, 2012). Seneca the Elder, Suasoria 6 (Krivolapov–Snedkova 2024). Plutarch's De Alexandri fortuna is sold in Russian (MyBook, 'О судьбе и доблести. Александр Македонский'); the translator was not checked. From the previous sweep, not re-checked: Palladius, De gentibus Indiae (Taronyan 2007); Collatio, Epistola ad Aristotelem and Commonitorium Palladii (Gorelov 2006); Egunov's α excerpts (1960/61).

verification.title: Papyrus letters of Alexander and Darius (the "Briefroman" dossier): PSI XII 1285 (TM 63399, MP3 2114, LDAB 4606) + P.Hamb. II 129 (Hamburg SUB inv. 605, TM 65529, MP3 2115, LDAB 6780)
verification.ru_found:
The sweep's "RU none" is refuted, but only in part. Б. Г. Деревенский, «Письма Александра Великого» (СПб.: Алетейя, 2022; LitRes e-book 4 Jan 2023; ISBN 978-5-00165-511-4; 401 pp.). LitRes lists the translator as Р. А. Гимадеев. The book is an anthology of Alexander's letters with Greek or Latin text, Russian translation and commentary. I checked it through Google Books search-within (https://books.google.com/books?id=3M2lEAAAQBAJ). Its table of contents includes:
- No. 130а «То же послание на Флорентийском папирусе», p. 266: Greek text of PSI XII 1285 col. IV 17–41 followed by a Russian translation. The translation renders papyrus-only wording, e.g. «…надменное, через которое ищешь, чтобы встретились мы с тобой в Финикии … приняв прежде согласованное с тобой в прежнем письме?».
- p. 268: a note on PSI 1285 col. IV 42–48, Alexander's reply. It says only the opening of the letter survives on the papyrus and gives its content in summary.
- No. 133а «То же послание на Гамбургском папирусе», pp. 272ff.: P.Hamb. 129 ll. 31–56, with Russian lemmata such as «ради … родства, существующего меж нами от Персея».
- No. 133б: the same letter on the Tabula Iliaca (SEG 33.802).
- The Porus letter (No. 137/137а) is given only in its Romance and Metz Epitome forms; the P.Hamb. version is only mentioned.
Searches within the book for Полиид, the cups of Dionysus and col. I–III passages found nothing. So PSI 1285 letters 1–3 (cols. I–IV 16) and P.Hamb. 129 ll. 1–30, 57–78 and 79–105 appear not to be translated.
Other Russian searches found nothing more (CyberLeninka API ×8, Internet Archive full text ×3, Google Books in Russian ×2, ru.wikipedia, facetia.ru). Braginskaya's bibliography of Russian translations of ancient novels (Ancient Narrative 3, 2003, https://ancientnarrative.com/article/view/24306) lists only Egunov's α excerpt. Egunov covers I.39, the Romance parallel to P.Hamb. ll. 1–30, but not the papyrus text. Kuznetsova and Грабарь-Пассек in «Античный роман» (1969) and the 1963 survey summarise Merkelbach's papyri; the snippets show no translation. Botvinnik 1979 is about recension ε, not the papyri.
verification.en_found:
"Partial" is right but overstates the coverage: only one letter is translated in full, plus excerpts.
- Arthur-Montagne, "Persuasion, Emotion, and the Letters of the Alexander Romance", Ancient Narrative 11 (2014) 159–189, at p. 164 (https://ancientnarrative.com/article/view/24674): full translation of PSI 1285 col. IV 17–41 only, using Giuliano's text. Nawotka, The Alexander Romance by Ps.-Callisthenes: A Historical Commentary (Brill 2017) 166 cites this as the English translation and names no other.
- Whitmarsh, "Addressing Power: Fictional Letters between Alexander and Darius", in Hodkinson, Rosenmeyer and Bracke (eds), Epistolary Narratives (Brill 2013) 169–186 (DOI 10.1163/9789004253032_009); reprinted as ch. 6 of Beyond the Second Sophistic (UC Press 2013). It gives a concordance of letters and quotes short passages from the papyri (e.g. "my great master", letter 11; the Polyidus letter). Its note: "Translations of the Romance letters adapted from Dowden 1989; all others are mine". So these are his own excerpt translations, not full texts.
- Cropp, Minor Greek Tragedians II (2021), note on Chaeremon F 2: one sentence of the Polyidus letter (PSI 1285 II 12ff.).
- Checked and found to contain no translation: Stoneman, The Greek Alexander Romance (Penguin 1991); Rosenmeyer 2001 and 2006; Stephens–Winkler 1995 (excludes the Romance material); Hansen 1998; Monti 2023 (BMCR 2024.10.31; Arthur-Montagne's review in Histos 2025, DOI 10.29173/histos708).

- German: Merkelbach, "Pseudo-Kallisthenes und ein Briefroman über Alexander", Aegyptus 27 (1947) 144–158; ed. pr. P.Hamb. II 129 (1954) 51–74, commentary only with no running translation (checked in the IA scan); Quellen (1954; 2nd ed. 1977 with Trumpf), whose Anhang pp. 230–252 gives a Greek reconstructed "Alexandri Epistolae" with Latin apparatus and German summaries. Valla, Il Romanzo di Alessandro I (2007) xvii–cix announces the papyri in "Appendice 1" of vol. III, but the Valla catalogue still lists only vols I–II (checked Oct 2026).
- Spanish: Vicente Sánchez, Habis 50 (2019) 245–267 (DOI 10.12795/habis.2019.i50.11): Greek excerpts from both papyri with Spanish paraphrase, not a translation.
- French: Jouanno 2002, discussion only.
- Not checked: the Polish translation of the Romance (Nawotka 2010).
verification.source_text:
No public-domain online Greek text exists. The DCLP records (CC BY 3.0) for TM 65529 and TM 63399 have empty edition sections, i.e. metadata only, which corrects the sweep's statement that the Greek text is on papyri.info (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/papyri/idp.data/master/DCLP/65/65529.xml and …/DCLP/63/63399.xml).

Working texts:
- P.Hamb. 129: Merkelbach, P.Hamb. II 129 (1954) 51–74. A full scan is on the Internet Archive (https://archive.org/details/p-hamb-2), uploaded by a user; its copyright status is unclear, though German §70 UrhG protection for scholarly editions (25 years) has lapsed for the edited Greek text. Dating: Merkelbach puts it in the 1st c. BC; Cavallo–Maehler 2008 no. 38 and Giuliano put it in the first half or middle of the 2nd c. BC; DCLP gives 200–150 BC.
- PSI 1285: Pieraccioni, PSI XII 1285 (1951) 166–190 (Oxyrhynchus; verso of a land register; 4 columns; Cairo Museum; dated 100–150 AD). Images: PSIonline (http://www.psi-online.it/documents/psi;12;1285).
- The current reference text is Giuliano 2010 (in copyright); use Merkelbach–Trumpf 1977 for the integrated text.
- Images of P.Hamb. 129 at SUB Hamburg (HANSh605) and the Leipzig papyrus portal sit behind bot checks, so their licences were not verified.
verification.recommendation: This is still a good candidate if pitched as the first complete translation of the whole papyrus dossier, not as a fully untranslated text: two letters already exist in Russian (Derevensky/Gimadeev 2022) and one in English (Arthur-Montagne 2014). Start with PSI XII 1285 cols. I–IV 16 (Darius' letter, the Polyidus letter and Alexander's long reply; no translation of these was found in any language), then P.Hamb. 129 ll. 1–30, 57–78 and 79–105. Checking requires Greek papyrological skill (heavy restorations, so supplements must be marked strictly) but no oriental languages.

verification.title: Alexander and the Gymnosophists outside the Romance: P.Berol. 13044 recto (FGrHist 153 F 9) + P.Genev. inv. 271 (+ P.Rob. inv. 40 / P.Köln inv. 907) + Boissonade, Anecdota Graeca I 145–146
verification.ru_found:
REFUTED: the "none" claim is wrong. Both papyri were translated into Russian by I. M. Nakhov.
(1) Solopova M. A., «Античная философия и Восток: избранная библиография», Историко-философский ежегодник 2017, no. 124, lists: «Кинические диатрибы. Из Берлинского папируса № 1304[4]. Из Женевского папируса № 271 // Антология кинизма / Изд. подг. И. М. Нахов. М.: Наука, 1978 [sic], С. 232–236». The edition is in fact Наука 1984, series «Памятники философской мысли», 398 pp. (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/antichnaya-filosofiya-i-vostok-izbrannaya-bibliografiya-ch-i-mir-vostoka-glazami-antichnyh-filosofov-ch-ii-klassicheskaya-antichnaya).
(2) Popov A. A., «Истоки и зарождение греко-буддизма…», Вестник СПбГИК 2020 no. 1(42), cites the Berlin papyrus as «Антология кинизма», М.: Наука, 1984, pp. 271–273. These may be the notes pages, since Solopova gives the text as pp. 232–236. Popov cites the Geneva papyrus via Nakhov, Martin and Photiadès (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/istoki-i-zarozhdenie-greko-buddizma-v-indii-i-baktrii).
(3) Koroleva E. M., Вестник ПСТГУ сер. III, 2012, вып. 4(30), pp. 41–58, n. 52: «Перевод обоих фрагментов на русский язык см.: Нахов И. М. Киническая литература. М., 1981. С. 139–140, 142–144» (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/rasskaz-o-brahmanah-v-drevnerusskoy-i-latinskoy-versiyah-romana-ob-aleksandre-istochniki-i-ih-modifikatsiya).
(4) Possibly relevant but unchecked: Nakhov, «Три кинических диатрибы», in «Античность и современность» (Festschrift Петровский), М.: Наука, 1972, pp. 164–175. Its contents were not verified.
Extent: the anthology titles say «Из…», which suggests excerpts. 4–5 pages for both texts points to a partial version, or at most a near-complete one for the Alexander portion of P.Genev. I could not see Nakhov's books myself.
Not covered by Nakhov: the Willis–Maresch fragments (1988), because they were published after Nakhov's 1981 and 1984 books. The Russian Palladius (Taronyan, «Древний Восток в античной и раннехристианской традиции», Ладомир 2007) contains the expanded Christianized version of the Geneva diatribe. Popov also cites Taronyan 2007 p. 383 about the Berlin papyrus, so that volume might contain it too; not verified.
No Russian translation was found for the Boissonade text, Ἐννέα σοφῶν ἀποφθέγματα. Its content overlaps heavily with Plutarch, Alex. 64, which does exist in Russian.
verification.en_found:
(1) Confirmed: Stoneman R., Legends of Alexander the Great, revised edition, London: I.B. Tauris 2012 (ISBN 9781848857858). Appendix I "Fragmentary Texts from Antiquity": (i) "Berlin Papyrus 13044: Alexander Interrogates the Gymnosophists"; (ii) "Geneva Papyrus 271: A Cynic Diatribe of Dandamis to Alexander". Source: archive.org catalog contents note, https://archive.org/details/legendsofalexand0000unse. Whether the Geneva translation is complete, and whether the 1994 Everyman/Dent edition (ISBN 0460875140) already had both appendix texts, could not be checked (the full text is restricted).
(2) REFUTED, the sweep's claim that the Willis–Maresch fragments are untranslated: Willis & Maresch, ZPE 74 (1988) 59–83, pp. 82–83, print a section headed "Translation". It gives an English version of their tentatively reconstructed cols. i–iv (P.Rob. inv. 40 + P.Köln inv. 907), which are now numbered before the Geneva cols. v–xix. Checked directly in the PDF: https://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/zpe/downloads/1988/074pdf/074059.pdf
(3) No English translation was found for Boissonade's Ἐννέα σοφῶν ἀποφθέγματα (Anecd. Gr. I 145–146).
So all three papyrus components exist in English; only the short Byzantine text appears untranslated.
verification.other_found:
French: V. Martin, «Un recueil de diatribes cyniques. Pap. Genev. inv. 271», MusHelv 16 (1959) 77–115 (editio princeps). Its French translation is reported, not checked directly. P. Photiadès, MusHelv 16 (1959) 116–139, is a study of the ancient Greek and Latin reworkings («traductions et élaborations successives»), not a modern translation.
German: U. Wilcken, «Alexander der Große und die indischen Gymnosophisten», SBBerl 1923, 150–183 (papyrus text 161–162). Whether it includes a German translation is not verified. G. Chr. Hansen, «Alexander und die Brahmanen», Klio 43–45 (1965) 351–380, may contain German renderings; not checked.
Italian: U. Criscuolo, «Per la fortuna della diatriba cinica (pap. Genevensis inv. 271)», Annali Macerata 3–4 (1970–71) 455–467. Whether it translates the text is unknown.
Other studies listed by Willis–Maresch: Derrett, ClMed 21 (1960); Kakridis, MusHelv 17 (1960) and Serta Turyniana (1974); Berg, ClMed 31 (1970); Brunel 1978.
Early modern: Boissonade's note says a related version, «Ἀποκρίσεις φρονίμων», was printed earlier by Vulcanius and then by Berkel after Epictetus. These were probably bilingual Greek–Latin printings; not verified.
Spanish: nothing found.
Method caveat: WebSearch was unavailable (session budget of 200 already used), so I could not run the required 4+4 Russian/English web searches. Evidence comes from direct fetches: the ZPE PDF, the archive.org and Open Library catalogs, CyberLeninka catalog queries in Russian (about 11), and the Russian Wikipedia API.
verification.source_text:
(a) Anecdota version: Boissonade, Anecdota Graeca vol. I (Paris 1829), pp. 145–146, Ἐννέα σοφῶν ἀποφθέγματα πρὸς Ἀλέξανδρον τὸν Μακεδόνα. It comes from a Paris codex; the shelfmark reads "1630" or "1680" depending on how the OCR is read. Boissonade's notes compare Plutarch, Alex. 64 and Zonaras IV 14. Public domain, confirmed on archive.org: https://archive.org/details/anekdotaanecdot01boisgoog (vol. I).
(b) Berlin papyrus: Wilcken, SBBerl 1923, 161–162. Probably public domain in the EU (Wilcken died 1944), but I did not locate a scan. FGrHist 153 F 9 is not public domain.
(c) Geneva papyrus: Martin, MusHelv 16 (1959) 77–115. Free to read via e-periodica, but in copyright; the URL was not verified. The new fragments are in Willis–Maresch, ZPE 74 (1988) 59–83: a free PDF (© Habelt, not openly licensed) at https://www.uni-koeln.de/phil-fak/ifa/zpe/downloads/1988/074pdf/074059.pdf. Large parts of the Geneva text can be reconstructed from Palladius, De gentibus Indiae II (Derrett, ClMed 21, 1960; Berghoff 1967).
verification.recommendation: Weak candidate as a "first translation": both papyri are already in Russian (Nakhov, Антология кинизма 1984 and Киническая литература 1981, apparently in excerpts) and in English (Stoneman 2012), and Willis–Maresch translated their new fragments themselves. The only text that seems untranslated is the 2-page Byzantine "Ἐννέα σοφῶν ἀποφθέγματα" (Boissonade I 145–146, public domain). Start with it, either alone or as the anchor of a fully annotated RU/EN "gymnosophist dossier" that would also be the first Russian version of the Willis–Maresch fragments. Only Greek is needed, plus some papyrological caution.

candidates.title: Dio Chrysostom, Or. 4 Περὶ βασιλείας δ΄ (Alexander and Diogenes), with Or. 2 (Alexander and Philip on Homer) / Fourth and Second Kingship Orations / «Четвёртая и вторая речи о царской власти»
candidates.author: Dio of Prusa (Chrysostom)
candidates.tradition: Rhetoric and philosophy (Cynic theory of kingship); Second Sophistic
candidates.size: Or. 4: 139 §§ (about 7,000 Greek words, estimated); Or. 2: 79 §§ (about 4,500, estimated)
candidates.edition: von Arnim 1893 (Weidmann; public domain, archive.org); de Budé, Teubner 1916–19; Cohoon, LCL 257 (1932)

Or. 2 has Alexander on Homer as the royal poet. Central to the imperial political reception of Alexander and readable for a general audience.
candidates.ai_feasibility: High: Attic prose, public-domain text, good commentaries

verification.title: Dio Chrysostom, Or. 4 (Περὶ βασιλείας δ΄: Alexander and Diogenes) with Or. 2 (Alexander and Philip on Homer). Fourth and Second Kingship Orations / Дион Хрисостом, Четвёртая и вторая речи о царской власти
verification.ru_found:
I could not refute "none" for Or. 2 or Or. 4. One weak point remains (Sidash, below). The WebSearch budget was used up (200/200), so these checks were done by fetching sources and catalogues directly, not through a search engine.
(1) Zvirevich's Russian translation is Or. 1 only. В.Т. Звиревич, «Дион Хрисостом. О царской власти», Известия УрФУ, Сер. 3, 2012, № 3(106), с. 147–159. I downloaded and read the PDF: it runs from 1.1 (Timotheus) to 1.84 and its own note says "первая из его четырёх речей". It was made from Greek with Cohoon/Thayer as a crib. https://elar.urfu.ru/handle/10995/20967
Zvirevich later translated Or. 70 «О философии» (Вестник Гуманитарного ун-та, Екатеринбург, 2014, № 1(4)). The UrFU repository has no other Dio translations of his.
(2) Danilova, ΣΧΟΛΗ 17.1 (2023), p. 263, checked in the PDF (https://classics.nsu.ru/schole/assets/files/17-1-danilova.pdf). She says that of Or. I–IV, LVI and LXII only Or. 1 (Звиревич) and Or. 62 (Сидаш 2012, с. 103–107) exist in Russian. She worked from Cohoon. Her own Russian renderings of Or. 2 and Or. 4 are phrase-level glosses only (e.g., IV.4, 52, 60, 77, 84; II.15, 73), not excerpts.
(3) Russian Wikipedia's translation list (raw wikitext, checked) gives Or. 6–12, 18, 21, 36, 51, 53 and 55, Скифия/Кавказ excerpts (ВДИ 1948), the India excerpts (Таронян 2007), Sidash 2012, and Межерицкая's Or. 29 (2017). It lists nothing for Or. 2–4. Нахов's «Антология кинизма» (1984/1996) has Or. 6, 8, 9 and 10 (pp. 270–296) and no Or. 4.
(4) Новое, но не относится к делу: Литпамятники № 760, «Дион Хрисостом. Вифинские речи», изд. подг. С.И. Межерицкая, перевод М.Е. Грабарь-Пассек (Ладомир–Наука 2024, 482 pp.; RSL catalogue). Судя по названию, это Bithynian orations; the volume's appendices were not checked.
(5) Weak point: Т.Г. Сидаш, «Кинические речи = Orationes Cynicae». Editions: Нестор-История 2012 (254 pp., 17 cm, Russian only); 2nd ed. Квадривиум 2021 (ISBN 978-5-7164-1063-3, 249 pp.). Both are in the NLR and RSL catalogues, which give no table of contents. Pieces I could confirm from other people's citations:
- Or. 72 «О внешнем виде» at pp. 7–14 (Светлов 2015)
- Or. 70 «О философии» (Афонасин 2013)
- probably Or. 64 «О судьбе II» (Куликова 2017, «кн. II, § 5»)
- Or. 62 at pp. 103–107 (Danilova)
So the book looks like a collection of the short diatribes. Danilova used it and still lists only Or. 1 for I–IV. Or. 4, as a Diogenes dialogue, cannot be completely ruled out until someone checks the book's table of contents (NLR shelfmark Л1 Ш6(0)33/Д-468).
Not checked: Вальденберг 1926–27 (Известия АН СССР), which may contain long Russian quotations, and «Антология мировой политической мысли» (1997).
verification.en_found: J.W. Cohoon, Dio Chrysostom vol. I (Discourses 1–11), Loeb Classical Library 257 (1932): complete Or. 2 and Or. 4. It is freely online at LacusCurtius: https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Dio_Chrysostom/Discourses/2*.html and .../4*.html (both return HTTP 200). Thayer states it is US public domain because the copyright was not renewed. Danilova cites the 2002 Henderson reprint.
verification.other_found:
- German, complete: W. Elliger, Dion Chrysostomos, Sämtliche Reden (Artemis, Bibliothek der Alten Welt, Zürich 1967), per the de.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia bibliographies.
- French, Or. 4 included: L. Paquet, Les cyniques grecs. Fragments et témoignages (Livre de Poche 1992), pp. 202–262, translates Discours IV, VI, VIII, IX and X (fr.wikipedia bibliography). No French translation of Or. 2 was found; the remacle.org Dio pages have only Or. 7 and 11.

verification.source_text:
H. von Arnim, Dionis Prusaensis quem vocant Chrysostomum quae exstant omnia, vol. I (Berlin: Weidmann 1893), public domain.
Digital TEI of this edition: Perseus canonical-greekLit, urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0612.tlg001.perseus-grc2, CC BY-SA 4.0. https://github.com/PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit/tree/master/data/tlg0612/tlg001 (checked: it contains speech n=2 and n=4).
Measured from the TEI: Or. 4 is about 6,400 Greek words in 139 §§; Or. 2 about 4,440 words in 79 §§; Or. 3, also untranslated into Russian, about 6,000 words.
Use de Budé (Teubner 1916–19) for comparison. The Cohoon Loeb text, with the LacusCurtius English, can serve as a crib.
verification.recommendation: Worth doing as a first Russian translation, but it does not meet priority (2): a complete, public-domain English translation is online, along with German and Italian ones (French for Or. 4 only), so the value is for Russian readers, with Alexander-reception commentary. Begin with Or. 4, about 6,400 words of Greek only. First check the table of contents of Sidash's «Кинические речи» (2012/2021) to make sure Or. 4 is not in it, then do Or. 2 and possibly Or. 3, which together with Zvirevich's Or. 1 would complete the four kingship orations in Russian.

verification.title: Alexander apophthegms in Byzantine gnomologia: Gnomologium Vaticanum (Vat. gr. 743, nos. 73–105 plus 112 and 379) and Florilegium Parisinum (Par. suppl. gr. 690, ff. 28v–29r) / «Изречения Александра в византийских гномологиях»
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of the Gnom. Vat. Alexander section, of the Florilegium Parisinum, or of the SAWS Alexander dossier. Searches run: Startpage (via script, because the WebSearch budget was used up and Google and Yandex returned CAPTCHAs) for «Ватиканский гномологий», «Гномологий Ватиканский перевод», «Gnomologium Vaticanum Александр перевод», «изречения Александра Македонского византийские гномологии перевод», «апофтегмы Александра Македонского перевод греческий флорилегий», «"Gnom. Vat." Александр перевод Диоген» and «facetia.ru изречения Александра Македонского». CyberLeninka API queries: «гномологий Александр», «Gnomologium Vaticanum», «апофтегмы Александра Македонского», «византийские гномологии изречения». I also checked the facetia.ru Alexander index. The only Russian hits for «Ватиканский гномологий» are Presocratic and Sophist fragment editions (Scholae: Antiphon 2021, Gorgias 2020, Protagoras 2020; Lebedev on Heraclitus). They translate single non-Alexander GV items. Russian coverage exists only through parallel versions in other works, not through these gnomologia: (a) Plutarch, Regum et imperatorum apophthegmata, Alexander section, tr. S. V. Polyakov (ancientrome.ru/antlitr/t.htm?a=1438015000, citing «Плутарх. Сочинения», М. 1990). (b) «Пчела», the Old Russian Melissa. Its modern Russian translation by V. V. Kolesov is reproduced at facetia.ru/node/2966 and contains several Alexander sayings parallel to GV, e.g. the refusal to "steal a victory" = GV 77. Plutarch, Alex. and De Alexandri fortuna (Borovsky; facetia.ru/node/2763) also exist in Russian. In each case the wording differs from the gnomologia.
verification.en_found: This refutes "partial". There are two independent complete English translations online. (1) Ryan Baumann & Clinton Kinkade, "English translations from the Gnomologium Vaticanum", https://ryanfb.xyz/gnomvat/gnomvat.html (GitHub ryanfb/gnomvat, CC BY 4.0, 633 commits, last commit Feb 2023, labelled "work-in-progress"). It gives Sternbach's Greek with an English version for every item: 591 list entries, all with Greek and English, ending with Phryne. This includes the whole Alexander block GV 73–105, which I checked one by one. A companion page translates Die Wiener Apophthegmen-Sammlung (WA) (ryanfb.xyz/gnomvat/wa.html). It was announced on Reddit r/AncientGreek in March 2022. (2) Denis Searby (with M. Bylund and P. Österdahl), SAWS edition "Apophthegmata et gnomae secundum alphabetum" (2013), https://ancientwisdoms.ac.uk. It has a dedicated "Alexander" chapter: Greek at urn:cts:greekLit:sawsEdGr.Alexander.sawsEd01 and "Alexander, English translation" at sawsEd02 (https://ancientwisdoms.ac.uk/mss/xmlcache/AT__greekLit__sawsEdGr.Alexander.sawsEd02.html). It contains 49 apophthegm units, all translated, with a synoptic apparatus. The witnesses are GV 73–105, 112 and 379; FP 1–16, 18, 21 and 24–31; plus WA, Corpus Parisinum VI (Paris and Digby), Fl. Leidense, Monacense, Vindobonense, Vaticanum, Baroccianum, Chisianum, Neapolitanum, App. Vaticana I–II and the three Appendix Gnomica witnesses. SAWS describes FP as "a previously unedited collection of 35 sayings" in Par. suppl. gr. 690 (12th c.), ff. 28v–29r, "mainly apophthegms attributed to Alexander". So FP's editio princeps came with an English translation. Further English: Searby, Corpus Parisinum (Edwin Mellen 2007; vol. 2, Notes and Translation), which covers the CP witnesses of the same sayings. Scattered single items: sententiaeantiquae.com (e.g. GV 78 on Achilles' tomb, 2024). Stoneman's Legends of Alexander the Great: I did not search it specifically and no hit linked it to these gnomologia; I did not check further.
verification.other_found: ITALIAN (full): Anna Busetto, "La vita è come un cetriolo. Una raccolta di aforismi greci" (Roma: Inschibboleth, 2025; Classici smarriti 4; 254 pp.; ISBN 978-88-552-9573-4). It is the first complete Italian translation of the Gnomologium Vaticanum (all 577 items), with Sternbach's Greek on facing pages (pp. 32–159), introduction and commentary. It was reviewed by L. M. Ciolfi in Estudios bizantinos 13 (2025) 299–302 (https://erevistas.publicaciones.uah.es/ojs/index.php/ebizantinos/es/article/download/3172/1876/12906); publisher page: inschibbolethedizioni.com. Lelli (ed.), Proverbi, sentenze e massime di saggezza in Grecia e a Roma (Bompiani, Milano 2021), pp. 968–997 and 1815–1825. Whether it includes Alexander items is not verified. GERMAN: only informal forum translations ("Aus dem Gnomologium Vaticanum #5", albertmartin.de), seen only as a search snippet that includes an Alexander–Diogenes item; no published German translation found. There is a German-language study with a concordance that covers the Alexander items: "Das Gnomologium, das Gnomologium Vaticanum und die Tradition" (GFA, journals.ub.uni-heidelberg.de); I could not access the full text (403). FRENCH and SPANISH: nothing found in one search each.
verification.source_text: Gnom. Vat.: L. Sternbach, "De gnomologio Vaticano inedito", Wiener Studien 9 (1887) 175–206; 10 (1888) 1–49, 211–260; continued in vol. 11 (1889), pages not verified. Public domain. Volumes 9–10 are on archive.org as https://archive.org/details/WienerStudien09_10. The Alexander block falls at the end of WS 9 and the start of WS 10 (OCR shows nos. 76 and 84 on WS 10 pp. 6–7). The Greek OCR is unusable. Reprint: Sternbach, Gnomologium Vaticanum e codice Vaticano graeco 743 (Berlin: de Gruyter 1963, TuK 2). The most practical digital Greek is the Sternbach transcription in github.com/ryanfb/gnomvat (CC BY 4.0, with Sternbach's corrigenda; the Greek itself is public domain). I found no explicit licence statement on the SAWS pages, so reuse terms need checking. The editors themselves say they worked from a poor microfilm of Par. suppl. gr. 690 (BnF IIIF manifest exists via Biblissima).
verification.recommendation: Weak candidate. The English status is "full", not "partial": two complete open translations (Baumann–Kinkade CC BY of all 577 GV items; Searby/SAWS of the whole Alexander dossier, including the editio princeps of FP). A full Italian GV appeared in 2025 (Busetto). Only Russian remains open. If wanted as a small Russian-only item, the unit should be the SAWS "Alexander" chapter (49 units, a synopsis of GV 73–105/112/379 plus FP and the parallel florilegia), with Russian translation and commentary on parallels in Plutarch, Diogenes Laertius, the Melissa/«Пчела» and Arabic gnomologia. Verification needs only Greek, but the dossier adds little new.

verification.title: Seneca Maior, Suasoriae 1 (Deliberat Alexander an Oceanum naviget) and 4 (Deliberat Alexander an Babylona intret) / «Свасории (свазории) I и IV»
verification.ru_found:
I found no complete or substantial Russian translation of Suas. 1 or 4. The "none" claim holds, except for short quotations inside scholarly articles.
(1) Krivolapov & Snedkova cover only Suas. 6 and 7. Their book is «Луций Анней Сенека (Старший). Свазории VI и VII. Антоний и Цицерон», пер., введ., коммент. Г.Л. Криволапова и Е.В. Снедковой (М.: Альма Матер, 2025; серия «Эпохи. Античность. Тексты»; 158 pp.; ISBN 978-5-00264-043-0; DOI 10.63952/7544.2025.16.38.001). Publisher page: https://almamater-book.ru/shop/tproduct/228798383182-svazorii-vi-i-vii-antonii-i-tsitseron. The publisher bills it as the first Russian edition of VI–VII and says nothing about I–V. This book is new compared with the sweep, which knew only the ПИФК 2024 Suas. 6 articles. Because the series is ongoing, I–V could be next; watch it or ask the translators. Note their spelling «свазории», which matters for searches.
(2) Excerpt: А.В. Подосинов, «Alter orbis terrarum: "другие миры" в античной географии», Индоевропейское языкознание и классическая филология 2020 (https://cyberleninka.ru/article/n/alter-orbis-terrarum-drugie-miry-v-antichnoy-geografii). It quotes Suas. 1.1 in Latin with the author's own Russian translation («Нет ничего столь бесконечного, как Океан…»). It is one sentence group only.
(3) Not verified, though excerpts are likely: Т.И. Кузнецова, ch. 4 «Сенека Старший» in Кузнецова & Стрельникова, «Ораторское искусство в древнем Риме» (М., 1976), pp. 136–173. I could not reach the text.
Checked with nothing found: ru.wikipedia (Сенека Старший lists only the Loeb; the Педон Альбинован article does not translate the Suas. 1.15 fragment); ru.wikisource; ancientrome.ru (only Seneca the Younger); CyberLeninka API (about 15 Russian queries: свасории/свазории, Сенека Старший, Ареллий Фуск, Альбинован Педон, Кестий, Латрон, etc.); Crossref; Internet Archive. Pistellato 2020 (Вестник ННГУ) gives the Pedo fragment in Latin only. Caveat: the WebSearch budget was used up and Bing/Yandex/DDG were blocked or captcha'd, so elibrary.ru and general web pages were not searched.
verification.en_found:
The "full" status is confirmed by two complete English translations.
(1) W.A. Edward, The Suasoriae of Seneca the Elder: Introductory Essay, Text, Translation and Explanatory Notes (Cambridge UP, 1928). Reviewed in CR 1929 (doi:10.1017/s0009840x00052379), CW 1930, JRS. Reprinted Bristol Classical Press 1996. It has been public domain in the US since 2024, but I could not confirm an online scan: HathiTrust was blocked, and Internet Archive search found nothing.
(2) M. Winterbottom, The Elder Seneca: Declamations, LCL 463–464 (1974); Suasoriae in vol. II (Digital Loeb doi:10.4159/dlcl.seneca_elder-suasoriae.1974).
Studies with partial translations or paraphrase: B. Huelsenbeck, "The Ocean (Seneca Suas. 1)", in Dinter, Guérin & Martinho (eds.), Reading Roman Declamation: Seneca the Elder (OUP 2020) 151–185 (doi:10.1093/oso/9780198746010.003.0008). This is a close-reading study; I could not see whether it includes a full translation.
Not confirmed: the sweep's "attalus.org (Suas. 1)". The attalus.org translations index has no Seneca entry, and ToposText's text list has none either.
verification.other_found:
Translated in full in other languages:
- FR: H. Bornecque, Sénèque le rhéteur, Controverses et Suasoires (Garnier, 1902, 2 vols; rev. 1932). On archive.org as ControversesEtSuasoiresTraditionNouvelleTexteRevueParM.Henri (v.1) and …Henri_517 (v.2). Reissued as Sentences, divisions et couleurs des orateurs et des rhéteurs (Aubier, 1992).
- DE: O. & E. Schönberger, Sentenzen, Einteilungen, Färbungen von Rednern und Redelehrern (Würzburg: Königshausen & Neumann, 2004). Complete.
- IT: Seneca il Vecchio, Oratori e retori (Bologna: Zanichelli, Prosatori di Roma, 1986–; 4 vols, Latin and Italian; Suasoriae in vol. 4). The translator is normally cited as A. Zanon dal Bo, but the catalogue record I saw does not name him.
- ES: Séneca el Viejo, Controversias; Suasorias (Madrid: Gredos, BCG, 2005), 2 vols; Suasorias in vol. II (ISBN 978-84-249-2778-3). Translated by I.-X. Adiego Lajara with E. Artigas and A. de Riquer.
Not translations:
- S. Feddern, Die Suasorien des älteren Seneca: Einleitung, Text und Kommentar (De Gruyter, 2013). BMCR 2013.11.19 mentions no translation.
- E. Migliario, Retorica e storia: una lettura delle Suasoriae di Seneca Padre (Edipuglia, 2007). Latin text from Håkanson, no translation (BMCR 2010.01.20).
Pattern elsewhere: the Cicero suasoriae (6–7) have had separate translations (IT «Cicerone è stato assassinato!», Palomar 2008; RU Krivolapov–Snedkova 2025). The Alexander suasoriae have had none in Russian. Polish, Czech, Ukrainian and Modern Greek Wikipedias showed nothing.
verification.source_text: Modern critical texts (copyrighted; use for collation): L. Håkanson, Teubner 1989, and S. Feddern 2013 (newest text and commentary for the Suasoriae). Public-domain texts: A. Kiessling, Teubner 1872, https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_Y4YDAAAAQAAJ (a 1967 Stuttgart Teubner reprint is also at https://archive.org/details/lannaeisenecaeo00mullgoog, despite the "mull" in its ID); C. Bursian, Leipzig 1857, https://archive.org/details/bub_gb_Wos9AAAAcAAJ; H.J. Müller, Vienna 1887 (PD, but no online scan found in this check); Edward 1928 Latin text (US PD). Bornecque's 1902 French translation is a PD control version on archive.org.
verification.recommendation: A good Russian-first candidate. In Russian it is effectively untranslated (only one-sentence quotations such as Podosinov 2020 on Suas. 1.1), but English (Edward 1928, Winterbottom 1974), French, German, Italian and Spanish versions are complete, so the English output adds little. Start with Suas. 1 and 4 together as an "Alexander suasoriae" unit, about 20 short sections. Verification needs only Latin and Greek (Greek declaimers' sententiae in Suas. 1, the Pedo hexameters at 1.15, textual cruxes per Håkanson and Feddern). Before committing, check whether Krivolapov and Snedkova, whose Alma Mater series is ongoing, plan Suas. I–V.

verification.title: Libanius, Progymnasmata: Chreia 1 (Alexander: "my friends are my treasures"); [Libanius]/Ps.-Nicolaus, Descriptions 25 (Tychaion with Alexander) and 27 (Alexander the Founder) — «Александр в прогимнасмах Либания»
verification.ru_found:
I found no Russian translation. The check was limited because the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls) ran out before any search for this candidate could run, so I could not do the four Russian searches the task asked for. I checked these pages directly instead:
(1) The Russian Wikipedia article «Либаний» (https://ru.wikipedia.org/wiki/Либаний). Its list of Russian translations covers Shestakov's speeches (1912–16, reprinted 2014), Grabar-Passek 1964 (orations VI, XXV, XXXI, XXXV, LX, letters, and Declamation 28 in 1961), Rabinovich 1985 (Or. XVIII), Raitsina 1997 (Declamation 1) and Shabaga 2015 (Or. XIX–XXIII). It lists no progymnasmata, no chreiai and no ekphraseis.
(2) The Russian Wikipedia article «Хрия». It mentions only Hermogenes, Aphthonius and the 19th-century Russian school tradition (Koshansky). Libanius is not mentioned.
(3) The ancientrome.ru author index (antlitr/index.htm). It has no Libanius entry at all.
(4) cyberleninka. Its search page only works with JavaScript, so I got no results from it.
I could not check elibrary, Russian dissertation catalogues or art-history anthologies, which could hold a partial translation such as a quoted ekphrasis. "None" is therefore likely but not exhaustively verified.
verification.en_found:
(1) Craig A. Gibson, Libanius's Progymnasmata: Model Exercises in Greek Prose Composition and Rhetoric (SBL Writings from the Greco-Roman World 27; Atlanta: SBL / Leiden: Brill, 2008), xxix + 572 pp., ISBN 9781589833609 / 9789004157507. Greek and English. The BMCR review by L. Pirovano (BMCR 2012.03.31, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2012/2012.03.31/) calls it the first modern translation of the Progymnasmata in their entirety. It translates the whole of Foerster VIII (pp. 1–571), including Severus of Alexandria, Ps.-Nicolaus and the anonymous pieces, so it includes Chreia 1 and the spurious Descriptions 25 and 27. Open Library confirms the bibliographic details (OL3591471W). I could not confirm a free PDF on sbl-site.org because the site returns 403/404 to automated fetches.
(2) This one the sweep missed: R. F. Hock and E. N. O'Neil, The Chreia and Ancient Rhetoric: Classroom Exercises (SBL WGRW 2, 2002), xi + 411 pp., ISBN 9781589830189. It contains Libanius' chreia elaborations in Greek and English, with an introduction on pp. 113–125. The BMCR review (2004.10.20, https://bmcr.brynmawr.edu/2004/2004.10.20/) discusses the elaborations' portrayal of Alexander's affability, perhaps modelled on Julian, citing pp. 127 and 143. That points to the Alexander chreia, so Chreia 1 probably has a second, earlier English translation. The reviewer does not name the chreia directly.
(3) A. Stewart, Faces of Power (1993), pp. 383–84 and 397–400, which the sweep says gives English translations of Descriptions 25 and 27. I could not open it here, so this is unverified.
verification.other_found:
French: J.-P. Callu, "Julius Valère, le Pseudo-Libanius et le tombeau d'Alexandre", Ktèma 19 (1994) 269–284 (https://www.persee.fr/doc/ktema_0221-5896_1994_num_19_1_2120). The article exists and is about Ps.-Libanius' Tychaion ekphrasis (Descr. 25). Whether it gives a full or partial French translation could not be checked: Persée showed only p. 269 and blocked the PDF.
German: B. Hebert, Spätantike Beschreibungen von Kunstwerken: archäologischer Kommentar zu den Ekphraseis des Libanios und Nikolaos (Diss. Graz 1983), as reported by the sweep. I could not check it: the DNB catalogue blocked access and Open Library has no record. It is likely to contain German translations of the ekphraseis.
Italian: G. Ventrella has translated Libanius' Medea ethopoeia (per BMCR 2012.03.31). That piece does not concern Alexander. I found no Italian translation of Chreia 1 or Descr. 25/27.
Spanish: none found. I could not search Gredos.
Two leads I could not check: French anthologies of Alexandria sources, such as Méla and Möri (eds.), Alexandrie la Divine (2014), might quote Descr. 25. So might English source-books on Alexandria's topography, such as McKenzie 2007.
verification.source_text: Public domain: R. Foerster, Libanii opera VIII: Progymnasmata, Argumenta orationum Demosthenicarum (Leipzig: Teubner, 1915). The scan is at https://archive.org/details/foerster-libanii-opera, file "Foerster (1915), Libanii opera 8.pdf", 30.6 MB, marked Public Domain Mark 1.0. Its djvu.txt Greek OCR is poor and unusable without correction, so work from the page images. Chreia 1 ("Ἀλέξανδρος … ἐρωτηθεὶς … θησαυροὺς") is in the Chreiai section (OCR locates it around p. 60). Descriptions 25 and 27 are in the Ekphraseis section, which Foerster marks as partly spurious (Ps.-Nicolaus). Gibson 2008 reprints Foerster's text with minor departures, but it is under copyright.
verification.recommendation: This is a weak candidate. It passes priority 1 (no Russian translation found), but the English is full: Gibson 2008 covers everything, and Hock and O'Neil 2002 also covers Chreia 1, with a French study (Callu 1994) and probably a German translation (Hebert 1983) as well. It is worth doing only as a short Russian-only dossier, «Александр в прогимнасмах Либания», combining Chreia 1 with Descr. 25 and 27 (about 8–10 Teubner pages) and taken from Foerster 1915; LLM translation is feasible and a Greek specialist alone can verify it. Start with Chreia 1, and flag that Descr. 25 and 27 are spurious (Ps.-Nicolaus).
