verification.title: Laments of the philosophers over Alexander (Syriac collection; Brock 1970) / «Плачи философов над гробом Александра» (сирийская версия)
verification.ru_found: I found no Russian translation of the Syriac text. What exists in Russian is the Arabic parallel tradition, which is why the colleague called RU status "partial". (1) Н.Н. Селезнев, «Изречения философов над гробом Александра Великого по "Истории" ал-Макина ибн ал-Амида», История философии (2013; vol. 18 according to the sweep). The companion piece is Джирджис ал-Макин ибн ал-Амид, «Благословенное собрание. Девяносто второй от Адама, Александр… (фрагмент)», translated by Селезнев, edited by Д.А. Морозов, in the same issue around pp. 264–266. It gives a critical Arabic text from BnF ar. 294, Vat. ar. 168 and 169, and Munich ar. 376, with a Russian translation. The variant notes cite Budge's Ethiopic, Eutychius and al-Yaʿqubi; I found no Russian rendering of the Syriac there. URLs: cyberleninka.ru/article/n/izrecheniya-filosofov-nad-grobom-aleksandra-velikogo-po-istorii-al-makina-ibn-al-amida and cyberleninka.ru/article/n/blagoslovennoe-sobranie-devyanosto-vtoroy-ot-adama-aleksandr-syn-filippa-greka-makedonskiy-fragment-perevod-n-n-selezneva. (2) The Latin Western parallel (Petrus Alfonsi, Disciplina clericalis XXXIII, "О золотой гробнице Александра") is in Russian at facetia.ru/node/2859. (3) Not checked: Russian parallels in Жамкочян 1995 (Samaritan chronicle of Abu-l-Fath, p. 92, cited by Seleznyov), the Russian Шахнаме, and Сагадеев's selection from Mubashshir (1998/2010). Аржанов's Символ 61 (2012) articles deal with the Syriac "On the Soul" gnomologia, not the laments. Search limits: WebSearch quota was used up, and Google, Yandex and Brave returned CAPTCHAs, which I did not bypass. Russian searches therefore ran through the CyberLeninka API (9 queries, e.g. «плачи философов», «философы над гробом Александра», «ал-Макин Александр», «сирийская гномология Александр Македонский», «Хунайн ибн Исхак изречения философов»), plus cached facetia.ru/vostlit pages and Solopova's 2017 bibliography of Syriac and Armenian translations.
verification.en_found: Confirmed full. S.P. Brock, "The Laments of the Philosophers over Alexander in Syriac", JSS 15.2 (1970) 205–218, doi 10.1093/jss/15.2.205; reprinted in Brock, Studies in Syriac Christianity (Variorum 1992), ch. VIII. It gives the Syriac text from Mingana syr. 47, fol. 267a–b (pp. 209–211), and the English translation with the Arabic of Eutychius alongside (pp. 211–214). This is per Monferrer-Sala's chapter in Zuwiyya (ed.), Brill Companion 2011, pp. 49–50. Two points of clarification. First, the "Sayings of Alexander" passage Monferrer-Sala lists separately (BL Add. 14618/14614, Sachau, Inedita Syriaca 1870) is not a lament. It is Alexander's saying about Darius' daughters, already in English in Cowper, Syriac Miscellanies 1861, p. 45 (checked in the archive.org text), and in Arzhanov, Syriac Sayings of Greek Philosophers (CSCO 669, 2019; MSS F and G). Second, the Syriac Pseudo-Callisthenes (Budge 1889) has no laments; I checked the full text. English parallels: Seleznyov, Scrinium 10 (2014) 97–114, doi 10.1163/18177565-90000093 (al-Makin, Arabic plus English); R. Pearse, roger-pearse.com, 2 Sept 2017 (Eutychius, Annals ch. 7 pt. 6, English made from an Italian edition); Budge, Life and Exploits 1896 (Ethiopic versions). English-language searches: 9 Crossref queries (5 English; French/Italian/Spanish/German variants), archive.org, JSTOR, publisher sites.
verification.other_found: The sweep missed two complete translations of the Syriac. (1) Spanish: J.P. Monferrer-Sala, "Alexandri magni de anima dictum fictitium apud philosophos enuntiavit", Hikma 5 (2006) 155–169, doi 10.21071/hikma.v5i5.6689. His own Brill Companion chapter describes it as a Spanish translation of the Mingana text with a study. The open-access PDF was down (502) when I checked. (2) French: Muriel Debié, Alexandre le Grand en syriaque. Maître des lieux, des savoirs et des temps (Paris: Les Belles Lettres, Bibliothèque de l'Orient chrétien 7, 16 Feb 2024, 656 pp., ISBN 9782251454900). It is billed as "Traductions, introductions et commentaires", and Part II, ch. 4 "Les derniers jours d'Alexandre" contains "Les sentences funèbres des philosophes" (lesbelleslettres.com/livre/9782251454900; reviewed by M. Sartre, Syria 2024, doi 10.4000/12c7h). The book appears to translate almost the whole Syriac Alexander corpus into French, which matters for other Neoscholia candidates too. Parallel versions in other languages: Arabic (Ḥunayn, Ādāb al-falāsifa, ed. Badawi 1985; Pseudo-Eutychius, Pococke 1656 and Cheikho 1906; Mubashshir, ed. Badawi 1958; Ibn al-Rāhib; al-Makin; al-Yaʿqubi; al-Masʿudi; the Samaritan Abu-l-Fath, ed. Vilmar 1865); Ethiopic (Budge, English); Persian (Ferdowsi); Hebrew (al-Ḥarizi, Musre ha-filosofim; a German translation by Loewenthal 1896 exists from memory, not verified here); Old Spanish (Bocados de oro, Buenos proverbios); Latin, Middle English and Old Russian derivatives. I found no German or Italian translation of the Syriac itself.
verification.source_text: No public-domain or openly licensed edition of the Syriac exists. Brock's edition (JSS 15, 1970, pp. 209–211) is under OUP copyright. According to Seleznyov 2014, the only witness is Birmingham, Cadbury Research Library, Mingana Syr. 47, fol. 267a–b, an East-Syriac copy made at Alqosh in 1907. I could not confirm online images: the old Virtual Manuscript Room host no longer resolves. The licensing of the Cadbury digitisation needs checking. Public-domain parallels: Pococke, Contextio gemmarum/Annales (Oxford 1656, Arabic plus Latin); Cheikho, CSCO Script. Arab. III.6 (1906); Budge, Life and Exploits of Alexander (1896, Ethiopic in English, archive.org/details/lifeandexploits00budggoog).
verification.recommendation: This is a poor standalone candidate. The Syriac is about one folio, survives only in a 1907 copy, and is already fully translated into English (Brock 1970), Spanish (Monferrer-Sala 2006) and French (Debié 2024). The only gap is Russian, and there is no public-domain source text. If wanted at all, use it as a short Russian pilot or inside a synoptic Russian dossier: Mingana Syr. 47 plus Ḥunayn's Ādāb al-falāsifa version and Pseudo-Eutychius (Cheikho 1906, public domain). Checking that would need both Syriac and Arabic expertise, which goes beyond Greek and Latin.

Public domain:

verification.recommendation: Weak candidate. The Greek Alexander chapters already exist in Russian (Derevensky 2000/2007), the Slavonic text has a full Russian translation (Smolnikova 1997), and English is full for both the Syriac and the Greek/Latin. The only real gap is a Russian translation of the Syriac original: Kushyat daughter of Pil king of Kush, the gates, Byzas and Rome, and the Ps 68:31 exegesis (roughly chs. VIII–X), plus the release of the nations (ch. XIII), in Reinink's numbering. That unit needs Syriac expertise to verify, and its base text, Reinink's CSCO edition, is in copyright. It would be worth doing only as a Syriac–Greek–Slavonic side-by-side with commentary, not as a first translation.

verification.title: George the Monk (Georgios Monachos / Hamartolos), Chronicon I.19: the Alexander chapter (Nectanebo and Philip, the Jaddus/Jerusalem visit, Candace, Brahmans after Palladius, the 'laws of nations' after Ps.-Caesarius, the Diadochi). De Boor I pp. c. 25–40.
verification.ru_found: This refutes the sweep. A complete modern Russian translation of the chapter exists, though it was made from the Slavonic version rather than directly from de Boor's Greek. Матвеенко В.А., Щеголева Л.И. «Временник Георгия Монаха (Хроника Георгия Амартола) = Книга временная и образная Георгия Мниха: Рус. текст, коммент., указ.» М.: Богородский печатник, 2000, 543 с. It is translated from the Old Russian Troitsky (Tver) MS, early 14th c., in Istrin's text. The publisher says it was checked throughout against the Greek parallel text, with commentary on the main divergences. I checked the online text. Book 1, chapters 21–28 correspond to Greek I.19, with de Boor page markers Б25–Б40 and Istrin markers И42–И51 in the text. They cover: ch. 21–22 Ochus, Nectanebo and Philip; ch. 23 Alexander's accession and the march on Judaea; ch. 24 the high priest Jaddus, the full vestments excursus, the proskynesis, the dream and Parmenion, Daniel's prophecy and the Mosomachos story; ch. 25 Issus, Candace, Alexandria and the death; ch. 26 Brahmans and Makrobioi (Palladius); ch. 27 the laws of nations (Caesarius); ch. 28 the partition among the Diadochi. That is about 3,300 Russian words. Full text online: azbyka.ru/otechnik/Istorija_Tserkvi/vremennik-georgija-monaha/ (section ./3); drevlit.ru/texts/g/georgiy_monah1.php (Book 1 including the Jaddus chapter; drevlit is the sister site of vostlit); facetia.ru/node/2775, which also gives a PDF and tags it «Александр Македонский». Older printed text: Истрин В.М. «Книгы временьныя и образныя Георгия Мниха», 3 vols., Пг./Л. 1920–1930 (Slavonic, Greek parallel in vol. 2; Munich reprint 1972). On the Slavonic Jaddus episode there is also an article in Український історичний журнал 2011 No. 5, pp. 162–178, on 'Въшествіє в Ієроусалимъ' of Alexander in the Chronographic Alexandria (academia.edu/1467557); author not verified. Caveat: the Slavonic follows the base version (the Coislin 305 type), not de Boor's vulgate. A direct Russian translation from de Boor's Greek was not found.
verification.en_found: 1) R. Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (Everyman/Dent 1994; I.B. Tauris 2012). The table of contents (dandelon.com scan) lists '3. Excerpt from "The Chronicle of George the Monk"', pp. 25–33. BMCR 1995.08.06 describes it as 'a translation of I.19' that stresses the Jerusalem visit. Di Serio (Studia Ceranea 11, 2021) cites Stoneman 2012 pp. 30–33 for de Boor 35,6–39,10. I could not check line by line whether every sentence, e.g. the whole vestments excursus, is included. A borrowable scan is on archive.org (legendsofalexand0000unse). 2) Ph. A. Harland, 'Ethnic Relations and Migration in the Ancient World' blog, Feb. 2023, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0: partial only. It translates the Brahmans and Makrobioi section and the Caesarius catalogue, and explicitly omits 'Alexander's interactions among Judeans' and the animal list. 3) Forthcoming complete translation: Craig A. Gibson, The Concise Chronicle of George the Monk, Translated Texts for Byzantinists 17, Liverpool UP. Indigo lists 11 June 2027 and 560 pp.; Gibson's University of Iowa profile confirms the project. 4) Di Serio 2021 (open access, CC BY-NC-ND) quotes and lightly adapts Stoneman's English for the catalogue passages.
verification.other_found: FRENCH: Thomas Picciola, 'La Chronique de Georges le Moine, avant-propos, livre I et extraits des livres II à VI : traduction et commentaire', doctoral thesis, Aix-Marseille, defended 18.06.2024 (supervisor E. Caire), theses.fr 2024AIXM0146. It gives the Greek text (a reworking of Dmitry Afinogenov's unpublished edition based on Coislin 305, with apparatus against de Boor) plus a French translation of the whole of Book I, so I.19 is included. theses.fr marks it 'accessible: non', so it is not openly available. LATIN: E. de Muralt's 1859 edition with Latin version, reprinted in PG 110 (1863). MEDIEVAL: the Slavonic translation (11th c.), the second Slavonic version (the 14th-c. Lětovnik) and the Georgian translation by Arsen of Iqalto. GERMAN, ITALIAN, SPANISH, MODERN GREEK: no translation of I.19 found. Studies: C. Di Serio, 'An Ethnographic Catalogue in George the Monk's Chronicle', Studia Ceranea 11 (2021).
verification.source_text: C. de Boor, Georgii Monachi Chronicon, vol. I, Leipzig: Teubner 1904, Book I ch. 19, about pp. 25–40. Public domain; on archive.org as georgiimonachic01boorgoog (vol. I confirmed; the scan Harland links to, at p. 35) and bub_gb_dp1EAAAAMAAJ. The archive.org OCR of the Greek is unusable, so the text must be re-keyed or re-OCRed. Do not use the corrected reprint by P. Wirth (Stuttgart 1978), which is in copyright. Textual caveat: de Boor prints the expanded vulgate. The base version (Coislin 305, plus the Slavonic, plus Afinogenov's unpublished edition now used by Picciola 2024) differs in places. Parallel: Istrin 1920–1930 (Slavonic and Greek), public-domain status in RU/US to be checked.
verification.recommendation: Not a good Neoscholia candidate. A full Russian version exists (Matveenko–Shchegoleva 2000, online at azbyka.ru and drevlit.ru), English has Stoneman's translation of I.19 plus a complete Liverpool TTB translation due in 2027, and a French thesis translation of all of Book I exists. The only remaining niche is a direct Russian translation of de Boor's Greek I.19 (about 15 Teubner pages), annotated against the Slavonic and Coislin 305 version; that is low priority and should come only after truly untranslated Alexander texts.

verification.title: Alexandri Magni Iter ad Paradisum (Alexander's Journey to Paradise; «Путешествие Александра к раю»), anonymous Latin, 12th c.
verification.ru_found: REFUTED: a Russian translation of the Latin Iter does exist. The earlier sweep was wrong to say Gorelov does not contain it. Source: «Повесть о рождении и победах Александра Великого» [= Nativitas et Victoria Alexandri Magni Regis], пер. с лат. и ст.-фр., сост., вступ. ст. и ком. Н. Горелова. СПб.: Азбука-классика, 2004 (1st ed., 224 pp., cited by Saltykova 2024 and in Книжная летопись 2004); reissued 2006 (256 pp.). The table of contents, under «Средневековые истории об Александре Великом», includes «О путешествии Александра Македонского в Рай». It opens with Gorelov's introduction, which quotes Tamid 32b in Orshansky's Russian version and says the Latin version is known from a 13th-c. Paris MS. The translation itself follows under the subheading «Путь к раю». facetia.ru reprints only the opening three paragraphs and then breaks off with «<...>» (https://facetia.ru/node/2837; book contents at https://facetia.ru/povest-o-rozhdenii-i-pobedah-aleksandra-velikogo). That opening closely matches Zacher's Latin, pp. 19–20: "Igitur Alexander ... praeda onustus ... a finibus Indorum"; "Gangem, qui et Physon, cujus origo est Paradisus voluptatis" rendered «Ганг, то есть Фисон, берущий свое начало в райских кущах»; "quingentos clipeos" rendered «пятьсот щитоносцев». So it is a direct translation of the Latin, not a retelling. I confirmed only this partial text. Whether the print edition gives the whole text is unverified but likely, since it is a short self-contained piece with its own heading; check the printed pages. Related Russian material that is NOT a translation of the Iter: (a) Russian versions of the source, Bavli Tamid 32b: И. Г. Оршанский, «Талмудические сказания об Александре Македонском» (19th c.; facetia.ru/node/2963); «Агада», tr. С. Фруг (Одесса 1910–14; Берлин 1922, p. 232); Жуковский, «Две повести» (1844), a free version of Chamisso's Talmud-based poem; (b) summaries and discussions: Веселовский, «Из истории романа и повести» I (1886), pp. 278–279; Костюхин 1972; А. А. Панченко, Studia Litterarum 2021 (cyberleninka); Гаркави 1892, a Russian rendering of a Hebrew Alexander romance with the paradise episode; С. Б. Чернецов, «Путешествие Александра Великого из Иерусалима в рай и обратно», Живая старина 1997/3 (apparently a different, likely Ethiopic, tradition; content not checked). Searches with no hits for a separate Russian translation: ru.wikipedia (no article on the Iter), CyberLeninka API (4 queries), facetia site search (3 queries), Google Books (Russian phrase queries). vostlit does not apply, since the text is Latin.
verification.en_found: Two complete English translations. (1) Dennis M. Kratz, The Romances of Alexander (Garland Library of Medieval Literature B/64, New York/London 1991), "Alexandri Magni Iter ad Paradisum", pp. 127–134. Reissued by Routledge in 2025, DOI 10.4324/9781003682912-6; cited as "Kratz 1991: 127–34" by Su Fang Ng, OUP 2019. Note for the master list: Kratz 1991 also has HdP J2 excerpts (pp. 83–88), J3 excerpts (pp. 89–106) and the Epistola ad Aristotelem (pp. 107–125), not only J1. (2) Richard Stoneman, Legends of Alexander the Great (Everyman/Dent 1994; I.B. Tauris 2012), "Alexander the Great's Journey to Paradise", ch. 6 (DOI 10.5040/9780755625741.ch-006). Confirmed by BMCR 1995.08.06, which describes Papas' eye parable. Also in English: Lascelles, Medium Ævum 5 (1936), a study with paraphrase; Mimekor Yisrael (Bin Gorion, tr. I. M. Lask, 1976) may contain a version derived from Hertz's German, not checked.
verification.other_found: ITALIAN: "Iter Alexandri in Paradisum", ed. and tr. M. Liborio, in Boitani, Bologna, Cipolla, Liborio (eds.), Alessandro nel Medioevo occidentale (Fondazione Lorenzo Valla/Mondadori 1997; texts with facing Italian translation). T. Gregory (2002/2003/2007) cites it at p. 378. Probably complete; not checked page by page. A 2026 Italian translation of Bin Gorion ("Storielle e insegnamenti", Free Ebrei) reuses Hertz's German version. GERMAN: Wilhelm Hertz, Aristoteles in den Alexanderdichtungen des Mittelalters (Abh. bayer. Akad. 1889/90; separate printing 1892, pp. 59–62; repr. Gesammelte Abhandlungen 1905). I checked the OCR on archive.org (bub_gb_tSkEAAAAIAAJ): it is a close, abridged German paraphrase of the whole narrative ("Der Inhalt ... ist folgender"), with one Latin quotation, so excerpt or summary level. Bin Gorion's Der Born Judas (Insel 1916–) used Hertz's version. FRENCH: I found no translation. There are summaries in I. Lévi, REJ 2 (1881) and 7 (1883), and in P. Meyer, Alexandre le Grand dans la litt. fr. (1886). Gaullier-Bougassas wrote the Iter notice in La Fascination pour Alexandre (Brepols 2014), pp. 48–52. Rothschild's study in Les voyages d'Alexandre au paradis (Brepols 2013), pp. 93–125, was not accessible, so I could not check whether it includes a translation. Medieval adaptations: Old French Voyage d'Alexandre au paradis terrestre (ed. Peckham–La Du 1935), the Straßburger Alexander, and Middle English and Scots versions. SPANISH: none found.
verification.source_text: J. Zacher, Alexandri Magni Iter ad Paradisum ex codd. mss. latinis primus edidit (Regimonti Pr.: Th. Theile, 1859). The text with apparatus from 2 MSS (A, B) is on pp. 19–32, about 2,300–2,600 Latin words. Public domain, scanned by Google and uploaded by ARLIMA under the CC Public Domain Mark: https://archive.org/details/AlexandriMagniIterAdParadisumA and https://archive.org/details/AlexandriMagniIterAdParadisumB (part B holds the text; the djvu.xml OCR is usable). The better critical text is A. Hilka's, printed in L. P. G. Peckham & M. S. La Du, La Prise de Defur and Le Voyage d'Alexandre au Paradis terrestre (Elliott Monographs 35, Princeton 1935). It is on archive.org as lending-only (bwb_P8-AGX-468). Hilka died in 1939, so his text is PD under EU rules; US status is not checked. I took its inclusion in that volume from the standard bibliography and did not open the book. Reprint: F. Pfister, Kleine Schriften zum Alexanderroman (1976), pp. 359–365 (in copyright).
verification.recommendation: Weak candidate: it fails priority (1). Gorelov's Russian translation from the Latin is in print (2004/2006), and there are two full English translations (Kratz 1991, Stoneman 1994) plus an Italian one (Valla 1997). Consider it only if Gorelov's printed text proves seriously abridged. In that case the unit would be the whole text (Zacher pp. 19–32, checked against Hilka), offered as a philological edition with facing Latin and commentary; Latin only, no extra language expertise needed beyond Hebrew/Aramaic for the Tamid 32b parallel.
